t: Poly(I:C) treatment increased baseline platelet activation (CD62P expression) and platelet aggregation, and reduced prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times, together indicating a hypercoagulable state during viral inflammation.
Ileal Maoa transcript levels were increased following SARS-CoV-2, VSV, or poly(I:C) treatment in a TLR3-dependent manner, indicating enhanced serotonin degradation capacity during viral inflammation.

Urinary levels of the serotonin degradation product 5-HIAA were increased in VSV- and LCMV-infected mice and in poly(I:C)-treated mice, an effect abolished in STAT1-deficient mice, indicating enhanced serotonin turnover.
Pharmacological inhibition of MAO with phenelzine prevented 5-HIAA accumulation and restored platelet serotonin levels in poly(I:C)-treated mice.
Mice infected with VSV or chronic LCMV, and mice treated with poly(I:C), showed impaired novel object recognition memory, an effect dependent on TLR3 and type I interferon receptor signaling.
Antibody-mediated platelet depletion alone was sufficient to impair novel object recognition memory in mice, linking platelet-mediated serotonin loss to cognitive dysfunction.
Treatment of mice with the SSRI fluoxetine restored novel object recognition performance in poly(I:C)-treated mice, supporting a causal role for serotonin signaling in the cognitive deficit.
In an independent metabolomics cohort from Cork, Ireland, serotonin was again among the most strongly depleted metabolites in Long COVID patients, replicating the Penn Medicine finding.

No reduction in serotonin was observed among PASC patients in the longitudinal UNCOVR cohort, possibly reflecting lower symptom severity in this recruitment setting compared to the Penn Medicine clinic cohort.
In the UCSF LIINC cohort, plasma serotonin levels negatively correlated with the number of symptoms reported three to four months after acute SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Serotonin levels measured during the acute phase of SARS-CoV-2 infection did not predict subsequent development of PASC.
Kynurenine levels were elevated during acute COVID-19 but this increase did not persist in individuals with PASC.

Mice genetically deficient in the kynurenine-producing enzyme IDO1 still exhibited reduced serotonin after poly(I:C) treatment, indicating kynurenine production is not the major driver of viral-inflammation-induced serotonin depletion.

Pharmacological inhibition of the alternative kynurenine-producing enzyme TDO2 with 680C91 did not restore serotonin levels in poly(I:C)-treated mice, further ruling out kynurenine pathway involvement in serotonin depletion.

Pharmacological inhibition of the serotonin-synthesizing enzyme TPH1 enhanced viral loads and pathogenesis during VSV infection but had no effect on SARS-CoV-2 replication, indicating serotonin depletion is not a host defense mechanism.

Isotope tracing with orally administered 13C-labeled tryptophan confirmed that poly(I:C) treatment impairs intestinal tryptophan absorption, as circulating tryptophan derived from the labeled oral source was reduced.

Successive loss of functional Ace2 alleles produced a stepwise reduction in plasma tryptophan levels, and poly(I:C) treatment of heterozygous Ace2-deficient mice phenocopied the homozygous knockout state.

The number and size of bone marrow megakaryocytes increased with poly(I:C) treatment, while thrombopoietin levels remained unchanged, suggesting a compensatory marrow response rather than reduced platelet production as the cause of thrombocytopenia.
Poly(I:C) treatment increased baseline platelet activation (CD62P/P-selectin expression) and platelet aggregation, consistent with a hyperactivated, procoagulant state during viral inflammation.
Prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time were both reduced by poly(I:C) treatment, further indicating a hypercoagulable state during viral inflammation.
Levels of fibrinogen, tissue factor, and thrombin-antithrombin complexes were unchanged by poly(I:C) treatment, ruling these out as alternative explanations for the observed hypercoagulability.

Single-cell transcriptomics of nodose ganglia revealed high and selective expression of the serotonin receptor 5-HT3 on vagal neurons, providing a plausible receptor mechanism linking peripheral serotonin to vagal signaling.
Cultured nodose ganglion (vagal) neurons exposed to serotonin exhibited rapid calcium influx, demonstrating a direct excitatory effect of serotonin on vagal sensory neurons in vitro.

Chemogenetic activation of Phox2b-expressing vagal neurons during poly(I:C) treatment restored hippocampal neuron activation and short-term memory formation, implicating the vagus nerve as a mediator of cognitive rescue.

Autopsy tissue analysis showed that while viral RNA could be detected in several organs during the acute phase of COVID-19, the gastrointestinal tract remained specifically viral-RNA-positive in samples from the post-acute phase (>2 weeks).

Viral RNA was detected in stool samples from a subset of individuals with PASC, suggesting a possible link between gastrointestinal viral persistence and long-term symptoms, compared with recovered individuals with prior infection but no persistent symptoms.

Reduced serotonin levels have also been reported in dengue virus infection, another trigger of post-viral syndrome, suggesting the interferon-driven mechanism described here may generalize beyond SARS-CoV-2.

Low serotonin levels are also reported in non-viral conditions characterized by elevated type I interferon, such as systemic lupus erythematosus and multiple sclerosis, suggesting the interferon-serotonin pathway described may extend beyond viral infections.

The TRPV1 agonist capsaicin rescued cognitive performance in poly(I:C)-treated mice without altering peripheral serotonin levels or brain interferon-stimulated gene responses, showing that sensory neuron stimulation alone can bypass serotonin deficiency to restore cognition.

Off-label low-dose naltrexone use in a retrospective cohort of 59 PASC patients was associated with fewer symptoms, improved fatigue, post-exertional malaise, unrefreshing sleep, and abnormal sleep pattern, and better functional status.
PASC prevalence estimates vary substantially, with global estimates around 43% of prior COVID-19 cases compared to approximately 11% in the US per NCHS data.
A leading hypothesis for the cause of PASC is persistent activation of innate immune cells with increased systemic inflammation.
Higher absolute CD4+ T cell counts were positively correlated with fatigue severity across all three convalescent COVID-19 severity groups.
Multivariate regression showed FAS fatigue score increased by 0.7 points for every 100 CD4+ T cells/µL of whole blood.
Post-acute lymphocyte counts, particularly CD3+ T cells, were associated with initial COVID-19 disease severity.
Hospitalized non-ICU patients had higher CD45+ intermediate monocyte counts than ICU-treated patients post-acutely.
Absolute blood immune cell counts post-acutely did not differ between unexposed controls and convalescent COVID-19 patients, regardless of initial severity.
CD19+ B cell, NK cell, CD4+ and CD8+ T cell counts, and activated CD56+CD4+/CD8+ T cell counts did not differ between COVID-19 severity groups.
Clinically relevant fatigue (FAS ≥22) was present in 29.5% of convalescent patients overall, with similar incidence across non-hospitalized, non-ICU, and ICU groups.
Extreme fatigue (FAS ≥35) was reported by 18.8% of patients, being most common in non-hospitalized patients.
All three patient groups showed a statistically significant and clinically relevant increase in fatigue scores from before to after COVID-19 infection.
S1-, S2-, RBD-, and N-specific IgG antibody levels were significantly higher in hospitalized (non-ICU and ICU) convalescent patients compared with non-hospitalized patients.
All convalescent groups showed a hierarchical increase of antigen-specific IgG levels from S1 (lowest) to RBD, N, and S2 (highest), consistent with a stepwise humoral response.
Levels of spike- and nucleocapsid-specific IgA and IgM antibodies were significantly lower than IgG in convalescent patient plasma.

Hospitalized (non-ICU and ICU) patients displayed higher SARS-CoV-2 variant neutralization/inhibition capacity than non-hospitalized patients, indicating antibody inhibition capacity increases with COVID-19 severity.
Non-hospitalized patients showed reduced in vitro antibody inhibition capacity against delta and beta SARS-CoV-2 variants, potentially explaining breakthrough infections in mild disease.
No significant correlations were found between IgG antibody levels and clinical outcomes, including fatigue prevalence or severity.
ICU-treated patients had lower DLCO, absolute and adjusted 6-minute walking distance, and lower resting paO2 and sO2 compared with other groups.
Total T cell count correlations with DLCO differed by severity group: positive correlation in non-hospitalized patients but negative correlation in hospitalized non-ICU patients.
In ICU patients, DLCO positively correlated with CD4-CD8- T cell counts, adjusted 6MWD positively correlated with CD3-CD16/56+ NK cell counts, and PaO2 positively correlated with CD8+ T cell counts.
Overall quality of life and depression symptom severity were independently associated with fatigue, potentially reflecting overlapping symptom domains across questionnaires.
Roughly a quarter of patients reported moderate to severe anxiety/depression symptoms, unrelated to their initial COVID-19 disease severity.
Patients with lingering neurologic PASC symptoms showed reduced growth hormone secretion compared to recovered COVID-19 patients without lingering symptoms.
Inflammatory markers were not significantly associated with neurologic PASC symptoms.
Adrenal insufficiency was not associated with neurologic PASC symptoms.
PASC subjects reported significantly worse fatigue, sleep quality, depression, quality of life, and gastrointestinal discomfort compared to non-PASC subjects.
Despite self-reported poor mental resilience, objective cognitive testing did not reveal significant differences between PASC and non-PASC groups.

A unique infrared spectral band at 1565 cm-1, attributed to carboxylate side chains and specifically glutamate, was identified as a distinguishing biomarker in fibromyalgia patients but was absent in Long COVID and healthy control spectra.

The relative percentage area of the deconvoluted IR band at 1580 cm-1 (associated with -C=N and carboxylate side-chain vibrations) was significantly higher in Long COVID patients compared to fibromyalgia patients.

An OPLS-DA model built from FT-MIR spectral data in the 1528-1624 cm-1 region correctly classified Long COVID versus fibromyalgia patients with 100% sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy in both cross-validation and external validation, with an AUC of 1.0.

IR bands at 1639 and 1670 cm-1, linked to β-sheet and α-sheet amide I conformations of the peptide backbone, showed no statistically significant difference between fibromyalgia and Long COVID patients.
Self-reported pain and functional impact scores (FIQR in FM, SIQR in Long COVID) were statistically similar between the two groups, suggesting comparable levels of pain and functional impairment.
Within the Long COVID cohort, there was no statistically significant difference between male and female subjects in age, BMI, or SIQR scores.

Healthy control subjects lacked the FM-specific 1565 cm-1 spectral band but showed a distinct IR band at 1545 cm-1 (linked to amide II C-N stretching/N-H bending or deprotonated carboxylate groups) not seen in FM or LC patients.

Medication usage patterns differed between cohorts, with tricyclic antidepressants more prevalent among fibromyalgia patients and naltrexone use more common among Long COVID patients, while gabapentin, opioid analgesics, and SSRIs were used at similar rates in both groups.
Mounting evidence suggests that acute SARS-CoV-2 infection and PASC may lead to reduced growth hormone secretion as demonstrated by stimulation testing.
Ongoing clinical research has shown that PASC patients with fatigue and cognitive complaints show promising improvement following growth hormone replacement therapy.
Both acute SARS-CoV-2 infection and PASC are associated with gut microbiome dysbiosis and alterations in the gut-brain and HPA-axis.
SARS-CoV-2 commonly impacts tissues with cells expressing the ACE-2 receptor, contributing to extrapulmonary manifestations of both acute and post-acute infection.
Long-COVID is associated with abnormalities in both parasympathetic and sympathetic autonomic nervous system function as assessed by various testing techniques.
No studies to date have tested treatment options specifically for autonomic disorders in Long-COVID patients.
There is a high prevalence of clinical autonomic disorders (e.g., POTS-like presentations) among Long-COVID patient cohorts as reported in recent studies.
Frequent EBV reactivation was observed during the acute phase of hospitalized COVID-19 patients, which may contribute to post-COVID fatigue given EBV's own association with prolonged fatigue.
Adolescents with more severe fever and a more difficult clinical course during infectious mononucleosis were more likely to subsequently develop ME/CFS.
Adolescents who met CFS criteria 6 months after illness could perform physical activity to the same extent as a recovered control group.

Despite similar physical activity capacity, adolescent CFS patients showed significant differences in autonomic symptomatology, cytokine biomarkers, and psychological risk factors compared to recovered controls.

A cohort study using metabolic equivalent scores found that exertional dyspnea, fatigue, shortness of breath, and anxiety were common in acute PASC (up to 12 weeks), while fatigue was the most common symptom in chronic PASC beyond 12 weeks.

COVID-19-recovered patients without cardiopulmonary sequelae showed significantly reduced peak CO2 attributable to peripheral (not central cardiac) limitation, with exaggerated hyperventilation during exercise.
A systematic review found 41% of patients with acute lung injury had reduced aerobic capacity 3 months after illness, and weakness persisted in 14% of COVID-19 patients at 12 months.

PASC patients show a persistent prothrombotic/hypercoagulable state associated with endothelial dysfunction and microthrombi in capillary blood flow of large muscles, reducing oxygen capacity and promoting anaerobic respiration and fatigue during exercise.
A study of ME/CFS patients found excessive production of reactive oxygen species with altered resting oxidant/antioxidant blood balance, associated with muscle fatigue symptoms.
Stress-induced hyperglycemia was correlated with a pro-inflammatory immune response and increased reactive oxygen species production in ME/CFS.
Mitochondrial myopathy in ME/CFS patients with exercise intolerance involves increased reliance on anaerobic metabolism, increased free radical production, and decreased oxygen extraction.
Elevated IL-6 levels have been consistently reported in patients affected by SARS-CoV-2, alongside acute inflammation and oxidative stress.
Elevated TNFα levels have been consistently reported in patients affected by SARS-CoV-2, alongside acute inflammation and oxidative stress.

A review of physiological changes underlying post-COVID conditions concluded that shared pathophysiological mechanisms with ME/CFS may include dysregulated energy metabolism, exercise-induced plasma metabolome alterations, dysbiosis, and immune cell dysfunction.

Exercise intolerance in post-COVID patients is associated with higher arterial blood lactate accumulation and lower fatty acid oxidation during graded exercise tests, with altered levels of carboxylates, polyamines, and taurine indicating dysfunctional mitochondria-dependent lipid catabolism.

Cultured skeletal muscle cells from ME/CFS patients are less able to utilize glucose oxidation than healthy control cells, leading to decreased basal and maximal mitochondrial respiration, while galactose and fatty acid use remain normal, localizing the defect between glycolysis and the TCA cycle.
Research shows a correlation between the state of the gut microbiome, immune system functionality, and the pathology of ME/CFS.

The gut microbiome of COVID-19 patients showed significantly reduced bacterial diversity, depletion of beneficial commensal bacteria, and expansion of opportunistic pathogens such as Clostridium, Actinomyces viscosus, and Bacteroides.
Evidence across 29 ethnic groups shows that obesity and high BMI are significant risk factors for more severe COVID-19 outcomes.

During COVID-19 lockdown, individuals who increased or maintained physical activity reported better mental health scores than those who reduced activity, and lower physical activity correlated with increased anxiety.
Low CoQ10 levels have been linked to abnormal oxidative stress regulation in ME/CFS patients.
A significant correlation has been reported between increased CoQ10 concentration and reductions in oxidative stress and fatigue.
Increased CoQ10 concentration correlates with reduced oxidative stress and fatigue, and low CoQ10 levels have been linked to increased oxidative stress in ME/CFS patients.
In a non-randomized clinical trial, oxaloacetate (AEO) capsules at 500 and 1000 mg over 6 weeks improved fatigue from baseline in ME/CFS and post-SARS-CoV-2 chronic fatigue patients.
COVID-19 patients showed severe glutathione deficiency with increased oxidative stress and oxidative damage across all age groups compared to uninfected controls.

Supplementation with glycine and N-acetylcysteine (a glutathione precursor) was highly effective in correcting glutathione deficiency and reducing oxidative stress in HIV patients, suggesting a similar approach could help COVID-19 patients.

Omega-3 fatty acids and their metabolites have beneficial effects on immunity, inflammation, oxidative stress, and psychoneuroimmunity across stages of SARS-CoV-2 infection, offering a promising strategy for PASC patients.

Eccentric contraction (ECC)-based pulmonary rehabilitation was proposed as a well-tolerated alternative to conventional concentric contraction (CONC) exercise, increasing muscle mass without significant cardiopulmonary stress and improving functional capacity in patients with SARS-CoV-2-related hospitalization.

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) has been investigated as a treatment for chronic fatigue and ME/CFS, with reported benefits including reduced fatigue and pain, improved cognitive function, increased energy, improved fitness, and improved quality of life; it is also suggested as promising for PASC including alleviating psychiatric symptoms and pain interference.
A reanalysis of CBT studies in ME/CFS patients found that cognitive behavioral therapy did not lead to objective improvements in physical performance or restore ability to work.

Meditation, as a mind-body practice, is suggested to help PASC patients by balancing pro- and anti-inflammatory effects, reducing excessive sympathetic activation, and producing positive immunomodulatory effects.

Regular 14-day inhalation of molecular hydrogen (H2) positively affected physical and respiratory function in patients with SARS-CoV-2 infection, with no evidence of toxic effects even at high levels.

Enhanced external counterpulsation (EECP) has shown positive effects in PASC patients, improving fatigue, shortness of breath, brain fog, and overall quality of life, based on the concept of PASC as an endothelial dysfunction disorder similar to angina pectoris.
Pulsed electromagnetic field (PEMF) therapy has recently been applied to manage post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 by reducing inflammation and pain, though more sham-controlled trials are needed.

Photobiomodulation therapy has been shown to reduce inflammation and control exacerbated pulmonary responses caused by SARS-CoV-2, and is beneficial at the cellular/mitochondrial level and in preventing thrombosis, though evidence in SARS-CoV-2 infection remains limited.
Obesity and high body mass index (BMI) are significant risk factors for more severe COVID-19 outcomes, based on evidence across 29 ethnic groups.
Individuals who increased or maintained physical activity levels during COVID-19 lockdown reported better mental health scores, while lower physical activity levels correlated with increased anxiety.

A systematic review of longitudinal studies in university students during the COVID-19 pandemic concluded that lifestyle changes including increased sedentary behavior and decreased physical activity were significant risk factors for worsened mental health status.
Relapses in ME/CFS patients can be partially induced by excessive exercise and other physical or mental activity that causes stress.

Petracek et al suggested that COVID-19 can trigger ME/CFS in adolescents and young adults, noting that the allergic terrain, increased mast cell activation, and neurological abnormalities in these patients require individualized treatment, including manual therapy for neuromuscular limitation and existing therapies for orthostatic intolerance and POTS.
95% of patients diagnosed with Long COVID showed severe functional limitations compared to the acute COVID-19 (non-Long COVID) group.

44.7% of Long COVID patients experienced a worsening of physical activity from a high pre-infection level (60.2%) to a low current level (79.3%), while the acute infection group's activity level remained stable in 84.7% of cases.
Quality of life deteriorated significantly in 54.1% of Long COVID patients, whereas it remained unchanged in 88.2% of the acute infection (non-Long COVID) group.
Fatigue severity worsened significantly in 94.7% of Long COVID patients relative to the acute infection group.
92.4% of patients diagnosed with Long COVID met diagnostic criteria for Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (CFS).

In stepwise regression, functional status was the sole significant predictor of quality of life, explaining approximately 67.5% of the variance, excluding physical activity and fatigue from the final model.
Among all participants, 75% of those without functional limitations reported excellent quality of life, compared to 80% of those with severe functional limitations reporting poor quality of life.
75% of participants with no fatigue before or currently reported excellent quality of life, while 30% of those whose fatigue significantly worsened reported poor quality of life.
The non-Long COVID group had a significantly higher percentage of participants actively employed and less prolonged sick leave compared to the Long COVID group.
A significantly higher percentage of Long COVID patients had COVID-19-related sick leave compared to the acute infection group.
Multivariable logistic regression identified asthma as an independent risk factor for persistent general fatigue at the 12-month follow-up in long COVID patients.
Univariate logistic regression identified younger age as a risk factor for prolonged general fatigue at the 3-, 6-, and 12-month follow-ups.
Univariate logistic regression identified female sex as a risk factor for prolonged general fatigue in long COVID patients.
Among prolonged symptoms observed through 1-year follow-ups, general fatigue was the symptom most interfering with daily life in long COVID patients.
Patients with protracted fatigue at all follow-up time points had lower quality-of-life scores at the 12-month follow-up compared with those without protracted fatigue.
Longitudinal symptom tracking showed that general fatigue, but not cough or dyspnea, was significantly prolonged in long COVID patients with asthma compared with those without asthma.

In non-hospitalized long COVID patients, mean peak oxygen uptake was 92% of predicted, with two-thirds of participants having normal exercise capacity and 35% having reduced exercise capacity (<85% predicted).
Among participants with reduced exercise capacity, deconditioning (65%) and peripheral muscle limitation (35%) were identified as the main explanatory reasons.
Oxygen pulse during CPET was significantly lower in patients with reduced exercise capacity compared to those with normal exercise capacity.

Breathing reserve during CPET was significantly higher in patients with reduced exercise capacity compared to those with normal exercise capacity, suggesting the limitation was not primarily ventilatory.
Participants with normal V̇O2peak completed the stair climbing test significantly faster than those with reduced exercise capacity.
There was no significant difference in 30-second sit-to-stand test repetitions between patients with normal versus reduced peak oxygen uptake.
Nearly all participants (95%) met criteria for fatigue and 65% met criteria for severe fatigue, with a mean CFQ-11 score of 24 indicating a high symptom burden.
Dyspnea (mMRC ≥1) was reported by 66% of participants.
There was no significant difference in fatigue or dyspnea burden between patients with normal versus reduced peak oxygen uptake.
Lung function measures (FEV1, FVC, FEV1/FVC ratio) were within normal predicted values overall in the cohort.
DLCO was ≤75% predicted in 13% of participants, and DLCO values were significantly lower in patients with reduced versus normal exercise capacity.
In adjusted linear regression, V̇O2peak kg-1 was negatively associated with dyspnea severity (mMRC score).
In adjusted linear regression, V̇O2peak kg-1 was positively associated with DLCO.
Time on the stair climbing test was associated with the same variables (mMRC and DLCO) as V̇O2peak, but with reversed direction of association (i.e., worse SCT time with higher mMRC and lower DLCO).
30STST score was negatively associated with fatigue burden (CFQ-11 total score) in adjusted regression.
30STST score was negatively associated with dyspnea severity (mMRC score) in adjusted regression.
FEV1 was associated with V̇O2peak kg-1 and SCT in unadjusted regression, but this association did not persist after multivariate adjustment.
No association was found between time since initial COVID-19 infection (3-24 months) and exercise capacity.
The overall group of long COVID patients had significantly increased circulating leukocyte and total T-lymphocyte counts compared to healthy controls, driven by increased CD8+ T-lymphocyte counts.
Increased CD8+ T-lymphocyte counts correlated significantly with greater fatigue severity in long COVID patients.
Long COVID patients showed increased percentages of CD8+ TEMRA T-lymphocytes, including senescent/exhausted CD279+CD57+ and CD27-CD28- subsets, compared to healthy controls.
Naive CD4+ T-lymphocyte percentages were significantly reduced in long COVID patients compared to healthy controls.
Regulatory CD4+FOXP3+ T-lymphocyte percentages were significantly reduced in long COVID patients compared to healthy controls.
Exhausted/senescent CD4+ TEM lymphocytes (CD279+CD57+) were significantly increased in long COVID patients compared to healthy controls.
Classical monocyte (CD14++CD16-) percentages were significantly reduced in long COVID patients compared to healthy controls.
Non-classical monocyte (CD14+CD16++) percentages were significantly increased in long COVID patients compared to healthy controls.
The percentage of classical monocytes negatively correlated with fatigue severity in long COVID patients.
The percentage of intermediate monocytes positively correlated with fatigue severity in long COVID patients.
The percentage of non-classical monocytes positively correlated with fatigue severity in long COVID patients.
Monocyte IL-6 gene expression was significantly overexpressed in long COVID patients compared to healthy controls, part of a pro-inflammatory monocyte gene cluster.
Monocyte CCL7 gene expression was significantly overexpressed in long COVID patients compared to healthy controls.
Monocyte cholesterol efflux gene ABCA1 was significantly downregulated in long COVID patients compared to healthy controls.
The M2 macrophage marker gene MRC1 was significantly downregulated in monocytes of long COVID patients compared to healthy controls.

Monocyte type 1 interferon-induced gene cluster (ISGs, e.g. IFI44, IFI44L, IFIT1, IFIT3, MX1) showed normal expression levels in long COVID patients compared to healthy controls, suggesting impaired antiviral IFN response.
Upregulated monocyte CCL2 gene expression significantly correlated with increased fatigue severity in long COVID patients.
Upregulated monocyte CCL7 gene expression significantly correlated with increased fatigue severity in long COVID patients.
Upregulated monocyte SERPINB2 (PAI-2) gene expression significantly correlated with increased fatigue severity in long COVID patients.
Serum Galectin-9 was significantly elevated in the entire long COVID group compared to healthy controls.
Serum TNF-α was significantly elevated in long COVID patients compared to healthy controls, consistent with a prior study at similar follow-up.
Serum CXCL10 (IP-10) was significantly elevated in long COVID patients compared to healthy controls.
Serum soluble CD163 was significantly elevated in long COVID patients compared to healthy controls.
Serum CXCL9 was significantly reduced in long COVID patients compared to healthy controls.
Serum IFN-β was significantly reduced in long COVID patients compared to healthy controls, suggested to reflect poor innate antiviral immunity.
Serum IFN-γ was significantly reduced in long COVID patients compared to healthy controls.
Serum Galectin-9 levels positively correlated with fatigue severity in long COVID patients.
Serum CD163 showed only a non-significant trend toward positive correlation with fatigue severity in long COVID patients.
No active EBV or CMV viral loads were detected in a randomly tested subset of fatigued and non-fatigued long COVID patients, arguing against ongoing herpesvirus reactivation as a driver of fatigue.

At the group level, immune parameters (leukocyte/lymphocyte subsets, monocyte subsets, gene expression, serum cytokines) did not differ significantly between fatigued and non-fatigued long COVID patients, with both groups showing similar abnormalities relative to healthy controls.
Serum Galectin-9 levels were significantly higher in the combined long COVID group than in healthy controls.
Serum IL-6 was significantly elevated in long COVID patients compared with healthy controls.
Serum TNF-α was significantly higher in long COVID patients than in healthy controls, consistent with a similar prior study.
Serum CXCL10 (IP-10) was significantly increased in long COVID patients compared with healthy controls.
Serum soluble CD163, a marker of monocyte/macrophage activation, was significantly elevated in long COVID patients versus healthy controls.
Serum CCL2 (MCP-1) was significantly increased in long COVID patients compared with healthy controls.
Serum CXCL9 levels were significantly reduced in long COVID patients compared with healthy controls.
Serum SERPINB2 (PAI-2) levels were significantly reduced in long COVID patients compared with healthy controls, contrasting with its monocyte gene expression which correlated positively with fatigue.
Serum IFN-β levels were significantly reduced in long COVID patients compared with healthy controls, suggested by the authors as a sign of poor innate antiviral immunity.
Serum IFN-γ levels were significantly reduced in long COVID patients compared with healthy controls.
Higher serum Galectin-9 levels were significantly positively correlated with greater fatigue severity in long COVID patients.
Serum CD163 levels showed a non-significant trend toward positive correlation with fatigue severity.

No active EBV or CMV viral loads exceeding the limit of quantification were detected in randomly tested fatigued or non-fatigued long COVID patients, arguing against herpesvirus reactivation as an explanation for fatigue.
Fatigued long COVID patients reported significantly more concurrent symptoms and worse health-related quality of life than non-fatigued long COVID patients.
Fatigued long COVID patients showed little clinical improvement over one year, with 95.0% still reporting ≥3 symptoms at 12-month follow-up, versus 55.6% of non-fatigued patients.

The authors hypothesize that anti-inflammatory agents such as minocycline, dexamethasone, and anti-IL-6 therapy might help dampen excessive inflammation in long COVID, though this was not tested in this study.
The authors suggest low-dose IL-2 might help correct the reduced CD4+ Treg-lymphocytes and naïve CD4+ T-lymphocytes seen in long COVID, based on prior literature, though this was not tested here.

The authors propose that TLR-7/TLR-9 stimulating agents such as rintatolimod, which has shown some success in ME/CFS, could help induce type 1 interferon production in long COVID and is being tested for this condition.
Children with long COVID had significantly lower PedsQL Core quality of life scores compared with previously published normative samples.
Children with long COVID had significantly lower PedsQL Fatigue scores compared with previously published normative samples.
Families of children with long COVID reported significantly lower PedsQL Family Impact scores compared with previously published normative samples.
The number of long COVID symptoms, patient age, and preexisting depression, allergies, and developmental delay were associated with overall fatigue PedsQL scores.
Preexisting mood disorders were associated with a higher prevalence of worsening anxiety symptoms in children with long COVID.
Preexisting mood disorders were associated with a higher prevalence of worsening depression symptoms in children with long COVID.
Preexisting mood disorders were associated with a higher prevalence of dizziness, lightheadedness, or vertigo in children with long COVID.
Preexisting mood disorders were associated with a higher prevalence of appetite change in children with long COVID.
Multiple studies have identified fatigue as the most prevalent symptom of long COVID.
The European Burden of Disease Network's consensus model used the disability weight for 'infection, post-acute consequences' (0.219) as a single fixed health state to estimate YLD from long COVID.

The authors propose a graded set of disability weights (borrowed from mild/moderate/severe anemia health states) to better capture the range of severity of fatigue-related long COVID, ranging from 0.004 to 0.219.

The GBD Long COVID Collaborators assessed non-fatal disease burden using three symptom clusters: persistent fatigue with bodily pain or mood swings, cognitive problems, and ongoing respiratory problems.

One hypothesis proposes that long COVID arises from a prolonged pro-inflammatory response to SARS-CoV-2 that induces atypical activation of the immune system and mast cells, driving persistent symptoms.
The symptomatology of long COVID has been compared to that of fibromyalgia, though fibromyalgia lacks a disability weight in the GBD study.
Another hypothesis is that long COVID relates to organ damage from acute COVID-19 infection, such as myocardial infarction or renal failure, causing persistent symptoms.
About a fifth of long-COVID patients were found to have prediabetes on blood glucose/HbA1c assessment.
Low DHEA-S levels were found in 21.4% of long-COVID patients.
Subclinical hypothyroidism was identified in 3.6% of long-COVID patients based on thyroid hormone testing.
A non-specific thyroid function abnormality was found in 7.1% of long-COVID patients.
Thyroid autoimmunity, indicated by anti-thyroperoxidase and/or antithyroglobulin autoantibodies, was present in 7.1% of long-COVID patients.
Low total testosterone was found in 6.6% of male long-COVID patients.
Low IGF-1 levels were found in 3.6% of long-COVID patients.
All long-COVID patients showed normal adrenal reserve on ACTH stimulation testing.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported long-COVID symptom, occurring in 89.3% of patients.
The fatigue assessment scale score was above normal threshold (≥22) in 42.8% of long-COVID patients.
No significant associations were found between long-COVID patients' symptoms and their hormone levels.
Long-COVID patients with prediabetes/diabetes reported confusion and hair loss more often than non-diabetic patients.
Fatigue was the most frequently reported persistent symptom among PASC patients at both baseline and 6 months.
By 6 months, the prevalence of persistent symptoms including fatigue had decreased from baseline but had not resolved for most patients.
Approximately one in five PASC patients completing FACIT-F scored in the severe fatigue range at baseline, with the total number of severe fatigue cases roughly halving by 6 months.
Patients with severe fatigue at baseline were over five times more likely to report headache than those without severe fatigue.
Patients with severe fatigue at baseline were more than three times as likely to report shortness of breath compared to those without severe fatigue.
Those categorized as severely fatigued by FACIT-F were also almost three times more likely to self-report fatigue as a specific named symptom.
Patients with severe fatigue at baseline reported significantly worse diet quality compared to before their acute SARS-CoV-2 infection than those without severe fatigue.
Patients with severe fatigue at baseline reported significantly worse weight status than those without severe fatigue.
Patients with severe fatigue at baseline reported significantly worse sleep quality than those without severe fatigue.
At 6 months, shortness of breath was the only symptom that remained statistically significantly associated with fatigue severity.
Young women were disproportionately more likely to report severe, persistent, and disruptive fatigue after SARS-CoV-2 infection, and also reported low pre-COVID exercise levels.
A substantial proportion of patients reporting severe fatigue also had a past medical history of anxiety or depression.
Patients with severe fatigue reported less regular physical activity both before and after their acute SARS-CoV-2 infection compared to those without severe fatigue.
Nasal congestion was the only reported symptom that fully resolved by 6 months, while most other symptoms persisted at reduced frequency.
Anosmia (loss of smell) cases were reduced by roughly half from baseline to 6 months but did not fully resolve, illustrating incomplete symptom resolution even for acute symptoms.
Regular exercise (30 minutes 5x/week or 150 minutes/week) was associated with fewer symptoms and faster symptom resolution among PASC patients.
The CDC estimates that 7.5% (1 in 13) of US adults report long COVID, and global PASC prevalence is estimated at approximately 65 million people.
Among 209 people with long COVID, 26% reported persistent dizziness as a long-COVID symptom.
15.3% of the 209 participants reported perceived hearing loss as a persistent long-COVID symptom.
Female sex and higher fatigue levels were significant predictors of reporting dizziness in people with long COVID, controlling for age and dizziness severity, explaining 31% of variance.

The severity of dizziness (DHI) and having neurological symptoms during acute COVID-19 were significant predictors of reporting hearing loss in long COVID, controlling for age, explaining 10.4% of variance.
Individuals with perceived dizziness in long COVID had a significantly higher rate of respiratory or neurological symptoms during acute COVID-19 than those without dizziness.

A UK prospective study found persistent cardiac MRI abnormalities in over half of long COVID-19 patients at 12 months, but troponin and BNP biomarkers could not predict these findings.
Fogarty et al. measured endothelial activation markers in 55 patients at a median of 68 days post-infection and found elevated von Willebrand factor, factor VIII, and thrombomodulin.
COVID-19 survivors had elevated circulating endothelial cell levels correlated with high cytokine levels, suggesting endothelitis results from inflammation.

SARS-CoV-2 binding to ACE-2 on endothelium triggers angiotensin II release and reduced nitric oxide production, causing endothelial damage via oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, with implications for RAAS dysregulation.

Cytokine studies showed increased TNF, IL-1β, IL-4, IL-6, IL-7, IL-8, IL-10, and IL-15 two months post-infection, and increased IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF-α eight months post-infection, indicating persistent inflammation and immune cell differentiation.
Small-fiber neuropathy has been implicated as a cause of dysautonomia in post-COVID-19 syndrome.
A US study of over 16,000 long COVID-19 patients found that 40% experienced persistent shortness of breath.
Predictors of pulmonary fibrosis in long COVID-19 include advanced age, comorbidities, male sex, elevated d-dimer, and elevated inflammation markers at four weeks post-infection.
CNS symptoms account for approximately 22% of long COVID-19 manifestations, with hospitalization history and female gender as risk factors for neurological manifestations.
An autopsy study of 33 COVID-19 patients detected ACE2 in olfactory mucosa, supporting a nasal-olfactory-brainstem route of CNS viral invasion.
Autopsies of 44 COVID-19 patients and an observational plasma viral RNA study support a hematogenous route of viral spread to the brain, facilitated by BBB vulnerability during infection.
A prospective study of human gut samples supports the hypothesis that SARS-CoV-2 reaches the CNS via the gastrointestinal tract and vagus nerve, since virus is present in enterocytes.
A PET study found hypometabolism in the hippocampus and brainstem of long COVID-19 patients with normal CSF, suggesting an immunological rather than infectious basis for these metabolic changes.
Corticosteroid and immunoglobulin administration improved brain hypometabolism/symptoms in long COVID-19 patients with suspected immune-mediated CNS involvement.
Neuropsychiatric and neurophysiological testing found central neuromuscular fatigue, apathy, and executive dysfunction in long COVID-19 patients, attributed to prolonged brain inflammation.
Elevated IL-6 appears to decrease GABA receptor expression, a proposed mechanism for neuromuscular fatigue in long COVID-19.
IL-6 overproduction is associated with depressive symptoms in long COVID-19 as an independent risk factor, and normalization of IL-6 levels relieves depressive symptoms.

A genome-wide association study found a single nucleotide polymorphism in the FOXP4 locus on chromosome 6 significantly associated with increased risk of long COVID-19, suggesting genetic predisposition.
Receipt of two doses of a COVID-19 vaccine was associated with a reduced likelihood of developing long-term effects of COVID-19.
Female sex, older age, smoking, high BMI, comorbidities, and prior hospitalization or ICU admission were identified as risk factors that increase the likelihood of developing long COVID-19.
Increased IL-6 crossing the blood-brain barrier appears to decrease GABA receptor expression, contributing to neuromuscular fatigue in long COVID-19.
IL-6 overproduction is associated with depressive symptoms in long COVID-19, acting as an independent risk factor, and normalization of IL-6 relieves depressive symptoms.
Overproduction of IL-4 causes persistent neuroinflammation mainly involved in memory symptoms and alters neuronal-enriched extracellular vesicle (nEV) protein content.
Elevated levels of TGF-β and IL-8 have been observed in long COVID-19 patients with brain fog.

High levels of neuronal dysfunction biomarkers, including amyloid-beta, neurogranin, total tau, and phosphorylated tau (pT181-tau), have been observed in patients with persistent long COVID-19 symptoms.
Increased levels of IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α may stress cochlear cells and, combined with direct viral infiltration, lead to irreversible hearing loss in long COVID-19.

Elevated antiganglioside antibodies, potentially arising from cross-reactivity with the virus, have been found in long COVID-19 patients with peripheral nervous system symptoms such as Guillain-Barré syndrome and encephalomyelitis.

Some long COVID-19 patients with cerebral infarct were positive for anticardiolipin, anti-β2 microglobulin antibodies, and lupus anticoagulant, though these positivities may be non-specific artifacts of inflammation.
Increased IL-8 and TNF levels lead to increased von Willebrand factor and consequent platelet aggregation, contributing to cerebral microthrombosis in long COVID-19.
Neurofilament light chain, a marker of brain damage, has been detected at elevated levels in peripheral blood of long COVID-19 patients.
Anti-ACE-2 autoantibodies have been described in several long COVID-19 patients and could theoretically interfere with ACE-2's role in blood pressure control and renin-angiotensin system function.
Autoantibodies targeting type I interferons have been detected in long COVID-19 patients, potentially impairing immune response and causing viral persistence, and are used as predictive biomarkers.

Cervia and colleagues identified a SARS-CoV-2-specific immunoglobulin signature driving post-COVID-19 syndrome, with low IgM and IgG3 titers accompanied by diminished type I interferon secretion increasing susceptibility to long COVID-19.
Patients with COVID-19-associated macrophage activation syndrome showed significantly elevated tryptase levels compared to healthy controls, correlating with IL-6 levels.

Immune hyperactivation produces autoantibodies against GPCRs, cytokines, and tissue structures that inhibit catecholamine and acetylcholine signaling, resulting in autonomic nervous system dysfunction.
In a case report, administration of a DNA aptamer neutralized anti-GPCR autoantibodies, improved retinal microcirculation, and eliminated long COVID-19 symptoms.

Circulating autoantibodies in long COVID-19 patients contribute to connective tissue disorders such as myositis, lupus, and arthritis, and can trigger other autoimmune diseases including rheumatoid arthritis and fibromyalgia.
SARS-CoV-2-induced immune dysregulation causes prolonged T-cell activation with expression of exhaustion markers PD1 and TIM-3 on CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells persisting up to eight months after infection.
There is a decrease in the absolute number of lymphocytes and dendritic cells in long COVID-19, with severe forms linked to elimination of B and T lymphocytes contributing to chronic inflammation.

Kidney function impairment occurring in the acute phase of COVID-19 can persist for up to three months in patients with long COVID-19, attributed to hemodynamic instability, coagulation disorders, and systemic inflammation.
SARS-CoV-2 can enter renal cells via ACE-2, causing glomerulopathy manifesting as proteinuria, hematuria, and renal failure, particularly in patients with risk factors.
Two months after initial COVID-19 infection, previously normoglycemic patients frequently develop hyperglycemia and insulin resistance.

SARS-CoV-2 enters pancreatic cells directly via ACE-2 receptors and destroys them, which can lead to the development of diabetes mellitus, and can worsen glycemic control in patients with pre-existing diabetes.
Reports describe dysregulated thyroid and parathyroid function along with deficient vitamin D levels in patients with long COVID-19.
SARS-CoV-2 inhibits osteoblast function and enhances osteoclast activity, and cytokine storms combined with corticosteroid therapy and low vitamin D may further worsen bone health in long COVID-19.
SARS-CoV-2 persists in the gut and causes changes in the intestinal microbiome that persist for up to six months, with dysbiosis significantly associated with long COVID-19.
A genome-wide association study identified a single nucleotide polymorphism in the FOXP4 locus significantly associated with increased risk of developing long COVID-19.
Impairment of kidney function occurring during acute COVID-19 can persist for up to three months in patients with long COVID-19.
SARS-CoV-2 can enter renal cells via ACE2 receptors, causing glomerulopathy that manifests as proteinuria, hematuria, and renal failure, particularly in patients with risk factors.
Two months after initial SARS-CoV-2 infection, patients with previously normal glucose levels frequently developed hyperglycemia and insulin resistance.
Deficient levels of vitamin D, along with dysregulated thyroid and parathyroid function, have been reported in patients with long COVID-19.
SARS-CoV-2 directly inhibits osteoblast function while enhancing osteoclast activity, contributing to impaired bone health, worsened by cytokine storms, corticosteroid therapy, and low vitamin D.
SARS-CoV-2 causes changes in the intestinal microbiome that persist for up to six months, with dysbiosis significantly associated with long COVID-19.
Four months after infection, SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid proteins and viral RNA have been detected in intestinal biopsies and feces even in patients with a negative nasopharyngeal PCR.
SARS-CoV-2 has been detected in hepatocytes on biopsy in long COVID-19 patients and, together with chronic inflammation and microbiome-driven dysbiosis, is proposed to cause abnormal liver function.
Low titers of IgM and IgG3, accompanied by diminished secretion of type I interferons, were found to increase individuals' susceptibility to long COVID-19.
Tryptase levels were found to be significantly elevated compared to healthy controls in COVID-19 patients who developed macrophage activation syndrome, and correlated with IL-6 levels.

Immune hyperactivation causes production of autoantibodies against G-protein-coupled receptors, cytokines, or tissue/cell structures, leading to inhibition of catecholamine and acetylcholine signaling and dysfunction of the autonomic nervous system.
In a case report, administration of a DNA aptamer neutralized anti-GPCR autoantibodies, improved retinal microcirculation, and eliminated long COVID-19 symptoms.

Autoantibodies accumulating in the circulation of long COVID-19 patients can trigger other autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and fibromyalgia, as well as connective tissue disorders including myositis, lupus, and arthritis.

SARS-CoV-2-induced immune dysregulation causes prolonged T-cell activation and expression of exhaustion markers PD1 and TIM-3 in CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells even eight months after infection, decreasing cytokine production and memory cell formation.
There is a decrease in the absolute number of lymphocytes and dendritic cells in severe COVID-19, with elimination of B and T lymphocytes linked to chronic inflammation in post-COVID-19 syndrome.

Elevated antiganglioside antibodies, possibly produced by cross-reactivity with SARS-CoV-2, have been found in patients with peripheral nervous system symptoms such as Guillain-Barre syndrome and encephalomyelitis.

Patients have been described with cerebral infarct and positive anticardiolipin, anti-β2 microglobulin antibodies, and lupus anticoagulant, though positivity may be a false finding due to inflammation without clinical impact.
Increased IL-6 decreases the expression of GABA receptors, which can lead to neuromuscular fatigue in long COVID-19 patients.
IL-6 overproduction is associated with depressive symptoms and is an independent risk factor; normalization of IL-6 relieves depressive symptoms.
Overproduction of IL-4 causes continuous neuroinflammation mainly involved in memory symptoms and can lead to changes in neuronal-enriched extracellular vesicle (nEV) proteins.

Elevated TGF-β and IL-8 have been observed in patients with brain fog, alongside high levels of neuronal dysfunction biomarkers such as amyloid-beta, neurogranin, total tau, and pT181-tau in patients with persistent symptoms.
Increased levels of cytokines such as IL-8 and TNF lead to an increase in von Willebrand factor and consequently platelet aggregation and thrombosis in the brain.
Markers of brain damage, such as neurofilament light chain, have been found in the peripheral blood of long COVID-19 patients.
Production of anti-ACE-2 autoantibodies has been described in several patients, potentially affecting the action of ACE-2 in controlling hypertension and renin-angiotensin system function.

Autoantibodies targeting interferons have been detected in COVID-19 patients, affecting the immune response and causing viral persistence, as well as antibodies causing Guillain-Barre syndrome, thrombocytopenia, and systemic lupus erythematosus.
Small-fiber neuropathy has been implicated in post-COVID-19 syndrome and is considered a cause of dysautonomia.
Cases of dysregulated tissue oxygen supply, such as POTS and orthostatic hypotension, can contribute to dysautonomia via peripheral vasoconstriction in long COVID-19.

In a mouse model of mild respiratory COVID-19, CSF CCL11 concentration rose further at seven weeks post-infection in parallel with rising circulating blood CCL11, a chemokine linked to age-related cognitive impairment.

At seven days post-infection, mice with mild respiratory COVID-19 showed CSF elevation of interferon-gamma, IL-6, TNF-alpha, CXCL10, CCL7, CCL2, CCL11, GM-CSF, and BAFF, with a distinct but overlapping panel (CXCL10, CCL7, CCL2, CCL11, GM-CSF, IL-10, CCL5) elevated at seven weeks.
IL-6 has been shown to directly inhibit hippocampal neurogenesis by inducing apoptosis of healthy adult hippocampal neural stem cells.
Systemic administration of CCL11 in mice induced microglial/macrophage reactivity in the hippocampal white matter and reduced hippocampal neurogenesis.

CCL11 concentration in circulating blood was increased in 48 long-COVID patients with cognitive 'brain fog' after mild SARS-CoV-2 infection compared to 15 long-COVID patients without cognitive impairment, though CCL11 was surprisingly higher in male patients despite cognitive impairment being more common in females.
Post-COVID-19 mice showed increased CD68 expression indicating microglial/macrophage reactivity in subcortical white matter but not in cortical gray matter.

Postmortem brain tissue from 7 patients who died suddenly or within days to weeks after COVID-19 symptom onset showed microglial reactivity in the subcortical white matter, corroborating the mouse model findings in humans.

Single-cell RNA sequencing of cortical and white matter microglia after SARS-CoV-2 infection identified five transcriptional states, including three clusters overexpressing chemokine, inflammation, and interferon-response genes with elevated TNF-alpha, IL-1a, and IL-1b, resembling disease-associated microglia in Alzheimer's disease and white-matter-associated microglia of aging.

Exposure of microglia to SARS-CoV-2 spike protein altered purinergic signaling, upregulating and activating P2Y6 and P2Y12 receptors linked to neuroinflammation; P2Y12 activation is associated with increased iNOS and inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and TNF-α, while P2Y6 stimulates phagocytosis that can cause neuronal loss and memory impairment.

Post-COVID-19 mice showed decreased numbers of doublecortin-positive newly born neurons in the subgranular zone-granule cell layer of the dentate gyrus at seven days post-infection, which persisted at seven weeks post-infection.
A separate hamster study reported decreased hippocampal neurogenesis associated with microglial activation and upregulation of IL-1b and IL-6.

Post-COVID hippocampal pyramidal and granule cell layer neurons showed morphological changes including shortened dendrites, decreased dendritic spines, reduced cellular branching, and altered neuronal distribution.
The oligodendrocyte precursor cell population was unaffected at seven days post-infection but showed a mild decrease at seven weeks post-infection in the post-COVID-19 mouse model.
Mature oligodendrocytes were depleted by approximately 33% at seven days post-infection, a reduction that persisted at seven weeks with significant myelin loss in the post-COVID-19 mouse model.
White matter areas in the post-COVID-19 mouse model showed decreased myelinated axon density at seven days post-infection, which did not recover by seven weeks post-infection.
A prior study suggested that decreased levels of CCL11 can increase stroke severity, contrasting with its presumed pathogenic role in long-COVID neuroinflammation.
A 73-year-old woman with mild acute XBB.1.5 infection developed persistent fatigue lasting over one month, meeting criteria for Long COVID-19 despite having no pre-existing comorbidities.
At the time of infection, eight months after her last vaccine dose, the patient had only low levels of anti-Spike Protein S1 IgG despite having received four vaccine doses.

One month post-infection, inflammatory and organ function biomarkers including ferritin, C-reactive protein, creatinine, creatine phosphokinase, albumin, total proteins, amylase, and lipase were all normal, as were liver enzymes throughout follow-up.
In the RECOVER cohort of 9,764 participants, the prevalence of Long COVID-19 was reported as 10% at six months after infection.
The XBB.1.5 Omicron lineage carries the F486P spike mutation, which confers higher binding affinity to the ACE2 receptor.
XBB.1.5 appears to elicit lower neutralizing antibody titers than previous Omicron lineages, even among vaccinated individuals or those with hybrid immunity.

Viral load, measured by RT-PCR cycle threshold for the nucleoprotein gene, declined from Ct 19.44/20.94 at diagnosis to Ct 32.29/33.63 one week later, becoming undetectable one month after infection, despite persistence of fatigue symptoms.
Among kidney transplant recipients surveyed after SARS-CoV-2 infection during the Omicron predominance, 52% reported symptoms consistent with Long COVID.
Weakness was the most commonly reported Long COVID symptom, affecting 46% of respondents.
Myalgia was reported by 41% of patients as a Long COVID complaint.
Dizziness was reported by 33% of patients as a Long COVID complaint.
Headache was reported by 31% of patients as a Long COVID complaint.
Among employed kidney transplant recipients with Long COVID, 94% were able to resume their normal work activities, suggesting a milder functional impact during the Omicron era.
Female gender was independently associated with more than double the risk of developing Long COVID among kidney transplant recipients.
A previous SARS-CoV-2 infection prior to the study period was independently associated with markedly higher risk of Long COVID.
Fatigue during the acute COVID-19 phase was independently associated with more than double the risk of subsequent Long COVID.
Hospitalization due to COVID-19 during the acute phase was independently associated with increased risk of Long COVID in kidney transplant recipients.
Unlike in the general population, vaccination status was not identified as a risk factor for Long COVID among kidney transplant recipients in this cohort.
Nearly 60% of long COVID patients had elevated CH50 (complement activity) levels.
High CH50 levels were significantly more frequent among long COVID patients reporting poor concentration and were independently associated with poor concentration in multivariate analysis.
High CH50 levels were significantly associated with brain fog in multivariate analysis of long COVID patients.
High CH50 levels showed no significant association with other long COVID symptoms including fatigue, headache, insomnia, dyspnea, and tiredness.
The prevalence of long COVID among patients attending the outpatient department was 37.3%.
Long COVID prevalence was higher among females (41.4%) than males (33.6%).
Higher PHQ-9 depression scores were significantly associated with long COVID in both bivariate and multivariate logistic regression.
Greater severity of the acute COVID-19 illness was significantly associated with development of long COVID in multivariate analysis.
A small proportion of participants showed ECG abnormalities including left ventricular hypertrophy, right atrial enlargement, and sinus tachycardia after recovering from COVID-19.
Over one-fifth of participants had abnormal chest X-ray findings including hilar lymphadenopathy, lung opacities, pleural effusion, and cardiomegaly following COVID-19.
Nearly one-fifth of participants had reduced FEV1/FVC ratio (<0.7) indicating impaired lung function after COVID-19, though this was not significantly associated with long COVID status.
Fatigue, body pain, cough, joint pain, and breathlessness were the most frequently reported symptoms consistent with long COVID among study participants.
Pre-existing comorbid conditions showed a greater but statistically non-significant risk of long COVID.
Biochemical and anthropometric parameters, including BMI, showed no significant differences between participants with and without long COVID, aside from PHQ-9 score.
Lack of vaccination was an independent predictor of long COVID after adjusting for age, gender, comorbidities, and disease severity.
Fully vaccinated patients had a 62% reduced risk and partially vaccinated patients had a 56% reduced risk of developing long COVID compared to unvaccinated patients.
Severe/critical disease during hospitalization was more common in unvaccinated patients than vaccinated patients.
Unvaccinated individuals required readmission to emergency/inpatient services more often than vaccinated individuals.
New/worsened/persistent long COVID symptoms were more common in unvaccinated patients compared to vaccinated patients.
Severe fatigue was more common in unvaccinated than vaccinated patients at 1-year follow-up.
A higher proportion of vaccinated patients were able to return to work compared to unvaccinated patients.
At 1-year follow-up, 29.9% of survivors reported new/worsened/persistent symptoms consistent with long COVID, more prevalent among those with severe/critical initial disease.
Fatigue at 1 year was the most prominent persistent symptom and was significantly higher in patients with severe/critical disease compared to non-severe disease.
Shortness of breath/chest tightness was significantly more common in severe/critical disease survivors than non-severe survivors at 1 year.

A substantial proportion of survivors, especially those with severe/critical disease, required home oxygen supplementation for weeks to months after discharge, though none required it by the time of the 1-year interview.
Among survivors who answered employment questions, 45% had returned to employment while 12.8% had not, with most returning within 60 days of discharge.
A substantial proportion of survivors reported emotional and financial difficulties even one year after discharge, with greater emotional impact in the severe/critical disease group.
Clinically significant anxiety or depression (HADS score >11) was present in 6.1% of survivors, with no significant difference between severity groups.
One year after infection, a subset of patients showed worsened functional class (NYHA class 4) compared to their pre-COVID baseline, though most remained NYHA class 1.
Long COVID was not found to be a contributing factor for post-discharge hospital readmissions, which were instead driven by respiratory failure and infections.
Among survivors who had outpatient chest X-rays, a minority showed fibrosis or consolidation, with the majority being normal.
Ginsenoside Rb1 was found to suppress JAK kinase activity.
Total ginsenosides may down-regulate c-Jun gene expression, inhibiting the TNF signaling pathway.
Ginsenoside CK inhibits NLRP3-inflammasome activation, suppressing IL-1 release and dampening the overactive immune response.
Down-regulation of miR-34a-5p inhibits ERK-mediated signaling and decreases natural killer cell cytotoxicity.
Ginsenoside 20(R)-Rg3 promotes ERK1/2 phosphorylation, enhancing the cytotoxicity of natural killer cells.
Total ginsenosides may activate STAT1 to promote type I and type III interferon anti-viral signaling.
Fermented (black) Ginseng Radix et Rhizoma suppressed SARS-CoV-2 replication and lowered viral RNA copies in the extracellular environment.
In HIV-infected patients, Ginseng Radix et Rhizoma combined with zidovudine preserved CD4+ T cell counts, alongside inducing genetic defects in the viral nef gene.
Diets containing Ginseng Radix et Rhizoma protected mice and ferrets from lethal H5N1 influenza infection.
Ginsenosides Rb1, Rg1, and Rg3 inhibited replication of hepatitis A and B viruses in vitro.
A small clinical study found that Ginseng Radix et Rhizoma Rubra extract reduced production of the inflammatory cytokines TNFα and IFNγ after chemotherapy.

In a chemotherapy-related fatigue mouse model, BST204 (a purified ginseng extract) improved running wheel activity and forced swimming performance by 50% after 27 days, by raising muscle glycogen and lowering peripheral TNF-α and IL-6.
In a weight-loaded swimming fatigue rat model, Ginseng Radix et Rhizoma down-regulated protein expression of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-1β.
Fermented Ginseng Radix et Rhizoma powder was clinically shown to increase testosterone levels.
Ginsenoside Rg1 reverted hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis function toward normal by improving serum cortisol and testosterone levels.
Ginsenoside Rg3 resists neurotoxicity by increasing nerve growth factor expression.
Ginsenoside Rg1 has a neuroprotective effect associated with decreased AQP4 expression, reducing blood-brain barrier permeability and brain edema.
Panaxydol, an active component of wild ginseng, enhanced forced swimming performance in a fatigue model by changing LDH levels.
Mixed water-soluble ginseng polysaccharides reduced immobility periods in a fatigue model by lowering LDH and creatine phosphokinase activities.

20(S)-protopanaxatriol significantly extended forced-swimming and rotarod running times, increased glucose, and decreased corticosterone, blood lactic acid, free fatty acid, and LDH activity in a fatigue model.
In a postoperative fatigue syndrome rat model, ginsenoside Rb1 increased maximum grip strength and reversed the increases in blood lactic acid and LDH activity.
Qingjin Yiqi granules, a ginseng-based formula, significantly alleviate fatigue and are recommended by rehabilitation guidelines for long COVID treatment.
Long COVID symptoms are reported to be infrequent in children compared with adults, while women are more susceptible to long-COVID-associated fatigue.
Long COVID patients show highly activated innate immune cells, a lack of naive T and B cells, and persistent cytokinemia.
Elevated LDH levels in COVID-19 indicate impaired energy generation and reflect mitochondrial dysfunction.

Three patients with severe, disabling long COVID experienced complete, rapid remission of symptoms within about a week of receiving the casirivimab/imdevimab monoclonal antibody cocktail, with remission sustained for over two years.
Prior to MCA treatment, all three subjects developed chronic, unrelenting fatigue and cognitive impairment along with other severe, disabling symptoms following acute COVID-19 infection.
A 4-week course of intranasal oxytocin reduced intrinsic amygdala-orbitofrontal functional connectivity in children with autism compared to placebo, an effect most pronounced at the 4-week follow-up.
Reductions in amygdala-orbitofrontal connectivity following oxytocin administration were correlated with improved social symptoms in the children.
Oxytocin administration was associated with improved cardiac autonomic balance, reflected by lower cardiac autonomic arousal correlating with reduced amygdala-orbitofrontal connectivity.

Epigenetic methylation of the oxytocin receptor gene (OXTR) modulated the neural and cardiac autonomic effects of oxytocin, with more pronounced effects in children with reduced methylation (implying higher OXTR expression).
In a cohort of 53 children with autism spectrum disorder, 34% were diagnosed with obstructive sleep apnea via polysomnography.
Ferritin levels and BMI were not significantly correlated with OSA in children with ASD, suggesting other factors contribute to SDB in this population.
Higher numbers of pain-related behaviors in the previous week were associated with increased overall sleep-related problems, including shorter sleep duration, parasomnias, and SDB.

Sleep behaviors and vocalizations were found to influence scores on the SDB subscale of the CSHQ, suggesting SDB may be linked to specific vocal behaviors and overall sleep quality in children with ASD.
Children with ASD had a 96% increased risk of developing sleep disorders, including OSA, compared with non-autistic children.
Children with ASD had a 274% increased likelihood of undergoing polysomnography compared to non-autistic controls.
Children with ASD had a 50% increased likelihood of undergoing ENT surgery compared to non-autistic controls.
Loud snoring and other abnormal breathing behaviors were rarely reported in children with ASD assessed via the CSHQ, despite the known association between ASD and SDB.
Treatment of OSA with adenotonsillectomy improved behavioral outcomes in children with ASD, regardless of obesity or age.
Among 45 children with ASD, 58% were diagnosed with OSA via PSG and 33% were obese.
Obesity was identified as a significant predictive factor for severe OSA in children with ASD.
Autism severity and age at OSA diagnosis were not significantly associated after adjusting for other factors, but both BMI and age at autism diagnosis independently predicted age at OSA diagnosis.
Hypotonia was the most common motor symptom in a cohort of 154 children with ASD, present in 51% overall and in 63% of children aged 2-6 years, an age range with high SDB prevalence.
Children with ASD showed a higher prevalence of asthma and allergic rhinitis, at a ratio of 5:1 compared to healthy subjects.
Very young children with common ear and upper respiratory symptoms appear to have an elevated risk of subsequently receiving an autism diagnosis or exhibiting high levels of autism-related traits.

A straightforward linear correlation between degree of nasal obstruction and severity of SDB is not consistently observed, and nasal obstruction is not the primary underlying factor in most cases of moderate or severe OSA.
The risk and rate of obesity in pediatric individuals with ASD are elevated compared to the general population, attributed primarily to sedentary lifestyles and improper dietary habits.
Joint hypermobility has a high prevalence in ASD, leading some authors to include autism among hypermobility spectrum disorders.

Patients with a neurodevelopmental diagnosis of identified genetic etiology (NPD) showed higher rates of autonomic symptoms across all four assessed symptom categories compared to ASD patients without a known genetic cause and matched controls.
The study identified several significant relationships between individual differences in autonomic symptoms and quantitative measures of ASD traits.
Sleep disturbances, gastrointestinal problems, and atypical heart rate are commonly observed in patients with ASD and may relate to underlying autonomic nervous system function.

Individuals reporting current long COVID symptoms had significantly greater stress, anxiety, and depression severity than those with no history of long COVID, after adjusting for demographic and lifestyle factors.

Individuals reporting a previous history of long COVID symptoms had significantly greater stress, anxiety, and depression severity than those with no history of long COVID, though effect sizes were smaller than for those with current symptoms.

The paper analyzes two first-person illness narratives (Lucy Adams's long COVID account and Laura Hillenbrand's 1987 post-viral/CFS essay) using literary close-reading focused on temporality and suffering.
Approximately half of people with long COVID are estimated to meet diagnostic criteria for ME/CFS, and studies are finding shared clinical abnormalities between the two conditions.
An estimated 2.1 million people in the UK and 65 million people worldwide reported living with long COVID as of January 2023.
US long COVID patients seeking medical care in the first 18 months of the pandemic frequently experienced 'medical gaslighting' characterized by dismissal, delayed diagnosis, and deferred treatment.

Both Hillenbrand's and Adams's narratives describe severe post-exertional symptom exacerbation, where even minor activity (e.g., a short walk or bike ride) could trigger relapse, fever, or being bed-bound for extended periods.
In the BBC Panorama documentary, a voice-over states that one in five people with long COVID struggle with memory, concentration, or brain fog.

Gulf War Syndrome, once attributed by some researchers to rumor/narrative transmission, was later determined to result from a gene-environment interaction in which veterans with a weak variant of a particular gene were predisposed to chronic symptoms following low-level nerve agent exposure.

Some commentators (Shure 2022; Saunders et al. 2023) have proposed that long COVID may be driven by psychosocial distress, pandemic-related trauma, or a biopsychosocial causal model including 'legitimised illness narratives,' a framing the authors of this paper critique as echoing historically discredited claims about post-viral illness.
EBV DNA was undetectable by qPCR at any timepoint (pre-pandemic to 9 months post-infection) in any participant reporting post-COVID-19-syndrome, arguing against EBV reactivation as a cause of PCS.
EBV VCA IgM antibody levels showed no significant differences between PCS and non-PCS groups relative to pre-pandemic baseline, indicating no evidence of acute EBV reactivation.
EBV VCA IgG antibody levels showed no significant differences between PCS and non-PCS groups over the study period, providing no evidence for EBV reactivation.
EBNA IgG antibody levels showed no significant differences between PCS and non-PCS groups, and no specific increase over time in PCS individuals, arguing against EBV reactivation.

Neopterin levels, a marker of pro-inflammatory antiviral T-helper cell-mediated immune activation, were not elevated (>11 nmol/L) and showed no significant differences between PCS and non-PCS groups at the seropositive blood donation timepoint.
Relative change in neopterin levels compared to each participant's own pre-pandemic baseline showed no significant or visual differences between PCS and non-PCS groups.

SARS-CoV-2 anti-N total antibody levels declined similarly over the first year post-infection across asymptomatic, symptomatic non-PCS, and PCS groups, with no significant group differences, suggesting successful viral clearance rather than persistence in PCS.

18% of the 163 healthy blood donors with asymptomatic or mild SARS-CoV-2 infection developed post-COVID-19-syndrome with symptoms lasting up to one year, with fatigue, altered sense of taste (hyposmia/dysgeusia), and shortness of breath being the most common persisting symptoms.

Individuals who developed PCS showed numerically higher rates of acute-phase symptoms (cough, shortness of breath, headache, body ache, hyposmia, dysgeusia, GI issues) compared to those without PCS, but these differences were not statistically significant by Fisher's exact test.

Serum 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol, the active form of vitamin D) was significantly elevated in gynecologic cancer patients with PASC/Long COVID compared to gynecologic cancer patients without PASC/LC.
No significant difference was found in serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (calcifediol, the storage form of vitamin D) between PASC/LC patients and controls.

Longitudinal monitoring in two representative PASC/LC patients showed persistently abnormal, elevated 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels over more than two years, coinciding with ongoing debilitating symptoms.

The authors hypothesize that chronic macrophage/dendritic cell activation driven by persistent SARS-CoV-2 viral RNA or antigens may trigger CYP27B1-mediated extrarenal hydroxylation of vitamin D, analogous to sarcoidosis, explaining the elevated active vitamin D observed in PASC/LC patients.

Cited literature indicates cancer patients with COVID-19 may be especially prone to developing PASC/Long COVID, including dysautonomia such as postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), with up to 60% affected in some cohorts followed up to 14 months.
Prior studies cited by the authors reported that female cancer patients were more likely than male cancer patients to report persistence of PASC/LC symptoms.

Prior studies found that a significant proportion of non-classical monocytes contained or transported SARS-CoV-2 S1 protein in PASC/LC patients up to 15 months post-infection, supporting a model of persistent viral antigen reservoir driving chronic immune activation.
Occipital cortical GABA+/water levels were significantly lower in the PASC group than in healthy controls after controlling for tissue composition, alcohol intake, and sex.
Lower GABA+/water levels were strongly associated with poorer sleep quality (sleep-aid medication use subscale of the PSQI) in the sample.
Within the PASC group, lower GABA+/water was associated with higher depression scores, an association not seen in controls.
In the control group, GABA+/water was not associated with depression scores, unlike in the PASC group.

Mediation analysis suggested that lower GABA+/water partially mediates the effect of PASC on depression, accounting for roughly 43% of the total effect, though this indirect effect did not reach significance.
PASC was associated with a significant increase in depression severity (PROMIS t-score) relative to controls in the full mediation model.
NAA concentration showed a non-significant trend toward being lower in the PASC group compared to controls.
Within the PASC group, lower NAA levels were associated with worse verbal recall performance.
Combined glutamate/glutamine (Glx) levels did not differ significantly between the PASC and control groups.
PASC participants reported significantly greater depression and anxiety than general population normative scores on PROMIS scales.
PASC participants scored lower than population norms on a subjective cognitive impairment scale, indicating greater self-perceived cognitive deficits (brain fog).
The PASC group reported worse sleep quality than the demographically matched control group.
The PASC group reported higher weekly alcohol intake than controls.
Since recovering from acute COVID-19, PASC participants reported the greatest perceived deterioration in memory, brain fog, attention, mood, and fatigue.
Weekly alcohol intake did not correlate with GABA+/water levels, supporting its use as a covariate rather than a confound.
Insomnia and depression scores were positively correlated within the study sample, consistent with these being co-occurring core PASC symptoms.

Two PASC participants who used GABA-enhancing medications (fluoxetine, lisdexamfetamine) had GABA+/water z-scores close to the PASC group mean, indicating medication use did not drive or mask the observed GABA reduction.
Among initially symptomatic individuals with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, half reported at least one persistent symptom 3-6 months after acute infection.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported persistent symptom, occurring in about one in five previously symptomatic individuals.
Headache was the second most common persistent symptom reported after acute COVID-19.
Cough was the third most common persistent symptom reported after acute COVID-19.
Individuals hospitalized with moderate acute COVID-19 disease had approximately twice the prevalence of PASC compared with those who were not hospitalized.
Individuals hospitalized with severe/critical acute COVID-19 disease had over twice the prevalence of PASC compared with those who were not hospitalized.
Females were more likely than males to report persistent fatigue following COVID-19 infection.
