The most prevalent symptoms among Long COVID clinic patients were fatigue, brain fog, trouble concentrating, dizziness/lightheadedness, and post-exertional pain/fatigue.

More than three-quarters of patients experienced constitutional and neurological symptoms, while respiratory, psychiatric, cardiovascular, and rheumatologic symptoms occurred in over half of the cohort.
Patients experienced a median of 18 new symptoms (IQR 14) attributable to COVID-19 infection and a median of only 1 resolved symptom (IQR 4) by their initial clinic visit.
Patients had markedly reduced self-reported mental health, with a mean PROMIS mental T-score of 37.9 and 65% rating mental health as fair or poor.
Patients had markedly reduced self-reported physical health, with a mean PROMIS physical T-score of 37.5 and 73% rating physical health as fair or poor.
Nearly half of the cohort (46%) showed mild cognitive dysfunction on the MoCA despite almost universal subjective neurocognitive complaints.
Patients who were hospitalized during acute COVID-19 had significantly lower MoCA cognitive scores than those who were not hospitalized.
PHQ-9 depression scores were inversely correlated with MoCA cognitive scores, suggesting overlap between depressive and cognitive symptoms.
42% of patients screened positive for moderate to severe depression on the PHQ-9.
38% of patients screened positive for moderate to severe anxiety on the GAD-7.
63% of patients had a positive PC-PTSD-5 screen (score ≥1), suggesting a high burden of trauma-related symptoms.
19% of patients reported an unmet health-related social need, most commonly inability to obtain needed medicine or health care.
12% of patients endorsed housing insecurity.
Patients with pre-existing vascular disease had significantly higher odds of reporting a high symptom burden (>30 symptoms) compared to those with fewer than 16 symptoms.
PASC significantly impacted patients' ability to work, with reduced full-time employment, increased part-time employment, and a doubled unemployment rate compared to pre-pandemic employment.
Most patients reported no reliable improvement in PASC symptoms after vaccination, with the majority experiencing no change and some worsening.

Based on reported review-of-systems symptom patterns (fatigue, post-exertional malaise, sleep disturbance plus additional symptoms), the authors estimate at least 60% of the Long COVID cohort would meet diagnostic criteria for ME/CFS.
Cited literature suggests persistently positive antinuclear antibodies are associated with ongoing symptoms and inflammation in COVID-19 survivors, supporting an autoimmune hypothesis for PASC.
Cited literature links antibodies targeting ACE2 to a pro-inflammatory state in PASC, supporting an autoimmune/inflammatory mechanism.

A cited external study found elevated odds of an abnormal MoCA score in patients with high premorbid vulnerability (NHS score) and more severe pulmonary disease, a pattern the authors state is consistent with their own hospitalization-related MoCA findings.
Symptom prevalence was similar regardless of the severity of the initial acute COVID-19 illness.
Pooled incidence of chest pain among post-acute COVID-19 patients was 17%, the highest among pain-related symptoms.
Pooled incidence of headache among post-acute COVID-19 patients was 16%.
Pooled incidence of arthralgia (joint pain) among post-acute COVID-19 patients was 13%.
Pooled incidence of neuralgia among post-acute COVID-19 patients was 12%, based on only three studies.
Pooled incidence of abdominal pain among post-acute COVID-19 patients was 11%.
Pooled incidence of fatigue among post-acute COVID-19 patients was 45%, the most frequent symptom overall.
Pooled incidence of insomnia among post-acute COVID-19 patients was 26%.
Pooled incidence of dyspnea among post-acute COVID-19 patients was 25%.
Pooled incidence of weakness among post-acute COVID-19 patients was 25%.
Pooled incidence of anosmia among post-acute COVID-19 patients was 19%.
Meta-regression showed the incidence of insomnia was significantly higher with longer follow-up periods after acute COVID-19.
Meta-regression showed the incidence of ageusia was significantly higher in study populations with a lower ratio of males, indicating a sex difference.
Meta-regression indicated neuralgia incidence increased by approximately 45% for every additional month of follow-up, though based on only three studies.
An inverse association was found between age and the incidence of weakness in post-acute COVID-19 patients, which the authors could not explain.
Fatigue, dyspnea, cough, anosmia and fever were the symptoms most frequently ranked as top-3 symptoms across the individual included studies.
The authors note that long COVID fatigue shows proposed similarities and pathological overlap with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS).
Patients with low CCDC18 expression in whole blood tended to report better quality of life after recovering from COVID-19.
Patients with high CPED1 expression in whole blood tended to report better quality of life after recovering from COVID-19.
Patients with low CDC16 expression in whole blood tended to report worse quality of life after recovering from COVID-19.

A machine learning-based workflow applied to whole blood RNA-seq data identified gene expression patterns distinguishing PASC patients whose quality of life was better, the same, or worse after COVID-19 recovery, with top genes implicated in immune response to viral infection.

Elevated levels of IL-1β, IL-2, IL-6, IL-10, IFN-γ, and TNF-α have been reported in COVID-19, with the degree of elevation proportional to illness severity, supporting a cytokine-storm mechanism potentially driving Neuro-PASC.

In a case-control 18F-FDG-PET/CT study, post-COVID syndrome patients showed brain hypometabolism in limbic, paralimbic, brainstem, and cerebellar regions with no regions of hypermetabolism, and limbic/orbitofrontal hypometabolism correlated with acute-phase anosmia.

Whole-body 18F-FDG-PET/CT in the same post-COVID cohort showed hypermetabolic activity in both ACE2-target and non-target organs despite brain hypometabolism, supporting a role for systemic inflammation independent of direct ACE2-mediated viral invasion.
In 143 patients with suspected Neuro-PASC, 47% of 18F-FDG-PET/CT scans showed hypometabolism in limbic/paralimbic and fronto-orbital olfactory regions, as well as brainstem and cerebellum.
Karimi-Galougahi et al. found reduced metabolic activity in the orbitofrontal cortex on 18F-FDG-PET/CT in Neuro-PASC patients.
Donegani et al. reported bilateral parahippocampal and fusiform gyri hypometabolism along with left insula hypometabolism on 18F-FDG-PET/CT in Neuro-PASC patients.

Hosp et al. found frontoparietal hypometabolism on 18F-FDG-PET/CT that correlated with cognitive decline measured by the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, while structural 3T MRI showed no signs of cerebral damage in the same patients.

Guedj et al. identified distinct hypometabolic clusters on 18F-FDG-PET/CT that reliably distinguished Neuro-PASC patients from controls, with cerebellar hypometabolism linked to hyposmia/anosmia/memory impairment and frontal-brainstem-cerebellar hypometabolism linked to pain and insomnia.

Post-COVID patients with vascular hypermetabolism on whole-body PET at 1-month post-infection also showed brain hypometabolism, indicating a temporal/regional sequence in how COVID-19 affects different tissues.

Dressing et al. found that post-COVID patients with symptoms lasting over 3 months showed only mild cognitive impairment on MoCA testing despite having distinct pathologic 18F-FDG-PET/CT findings, and Ferrucci et al.'s review noted not all patients with cognitive decline showed hypometabolism.

Debs et al. observed time-dependent brain PET changes: hypometabolism in bilateral frontal, parietal, occipital, and posterior temporal lobes and cerebellum peaked at 2 months post-infection, nearly resolved at 6 months, and disappeared by 12 months; hypermetabolism in brainstem, cerebellum, limbic structures, frontal cortex, and periventricular white matter was seen at 2-6 months.
Takao et al. described SPECT-detected hypoperfusion in various brain areas, particularly the frontal lobes, in Neuro-PASC patients, concordant with prior 18F-FDG-PET/CT hypometabolism findings.

In 32 patients with severely impaired functional status, SPECT-CT showed cerebral perfusion changes in 29 patients (90%); on follow-up 3-9 months later in 15 patients, imaging improved in 8 and worsened in 7.

Ferrucci et al. detected amyloid plaques via 18F-amyloid PET/CT in the superior/middle frontal cortex and posterior cingulate cortex of one Neuro-PASC patient 12 months after hospital discharge, with concurrent hypometabolism in the left mesial temporal cortex on 18F-FDG-PET/CT.

Sun et al. found significantly higher plasma levels of amyloid beta in participants recovered from acute COVID-19 compared to controls, regardless of whether they had persisting neurological symptoms.

Thapaliya et al.'s pilot 7T MRI study found increased volume of the superior cerebellar peduncle, pons, and entire brainstem in Neuro-PASC patients compared to controls, biomarkers also observed in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome, suggesting shared pathophysiology.

A UK Biobank longitudinal imaging study of 785 participants scanned before and ~141 days after COVID-19 infection found statistically significant gray matter atrophy in limbic cortical areas linked to olfactory and gustatory systems.

Kandemirli et al. found that nearly three-quarters of 23 patients with persistent post-COVID olfactory dysfunction had olfactory cleft opacification, reduced olfactory bulb volume, and changes in bulb shape or signal on structural MRI.

Besteher et al. found increased gray matter volume clusters bilaterally in frontal lobe, temporal lobe, insula, amygdala, hippocampus, basal ganglia, and thalamus 8 months after acute COVID-19 in patients compared to controls using voxel-based morphometry, with four of these clusters decreasing over time, hypothesized to reflect compensatory processes or inflammation.

Hellgren et al. found subcortical white matter lesions near the gray-white matter junction (frontal/parietal lobes) in 71% of 35 hospitalized post-COVID patients (mean 6.5 months post-discharge); patients with lesions had lower RBANS visuospatial index scores than those with normal MRI.

Campabadal et al. found reduced gray matter volume in the caudate nucleus, putamen, olfactory cortex, parahippocampal gyrus, straight gyrus, left amygdala, and superior/inferior orbital gyri using voxel-based morphometry in Neuro-PASC patients.

Campabadal et al. found that Neuro-PASC patients with olfactory dysfunction had higher mean diffusivity in the genu of the corpus callosum, forceps minor, orbitofrontal white matter tracts, and anterior thalamic radiations, and higher radial diffusivity in the genu of the corpus callosum, anterior corona radiata, and uncinate fasciculus compared to post-COVID patients without olfactory dysfunction.
Yus et al. found no statistically significant findings in brain volumes on 3T structural MRI (3D-T1, T2-FLAIR) and no statistically significant DTI findings in patients with Neuro-PASC.

Kiatkittikul et al. showed abnormal brain connectivity on resting-state fMRI concordant with 18F-FDG-PET/CT findings, illustrated by a patient with COVID-19-related sensorineural hearing loss showing left temporal hypometabolism and corresponding rsfMRI anomalies in the same region.

Churchill et al. found that patients with a larger number of Neuro-PASC symptoms had altered connectivity between parietal, temporal, occipital, and subcortical regions on BOLD resting-state fMRI, with distinct connectivity patterns correlating with symptom intensity.

Ajčević et al. found that Neuro-PASC patients with cognitive impairment 2-10 months post-infection had cerebral hypoperfusion on ASL MRI, primarily in the frontal cortex but also temporal and parietal cortex (more pronounced in the right hemisphere), with overall lower gray matter cerebral blood flow than healthy controls.
Yus et al.'s ASL study found lower perfusion in the orbital and medial frontal lobes of post-COVID patients.

Douaud et al. found a greater increase in diffusivity (an indicator of tissue damage) in areas functionally connected to the piriform cortex, olfactory tubercle, and anterior olfactory nucleus in SARS-CoV-2-infected patients compared to healthy controls, in the same UK Biobank cohort.

Mishra et al. (preprint, not peer-reviewed) found abnormal susceptibility bilaterally in the brainstem (midbrain), gray-white matter junction, and frontal lobe white matter (uncinate fasciculus and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus tracts) using susceptibility-weighted imaging in post-COVID condition patients.
Hellgren et al.'s susceptibility-weighted imaging found subcortical abnormalities near the gray-white matter junction in the frontal and parietal lobes in 8 of 35 post-COVID patients.

Elevated levels of pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines including IL-1β, IL-2, IL-6, IL-10, IFN-γ and TNF-α were reported in COVID-19 patients, with the degree of elevation proportional to illness severity, supporting a cytokine-storm mechanism for Neuro-PASC.

SARS-CoV-2 is proposed to invade the nervous system via ACE2 receptors on the olfactory mucosa, crossing the neural-mucosal interface and migrating along neuronal structures to cardiorespiratory control centers, supporting a direct neurotropism hypothesis for Neuro-PASC.
Approximately one-third of people with COVID-19 overall, and nearly two-thirds of hospitalized COVID-19 patients, experienced neurological complications from their infection.
Nearly 10% of people affected by COVID-19 develop signs or symptoms persisting over 3 months, classified as post-COVID syndrome.
Up to 55% of hospitalized COVID-19 patients reported neurological manifestations 3 months after infection.

18F-FDG-PET/CT detected frontoparietal hypometabolism correlating with cognitive decline on MoCA testing, whereas a concurrent structural 3T MRI in the same patients found no relevant structural or vascular abnormality besides a few subacute infarcts.

A pilot 7T T1-weighted MRI study found increased volume of the superior cerebellar peduncle, pons, and entire brainstem in Neuro-PASC patients compared to controls, biomarkers also reported in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome, suggesting a shared substrate for symptom overlap.
COVID-19 patients showed interrelated cognitive, EEG, and structural 3T T2-weighted MRI abnormalities two months after hospital discharge.

A UK Biobank longitudinal imaging study of 785 participants scanned before and approximately 141 days after testing positive for COVID-19 showed statistically significant gray matter atrophy in limbic cortical areas directly linked to olfactory and gustatory systems.

Among 23 patients with persistent COVID-19 olfactory dysfunction, nearly three-quarters showed olfactory cleft opacification, reduced olfactory bulb volume, altered bulb shape, or signal anomalies on structural MRI.

Post-COVID patients showed increased gray matter volume clusters bilaterally in the frontal lobe, temporal lobe, insula, amygdala, hippocampus, basal ganglia, and thalamus 8 months after acute infection compared to controls, with four of these clusters decreasing in volume over time, possibly reflecting compensatory processes or inflammation.

In 35 post-COVID patients hospitalized for acute infection and discharged on average 6.5 months prior, 71% had subcortical white matter lesions on MRI (mainly frontal/parietal, near the gray-white matter junction), and these patients had lower RBANS visuospatial index scores than those with normal MRI.

Campabadal et al. found reduced gray matter volume in the caudate nucleus, putamen, olfactory cortex, parahippocampal gyrus, straight gyrus, left amygdala, and superior/inferior orbital gyri in Neuro-PASC patients using voxel-based morphometry.
A study by Yus et al. using 3T structural MRI (3D-T1, T2-FLAIR) found no statistically significant differences in brain volumes in Neuro-PASC patients.

Resting-state fMRI showed abnormal brain connectivity concordant with 18F-FDG-PET/CT findings; a patient with COVID-related sensorineural hearing loss showed both hypometabolism and connectivity anomalies in the same left temporal region.

Patients with a greater number of Neuro-PASC symptoms showed altered BOLD resting-state connectivity between parietal, temporal, occipital and subcortical regions, with distinct connectivity patterns correlating with symptom intensity.

Participants with cognitive impairment 2-10 months after acute COVID-19 showed cerebral hypoperfusion on ASL MRI, primarily in the frontal cortex but also temporal and parietal cortex, more pronounced in the right hemisphere, with lower overall gray matter cerebral blood flow than healthy controls.
Yus et al. found lower cerebral perfusion in the orbital and medial frontal lobes of post-COVID patients using ASL MRI.

Douaud et al. found greater increases in diffusivity, an indicator of tissue damage, in brain areas functionally connected to the piriform cortex, olfactory tubercle, and anterior olfactory nucleus in SARS-CoV-2-infected patients compared to healthy controls.
Long-term fasting induced marked weight loss in all 14 long COVID patients.

Systolic blood pressure decreased or stayed unchanged after fasting, with the largest reduction (-55 mmHg) in the patient with the highest baseline value and minimal change (-2 mmHg) in the patient with the lowest baseline value.
Diastolic blood pressure changes followed a similar but less pronounced pattern than systolic blood pressure after fasting.
Blood glucose levels were reduced after long-term fasting compared to before fasting.
Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) remained unchanged after long-term fasting.
Lipid parameters, particularly total cholesterol, were predominantly reduced after fasting, with the largest reductions in patients with the highest initial values.

Changes in erythrocyte sedimentation rate were inconsistent, with reductions in three patients with higher baseline levels, increases in three others, and no change in three patients with low initial values.
High-sensitivity CRP decreased in two patients with high baseline values but increased in five patients after fasting.
EQ-5D-5L index score and visual analogue overall health scale improved after fasting, with 13 of 14 patients reporting improvement.

Common long COVID symptoms (fatigue, breathlessness, muscle pain, muscle weakness, headache, joint pains, sleep difficulties, chest pain/tightness) that improved after the acute phase were further improved by long-term fasting in the majority of patients.
Less frequent post-acute sequelae, including depression, cognitive impairment, cough/sore throat, dizziness, and smell and taste disorders, improved in all affected patients after long-term fasting.
Rare gastrointestinal and dermatologic symptoms (abdominal pain, skin rash, diarrhea, nausea) also improved during long-term fasting, while fever was mainly confined to the acute phase.

Ten of 14 patients subjectively identified fasting as the most helpful therapy for their symptom improvement, while six found physiotherapy helpful and others cited ozone therapy, acupuncture, psychotherapy, or osteopathy.
No adverse events were observed during the long-term fasting intervention in these long COVID patients.

The literature reviewed indicates that the ketone body beta-hydroxybutyrate, produced during fasting, directly increases CD8+ T effector cell cytokine production through effects on histone acetylation, a proposed mechanism for fasting's immune benefits in long COVID.

The authors speculate that fasting-induced inactivation of the mTOR pathway, which also activates the inflammasome, may promote autophagy that helps clear viral RNA and repair post-acute damage in long COVID.

The authors note that mouse studies show conflicting effects of fasting depending on infection type: fasting improved survival in bacterial inflammation models but glucose utilization was crucial for survival in viral inflammation models, raising safety concerns for fasting during acute infection.
All patients had evidence of coronary microvascular dysfunction, with an average baseline index of microcirculatory resistance of 63.6, far above the normal reference of <25.
EECP treatment produced a significant reduction in patient-reported angina symptoms.
EECP treatment produced a significant reduction in patient-reported fatigue.
Dyspnea, brain fog, and palpitations also improved after EECP, though no specific significance level was reported for these symptoms.
No change was observed in muscle pain or concentration impairment among the patients who had these symptoms at baseline.
The overall PASC symptom burden per patient was significantly reduced following EECP treatment.
Six-minute walk distance improved from a mean of 498.5 m at baseline to 528 m after EECP, but the change was not statistically significant.
Perceived exertion and angina/dyspnea ratings during the 6-minute walk test improved slightly after EECP (exertion 15 to 14.5; angina/dyspnea 3 to 2.5).
Depression scores measured with the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale decreased by a mean of 0.8 points after EECP treatment.
Anxiety levels showed no improvement after EECP treatment.
Mean health-related quality of life scores improved in seven of eight RAND-36 subscales after EECP, with changes ranging from +0.2 to +10.5 points.
The vitality (energy/fatigue) subscale of RAND-36 showed the largest improvement of all subscales after EECP.
Social function and physical function subscales of RAND-36 also showed large improvements after EECP (+8.6 and +7.5, respectively), suggesting improved social interaction and physical capacity.
No improvement was seen in the emotional role functioning subscale, with most patients reporting no change and some experiencing deterioration.
The mean D/S ratio, an indicator of EECP counterpulsation efficiency linked to endothelial shear stress, increased from 1.06 in the first week of treatment to 1.10 in the fifth week.
At the individual level, the D/S ratio improved over the treatment course in five of ten patients, remained unchanged in three, and decreased in two.
Two patients returned to part-time work from full-time sick leave following EECP treatment, indicating improved working capacity.
At baseline, the most commonly reported PASC symptoms were angina (100%), fatigue (80%), and dyspnea (80%), with about 70% of patients experiencing four or more symptom types.
Anxiety or depression was a pre-existing condition in 40% of the study patients prior to their PASC diagnosis.
One patient reported complete resolution of PASC symptoms after EECP treatment, and none of the patients experienced symptom worsening.
Vital parameters (blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation) remained stable during EECP sessions, and the treatment was well tolerated by all patients who completed the protocol.
At rest, Long COVID patients had a significantly shorter mean RR interval (faster heart rate) than controls.
Standard deviation of RR intervals (STD iRR) at rest was significantly lower in Long COVID patients than controls, indicating reduced overall heart rate variability.
Mean resting heart rate was significantly higher in Long COVID patients compared to controls.
Standard deviation of heart rate at rest was significantly lower in Long COVID patients than controls.
rMSSD, a marker of parasympathetic (vagal) tone, was significantly lower at rest in Long COVID patients compared to controls.
The RR triangular index, a measure of overall RR interval variability, was significantly lower at rest in Long COVID patients than in controls.
SD1, a nonlinear index reflecting short-term (parasympathetic-mediated) HRV, was significantly lower at rest in Long COVID patients than controls.
SD2, a nonlinear index reflecting overall (long-term) HRV, was significantly lower at rest in Long COVID patients than controls.
Alpha1, a short-term detrended fluctuation analysis index associated with sudden death risk, was significantly higher at rest in Long COVID patients than controls.
Alpha2, a long-term detrended fluctuation analysis index, was significantly lower at rest in Long COVID patients compared to controls.
Entropy-based nonlinear HRV measures (ApEn and SampEn) at rest did not differ significantly between Long COVID patients and controls.
During the deep-breathing (M-RSA) maneuver, mean RR interval remained significantly shorter in Long COVID patients than controls.
During M-RSA, the increase in RR interval standard deviation was significantly blunted in Long COVID patients compared to controls.
During M-RSA, mean heart rate remained significantly higher in Long COVID patients than controls.
During M-RSA, standard deviation of heart rate was significantly lower in Long COVID patients, reflecting a blunted parasympathetic response.
During M-RSA, the parasympathetic-tone marker rMSSD increased less in Long COVID patients than in controls, indicating a blunted vagal response to deep breathing.
During M-RSA, the RR triangular index was significantly lower in Long COVID patients compared to controls.
Despite a significant age difference between groups, linear regression showed age did not significantly influence the HRV outcomes.
Children with Long-Covid syndrome had significantly lower fractional exhaled nitric oxide values compared to asymptomatic children with previous COVID-19.
Lung function measured by spirometry, body plethysmography and DLCO was normal and similar between children with Long-Covid syndrome and asymptomatic controls.
The frequency of lung ultrasound abnormalities did not differ significantly between children with Long-Covid syndrome and asymptomatic controls.
Children with Long-Covid syndrome were significantly older than asymptomatic children with previous COVID-19.
Children with Long-Covid syndrome most frequently reported fatigue, cough, exercise intolerance, and dyspnea as persistent symptoms.
Both patients showed markedly reduced coughing episodes and eased intercostal tenderness after three MLD treatments, with neither symptom present at follow-up.
The Dyspnea-12 Questionnaire showed a positive trend of improved breathing-related symptoms, with both patients answering 'none' to ten of the twelve questions at follow-up.
Both patients scored above the clinically significant threshold on the Revised Piper Fatigue Scale before treatment but no longer met this threshold after a course of MLD.
Small improvements were recorded in peak expiratory flow, blood oxygen levels, and sit-to-stand test scores in both patients over the treatment and review period.
Patient B experienced a transient asthma symptom exacerbation with increased coughing and phlegm two days after the second MLD treatment, which resolved within four days.
Both patients reported sleeping better after receiving MLD treatments.
After the follow-up review, Patient A no longer required blood pressure medication or pain medication for aching joints that had been needed for post-infection symptoms.
By the follow-up review, Patient B no longer needed to use her Ventolin inhaler at the end of the day, which had been her primary reason for seeking treatment.
Cardiopulmonary studies cited in the background show significantly lower peak VO2 among people with long COVID compared to asymptomatic subjects.

A large Brazilian cohort of hospitalised COVID-19 patients found that 71% had daily activity limitations six months post-discharge, with 6% rating them severe, alongside high rates of pain/discomfort, breathlessness, and anxiety/depression.
A prior case series using the Perrin Technique (a different lymphatic drainage approach) reported an average 50% reduction in fatigue-related states after about nine sessions.
In breast cancer-related lymphoedema, therapist-delivered MLD produced greater improvement in dyspnoea scores than a self-administered home treatment protocol.
The authors propose that high levels of inflammatory mediators and activated immune cells persisting in affected organs and tissues may underlie or contribute to long-COVID symptoms.
At the initial visit approximately 7 months post-COVID-19, 38.7% of participants met criteria for low neuropsychological test performance.
At the initial visit, 21.3% of participants met criteria for extremely low neuropsychological test performance.
At 6-month follow-up, most previously abnormal neuropsychological domains normalized, but language performance remained significantly below normative values.
Delayed memory performance showed a statistically significant improvement between the initial visit and 6-month follow-up.
Fatigue measures showed a statistically significant improvement between the initial visit and 6-month follow-up.
No individual participant showed a decline in neuropsychological test performance from initial visit to 6-month follow-up, though relatively few made significant clinical improvement.

In the authors' preliminary case series of 16 Long COVID patients, 12 sessions of acupuncture and moxibustion treatment produced significant improvement in fatigue that persisted through 4 weeks of follow-up, with no severe adverse events other than mild blisters from moxibustion.
Fatigue is reported as the most common post-COVID condition among more than fifty recognized Long COVID symptoms, affecting 58% of patients.
Long COVID fatigue occurs significantly more often in women and is commonly accompanied by stress, anxiety, depression, and cognitive impairment.
A previous study found that moxibustion was more effective than acupuncture in improving fatigue in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome, although both treatments improved fatigue symptoms.

Acupuncture has been reported as an effective and safe modality for cancer-related fatigue and chronic fatigue syndrome, acting through alleviation of neuroinflammatory response, modulation of immune responses, regulation of neuropeptides such as dopamine and β-endorphin, promotion of oligodendrocyte proliferation, and stimulation of nitric oxide production.
All patients with long COVID in this cohort had chronic epipharyngitis on endoscopic examination.
Significantly more patients presented with long COVID during July-August 2022 (the seventh COVID-19 wave) than in March-June 2022.
There were significantly more cases of SARS-CoV-2 infection reported in July 2022 compared to December 2021.
Most long COVID patients sought clinic evaluation within the first two weeks to one month after COVID-19 onset.
There was no significant difference in gender distribution between long COVID and non-long COVID chronic epipharyngitis patients.
Patients with long COVID were significantly younger than non-long COVID patients, largely because no patients in their 70s or 80s had long COVID.
Fatigue, cough, and brain fog were significantly more frequent symptoms among long COVID patients compared with non-long COVID patients.
Throat discomfort, postnasal drip, sputum, and IgA nephropathy were significantly more common among non-long COVID chronic epipharyngitis patients than among long COVID patients.
Symptoms attributable to autonomic disturbance were significantly more common among long COVID patients than among non-long COVID patients.
Direct symptoms due to epipharyngitis and immune-mediated secondary disease (focal-inflammation-related) were more common in non-long COVID than in long COVID patients.

Applying Hotta et al.'s three-pathology classification, long COVID patients more often had neuroendocrine symptoms, while non-long COVID patients more often had inflammation-mediated local and autoimmune-related symptoms.
Endoscopic severity scores of epipharyngeal findings (coloration, swelling, mucus/crust adhesion) were significantly higher in long COVID patients than in non-long COVID patients.
A significantly higher proportion of long COVID patients (80%) than non-long COVID patients (64%) had moderate to severe epipharyngeal endoscopic findings.
There was no significant difference in pain awareness or pain duration during the first endoscopic EAT session between long COVID and non-long COVID patients.
There was no significant difference in treatment drop-out rate or follow-up duration between long COVID and non-long COVID patients undergoing EAT.
Persistence of SARS-CoV-2 spike protein in the epipharynx for months after infection is proposed to drive recurring chronic inflammation, since the epipharyngeal mucosa is a major viral target.

EAT is hypothesized to improve long COVID symptoms via improved cerebral microcirculation from mucosal scraping/phlebotomy and via an autonomic nerve stimulation effect, though prolonged treatment may be needed to fully resolve autonomic neuropathy and brain dysfunction.
Long COVID patients had significantly lower maximal pulmonary oxygen uptake (V̇O2max) than healthy controls during a maximal cycle ergometer test.
Peak power output achieved during the exercise test was significantly lower in long COVID patients than in healthy controls.
Muscle deoxygenated heme responses measured by near-infrared spectroscopy during exercise, indicative of peripheral oxygen extraction, were lower in long COVID patients than controls.
Central cardiovascular parameters were not compromised in long COVID patients, suggesting the cardiovascular system does not explain their limited exercise capacity.

Skeletal muscle capillary density and capillary-to-fiber ratio were not significantly different between long COVID patients and healthy controls, though there was a trend toward a lower ratio in patients.
Long COVID patients had a higher percentage of highly fatigable glycolytic type IIx muscle fibers in the vastus lateralis compared to healthy controls.
Fatigue-resistant type I muscle fiber cross-sectional area was lower in female long COVID patients compared to female controls, a finding not seen in males.
Succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) activity correlated with V̇O2max in healthy controls but not in long COVID patients, with significantly different correlation coefficients between groups.

Mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) capacity in skeletal muscle was significantly lower in long COVID patients than controls and remained lower one day after induction of post-exertional malaise.

SDH activity, a marker of mitochondrial density, was not different between groups at baseline but was significantly reduced after induction of post-exertional malaise in long COVID patients, unlike in controls.

Key TCA cycle metabolites (glutamate, FAD+, alpha-ketoglutarate, and citric acid) were lower in the skeletal muscle of long COVID patients compared to controls, indicating a lower reliance on oxidative metabolism.
Skeletal muscle creatine concentrations were lower in long COVID patients, likely contributing to their lower oxidative phosphorylation capacity.
Lower S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) was observed in skeletal muscle of long COVID patients, possibly linking to reduced methylation and SAM cycle activity.

Glycolytic metabolites in venous blood were significantly higher, while pyruvate and other TCA cycle metabolites were lower, in long COVID patients compared to controls; blood glycolytic metabolites decreased one week after induction of post-exertional malaise.

The concentration of amyloid-containing (Thioflavin T-positive) deposits in skeletal muscle was greater in long COVID patients than controls at baseline and increased similarly in both groups after induction of post-exertional malaise.

Amyloid-containing deposits in skeletal muscle were located in the extracellular matrix next to capillaries, not inside capillaries or lymphatic vessels, arguing against the hypothesis that they cause local vessel blockage and tissue hypoxia.

A larger percentage of long COVID patients displayed small atrophic fibers and focal necrosis in skeletal muscle, which increased significantly after induction of post-exertional malaise, indicating exacerbated exercise-induced tissue damage.

Centralized nuclei, a sign of skeletal muscle regeneration/repair, were significantly more abundant in long COVID patients than controls, even before induction of post-exertional malaise, but did not further increase with PEM.

More long COVID patients had CD3+ T-cell infiltration in skeletal muscle than controls, and the normal exercise-induced accumulation of T-cells was blunted in patients experiencing post-exertional malaise.
CD68+ macrophage infiltration in skeletal muscle was higher in long COVID patients than in healthy controls.
Circulating mitochondrial DNA fragments in plasma, hypothesized as a damage-associated molecular pattern triggering inflammation, were not different between long COVID patients and controls.
Circulating cortisol concentrations were not different between long COVID patients and healthy controls, with and without adjustment for time since waking.

SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein was detected in skeletal muscle of almost all participants but was not more abundant in long COVID patients than healthy controls, and its concentration did not change after induction of post-exertional malaise, arguing against a viral persistence explanation for post-exertional malaise.
CD20+ B-cells were not abundantly present in skeletal muscle and did not differ between long COVID patients and controls, though they tended to be higher one day after exercise in both groups.

All long COVID patients developed post-exertional malaise after maximal exercise, with significantly increased self-reported fatigue severity persisting up to one week after exercise, alongside muscle pain and cognitive symptoms.
Women have approximately a three-fold higher risk of being diagnosed with long COVID compared to men.
Women with long COVID more frequently report persistent weakness, chest pain, altered smell and taste, palpitations, muscle pain, and neurological, gastrointestinal and rheumatologic symptoms.
Long COVID clinical features are shaped by immune function, endothelial dysfunction and sex hormones, contributing to systemic dysfunction.
Therapeutic strategies for long COVID under exploration include anticoagulation, immuno-modulators, focused rehabilitation programs, and selected pharmacological treatments in specific cases.
Two-sample Mendelian randomization found a strong, mostly significant positive causal association between genetic predisposition to COVID-19 and increased risk of pneumonia.

MR analysis showed a positive and causal association between genetic predisposition to COVID-19 and onset of airflow-blockage/respiratory diseases (bronchitis, emphysema, asthma, rhinitis), though IVW and robust IVW estimates were not statistically significant.

Mendelian randomization results for the causal association between genetic predisposition to COVID-19 and anxiety/depression were inconclusive, with some methods showing positive and others negative associations, none robustly consistent.

The causal association between genetic predisposition to COVID-19 and Parkinson's disease remained undetermined, as median/IVW-type methods suggested a positive association while MR-Egger-based methods suggested a negative association.
A strong positive causal association was found between genetic predisposition to COVID-19 and development of headache in long COVID.

All eleven MR methods indicated a strong, consistent positive causal association between genetic predisposition to COVID-19 and increased risk of heart failure, with ten of eleven methods reaching high statistical significance.

The causal association between genetic predisposition to COVID-19 and chest pain remained inconclusive, with some methods showing significant positive associations and MR-Egger-based methods showing negative, non-significant associations; the chest pain dataset itself was non-specific in etiology.

A strong positive association was found between genetic predisposition to COVID-19 and risk of developing chronic fatigue (tiredness/lethargy), though standard IVW and MR-Egger estimates alone were non-significant.
Female COVID-19 patients had a significantly higher proportion of Long COVID than male patients.
Smoking history was inversely associated with Long COVID risk in binary logistic regression, with never-smokers as reference.
History of allergy was positively associated with increased risk of Long COVID compared with no allergy history.
Presence of first symptoms at admission was inversely associated with Long COVID compared to patients without first symptoms, possibly reflecting Omicron's mild/asymptomatic pathogenicity.
COVID-19 vaccine inoculation doses were associated with Long COVID, with basic vaccination (≤2 doses) linked to higher risk than booster vaccination (>2 doses).
Overall questionnaire scores (assessing functional/daily-life difficulty) were significantly associated with Long COVID status.
Approximately one-fifth of COVID-19 patients developed Long COVID three months after discharge in this Omicron-infected cohort.
The most common first symptoms on admission among COVID-19 patients were fever, cough, and dry or itchy throat.
Among Long COVID patients, the most frequently reported persistent symptoms were fatigue, amnesia, insomnia, and excessive sweating.
Age, past medical history, and length of hospital stay were not significantly associated with Long COVID.
Patients with persistent long COVID symptoms at 24 months had a higher proportion of women compared to those without symptoms.
Patients with persistent long COVID at 24 months had a lower median height than those without symptoms.

No significant differences were found between patients with and without long COVID at 24 months in age, age at infection, BMI, maximum disease severity, newly diagnosed disease, vaccination status, reinfection, or pre-existing comorbidity.
Fatigue was the most common long COVID symptom reported at 24 months, affecting 25.6% of patients.
Amnesia was reported in 23.1% of patients at 24 months and its incidence increased over time compared to earlier timepoints.
Difficulty concentrating increased in incidence over time, being reported by 19.0% of patients at 24 months, higher than at earlier timepoints.
Constitutional and sensory symptoms such as cough, fever, sputum production, anosmia, and ageusia improved (decreased in frequency) over the course of the study.
The frequencies of arthralgia, alopecia, and paresthesia did not change significantly over the course of the study.
At 24 months, there was no significant difference in major neuropsychiatric long COVID symptoms between vaccinated and unvaccinated patients.
There was no significant difference in the frequency of major neuropsychiatric long COVID symptoms between vaccinated patients receiving fewer than three doses versus three or more doses.
Patients with persistent long COVID symptoms at 24 months had significantly higher PHQ-9 depression scores than those without symptoms.
Patients with persistent long COVID symptoms at 24 months had significantly higher GAD-7 anxiety scores than those without symptoms.
PHQ-9 and GAD-7 scores were initially elevated in patients with severe acute COVID-19 illness but improved to levels similar to the milder illness group by 12-month follow-up.
The median PCL-5-K PTSD score decreased from 5 at 12 months to 3 at 24 months, indicating a nonsignificant trend toward improvement.
Pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression EQ5D categories were the most affected quality-of-life domains at 24 months, impacting 32.2% of patients, more than mobility, self-care, and usual activities.

Trouble walking or ascending steps and challenges remembering or concentrating were significantly more common at 2 years in patients who also had other persistent long COVID symptoms compared to those without.
There was no significant difference in long COVID symptom frequency between patients based on acute illness disease severity groups.

COMPASS-31 autonomic symptom scores were significantly higher in long COVID patients with palpitations (Group A) and without palpitations (Group B) than in asymptomatic post-COVID patients (Group C), with the highest score in Group A.
A greater proportion of long COVID patients with palpitations (65.71%) and without palpitations (41.13%) reported quality-of-life decline compared to asymptomatic post-COVID patients.

Both symptomatic long COVID groups (with and without palpitations) showed significantly lower levels of multiple HRV time- and frequency-domain parameters compared with asymptomatic post-COVID patients.

SDNN, HRVIndex, LF, and TP were specifically lower in long COVID patients with palpitations (Group A) compared to both the non-palpitation symptomatic group (Group B) and the asymptomatic group (Group C).
Multivariate logistic regression identified HRVIndex as a significant independent predictor of palpitation symptoms in female long COVID patients.
PNN50 and the LF/HF ratio did not differ significantly between the palpitation, non-palpitation, and asymptomatic groups.
Accompanying symptom profiles (fatigue, cough, memory impairment vs. fatigue, cough, menstrual changes) did not differ significantly between long COVID patients with and without palpitations.
In the palpitation group (Group A), fatigue (61.43%), cough (35.71%), and memory impairment (27.14%) were the most commonly reported accompanying symptoms.
In the non-palpitation symptomatic group (Group B), fatigue (58.87%), cough (34.68%), and menstrual cycle changes (30.65%) were the most commonly reported symptoms.
Of 300 participants interviewed, 155 (52%) had a history of COVID-19 illness.
Among those with prior COVID-19, 54 (35%) had persistent symptoms lasting more than 12 weeks, classified as long COVID.
Muscle problems and fatigue were the most frequently reported long COVID symptoms, occurring in 14.7% of affected participants.
Breathing problems were reported in 12.6% of long COVID participants.
Cognitive issues were reported in 12.6% of long COVID participants.
Decreased appetite during the acute infection phase was associated with subsequent development of long COVID.
Confusion or disorientation during the acute infection phase was associated with subsequent development of long COVID.
The majority of long COVID participants (83.3%) reported moderate levels of perceived stress on the Perceived Stress Scale.
Moderate to severe levels of perceived stress were observed in 17.3% of long COVID participants.
A high level of positive mental well-being, as measured by the Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-being Scale, was observed among participants in this long COVID cohort.
Among people with COVID, having a pre-existing chronic overlapping pain condition (COPC) increased the risk of developing long COVID features by 47%.
Headache showed the largest risk increase among individual long COVID features associated with pre-existing COPCs in the COVID cohort.
Pre-existing COPCs increased the risk of the 'pain' long COVID feature category in the COVID cohort.
Cognitive symptoms had the smallest, though still significant, increased risk associated with pre-existing COPCs among long COVID features.
Abnormal breathing showed a smaller but significant increased risk associated with pre-existing COPCs among long COVID features.
Female sex was associated with a 22% higher risk of long COVID features compared with males in the COVID cohort.
Hospitalization due to acute COVID increased the risk of developing long COVID features by 39%.
In the influenza cohort, pre-existing COPCs increased the risk of long COVID-like features by 39%, a magnitude slightly smaller than in the COVID cohort.
In the noninfected cohort with only a routine healthcare encounter, pre-existing COPCs increased the risk of long COVID-like features by 57%, a magnitude larger than in the COVID cohort.
In a sensitivity analysis using a stricter long COVID definition (3+ diagnostic features), pre-existing COPCs still increased risk of long COVID by 68% among those with COVID.
5.2% of surveyed residents with a history of COVID-19 reported persistence of one or more long COVID symptoms at 30 days post-onset.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported long COVID symptom, occurring in 1.75% of respondents.
Hair loss was the second most commonly reported long COVID symptom, occurring in 1.41% of respondents.
Cough was the third most commonly reported long COVID symptom, occurring in 1.28% of respondents.
Higher BMI was associated with an increased risk of experiencing long COVID symptoms.
Severe illness during the acute phase of COVID-19 was associated with increased risk of long COVID symptoms.
Infection with certain COVID-19 variant strains, including Alpha, Delta, and Omicron, was associated with increased risk of long COVID symptoms.
The incidence rate of long COVID appeared to decrease with the dominance of the Omicron variant, suggesting a lower prevalence of long COVID in the Japanese population after the Omicron wave.
Fatigue as an early symptom of COVID-19 was significantly associated with increased odds of developing Long COVID-19.
Myalgia as an early symptom of COVID-19 was significantly associated with increased odds of developing Long COVID-19.
Headache as an early symptom of COVID-19 was significantly associated with increased odds of developing Long COVID-19.
Need for emergency care during acute COVID-19 was strongly associated with increased odds of developing Long COVID-19.
SARS-CoV-2 reinfection was significantly associated with increased odds of developing Long COVID-19.
Presence of previous diseases (comorbidities) was significantly associated with increased odds of developing Long COVID-19.
Respiratory disease at symptom onset was significantly associated with increased odds of developing Long COVID-19.
Brain fog after COVID-19 was significantly associated with increased odds of developing Long COVID-19.
Carriers of the A allele in the ACE2 rs2106806 polymorphism (dominant model: AA or GA vs. GG) had increased risk of Long COVID-19 susceptibility.
Carriers of the T allele in the ACE2 rs6629110 polymorphism (dominant model: TT or TC vs. CC) had increased risk of Long COVID-19 susceptibility.
Under a recessive model, the T allele of ACE2 rs6629110 (CC or TC vs. TT) was associated with increased risk of Long COVID-19 susceptibility.
Allele-based analysis showed the ACE2 rs2106806 A allele was associated with a roughly four-fold increase in Long COVID-19 susceptibility.
Allele-based analysis showed the ACE2 rs6629110 T allele was associated with an approximately 3.75-fold increase in Long COVID-19 susceptibility.
No association was found between ACE-2 genotypes (rs2106806, rs6629110) and clinical features among patients who had Long COVID-19 syndrome.
Among U.S. adults who had COVID, 31.1% developed long COVID, corresponding to 14.3% of all adults.
Four in five people (80%) who developed long COVID reported that their symptoms limited their ability to carry out day-to-day activities.
Among adults who had COVID, being assigned female sex at birth was associated with 1.76-fold greater odds of developing long COVID compared to males.
Sexual and gender minority (SGM) individuals had 1.39-fold greater odds of developing long COVID compared to heterosexual, cisgender individuals.
Having at least a four-year college degree was associated with 0.62-fold lower odds of developing long COVID.
Asian non-Hispanic individuals had 0.71-fold lower odds of developing long COVID relative to white non-Hispanic individuals.

In the simple model, Hispanic and multiracial/other individuals had the greatest risk of developing long COVID relative to white non-Hispanic individuals, though no specific odds ratio value is given in text.
Nearly half of transgender respondents who had COVID developed long COVID, and over 90% of those with long COVID reported activity limitations.
Averaged across race/ethnicity, long COVID prevalence formed a step-like gradient by sex and education: 17.9% in college-educated men versus 40.6% in women without a degree.
Men without a college degree (27.6%) and women with a degree (27.9%) had nearly identical long COVID prevalence, a pattern driven mainly by white respondents.

When two-way and three-way interaction terms were added to the model, the previously significant associations of Hispanic and multiracial/other ethnicity with long COVID became non-significant, while Black non-Hispanic ethnicity became significant.
Black and Hispanic women had significantly higher odds of developing long COVID than both non-Black/non-Hispanic individuals and Black/Hispanic men.
The protective effect of a college degree against long COVID appeared to hold only for white or straight/cisgender individuals.

Asian sexual and gender minorities without a college degree had considerably lower odds of long COVID, but those with a college degree had a very high odds ratio for long COVID (a reversal in the three-way interaction).
Multiracial/other sexual and gender minority individuals with a college degree had lower odds of developing long COVID.

Among people who had long COVID, females and sexual/gender minorities had greater odds of reporting activity limitations, while multiracial/other race was the only racial/ethnic group with significantly greater odds relative to white non-Hispanic individuals.
In the full interaction model, Hispanic females, college-educated females, and especially Asian sexual/gender minorities had greater odds of reporting activity limitations due to long COVID.
Despite having very high odds of developing long COVID, Asian sexual/gender minorities with a college degree had particularly low odds of reporting activity limitations due to long COVID.
Although women were considerably more likely than men to develop long COVID, among those who developed it, women were slightly less likely than men to report activity limitations.

Consistent with other studies disaggregating by race, the authors found fairly small Black/white disparities in long COVID prevalence, possibly reflecting confounding factors including survivorship bias.
Three out of four adults who tested positive for COVID-19 in the PAMPA cohort reported experiencing long COVID symptoms for at least three months.
A higher proportion of women than men who tested positive for COVID-19 reported long COVID.
Female sex remained independently associated with a higher likelihood of long COVID after full adjustment for demographic, behavioral, and clinical factors.

Family income, race/ethnicity, and occupational status were significantly associated with long COVID in the demographic-only model but lost significance after adjusting for behavioral and COVID-19-related factors.
Age was not significantly associated with long COVID.

Obesity was associated with a higher probability of long COVID than normal BMI in the behavioral/clinical model, but this association was no longer significant after adjusting for hospitalization and vaccination status.
Participants who were unvaccinated or had received one or two vaccine doses had a higher likelihood of long COVID compared to those with three or more doses, showing a dose-response relationship.
Participants hospitalized due to COVID-19 infection had a higher likelihood of developing long COVID than those not hospitalized.
Participants living with chronic conditions had a higher likelihood of developing long COVID than those without chronic conditions.
Smoking status, alcohol consumption, and physical activity were not significantly associated with overall long COVID in the multivariable model.

The most commonly reported persistent symptoms after COVID-19 infection were fatigue, neurological complications (memory/concentration problems, irritability, depression, anxiety), headaches, coughing, hair loss, and loss of smell and taste.
Female participants had a higher likelihood of experiencing fatigue, neurological complications, headaches, and hair loss than males.
Higher-income participants (more than four minimum wages) were less likely to experience neurological complications and hair loss than lower-income participants (up to one minimum wage).

Occupational status was associated with differing risks of loss of smell/taste and continuous cough; unemployed and employed-and-student participants had lower risk of smell/taste loss, while employed-and-student, retired, and 'other' status participants had higher risk of continuous cough, relative to those only employed.
Smoking was associated with an increased likelihood of headaches and loss of smell and taste compared to never smokers.
Obesity was associated with an increased likelihood of neurological complications compared to normal weight.

Occasional alcohol consumption (<1 day/week) was associated with a lower likelihood of neurological complications, and consumption of 1-2 days/week was associated with a lower likelihood of headaches.
Physical activity was associated with a lower likelihood of fatigue, neurological complications, coughing, and headaches.
Participants hospitalized due to COVID-19 had a higher likelihood of experiencing fatigue, neurological complications, coughing, and loss of smell and taste.
Participants with incomplete vaccination schedules had a higher probability of experiencing fatigue and headaches than those with complete vaccination schedules.
Chronic conditions were associated with a higher likelihood of fatigue, neurological complications, and headaches.
Race/ethnicity was not associated with long COVID symptom-specific outcomes.
Hospitalized COVID-19 patients had a significantly higher incidence of any post-COVID condition than hospitalized influenza patients within 90–180 days.
COVID-19 survivors had a significantly higher risk of abnormal breathing compared to influenza survivors 90–180 days post-hospitalization.
COVID-19 survivors had a significantly higher risk of abdominal symptoms compared to influenza survivors.
COVID-19 survivors had a significantly higher risk of fatigue compared to influenza survivors.
COVID-19 survivors had a significantly higher risk of cognitive symptoms compared to influenza survivors, the largest hazard ratio among individual symptoms examined.
COVID-19 survivors had a significantly higher risk of the composite outcome of all-cause ED visits, hospitalizations, and death compared with influenza survivors.
COVID-19 survivors had a significantly higher risk of all-cause ED visits compared to influenza survivors.
COVID-19 survivors had a significantly higher risk of all-cause hospitalization compared to influenza survivors.
COVID-19 survivors had a markedly higher risk of death during follow-up compared to influenza survivors.

Among vaccinated patients, the risk of post-acute sequelae following COVID-19 hospitalization compared to influenza was not significantly higher, suggesting a protective effect of vaccination against long COVID.
In the non-Caucasian subgroup, COVID-19 patients did not show a statistically significantly higher risk of post-acute sequelae compared with influenza patients, unlike most other subgroups.
Anxiety/depression was the most common post-COVID-19 condition observed among the 12 clinical features assessed in the composite outcome.

The review discusses IVIG as a candidate treatment for autonomic dysfunction associated with long COVID, to be evaluated in the RECOVER-AUTO randomized trial, while noting its role in long COVID treatment remains uncertain.

IVIG is noted to have established use in immune thrombocytopenic purpura, Kawasaki disease, chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, and certain infections such as influenza, HIV, and measles, providing background rationale for exploring its use in long COVID.
In the control group (breathing exercises only), total creatine levels significantly decreased in the right frontal gray matter after 3 months.
Left parietal mesial gray matter total creatine also significantly decreased in the control (breathing-exercise-only) group at 3-month follow-up.
Breathing exercises alone failed to elevate tissue creatine levels at any measured location except for a nonsignificant rise in left precentral white matter.
Creatine monohydrate supplementation (4 g/day) combined with breathing exercises increased tissue total creatine levels at all 14 measured muscle and brain locations after 3 months.
Vastus medialis muscle total creatine significantly increased in the creatine plus breathing exercise group at 3-month follow-up.
Thalamic total creatine significantly increased in the creatine plus breathing exercise group at 3-month follow-up.
Right frontal gray matter total creatine significantly increased in the creatine plus breathing exercise group, in contrast to a decrease at the same site in the control group.
Right precentral white matter total creatine significantly increased in the creatine plus breathing exercise group and was significantly greater than the control group.
Right paracentral gray matter total creatine significantly increased in the creatine plus breathing exercise group.
Left parietal mesial gray matter total creatine significantly increased in the creatine plus breathing exercise group, contrasting with a decline in this region in the control group.
Cohen's effect sizes for creatine increment across six significant muscle/brain locations ranged from 0.77 to 1.76, indicating large effects of combined creatine and breathing exercise treatment.
Two-way repeated-measures ANOVA showed the creatine plus breathing exercise group had significantly greater increases in brain creatine at four locations compared to breathing exercise alone.
Breathing difficulty and respiratory discomfort were reduced to zero in both the creatine plus breathing exercise group and the breathing-exercise-only group after 3 months.

Time to exhaustion on a treadmill test significantly improved in the creatine plus breathing exercise group but not in the breathing-exercise-only group.
There was a nonsignificant trend toward creatine plus breathing exercises being superior to breathing exercises alone in extending time to exhaustion.
No significant changes were found in any of the five MFI-20 fatigue sub-domains throughout the study in either group.

Compliance with the intervention regimen was high and did not differ significantly between the creatine plus breathing exercise group and the breathing-exercise-only group, and no participant reported adverse effects.
Low creatine levels are reported to characterize long-COVID, based on prior literature cited by the authors.
The VDR TaqI genotype showed a possible association with COVID-19 severity, and one patient with the homozygous TaqI genotype experienced severe symptoms.
The VDR ApaI genotype was not significantly associated with COVID-19 severity.
The VDR FokI genotype was not significantly associated with COVID-19 severity.

Patients with the heterozygous VDR ApaI genotype had a significantly higher risk of long-COVID fatigue and muscle pain lasting over 4 weeks compared with patients with wild-type or homozygous genotypes.
Patients with the wild-type VDR TaqI genotype showed a significantly higher risk of long-COVID fatigue and muscle pain compared with those with the heterozygous or homozygous genotype.

The VDR TaqI genotype was significantly associated with persistent shortness of breath after COVID-19, with homozygous genotype carriers more likely to have this symptom than wild-type or heterozygous carriers.
The VDR FokI genotype was not associated with any of the assessed long-COVID persistent symptoms.
The VDR ApaI variant was found to be in strong linkage disequilibrium with the TaqI variant among COVID-19 patients.
The VDR FokI variant did not show linkage disequilibrium with the other investigated VDR variants (ApaI, TaqI).
The VDR ApaI(C)-FokI(C)-TaqI(T) haplotype was the most common haplotype among COVID-19 patients, occurring at a frequency of 28.2%.
Patient age, BMI, and cardiovascular disease comorbidity were non-genetic factors significantly associated with COVID-19 symptom severity.

Long COVID syndrome is reported to occur in at least 10% of SARS-CoV-2 infections.
The worldwide prevalence of long COVID syndrome varies widely, from 1% in a Danish study to 35-77% in a German study.
Long COVID syndrome is associated with autonomic nervous system imbalances including orthostatic hypotension, neurocardiogenic syncope, and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS).

Reported prevalence of true myocarditis in acute COVID-19 varied widely between studies, with lymphocytic infiltration and myocyte necrosis seen in 14% of cases in one study, while another found viral particles in the heart in 59% of cases with clinical relevance in 41%.
Persistent myocardial inflammation, detected by cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, occurred in up to 60% of previously hospitalized COVID-19 patients.

SGLT2 inhibitor treatment (e.g., empagliflozin) was associated with reduced inflammatory markers including ferritin, interleukin-6, and C-reactive protein, along with reduced prothrombogenic risk via effects on vascular endothelium.
In the Austrian EMMY trial, SGLT2 inhibitor treatment favorably affected structural and functional cardiac remodeling after acute myocardial infarction but did not reduce systemic inflammation.
Dapagliflozin was reported to reduce lactate levels and maintain stable cytosolic pH, potentially preventing severe chronic COVID-19 course and reducing viral load and chronic inflammation.

In the DARE-19 trial, dapagliflozin was safely and effectively used in hospitalized COVID-19 patients with cardiometabolic risk factors, but showed no significant efficacy in the acute infection phase, and was well tolerated without increased risk of volume depletion, diabetic ketoacidosis, or acute kidney injury.

Decreased ACE2 expression accompanied by elevated pro-inflammatory chemokines and cytokines was observed in acute COVID-19 patients and in SARS-CoV-2-infected cardiomyocytes, contributing to multiorgan dysfunction.

By improving abnormal apelin-ACE2 signaling, SGLT2 inhibitors are proposed as a potential therapeutic approach to ameliorate cardiorenal dysfunction in acute COVID-19 and as a possible treatment option for long COVID syndrome.
In the COVID-OUT trial, early outpatient treatment with metformin for acute COVID-19 significantly reduced the subsequent risk of long COVID syndrome by 41.3% over a 10-month follow-up.
In the COVID-OUT trial, fluvoxamine and ivermectin did not show significant benefit in reducing long COVID syndrome risk.
Diabetes is associated with increased risk of long COVID syndrome, likely due to pancreatic ß-cell dysfunction and aggravated insulin resistance from peripheral tissue inflammation.

Predictors of non-recovery after hospital admission for COVID-19 within the first 6 months included two or more cardiovascular/metabolic comorbidities, middle age, female sex, and initially severe clinical course.
Pre-existing comorbidities such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, ischemic heart disease, or immunosuppression are associated with a higher risk of developing long COVID syndrome.
Previously hospitalized COVID-19 patients showed an excessive risk of major cardiovascular events and an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes after infection.
At 3 months after COVID-19 infection, 66.8% of participants reported ongoing symptoms.
At 12 months, 44.8% of participants were still experiencing long-COVID symptoms.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported symptom at every follow-up point, ranging from 53.1% to 33.1% prevalence.
Pain symptoms increased in relative prevalence over the 12-month follow-up, becoming more problematic after 6 months.
Respiratory/pulmonary-type symptoms decreased substantially after 3 months of follow-up.
Females and younger people were more likely to experience symptoms in the early stages of long COVID.
Participants with more comorbidities were more likely to experience symptoms in the later stages of long COVID.
Vaccination showed a statistically significant protective effect against long-COVID symptoms and was associated with faster recovery.
Long COVID may affect at least 10% of patients recovering from SARS-CoV-2 infection and is often associated with debilitating symptoms.
The respiratory and cardiovascular systems are proposed to be central to common long COVID symptoms such as fatigue, dyspnea, chest pain, cough, and exercise intolerance.
At 2-year follow-up after hospital discharge, 5.2% (47/899) of female COVID-19 survivors met the case definition for fatigue based on a CIS-fatigue score of 27 or higher.
Older age was independently associated with increased risk of post-COVID-19 fatigue in multivariable logistic regression.
Pre-existing cerebrovascular disease was a strong independent risk factor for post-COVID-19 fatigue in multivariable analysis.
Hypertension was more prevalent among female fatigue cases than controls in univariable comparison, but was not retained as an independent risk factor in the final multivariable model.
Diabetes was more prevalent among female fatigue cases than controls in univariable comparison, but was not retained as an independent risk factor in the final multivariable model.
Tracheitis was more prevalent among female fatigue cases than controls in univariable comparison, but was not retained as an independent risk factor in the final multivariable model.
Female fatigue cases had significantly higher COPD Assessment Test (CAT) scores, indicating greater overall symptom burden, than non-fatigue controls.
Female fatigue cases had significantly higher anxiety scores and prevalence of anxiety symptoms (HADS-A) than non-fatigue controls.
Female fatigue cases had significantly higher depression scores and prevalence of depression (HADS-D) than non-fatigue controls.
