Among fatigue cases, chest pain was highly correlated with chest tightness.
Among fatigue cases, expectoration was highly correlated with cough.
Acute COVID-19 disease severity during hospitalization was not significantly different between fatigue cases and controls.
Abnormal neonatal heart rate characteristics collected in the first month of life were strongly associated with autism spectrum disorder symptoms assessed at 12 months.
Abnormal negative thermal gradients (central-peripheral temperature differences) measured during the neonatal period were associated with later autism spectrum disorder symptoms at 12 months.
Birth gestational age was associated with 12-month autism spectrum disorder symptoms in very preterm infants.
Birth weight was associated with 12-month autism spectrum disorder symptoms in very preterm infants.
Half of the very preterm infant sample showed significant autism spectrum disorder concerns by 12 months of age.
Adults with ASD had significantly higher single-eye K-grading of the Kobayashi structure in the corneal Bowman's layer compared to typically developing controls.
Bilateral-eye summed K-grading was significantly higher in ASD adults (median 8) than in TDC (median 5).
The higher K-grading in ASD participants remained significant even after adjusting for within-subject inter-eye correlation, supporting robustness of the finding.
Optimal diagnostic cutoffs to differentiate ASD from TDC were a bilateral-eye summed K-grading >6 and a single-eye K-grading >3, based on Youden Index.
Within the ASD group, higher K-grading was associated with fewer visual sensation-seeking behaviors.
In the TDC group, higher K-grading was associated with low visual registration, i.e., a higher sensory threshold.
Both longstanding and early type 2 diabetes groups required higher rectal balloon pressure to elicit earliest sensation than controls, indicating rectal hyposensitivity.
No significant between-group differences were found in the rectal pressure required to reach an unpleasant threshold, nor in evoked potential latencies or amplitudes.
The proportion of definite or borderline cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy did not differ significantly between longstanding diabetes, early diabetes, and control groups.
No between-group differences were found for heart rate variability scores or sudomotor function across the three groups.
The incretin effect was significantly reduced in both longstanding and early diabetes groups compared to controls.
Gastrointestinal-mediated glucose disposal (GIGD) was significantly reduced in a stepwise fashion from controls to early diabetes to longstanding diabetes.
Paracetamol AUC, used as a proxy for gastric emptying, was significantly higher (faster emptying) in longstanding diabetes compared to controls.
Faster gastric emptying (paracetamol AUC) was negatively correlated with GIGD but positively correlated with fasting glucose, 2-hour glucose, and HbA1c.
Gastric emptying (paracetamol AUC) did not correlate with the incretin effect.
Gastric emptying (paracetamol AUC) did not correlate with rectal pressure for first sensation.
Rectal sensitivity (pressure for earliest sensation) was not correlated with the incretin effect.
Rectal sensitivity was significantly correlated with GIGD, such that reduced rectal sensitivity (higher pressure threshold) was associated with lower GIGD, independent of diabetes duration.
The incretin effect did not differ significantly between participants with lower versus higher rectal sensory thresholds.
GIGD showed a borderline, non-statistically-significant trend toward being lower in participants with reduced rectal sensitivity.
Neither the incretin effect nor GIGD were significantly associated with other neuropathy tests, including cardiovascular autonomic reflex tests, HRV, sudomotor function, or evoked potentials.
The incretin effect was inversely correlated with OGTT glucose values (strongest at 80 minutes) and with HbA1c, confirming worsening incretin effect with greater dysglycaemia.
GIGD was strongly inversely correlated with OGTT glucose values (strongest at 90 minutes) and with HbA1c.

Overall, the meta-analysis found only a small and statistically insignificant difference in autonomic nervous system responses to social stimuli between autistic and neurotypical individuals, with high heterogeneity across studies.

A nested moderator analysis found a significant difference between autistic and neurotypical individuals specifically in physiological measures reflecting parasympathetic nervous system activity during social stimuli.

A significant difference between autistic and neurotypical individuals was also found in physiological responses reflecting combined sympathetic and parasympathetic activity, but only during experimental tasks requiring active participation in social interaction.
College students with high autistic traits showed significantly lower accuracy in recognizing negative facial emotions than those with low autistic traits.

During recognition of negative emotions, the high autistic traits group exhibited significantly lower pupil diameter than the low autistic traits group, suggesting reduced autonomic nervous system arousal.
The high autistic traits group spent significantly less proportional fixation time on the eye area of emotional faces than the low autistic traits group.
The high autistic traits group spent significantly more proportional fixation time on the mouth area of emotional faces than the low autistic traits group.
The frail cohort (mFI≥2) had a significantly higher proportion of geriatric-age patients than the nonfrail cohort.
The frail cohort had a significantly higher body mass index than the nonfrail cohort.
The frail cohort had more comorbidities in 9 of 14 measured categories compared to the nonfrail cohort.
Frail patients undergoing long-segment spinal fusion experienced significantly more postoperative urinary tract infections than nonfrail patients.
Hospital length of stay did not significantly differ between frail and nonfrail cohorts after long-segment spinal fusion.
Rate of home discharge after surgery did not significantly differ between frail and nonfrail cohorts.
30-day readmission rates did not significantly differ between frail and nonfrail cohorts, though a trend toward higher readmission in the frail group was observed.
The frail cohort did not differ significantly from the nonfrail cohort in overall rate of postoperative complications after long-segment spinal fusion.
When presented with rhythmic stimuli with predictable timing, children with autism showed reduced phase locking of neuro-oscillations and altered neural indices of predictive processing.

In autistic children (ages 6-9), the CNV build-up of preparatory activity across four rhythmic cues appeared temporally smeared and did not significantly differ between the first and last cue, unlike the clear cue-proximity build-up seen in typically developing controls.
Reduced phase concentration and inter-trial phase coherence to rhythmic cues in the autistic group suggested that impaired neural entrainment contributed to reduced temporal precision in the CNV.

In adults with ASD (ages 16-28), the CNV was less modulated by target probability and less temporally locked to target onset compared to controls, being more distributed across the cue-target interval.

Lawson and colleagues found reduced modulation of pupil size in ASD compared to controls when comparing unpredictable versus predictable targets, indicating altered ANS-environment phasic relationships.
Individuals with ASD are impaired in their ability to adapt to changes in auditory tempo during cued tapping tasks, though one cited study did not find this effect.
In one study, synchrony of neuronal activity within a parent-autistic child dyad was found to correlate with the child's autism traits as measured by AQ scores.
Studies report altered autonomic activity in ASD, with both hypo- and hyper-regulation observed across pupillometry, cardiac, and electrodermal activity measures.
ASD individuals have difficulty using prior information to anticipate goal-directed actions from others.
ASD individuals display impaired joint action coordination in motor coordination tasks.
Infants at high risk for autism exhibit reduced eye contact, joint attention, and reciprocal imitation relative to typically developing infants.
In a retrospective cohort of 185 tonsillitis patients, only 61% (112) underwent glandular fever (EBV) screening, leaving 39% (73) untested.
Among the 112 tonsillitis patients screened for glandular fever, 35 (31.3%) tested positive for EBV infection and 77 (68.7%) tested negative.
Gender distribution was similar between EBV-positive (18 females, 17 males) and EBV-negative (53 females, 24 males) patients, suggesting no strong sex predilection for EBV positivity in this cohort.

EBV-positive tonsillitis patients had a mean age of approximately 21 years, with 85% (30/35) aged over 16 years, consistent with known peak incidence of glandular fever in adolescents and young adults.

Among 35 EBV-positive tonsillitis patients, 26 (74%) had deranged liver function tests, compared with only 4 of the EBV-negative patients, suggesting a strong association between acute EBV infection and hepatic involvement.

Applying the 31% EBV positivity rate observed among tested patients to the 73 untested tonsillitis patients, the authors estimated approximately 23 additional EBV-positive cases (12% of the total cohort) may have been missed due to lack of screening.

Epstein-Barr virus infection (glandular fever) can lead to complications including splenic rupture, encephalitis, autoimmune diseases, chronic fatigue, acute acalculous cholecystitis, lymphoma, and other malignancies.
A large meta-analysis pooling 54 studies and nearly 1.2 million patients found that 6.2% of COVID-19 patients experienced symptoms persisting beyond 4 weeks.
A retrospective Canadian cohort study found that mean hospital days per-person-year increased by 47-53% at 8 or more weeks after a COVID-19 infection.
A large-scale survey of over 3,000 PASC patients found substantial compromise to family life, caregiving ability, work, and finances.
In a survey of 3,762 PASC participants, a substantial proportion reported reduced work capacity or inability to work at 6 months post-diagnosis.

The protocol describes a planned two-phase RCT testing an 8-week Education and Self-Management Strategies group versus a Mindfulness Skills group (and later a no-treatment control) for confidence to self-manage PASC symptoms, quality of life, and healthcare utilization, using a sample size calculation based on a prior concussion study effect size of 0.59.
Serum IL-1β levels showed no significant differences across the four groups stratified by COVID-19/PASC status.
Serum IL-6 levels showed no significant differences across the four groups stratified by COVID-19/PASC status.
Serum TNFα levels showed no significant differences across the four groups stratified by COVID-19/PASC status.
Serum cortisol levels did not differ significantly between the four COVID-19/PASC groups and remained within the normal range in all groups.
IL-6 and TNFα serum levels were strongly positively correlated within individuals.
IL-1β and IL-6 serum levels were moderately positively correlated within individuals.
IL-1β and TNFα serum levels were weakly-to-moderately positively correlated within individuals.
No correlation was found between individual serum cortisol levels and cytokine (IL-1β, IL-6, TNFα) concentrations.
Participants with comorbid bronchial asthma had higher cytokine levels than other participants, suggesting comorbidities may confound cytokine-based PASC biomarker studies.
Among PASC patients, the most commonly reported symptoms were concentration deficits, fatigue and word-finding difficulties.
12.44% of Mexican adults ≥20 years reported at least one persistent COVID-19 symptom lasting ≥1 month, meeting the CDC definition of PASC.

Using the NICE definition (≥1 persistent symptom ≥3 months), PASC prevalence was 4.67% overall, 5.51% among SARS-CoV-2 seropositive adults, and 21.21% among individuals with previously diagnosed COVID-19.

Using a symptom-severity PASC score ≥12 points, prevalence was 1.91% overall, 2.02% among seropositive adults, and 8.68% among individuals with previously diagnosed COVID-19, indicating a more severe PASC phenotype.
Among individuals meeting the PASC-CDC definition, 28.6% reported symptoms persisting until the date of interview (i.e., long-term persistence), while smaller proportions reported shorter durations.

14.06% of individuals meeting the PASC-NICE definition reported incapacitating symptoms (inability to perform self-care) compared to 7.13% of those with persistent symptoms not meeting PASC-NICE criteria.

The ten most frequently reported persistent symptoms among SARS-CoV-2 seropositive adults were fatigue, musculoskeletal pain, headache, cough, loss of smell or taste, fever, post-exertional malaise, brain fog, anxiety, and chest pain.
Crude PASC-CDC prevalence among seropositive adults was higher in males (14.12%) than females (10.50%), with differing top symptom rankings by sex.
In adjusted regression models, male sex was independently associated with a lower probability of PASC-NICE.
Having at least one SARS-CoV-2 reinfection was associated with a higher probability of PASC-NICE.
Infection during periods of Omicron variant predominance was associated with a lower probability of PASC-NICE compared to infection during periods of other variant predominance.
Moderate to severe depressive symptoms (CES-D) were associated with higher probability of PASC-NICE.
Living in states with higher sociodemographic inequality (highest DISLI quartile) was associated with higher probability of PASC-NICE compared to the lowest quartile.

COVID-19 vaccination (≥1 dose) was associated with a lower probability of severe PASC (PASC score ≥12), with a similar protective effect observed with increasing number of doses irrespective of vaccine platform.
Moderate to severe depressive symptoms were associated with higher risk of incapacitating PASC symptoms.
Age 50-59 years was associated with higher risk of incapacitating PASC symptoms compared to younger individuals.
Having had at least one SARS-CoV-2 reinfection was associated with higher risk of incapacitating PASC symptoms.
Infection during periods of Omicron variant predominance was associated with lower risk of incapacitating PASC symptoms.
A PASC score ≥12 points was the most significant predictor of incapacitating PASC symptoms after adjustment.

Hierarchical cluster analysis identified four distinct PASC symptom phenotypes: Cluster 1 (musculoskeletal pain and cough), Cluster 2 (fatigue, headache, breathlessness), Cluster 3 (dysgeusia, anosmia, fatigue), and Cluster 4 (fatigue, headache, musculoskeletal pain, brain fog, sleep disorders), with cluster 2 being the most common phenotype.

PASC-NICE prevalence declined across successive years of infection, from 25.82% in cases infected in 2020 to 21.96% in 2021 and 17.60% in 2022, consistent with the shift toward Omicron predominance and increasing vaccination coverage.

Individuals with PASC-NICE had significantly higher rates of cardiometabolic comorbidities including diabetes, hypertension, myocardial infarction, chronic angina, and heart failure compared to those without PASC.
Active prefrontal tDCS did not produce a significantly greater reduction in fatigue (Fatigue Impact Scale total score) than sham tDCS after four weeks of treatment.
Within-group analysis showed a significant reduction in fatigue severity only in the sham tDCS group, not in the active tDCS group.
At one-month follow-up, fatigue continued to improve in both groups but remained non-significantly different between active and sham tDCS.
Both active and sham tDCS groups showed similar reductions in overall PASC symptom severity (A-PASC score) at week four, with no between-group difference.
Anxiety (GAD-7) and depressive (PHQ-9) symptom scores declined similarly in both active and sham tDCS groups with no significant between-group difference.
Quality of life as measured by AQoL-6D showed no difference between active and sham tDCS groups during the study and follow-up, except an incidental difference in the senses dimension at follow-up.
Attention, working memory, and psychomotor tempo (assessed by Digit Span and DSST) were comparable between active and sham tDCS groups at all post-baseline visits.
Mild to moderate side effects (burning or tingling sensations) occurred at similar rates in active and sham tDCS groups, decreasing over the trial and resolving completely by one-month follow-up.
Bayesian analysis of the primary fatigue outcome provided moderate-to-strong evidence favoring the null hypothesis over a benefit of active tDCS.
Common PASC predisposing comorbidities did not significantly affect tDCS treatment outcomes in this cohort.

In a cohort of 43 patients evaluated 3 months after resolution of COVID-19, somatotropic axis deficits were found in 46.5% of patients.
In the same 43-patient post-COVID cohort, corticotrophic (ACTH) axis deficits were observed in 16.2% of patients.
Hypogonadism was reported in 9.3% of the 43 patients assessed 3 months after COVID-19 resolution.
Hyperprolactinemia was reported in 4.6% of the 43 patients assessed 3 months after COVID-19 resolution.
In a cohort of 61 SARS-CoV survivors, Leow et al. reported corticotropin deficiency in 39.4% of patients, concluding a likely secondary hypophysitis due to SARS-CoV that persisted post-infection.
Postmortem immunostaining in SARS-CoV victims showed decreased staining for corticotrope, somatotrope, and thyrotrope pituitary cell populations.
Anti-pituitary and anti-hypothalamic antibodies were found in 75% of COVID-19 patients with corticotropin deficiencies, suggesting an autoimmune origin for the hypophysitis.
In a large global registry of hospitalized COVID-19 patients (HOPE registry), hyponatremia was identified in 20.5% of cases and was associated with increased mortality and sepsis.
In the same HOPE registry, hypernatremia was identified in 3.7% of hospitalized COVID-19 cases and was associated with increased mortality and sepsis.
ACE2 receptor is expressed in the hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus, making this region susceptible to SARS-CoV-2 entry.
Postmortem examinations identified the presence of the SARS-CoV-2 genome in the hypothalamus, along with degenerated and edematous neurons.
SARS-CoV-2 was isolated in apoplexic pituitary tissue several months after infection, providing the first histological evidence of the virus at the pituitary level.

A literature review found the prevalence of adrenal insufficiency among COVID-19 patients ranged widely from 3.1% to 64.3%, with most studies lacking data to distinguish primary from secondary insufficiency.
A meta-analysis by Ospina et al. concluded that a normal Synacthen Test (at 1µg or 250µg dose) does not exclude a diagnosis of corticotropin deficiency in a clinically suggestive context.
Al Kuraishy et al. studied the gonadotropic axis specifically in Long COVID-19 patients with sexual disorders, reporting findings consistent with central gonadal axis inhibition.
Facondo et al. reported a case of Post COVID-19 syndrome in which the gonadotropic deficit mechanism appeared to be of hypothalamic rather than pituitary origin.
Nearly 40% of hypophysitis cases, including those related to COVID-19, are associated with moderate hyperprolactinemia attributed to pituitary stalk thickening.

A literature review by Ach et al. found only five cases of hypophysitis and three cases of pituitary apoplexy reported after COVID-19 vaccination, suggesting vaccination is an unlikely major contributor to hypopituitarism related to COVID-19.

A proposed mechanism suggests that SARS-CoV-2 exhibits molecular mimicry with ACTH, such that antibodies produced against the virus cross-react with host ACTH, contributing to relative ACTH and cortisol deficiency.

The 'Giustina Effect' describes functional inhibition of GH secretion caused by glucocorticoid deficiency, which is reversible with hydrocortisone replacement therapy, helping explain concurrent somatotrope and corticotrope impairment in post-COVID patients.

In a general (non-COVID) cohort of 33 patients with pituitary apoplexy (55% men, mean age 46 years), only 9% required acute pituitary surgery, and during a mean follow-up of 7.6±4.3 years none of the hormonal deficiencies regressed, while three patients died of unrelated causes.
Following the 4-week HRV biofeedback intervention, participants showed a statistically significant reduction (improvement) in the C19YRS-m symptom severity score.
Functional disability score on the C19YRS-m significantly improved (decreased) after the HRV-B intervention.
Overall health perception score on the C19YRS-m significantly improved (increased) after HRV-B intervention.
The total 'other' symptoms score on the C19YRS-m significantly improved after HRV-B intervention.

COMPASS-31 autonomic symptom burden score (covering orthostatic intolerance, vasomotor, secretomotor, GI, bladder and pupillomotor domains) significantly decreased after the 4-week HRV-B intervention.

WHODAS disability score significantly decreased after HRV-B intervention, indicating reduced disability across cognition, mobility, self-care, getting along, life activities and participation domains.
EQ-5D-5L quality of life global health score significantly improved after the HRV-B intervention.

Fitbit-derived RMSSD, a heart rate variability measure reflecting parasympathetic activity, significantly increased between the pre-HRV-B and post-HRV-B phases, though the effect size was smaller than for the clinical outcome measures.

There was a 92% compliance rate with the twice-daily 10-minute HRV biofeedback breathing sessions, with 720 sessions completed over the 4-week intervention period, supporting feasibility of home-based delivery.
Participants reported qualitatively that they appreciated the HRV-B technology, found it easy to use, and felt empowered by its effect on their Long Covid symptoms.
Estimates of the prevalence of dysautonomia in Long Covid range widely from 2.5% to 67% across cited studies.

An abnormal NASA Lean Test (heart rate increase ≥30 bpm or ≥120 bpm, or blood pressure decrease of ≥20 mmHg systolic/≥10 mmHg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing) was used as an inclusion criterion and objective marker of orthostatic cardiovascular instability/dysautonomia in this Long Covid cohort.
Neuro-PASC patients commonly reported fatigue (94.9%), brain fog (89.7%), and insomnia (74.4%).
Insomnia prevalence increased from only 2% before COVID-19 to approximately 75% at the time of the Neuro-COVID-19 clinic visit.
Half of Neuro-PASC patients had actigraphy-measured sleep efficiency ≤85%, compared to only 7% of matched healthy controls.
Neuro-PASC patients had significantly longer actigraphy-measured sleep latency compared to age- and sex-matched healthy controls.
Neuro-PASC patients had a significantly later sleep midpoint (delayed sleep timing) compared to matched healthy controls.
WASO, number of awakenings, and total sleep time did not significantly differ between Neuro-PASC patients and healthy controls.
Neuro-PASC patients performed significantly worse than the US normative population on a validated task of attention on the NIH Toolbox.
There was only a nonsignificant trend toward worse executive function performance in Neuro-PASC patients compared to normative population.

Neuro-PASC patients reported significantly worse quality of life across all PROMIS domains examined (cognition, fatigue, sleep disturbance, anxiety, depression) compared to the normative US population.
35% of Neuro-PASC patients had an Epworth Sleepiness Scale score ≥10, the threshold for moderate-to-severe daytime sleepiness.
The median STOP-BANG score of Neuro-PASC patients was 2, indicating low risk for obstructive sleep apnea in the cohort.
The microMCTQ indicated Neuro-PASC patients had a mid-sleep time on free days within the normal chronotype range.

Lower NIH Toolbox attention performance was associated with lower actigraphy sleep efficiency, and showed a near-significant trend with longer sleep latency, after adjusting for age and hospitalization history.

Lower processing speed on the NIH Toolbox was associated with lower sleep efficiency, longer sleep latency, more wakefulness after sleep onset, and more awakenings, after adjustment for age and hospitalization history.

Lower power law exponent from detrended fluctuation analysis (indicating more irregular ultradian activity rhythms) was associated with worse processing speed and, trend-level, worse attention performance.

Greater self-reported cognitive symptoms correlated with greater self-reported fatigue and depression, and a near-significant correlation with anxiety, but showed no correlation with self-reported sleep disturbance.
There were no significant associations between objective actigraphy-measured sleep metrics and any of the self-reported PROMIS measures.

PASC patients, regardless of ICU support type, showed higher rates of dysfunctional breathing patterns during cardiopulmonary exercise testing compared to controls.

PASC patients exhibited reduced oxygen uptake during cardiopulmonary exercise testing compared to controls, regardless of prior IMV need.

After adjusting for age, sex, ethnicity and BMI, long COVID cases had lower peak VO2 and lower extrapolated VO2max than healthy controls.
OUES was lower in long COVID cases compared with healthy controls after confounder adjustment.
Anaerobic threshold was lower in long COVID cases than controls, consistent with a peripheral limitation to exercise.
O2 pulse was lower in long COVID cases than controls, suggesting impaired stroke volume augmentation or peripheral oxygen extraction.
VE/VCO2 slope was higher (worse ventilatory efficiency) in long COVID cases than controls.
Long COVID cases reported higher Borg CR10 breathlessness and leg fatigue scores at exercise termination than healthy controls.
FEV1 and FVC (percent predicted and Z-scores) were lower in long COVID cases than controls, though means remained within normal ranges.

Abnormal LV relaxation (e') was observed in 19-25% of long COVID individuals, higher than anticipated, though no participant met formal diastolic dysfunction criteria and no systolic/diastolic dysfunction was found overall.

The time constant for recovery of muscle VO2 (an inverse marker of skeletal muscle oxidative capacity) was longer in long COVID cases than controls, indicating impaired mitochondrial oxidative function, while resting muscle VO2 was similar between groups.
Time to 95% peak hyperemia and change in tissue saturation index during exercise did not differ between long COVID cases and controls, suggesting normal microvascular/endothelial reactivity.

Knee flexor strength was below normal limits in 62% of long COVID cases, more affected than knee extensor (15%) or hand-grip strength (7%), possibly reflecting lower-limb detraining or reduced lean mass.
Heart rate recovery at 2 minutes post-exercise was less in long COVID cases than controls, despite cases achieving a lower peak heart rate, indicating autonomic dysfunction.

At least one resting HRV parameter fell outside normative ranges in 39% of long COVID cases, with 39% below normal limits for the LF variable and 18% below normal for RMSSD and HF, consistent with prior long COVID HRV studies.

On lying-to-standing testing, 2 (7%) of long COVID participants met criteria for POTS (heart rate increase >30 bpm on standing), and a further seven showed exaggerated heart rate increases (>20 bpm) suggestive of subclinical autonomic abnormality.
One long COVID individual met criteria for orthostatic hypotension (BP drop >20 mmHg on standing).
Objectively measured (actigraphy) sedentary time and sleep time were greater in long COVID cases than controls, though total activity time and average activity counts per minute did not differ.
20% of long COVID participants had hemoglobin levels below normal cutoffs, consistent with anemia contributing to exercise intolerance in a subset of patients.

In mediation analysis, adjusting for muscle oxidative capacity (time constant) attenuated the difference in extrapolated VO2max between cases and controls from -2.9 to -1.1, indicating partial mediation by skeletal muscle mitochondrial dysfunction.

Adjusting for HRR at 2 minutes partially attenuated the group difference in extrapolated VO2max, and also partially mediated OUES differences, implicating autonomic dysfunction as a partial contributor to reduced exercise capacity.

No single physiological system deficit (skeletal muscle, lung, or autonomic) fully explained the severely impaired exercise performance in long COVID; instead, exercise intolerance appears to arise from an accumulation of multisystem, often subclinical, dysfunction.

Focus group participants reported that the Energy Management Education (EME) program significantly improved their understanding of fatigue and equipped them with personal strategies for managing it, with some experiencing fewer energy crashes and re-engagement in valued activities.
At the two-month follow-up, participants reported having maintained newly learned energy management strategies and established new daily routines.

Participants and therapists both identified that cognitive fatigue and the cognitive aspects of daily activities were insufficiently addressed within the EME program and recommended greater focus on this domain.
The discussion cites prior literature reporting that cognitive impairment is among the most common and debilitating symptoms of post-COVID-19 syndrome, with an estimated prevalence of 22%.
The discussion notes that fatigue and cognitive impairment appear to be distinct post-COVID-19 symptoms, as only about 5% of patients experience both conditions concurrently, citing prior literature.

The prevalence of long COVID was lower among vaccinated adults (21.6%) compared to non-vaccinated adults (25.6%), a 4.0 percentage point difference.

Hierarchical cluster analysis of 24 long COVID symptoms at 3 months post-diagnosis identified five distinct symptom clusters in 935 Japanese patients.
Cluster 1 (n=54), defined by numerous symptoms across multiple organs, had a higher proportion of older patients with severe acute COVID-19.
Cluster 1 patients had higher lactate dehydrogenase levels at hospital admission compared with the other clusters.
Cluster 1 patients had higher C-reactive protein levels at hospital admission compared with other clusters.
Cluster 1 patients had higher haemoglobin A1c levels at admission compared with the other clusters.
Cluster 1 consistently had poorer quality-of-life scores across all QOL measures at 3 months compared with other clusters.
Using GEE analysis with cluster 2 as reference, clusters 1 and 4 had significantly worse QOL scores than cluster 2 at all time points (3, 6 and 12 months).

Cluster 2 (n=546), comprising patients with no or minor long COVID symptoms, showed no characteristic association with age, sex, acute severity, smoking history or comorbidities, and had higher QOL scores than other clusters.
Cluster 3 (n=76), defined by taste and olfactory disorders, had a higher proportion of young women with mild acute COVID-19 severity.
Cluster 3 patients showed mild acute severity with low white cell count, LDH and CRP, and high albumin at admission, consistent with a milder acute course.
Cluster 3 (taste/olfactory disorder phenotype) had QOL scores similar to cluster 2 and did not differ significantly from cluster 2 at any time point.

Cluster 4 (n=207) was characterized by fatigue, psychoneurotic symptoms (alopecia, headache, poor concentration, sleep disorder) and dyspnoea with low prevalence of cough/sputum, and had a high proportion of middle-aged patients.
Cluster 4 had lower mental-component QOL scores at 3 months and, along with cluster 1, remained significantly worse than cluster 2 across all follow-up time points.

Cluster 5, characterized by fatigue and dyspnoea with a high prevalence of cough and sputum, showed high white cell count and CRP and high frequency of ground-glass opacities/consolidation on CT in the acute phase, indicating a pure respiratory phenotype.
Cluster 5 had significantly worse EQ-5D-5L, SF-8 PCS and HADS-A scores than cluster 2 at all time points.

In cluster 5, EQ-5D-5L Visual Analogue Scale and SF-8 MCS scores worsened at 12 months compared with 6 months, coinciding with an increased prevalence of fatigue and dyspnoea and a higher background prevalence of COPD, an opposite trend to other clusters which generally improved over time.
The prevalence of long COVID symptoms decreased over time (3 to 12 months) within each cluster, but the characteristic symptom composition that defined each cluster was maintained at 6 and 12 months.
Across all five clusters, QOL scores tended to remain similar or improve over the 12-month follow-up period.
Among 935 long COVID patients, the most common symptoms at 3 months were fatigue, dyspnoea, muscle weakness, alopecia and poor concentration.
No significant association was observed between the epidemic wave (viral variant sub-lineage) and cluster assignment in this cohort, which covered only historical SARS-CoV-2 variants.

In a related analysis of patients from this cohort, COVID-19 vaccination did not appear to have a clinically important effect on long COVID symptoms, though notably no patients in this study were vaccinated at the time of COVID-19 onset since vaccination had not yet started in Japan.

Living in polluted areas was significantly associated with increased risk of long COVID in children after COVID-19 pneumonia.

Long COVID patients saw an average of 5.92 different health care providers seeking treatment for their symptoms.

Interest in long COVID research findings (60.5%) and willingness to participate in research (47.5%) varied by COVID vaccination status.

The hypoxic ventilatory response, a measure of carotid chemoreflex sensitivity, was substantially higher in long COVID patients than in controls.
During exercise, the VE/VCO2 slope and nadir, indicating poorer ventilatory/breathing efficiency, were higher in long COVID participants than controls.
A high proportion of long COVID patients had abnormally elevated VE/VCO2 slopes compared to controls, using both normal-range and heart-failure prognostic thresholds.
Carotid chemoreflex sensitivity (HVR) correlated with poorer breathing efficiency during exercise, measured by the VE/VCO2 slope and nadir.
Resting end-tidal CO2 was lower in long COVID patients than controls, consistent with resting hyperventilation.
Resting VE/VCO2 ratio was higher in long COVID patients, indicating resting hyperventilation despite similar minute ventilation.
Resting inspiratory flow (VT/Ti), a surrogate for neural inspiratory drive, was higher in long COVID patients than controls.
Peak oxygen consumption during exercise was lower in long COVID patients compared to controls.
The heart rate response relative to %VO2 peak was blunted in long COVID patients, suggesting some degree of chronotropic incompetence.
Peak oxygen pulse was lower in long COVID patients, indicating a cardiovascular limitation to exercise.
Heart rate recovery after exercise was similar between long COVID patients and controls, suggesting intact parasympathetic engagement post-exercise.
There was no significant orthostatic intolerance (excessive BP fall) detected via sit-to-stand testing in either long COVID or control groups.
The rise in heart rate upon standing was greater in the control group than in the long COVID group.
Long COVID participants reported multiple persistent symptoms, most commonly dyspnoea (rest and exertion), extreme fatigue, brain fog, and chest pain.
Unlike the ventilatory response, the heart rate and blood pressure responses to hypoxic challenge did not differ between long COVID and control groups.
The VE/VCO2 ratio at both peak exercise and anaerobic threshold was higher in long COVID patients compared to controls, and this relationship was not explained by blood pressure differences.
Volume of expired CO2 at peak exercise was lower in long COVID patients versus controls, while minute ventilation, tidal volume, and breathing frequency at peak were similar.

The authors propose that SARS-CoV-2 disrupts the carotid body's local renin-angiotensin system, shifting the balance toward higher ACE1 relative to ACE2 expression and increased angiotensin II receptor stimulation, which could drive chemoreceptor hyperactivity.

The authors propose P2X3 receptor antagonism (e.g. gefapixant, already shown effective for chronic cough) as a potential future treatment target to reduce carotid body hyperreflexia in long COVID, based on prior animal work in hypertension and heart failure models.

A cross-sectional study of American adults found significantly higher suicidal ideation/behavior scores in individuals with a prior COVID-19 diagnosis one year after infection compared to those without, despite similar rates of diagnosed depression and anxiety.
In a retrospective analysis of electronic health records of 153,848 COVID-19 survivors, suicidal ideation risk one year after infection was 46% higher than in unaffected controls.
Markedly elevated IL-1β, part of the cytokine storm in COVID-19, has been linked to increased suicide risk.
Markedly elevated IL-6, part of the cytokine storm in COVID-19, has been linked to increased suicide risk.
Markedly elevated TNF-α, part of the cytokine storm in COVID-19, has been linked to increased suicide risk.

Widespread ACE2 expression, the cellular entry receptor for SARS-CoV-2, may enable direct infection of multiple tissues including the brain, contributing to dysregulated peripheral inflammation and neurological complications.

A European cross-sectional study found that long-COVID-19 patients, defined by fatigue, muscle weakness, pain, headache, respiratory/cognitive impairment, paresthesia, and anosmia four months post-hospitalization, had increased risk of psychiatric disorders, new-onset psychiatric disorders, and suicidal ideation development.
The overall one-year suicidal ideation rate in the general European population has been documented at 11%, used as the expected baseline for the healthy control cohort in this study.
Circulating neurofilament light chain (NFL) has been proposed as a marker of long-COVID-19-associated brain injury and a potential etiological factor for suicidal ideation/behavior.
Circulating glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) has been proposed as a marker of long-COVID-19-associated brain injury and a potential etiological factor for suicidal ideation/behavior.

Long COVID participants had significantly lower whole-lung 129Xe RBC/Mem ratio compared with COVID-negative controls.
Long COVID participants had significantly higher (worse) SGRQ scores compared with both COVID-negative and fully recovered participants.

K-means cluster analysis of four 129Xe MRI gas-exchange/ventilation metrics identified four as the optimal number of long COVID phenotypic clusters, validated by Davies-Bouldin index, Dunn's index and silhouette width, with representation from all three sites.

Cluster 1 long COVID participants had normal 129Xe MRI metrics but a mildly increased RV/TLC ratio compared with COVID-negative participants, indicating air trapping, and were the youngest group with normal spirometry and no CT parenchymal abnormalities.
Cluster 2 was characterised by isolated low RBC/Mem with mildly reduced DLCO, normal spirometry/lung volumes, and no CT parenchymal abnormalities, and was the oldest cluster.

Cluster 3 was characterised by mildly elevated 129Xe membrane uptake (Mem/Gas) with preserved RBC/Mem, minimal CT abnormalities and normal PFTs, potentially reflecting residual interstitial inflammation or oedema.

Cluster 4 (~10% of long COVID participants) showed markedly elevated 129Xe membrane uptake with concomitantly low RBC/Mem, restrictive pattern on PFTs, high BMI, and the greatest CT abnormalities including GGOs in all members, and the worst SGRQ scores.
Dyspnoea and fatigue were the most commonly reported persistent symptoms among all long COVID participants and were common across all four clusters.

The proportion of participants hospitalised during acute COVID-19 infection differed significantly across the four imaging-derived clusters, with Cluster 4 having the greatest proportion hospitalised and longest hospital stays.
CT ground-glass opacities, reticulation and consolidation were significantly more prevalent across clusters, with all Cluster 4 participants who underwent CT showing ground-glass opacities.
SGRQ Activity score differed significantly across clusters, with lowest scores in Cluster 1 and highest (worst) scores in Cluster 4.
Despite distinct imaging phenotypes, the occurrence of self-reported persistent symptoms did not differ significantly across the four MRI-defined clusters.

129Xe ventilation defect percent did not strongly differentiate clusters, being only mildly elevated in Cluster 2, suggesting airway/ventilation abnormalities were a minor driver of long COVID pathophysiology compared with gas exchange abnormalities.
The median number of comorbidities per participant differed significantly across clusters, with Cluster 3 and Cluster 4 trending toward the most comorbidities compared with Cluster 1.
Pulmonary rehabilitation had a significant positive effect on reducing dyspnea in Long COVID patients.
Pulmonary rehabilitation significantly improved physical function in Long COVID patients.
Pulmonary rehabilitation significantly improved global and physical-domain quality of life in Long COVID patients.
Pulmonary rehabilitation significantly reduced anxiety symptoms in Long COVID patients.
Pulmonary rehabilitation significantly reduced depression symptoms in Long COVID patients.
Pulmonary rehabilitation did not have a significant effect on fatigue in Long COVID patients.

Age and study design were identified as potential moderators of pulmonary rehabilitation treatment effects in Long COVID.

A patient with persistent fatigue, dyspnea, and low-grade fever after SARS-CoV-2 infection was diagnosed with long COVID via telemedicine visits, but was later found to have Graves' disease causing thyrotoxicosis.
The patient's serum TSH was markedly suppressed, consistent with thyrotoxicosis rather than long COVID.
Free T3 was markedly elevated, confirming thyrotoxicosis.
Free T4 was elevated, confirming thyrotoxicosis.
TSH receptor antibody (TRAb) was elevated above the reference range, supporting a diagnosis of Graves' disease.
Anti-thyroglobulin antibody was markedly elevated, supporting an autoimmune thyroid process.
Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody was markedly elevated, supporting an autoimmune thyroid process.
Thyroid uptake of technetium-99m pertechnetate was markedly increased, consistent with Graves' disease rather than thyroiditis.
Treatment with oral thiamazole normalized thyroid hormone levels and resolved the patient's fatigue, low-grade fever, and dyspnea, and no relapse occurred after 1 year of tapering therapy.
Levels of multiple cytokines, including interleukin-6, are reported to increase after SARS-CoV-2 infection, which may contribute to subsequent Graves' disease development.

TSH receptor (TSHR) mRNA expression was reported to be upregulated in leukocytes of SARS-CoV-2-infected patients compared to healthy controls, suggesting a mechanistic link to post-COVID Graves' disease.
It has been reported that Graves' disease may be more likely to develop after SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Low-grade fever and tachycardia are common in thyrotoxicosis/hyperthyroidism but are rare or absent in long COVID, making these vital signs useful clues for distinguishing the two conditions in telemedicine visits.

Delayed diagnosis of Graves' disease increases the risk of thyroid storm, which carries approximately 10.7% mortality, and nearly half of thyroid storm cases occur within a year of, or before, GD diagnosis.

The most frequently reported Long COVID symptoms were weight loss (31.6%), inappetence (26.3%), chronic cough (21.1%), fatigue (21.1%), and sleep disturbances, wheezing, abdominal pain, and mood disorders (15.8% each).

Long COVID symptom presentation varied by age: fatigue, chronic cough, and cognitive/psychological symptoms were predominant in adolescents, whereas infants and toddlers more often showed recurrent wheezing, failure to thrive, and sleep disturbances.

At hospital admission, several acute symptoms differed significantly by age group, including shortness of breath, myalgia, arthralgia, fatigue, headache, altered consciousness, seizures, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and lymphadenopathy.

Neurological symptoms appeared more prevalent in children with Omicron infection and gastrointestinal symptoms more common with Delta infection, but neither difference reached statistical significance.
No statistically significant difference in Long COVID prevalence was found between male and female children in this cohort.

Long COVID symptoms caused frequent limitations in daily home activities for 70% of preschool-aged children and affected both home and school activities for all school-aged children studied, with 66.6% reporting interference with friendships, leisure, and physical activities.
Children aged 7 years and older with Long COVID self-rated their quality of life during the symptomatic period at an average of 4 out of 10 (range 0-8).
The majority of hospitalized children (80.2%) had not received SARS-CoV-2 vaccination prior to infection, primarily (71.6%) because they were age-ineligible.
T-cell dysfunction may contribute to Long COVID through autoimmune processes, whereby SARS-CoV-2 induces antigen-presenting cells to present antigens to autoreactive T-cells.
Antiphospholipid autoantibodies have been detected in 52% of COVID-19 patients, associated with neutrophil hyperactivity and more severe clinical outcomes.

Autoantibodies against interferons, neutrophils, connective tissues, cyclic citrullinated peptides, and cell nuclei have been identified in 10-50% of COVID-19 patients, resembling autoantibody profiles in chronic autoimmune diseases.

Residual inflammation following SARS-CoV-2 multisystem inflammatory syndrome (MIS), characterized by lymphopenia and elevated pro-inflammatory markers, has been proposed as a contributor to Long COVID.
Deep alterations in the gut microbiome have been observed up to 30 days after disease resolution and correlated with prolonged SARS-CoV-2 shedding, suggested as a contributor to Long COVID.

Children with Long COVID have been found to exhibit brain hypometabolism patterns similar to those seen in adults with Long COVID, suggesting underlying functional neurological pathophysiology behind cognitive and mood symptoms.
Participants with Long COVID reported a range of persistent symptoms including fatigue, shortness of breath, and cognitive impairments.
Most participants held a pessimistic view about achieving timely recovery from Long COVID.

Participants perceived medical support for Long COVID in Germany as inadequate, citing long waits for specialist appointments and lack of acceptance of their condition by some doctors, which increased their uncertainty.

Many participants avoided physical contact with friends and family due to a high level of fear of reinfection or transmitting infection.
Some participants distanced themselves from people in their environment who did not take their precarious health situation seriously.
The close circle of family and friends served as an important support resource for the majority of Long COVID interviewees.
Total SF-36 score improved progressively from baseline through week 12 in participants treated with LDN and NAD+.
Chalder Fatigue Scale total scores decreased significantly from baseline to week 12 after LDN and NAD+ treatment.
Among SF-36 subscales, role limitations due to physical health showed the most pronounced improvement at week 12.
Energy/fatigue SF-36 subscale scores improved substantially by week 12.
Pain-related SF-36 scores improved markedly by week 12, the largest single subscale change alongside energy.
The significant improvement in pain scores with LDN/NAD+ treatment was detected in women but the effect could not be confirmed in the small male subgroup.
In the female subgroup (n=22), SF-36 total scores and all subscales improved significantly from baseline to week 12.

In the male subgroup (n=9), total SF-36 score improved significantly, but role limitations due to emotional problems, emotional well-being, social functioning, pain, and general health did not reach significance.
Participants aged ≤39 years did not show significant improvement in physical functioning, emotional well-being, or pain SF-36 subscales after 12 weeks, unlike older age groups.

Approximately a third to half of efficacy participants (11 of 23 classified) were clinically responsive, defined as ≥20% SF-36 improvement and week-12 score ≥55, with responders showing significant SF-36 and Chalder improvements while non-responders did not significantly improve on SF-36.
No correlation was found between time from positive COVID-19 test to first treatment dose and whether a participant was clinically responsive to LDN/NAD+ treatment.
The most common adverse event was mild, temporary skin irritation at the NAD+ iontophoresis patch site.

The p.R462Q variant, the most frequent variant found (6 of 12 carriers), reduces AADC conformational dynamics and maximal kinetic rate, lowering serotonin levels according to prior in vitro enzyme assays.
Among the six p.R462Q carriers, three (patients IV, VI and VIII) presented with neuromuscular disorders, cognitive deficit, and autism spectrum disorder together.
One patient carried the heterozygous pathogenic p.F77L variant in exon 3, predicted to cause conformational anomaly and active-site alteration of AADC via loop1 mispositioning.

A novel splice-site variant, DDC c.714+3A>G, not previously reported in HGMD, was identified in two patients and predicted by Mutation Taster to be disease-causing with alteration of the splicing site.
A novel missense variant, DDC c.772G>A (p.G258S), was identified in one patient and predicted probably damaging/deleterious/disease-causing by PolyPhen-2, SIFT, and Mutation Taster.

The DDC carrier frequency in this Sicilian neurological patient cohort (2.57%, 1:39) was substantially higher than carrier frequencies reported in Taiwan (0.68%) and worldwide gnomAD estimates (0.17% overall; 0.78% East Asian, 0.07% Latino).

Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the observed Sicilian carrier frequency implies an AADC deficiency prevalence of about 1/6000, far higher than previously estimated global birth prevalence (1/90,000 US, 1/118,000 EU, 1/182,000 Japan).
Comparison of clinical outcomes (types/number of clinical signs) between patients with and without DDC variants did not reach statistical significance.

The identified DDC variants were mostly concentrated in patients born in northern and eastern Sicily (Messina, Enna, Catania), suggesting a possible founder effect or migratory pattern similar to that seen in other Sicilian founder-effect diseases (GSD II, ADOA).
Neuromuscular disorders and cognitive deficit were the most prevalent clinical sign categories in the overall screened population of 350 patients.

A prior biochemical study cited by the authors found that heterozygous carriers of DDC variants have decreased decarboxylase enzyme activity (residual activity about 35-40%), which is not sufficient to cause clinical AADC deficiency signs.

Among the 350 screened patients, about 33% presented one clinical sign category, 45% presented two, and 22% presented three of the neuromuscular, cognitive, behavioral or autism sign categories used as inclusion criteria.

Microstructural properties of the parvicellular reticular formation-alpha (PCRtA), a brainstem nucleus involved in mastication, digestion, and cardio-respiration, were associated with social communication features in children, and this association replicated in an independent adolescent sample.

Microstructural properties of the lateral parabrachial nucleus (LPB), a pain-network brainstem nucleus, were associated with repetitive behaviors, with partial replication in an independent adolescent sample.
The ventral tegmental parabrachial pigmented complex (VTA-PBP) was associated with autism features in the main sample, but this association failed to replicate in the independent adolescent sample.

SYNGAP1 dysfunction leads to postsynaptic 'mushrooming,' increased AMPA receptor number, and enhanced Ras-ERK signaling with altered gene expression.

Intraperitoneal IGF-1 in hemizygous Shank3-deficient adult mice reversed AMPA receptor deficits (I/O function) and restored hippocampal LTP after two weeks.
In Phelan McDermid syndrome patients, decreased cerebellar vermal volume correlated with severity of repetitive behaviors.

Syngap1 knockout mice show accelerated hippocampal dendritic maturation as early as postnatal day 14, with increased AMPA/NMDA receptor ratio and increased mEPSC amplitude and frequency.
CRISPR-generated human iPSC SYNGAP1 knockout neurons show increased GluA1 structures and larger postsynaptic structures, with early hyperactive synaptic maturation.

Approximately half of SYNGAP1-related developmental and epileptic encephalopathy patients develop autism spectrum disorder, and more than four-fifths develop epilepsy with characteristic myoclonic-atonic and eyelid myoclonia seizure types.

Disruption of UBE3A, a gene associated with autism and Angelman syndrome, increases internalization of AMPA receptors and decreases long-term potentiation.

Deletion of P-Rex1, a gene responsible for AMPA receptor endocytosis, results in increased AMPA receptor expression and defective long-term depression, with behavioral inflexibility and social deficits in animal models.
Preclinical studies of Neurobeachin, a gene associated with autism, showed altered dendritic spine morphology and reduced miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs).
Preclinical studies of Rbm8a, a nonsense-mediated decay regulatory gene associated with autism, showed abnormally increased mEPSCs, pointing to LTD-related alterations in autism.
Post-mortem analysis of individuals with autism revealed broadly increased AMPA receptor mRNA levels but regionally decreased AMPA receptor protein expression in the cerebellum.

In a Shank3 knockout mouse model, AMPAr-mediated mEPSCs in the anterior cingulate cortex and striatum showed decreased frequency, suggesting fewer functional synapses, independent of NMDA receptor or presynaptic changes.
