In hospitalized SARD patients from a Danish national registry, hospitalization due to COVID-19 was associated with a higher subsequent risk of hospitalization for respiratory diseases.
The same Danish registry cohort also showed a higher risk of subsequent hospitalization due to infections in SARD patients hospitalized for COVID-19.
Rheumatic disease patients with long COVID showed worse anxiety and depression scores compared with those without long COVID.
Among COVID-19-infected rheumatic patients, mental health components of the SF-36 were worse in those who developed long COVID, but physical components were not.
Hospitalization due to COVID-19 was associated with an increased risk of long COVID development in autoimmune rheumatic disease patients.
Non-Caucasian ethnicity was associated with a higher risk of long COVID development in rheumatic disease patients.
Underlying rheumatic disease activity did not differ between patients who developed long COVID and those who did not, in two separate studies.
Use of hydroxychloroquine during COVID-19 infection was positively associated with subsequent development of long COVID.
Prior use of systemic corticosteroids was associated with an increased risk of long COVID in rheumatic disease patients.
Prior use of cyclophosphamide was associated with an increased risk of long COVID in rheumatic disease patients.
Fibromyalgia patients who had COVID-19 infection had similar disease severity but higher anxiety scores and widespread pain index compared with fibromyalgia patients who did not contract COVID-19.
Fibromyalgia patients reported more long COVID symptoms and worse patient global assessment scores than systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease patients after COVID-19 infection.

Prior reports cited in the discussion showed that long COVID patients had elevated type I and III interferons, TNF-α, G-CSF, IL-17A, IL-6, IL-1β and IL-13 compared with levels during the acute phase of COVID-19.
IFN-γ-induced protein 10 (IP-10) levels were decreased in long COVID compared with the acute phase of COVID-19 infection, per cited prior reports.

Long COVID patients had activated innate and adaptive immune cell populations including myeloid cells, Th9 cells, CD4+ effector memory T cells, CD8+ effector T cells and naïve B cells, per cited prior reports.
Persistently elevated levels of anti-SARS-CoV-2 IgG antibodies were noted in long COVID patients, per cited prior reports.
Circulating CCL11 levels were elevated in long COVID patients with cognitive symptoms, consistent with murine data showing CCL11 impairs neurogenesis and glial activity after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
In a large multicentre Spanish telephone-interview study, pre-existing rheumatic disease was not independently associated with development of long COVID.
After excluding studies with serious risk of bias, the pooled prevalence of long COVID in ARD patients was even higher, at 65%.
In the sensitivity analysis excluding high risk-of-bias studies, arthralgia (41%) became the most common long COVID symptom, surpassing fatigue (39%).
Long COVID patients scored significantly higher on the mMRC dyspnea scale than fully recovered participants.
Long COVID patients had significantly lower EQ-5D health-related quality-of-life scores than recovered patients.
A composite Long COVID Score combining mMRC and EQ-5D was significantly higher in Long COVID patients, indicating more breathlessness and worse quality of life.
Vaccination rates at the time of Long COVID assessment were similar between Long COVID and recovered participants.
Seropositivity rates for IgG against SARS-CoV-2 spike protein and CMV did not differ between Long COVID and recovered groups.
All participants, regardless of Long COVID status, were IgG seropositive for EBV, indicating universal prior EBV exposure with no distinguishing serostatus between groups.
Routine biochemical and clinical laboratory parameters showed no significant abnormalities distinguishing Long COVID patients from recovered individuals.

Fatigue, myalgia, arthralgia, dyspnea, persistent coughing, persistent sore throat, anxiety, and lack of concentration were significantly more prevalent among Long COVID patients than recovered individuals.
Basal 8 a.m. serum cortisol levels were slightly lower in Long COVID patients but did not reach statistical significance compared to recovered individuals.
A subset of Long COVID patients (2/29, 6.9%) exhibited frank hypocortisolaemia, a proportion resembling that reported in ME/CFS.
Serum cortisol levels showed no significant correlation with overall Long COVID symptom severity as measured by the LCS.
Basal serum ACTH levels were comparable between Long COVID patients and fully recovered participants.
The cortisol rise 60 minutes after ACTH stimulation (ΔCortisol) was similar between Long COVID and recovered groups, indicating normal adrenal responsiveness.
A subset of 12 participants had an inadequate (<2-fold) cortisol rise after ACTH stimulation, but this suboptimal response was evenly distributed regardless of Long COVID status.

Participants with a suboptimal (<2-fold) cortisol response to ACTH stimulation were more likely to report rhinitis, persistent coughing, and persistent sore throat, but not depressive symptoms, anxiety, or fatigue.
Circulating neutrophil counts were significantly lower in Long COVID patients than recovered participants, though still within normal reference range.
Absolute counts of total T lymphocytes, T-helper cells, cytotoxic T cells, and their memory/effector subsets did not differ between Long COVID and recovered groups.
Long COVID patients showed a non-significant trend toward a higher proportion of activated CD4+ HLA-DR+ CD38+ Treg cells compared to recovered participants.
Long COVID patients had a significantly higher proportion of mature B cells than recovered patients, despite similar total B cell counts.
Long COVID patients had a significantly greater proportion of circulating CD103-expressing CD8+ T cells (tissue-resident memory phenotype) than recovered patients.
Long COVID patients had a significantly higher proportion of Tregs expressing the exonuclease markers CD39 and CD73 compared to recovered patients.
No significant differences were found in γδ-T cells, NK cells, or NK-T cell populations between Long COVID and recovered patients.
No single inflammatory cytokine among a seven-marker panel was found to be specifically elevated in Long COVID patients relative to recovered individuals, with most levels within normal ranges.

Type 2 diabetes was more commonly diagnosed among Long COVID patients than recovered individuals, but this and acute COVID-19 severity were not statistically significantly associated with Long COVID status.
Fatigue was the most commonly assessed Long COVID symptom and was reported by 32.35% of pooled patients across the 17 cohort studies.
Dyspnea was the most prevalent respiratory symptom of Long COVID, reported by 34.27% of pooled patients.
Cough, sore throat, and nasal congestion were commonly reported respiratory symptoms of Long COVID, at 23.40%, 14.01%, and 9.71% prevalence respectively.
PTSD was reported in the highest percentage of patients of any symptom assessed (49.41%), though it was only evaluated in two of the included studies.
Abdominal pain was reported by 31.22% of patients assessed for GI symptoms of Long COVID, despite being evaluated in only four of the included studies.
Loss of appetite and diarrhea were frequently reported GI symptoms of Long COVID (22.0% and 12.39% respectively), whereas nausea and vomiting were reported by fewer than 4% of patients.
Cardiovascular symptoms were less commonly assessed; chest pain/discomfort was reported by 11.3% of patients (16 studies) and heart palpitations by 7.9% (9 studies).
Dermatological symptoms of Long COVID included hair loss (9% of patients) and skin rashes (4.2% of patients).

Pulmonary sequelae were the most prevalent organ-system-level manifestation of Long COVID (23.54% mean prevalence), followed by general (18.10%), neuropsychiatric (17.01%), GI (16.71%), cardiovascular (9.90%), and dermatological (6.66%) sequelae.
Evidence on massage therapy for fatigue is mixed: some studies reported no change or minor increases in fatigue after massage, while multiple other studies found massage successfully reduced fatigue.
Massage therapy has shown improvement in muscular and joint pain in prior literature, suggesting potential benefit for Long COVID patients with these symptoms.
Massage therapy is reported to be effective in managing respiratory symptoms shared with Long COVID, including dyspnea, cough, and sore throat.
Elevated concentrations of C-reactive protein and creatine during acute COVID-19 infection have been associated with prolonged cardiovascular symptoms of Long COVID.

Massage therapy has been shown to decrease CRP and creatine levels when used to complement pharmacological treatment for musculoskeletal conditions, suggesting a possible mechanism for benefit in Long COVID cardiovascular symptoms.
Elevated levels of inflammatory cytokines, specifically IL-6 and TNF-α, are proposed to drive development of anxiety and depressive symptoms in Long COVID patients.
Massage therapy decreases both IL-6 and TNF-α levels, suggesting potential efficacy for the cytokine-driven neuropsychiatric symptom pathway in Long COVID.

Massage therapy has been reported to improve sleep quality, enhance trauma-related psychotherapy outcomes, reduce anxiety and depression, and relieve stress via increased dopamine/serotonin and decreased cortisol.
A small study found that lymphatic drainage massage reduced fatigue and pain in patients with Long COVID Syndrome specifically.

In a large analysis of 62,354 patients, the incidence of first or recurrent psychiatric disease at 90 days post-SARS-CoV-2 infection was 18.1%, significantly higher than matched cohorts with influenza or other respiratory infections.
Compared to patients with only acute COVID-19 symptoms, Long COVID Syndrome patients had lower levels of regulatory T cells and reduced PD-1 expression on CD4 and CD8 T cells.
Long-term COVID-19 symptoms were associated with high, prolonged circulating titers of IgG and IgM antibodies against SARS-CoV-2.

Massage frequency affects its immunomodulatory effect: a single session of Swedish massage decreased inflammatory cytokines, while twice-weekly sessions resulted in a minor increase in inflammatory cytokines.

Massage therapy had no effect on inflammatory markers associated with prolonged wake cycle and unbalanced circadian rhythm, suggesting it may need to be combined with other interventions for these symptoms.

Individuals with COVID-19 symptoms lasting longer than 12 weeks (post-COVID-19 syndrome) had the greatest risk of reporting being financially worse off compared with those who had not contracted SARS-CoV-2.
Long COVID with symptoms lasting more than 12 weeks was associated with an increased risk of making a new benefit claim during the pandemic compared with those who had not contracted SARS-CoV-2.
Symptoms lasting longer than 4 weeks showed a suggestive but statistically non-significant association with a decrease in weekly household income of at least 5%.

The association between long COVID and financial worse-off status differed by sex: men needed only 4-12 weeks of symptoms to show increased risk of financial hardship, whereas women required more than 12 weeks of symptoms to show a comparable increased risk.
Educational attainment did not modify the association between long COVID and any of the financial outcomes studied, unlike sex.

In the pooled sample, 13% of participants reported COVID-19 with symptoms that impeded normal function, and 0.6% reported symptoms lasting 12 or more weeks (post-COVID-19 syndrome), estimated to represent over 400,000 people in the UK.
Among long COVID participants who made new benefit claims, the most commonly claimed benefits were Universal Credit and the self-employed COVID-19 support scheme.

In a sensitivity analysis using OECD-equivalised household income adjusted for pre-pandemic income, participants with COVID-19 symptoms lasting longer than 4 weeks had decreased household income during the pandemic.

As a negative control exposure, participants with SARS-CoV-2 infection but no or mild symptoms that did not impede functioning showed no observed association with the financial outcomes, suggesting limited unmeasured confounding.
Long COVID is linked to reduced CD4+ and CD8+ T cell counts together with increased interferon expression, suggesting immune dysregulation.
Anti-ACE2 autoantibodies emerge after SARS-CoV-2 infection and are associated with lower soluble ACE2 plasma activity, potentially driving persistent inflammation.

A large cohort study of non-hospitalized SARS-CoV-2 patients identified three major Long COVID phenotype clusters: broad-spectrum symptoms (80%), respiratory symptoms (5.8%), and mental health/cognitive symptoms (14.2%).

SARS-CoV-2 shifts macrophage polarization toward the pro-inflammatory M1 subtype, increasing IL-1, TNF-alpha and TLR signaling, producing prolonged muscular inflammation linked to joint pain and myalgia.
Patients with Long COVID have roughly twice the risk of developing respiratory conditions.
In a large multi-center study, roughly one-third of patients undergoing pulmonary function testing six months after discharge showed abnormal FEV1, FVC, or TLC.

Over 40% of patients with abnormal chest CT during acute COVID-19 continued to show abnormal CT findings at 3-month follow-up, associated with higher initial severity, comorbidities, longer hospital stay, and ICU admission.
In a survey of 2550 Long COVID patients, 89% reported cardiopulmonary symptoms such as palpitations, chest pain, tachycardia and orthostatic intolerance.

An observational study of 100 patients found that more than three-quarters had abnormal cardiac MRI findings—including myocardial inflammation, regional scar, and pericardial enhancement—at 2-3 months post-COVID.

In patients hospitalized with severe COVID-19 pneumonia and myocardial injury, repeat echocardiograms at three months showed persistent right ventricular dilatation and dysfunction in nearly one-third of patients.
Elevated troponin levels in Long COVID cases indicate myocardial injury, which may activate fibrosis pathways and contribute to cardiac remodeling.

A retrospective PET study comparing 35 Long COVID patients with fatigue/neurological complaints to 44 healthy controls found brain hypometabolism in multiple regions that discriminated patients from controls and correlated with hyposmia, cognitive impairment, pain, and insomnia.
One-third of previously hospitalized COVID-19 patients with acute kidney injury demonstrated adverse renal outcomes.
COVID-19-associated nephropathy (COVAN), a severe form of COVID-19-related kidney injury, disproportionately affects patients carrying APOL1 gene polymorphisms, particularly those of African descent.
A systematic review of 50 studies found gastrointestinal symptoms in approximately 12% of Long COVID patients.

Analysis of 181,280 COVID-19-positive participants versus two control groups in VA databases found COVID-19 survivors had increased risk and burden of incident diabetes and antihyperglycemic medication use beyond 30 days post-infection.
Viral invasion and cytokine release in the thyroid gland can induce inflammation, potentially leading to hypothyroidism that may become permanent in some Long COVID patients.

A systematic review of 1,285,407 participants from 32 countries found that 20% of COVID-19 survivors exhibited psychiatric symptoms during the 12 months after recovery, consistent with rates in SARS and MERS survivors.
Approximately 42% of hospitalized COVID-19 patients reported some PTSD symptoms at 3-4 months after discharge.

An international dermatology registry documented 716 cases of new-onset dermatologic manifestations (morbilliform, pernio-like, urticarial, macular erythema, vesicular, papulosquamous, retiform purpura) in patients with confirmed or suspected COVID-19.
Approximately 28.6% of COVID-19 survivors experienced alopecia three months after hospital discharge, with a higher prevalence (48.5%) among women, and most cases (72%) began after discharge.
Female sex, belonging to an ethnic minority, smoking, higher BMI, and socioeconomic deprivation have been linked to a higher risk of developing Long COVID.
Pre-existing conditions such as anxiety, depression, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and fibromyalgia are associated with an increased risk of developing Long COVID.
A Louisiana retrospective study found that 76.9% of hospitalized COVID-19 patients and 70.6% of those who died were identified as Black, an overrepresentation relative to the general population.
The Louisiana study did not find a significant association between Black race and higher in-hospital mortality from COVID-19, a finding corroborated by Mackey et al.
Pan et al. found that Black and Hispanic populations had a higher likelihood of COVID-19 infection and hospitalization, but no subsequent differences in hospital treatment or in-hospital mortality.

Thaweethai et al. developed a data-driven PASC (Post-Acute Sequelae of SARS-CoV-2) scoring framework based on 12 specific symptoms, with higher PASC scores associated with increasingly poor well-being and functioning.
A French self-reported survey found that 85% of patients continued to report persistent Long COVID symptoms one year after symptom onset.

A meta-regression pooling 54 studies and two medical record databases (1.2 million people) found hospitalized patients had Long COVID symptom clusters lasting 9.0 months compared to 4 months in non-hospitalized patients.
Rintatolimod, a Toll-like receptor 3 agonist previously investigated for chronic fatigue syndrome/ME, has obtained FDA clearance for a clinical trial targeting Long COVID.
A trial of 60 patients with Long COVID demonstrated a potential benefit from administering selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs).
Clomipramine, an anti-inflammatory agent that efficiently crosses the blood-brain barrier, has been proposed as a candidate for managing neurological symptoms of Long COVID.
Melatonin has been proposed as an adjunct therapy for managing depression symptoms in Long COVID patients by restoring disrupted circadian rhythms.
A study of 52 patients with Long COVID found that Low Dose Naltrexone was safe and potentially beneficial in improving overall well-being and reducing symptoms.
Observational studies indicate antihistamines can alleviate Long COVID symptoms, thought to counteract abnormal mast cell activation and associated inflammatory responses.
A data-driven Post-Acute Sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC) scoring framework based on 12 symptoms was developed, and higher scores correlated with worse well-being and functioning.
A French self-reported survey found that 85% of patients continued to report persistent Long COVID symptoms one year after symptom onset.

A meta-regression pooling 54 studies and two medical record databases (1.2 million people) found that hospitalized patients had Long COVID symptom clusters lasting 9.0 months versus 4 months in non-hospitalized patients.
Rintatolimod, a Toll-Like Receptor 3 agonist not FDA-approved for ME/CFS, has obtained FDA clearance for a clinical trial specifically targeting Long COVID.
A trial of 60 patients with Long COVID demonstrated a potential benefit of SSRIs on symptoms.
Clomipramine, an anti-inflammatory agent able to cross the blood-brain barrier, has been proposed as a potential treatment for neurological aspects of Long COVID.
Melatonin, known for restoring disrupted circadian rhythms in depression, may hold promise as an adjunct therapy for depressive symptoms in Long COVID.
A study of 52 patients with Long COVID found low dose naltrexone to be safe and potentially beneficial for overall well-being and symptom reduction.
Observational studies suggest antihistamines may alleviate Long COVID symptoms by counteracting abnormal mast cell activation and inflammatory responses.
Vaccination against COVID-19 was shown to lower the rates of Long COVID symptoms.

Antiviral medications including nirmatrelvir, molnupiravir, and ensitrelvir may lower risk of all-cause hospitalization and emergency department visits compared with untreated COVID-19 patients, potentially reducing Long COVID risk.
Metformin exhibited in vitro activity against SARS-CoV-2 at physiologically relevant doses in cell culture and human lung tissue, suggesting it might reduce Long COVID risk.

A retrospective Louisiana study found 76.9% of hospitalized COVID-19 patients and 70.6% of those who died were Black, but Black race was not significantly associated with higher in-hospital mortality.

Pan et al. found Black and Hispanic populations had higher likelihood of SARS-CoV-2 infection and hospitalization, though no differences in subsequent hospital treatment or in-hospital mortality, suggesting greater burden is driven by exposure/susceptibility rather than treatment disparities.
Racial and ethnic minorities are more likely to experience persistent Long COVID symptoms and prolonged recovery than white patients.
Research in Latin American countries (Colombia, Brazil) and in South Africa has shown a high prevalence of Long COVID symptoms, highlighting need for post-acute care in resource-constrained settings.

A systematic review found limited evidence supporting the effectiveness of physical therapy, cardiopulmonary rehabilitation, nutritional supplements, and olfactory training in reducing fatigue, dyspnea, or improving quality of life in Long COVID.
A Swiss survey by the Federal Social Insurance Office reported an increasing percentage of disability insurance claims attributed to post-COVID-19 condition.
In a cohort of 28,375 non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients, 2.8% developed long COVID symptoms during 90-day follow-up.
Patients who developed long COVID tended to be younger, female, and of Caucasian race compared to those who did not.
Common long COVID symptoms in the cohort included fatigue, muscle pain, respiratory symptoms, abdominal and neurological symptoms, allergic reactions, skin rashes, and hair loss.
Diabetes mellitus was identified as a risk factor for developing long COVID.
Asthma was identified as a risk factor for developing long COVID.
Vitamin D deficiency was identified as a risk factor for developing long COVID.
Females and Caucasians had a higher risk of long COVID during the pre-Omicron period compared with the Omicron period.
Pre-COVID vaccination was associated with a reduced risk of long COVID across all patient subgroups.
Treatment with favipiravir during the acute phase of COVID-19 was linked to a decreased risk of long COVID, though it showed limited effectiveness in the high-risk group.
Treatment with sotrovimab during the acute phase of COVID-19 was linked to a decreased risk of long COVID.

All 25 one-on-one interview participants and 10 of 23 focus group participants reported having received at least one COVID-19 vaccination, indicating high vaccination uptake among people with long COVID.
Nine participants developed long COVID despite having been vaccinated against COVID-19 prior to their SARS-CoV-2 infection, though two of them were not fully immunized at the time.
Six participants had not been vaccinated against COVID-19 at the time of the SARS-CoV-2 infection that led to their long COVID, mostly because of national vaccination prioritization rules.

Ten participants reported vaccination reactions of varying type and severity, with three experiencing symptoms resembling acute COVID-19 (fever, limb and muscle pain, breathing problems, severe fatigue) and two reporting visible swelling or hematomas.

Two participants experienced cardiac symptoms after COVID-19 vaccination: one was hospitalized with myocarditis and one developed extrasystoles (heart palpitations), both already having pre-existing long COVID.
Two participants experienced a persistent (rather than temporary) deterioration of their long COVID health status and symptoms following COVID-19 vaccination.

Most participants believed COVID-19 vaccination contributed to milder acute COVID-19 courses and reduced long-term sequelae, though several with pre-existing long COVID expressed uncertainty about whether vaccination benefited or harmed their health.

Sixteen of the 48 participants had utilized outpatient (3) or inpatient (13) rehabilitation for long COVID, receiving programs with psychosomatic, neurological, or cardiological focus rather than dedicated long-COVID rehabilitation.

Four participants reported that rehabilitation improved their health status and alleviated long COVID complaints, with combined seaside inpatient rehabilitation plus follow-up rehabilitation sports and neurological rehabilitation cited as particularly helpful.

Four participants experienced their inpatient or outpatient rehabilitation as unhelpful or counterproductive for long COVID complaints, citing inadequate, inconsistent, and overly narrow therapeutic interventions, including a case of excessive physical exercise given as inappropriate treatment.

Participants attributed unhelpful rehabilitation experiences to rehabilitation clinics' lack of focus on long COVID and professionals' insufficient experience with the condition; two participants who received psychosomatic rehabilitation reported that long COVID was not addressed at all.
Two participants declined booster vaccinations specifically out of fear of intensifying existing long COVID complaints or triggering new cognitive symptoms.
Long COVID prevalence was 24% at months 6 and 12, declined to 15% at month 18 and 6% at month 24, with 33% of participants ever meeting long COVID criteria over 24 months.
Pre-COVID-19 obesity and hyperlipidemia were significantly associated with developing long COVID, while no other comorbidity or demographic characteristic was.
Long COVID status was not associated with acute hospitalization, COVID-19 treatment, or reinfection during follow-up.
No laboratory biomarkers, including high-sensitivity CRP, NT-proBNP, or high-sensitivity cardiac troponin, at any timepoint were associated with ever having long COVID.

Rates of orthostatic hypotension and orthostatic tachycardia in this cohort were consistent with general population prevalence estimates, suggesting long COVID is not accompanied by increased rates of postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome.
Within-person weight significantly increased over the follow-up period, particularly between months 1-3 and 6, and between months 1-3 and 24.

Participants with long COVID had higher median BMI at baseline and throughout follow-up, were more likely to be overweight or obese, and experienced less total weight gain than those without long COVID.
Long COVID was significantly associated with decreased quality of life in physical functioning at month 12, energy/fatigue at months 6, 12, and 24, and general health at months 12 and 18.

At month 6, participants with 3 or more symptoms had significantly worse quality of life than those with fewer than 3 symptoms in physical functioning, energy/fatigue, social functioning, pain, and general health domains.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported long COVID symptom across all follow-up timepoints, reported by at least 20% of participants at each visit.
Postexertional fatigue, a hallmark symptom shared with ME/CFS, was commonly reported, ranging from 17% to 50% of participants across timepoints.

Fatigue Severity Scale-9 scores among participants endorsing fatigue or sleep disturbances were similar to scores reported in known fatigue-related disorders such as multiple sclerosis and sleep-wake disorders.

The majority of participants endorsing sleep disturbances also screened positive for insomnia on the ISI, and 5%-11% reported both insomnia and hypersomnia concurrently, indicating multifaceted sleep-wake dysregulation.
Cognitive symptoms (brain fog/concentration problems, memory problems, confusion) increased from 5% at month 1-3 to 30% at month 6, 24% at month 12, 19% at month 18, and 29% at month 24.
Gastrointestinal symptoms, anosmia, and ageusia decreased consistently over the 24-month follow-up period.
Pre-existing anxiety or depression diagnoses were not associated with developing long COVID or with failing to return to usual health/activities at any timepoint.

Participants with diagnosed pre-COVID-19 anxiety or depression were more likely to report decreased quality of life in all domains across multiple timepoints, despite no association with long COVID risk itself.
The study did not observe an association between sex assigned at birth and long COVID risk, contrary to some prior studies, which the authors suggest may be due to limited sample size.
Symptom burden peaked and quality of life reached its nadir between 6 and 12 months postinfection, with gradual improvement thereafter.

A higher proportion of participants reported returning to pre-COVID-19 activities than to usual health status at each timepoint, and 16% reported relapse in activity status after initially recovering, indicating a waxing-waning course.
A majority of participants (139/196, 70.9%) continued to experience symptoms beyond four weeks post-diagnosis, with fatigue being the most prominent persistent symptom.
A total of 124 participants (63.3%) developed new symptoms after four weeks, most commonly hair loss, difficulty concentrating, anxiety, depression, and joint pains.
Female sex was significantly associated with development of Long COVID symptoms, with 74% of women affected compared to 52.6% of men.
No statistically significant association was found between ABO blood group and occurrence of Long COVID syndrome.
No significant associations were found between Long COVID occurrence and age, BMI, ethnicity, comorbidities, or smoking status.
Greater perceived severity of acute COVID-19 infection was significantly associated with the occurrence of Long COVID symptoms.
Nearly all participants (95.4%) experienced acute COVID-19 symptoms, most commonly fever, fatigue, body aches, and cough.

At Week 4 post-infection, the bivalent-vaccinated cohort had significantly lower prevalence of long COVID defined as ≥3 symptoms (24.2% vs 35.5%) and ≥2 symptoms (31.5% vs 47.8%) compared with the unvaccinated cohort.
At Month 6, the bivalent cohort had significantly lower prevalence of long COVID defined as ≥3 symptoms (17.2% vs 26.5%) and ≥2 symptoms (25.8% vs 37.0%) compared with the unvaccinated cohort.

Observed odds-ratio analyses at Month 6 showed bivalent vaccination was associated with a 41% reduced risk of long COVID (≥3 symptoms) and a 43% reduced risk of long COVID (≥2 symptoms) compared with unvaccinated participants.

After adjustment for demographics, comorbidities, prior infection, and antiviral treatment in a mixed-effects logistic model, bivalent vaccination remained associated with reduced odds of long COVID (≥3 symptoms and ≥2 symptoms) at Month 6.
At Week 4, the bivalent cohort reported a numerically but not statistically significantly lower mean number of long COVID symptoms than the unvaccinated cohort.
At Month 3, the bivalent cohort reported significantly fewer mean long COVID symptoms than the unvaccinated cohort.
At Month 6, the bivalent cohort reported a numerically lower but not statistically significant mean number of long COVID symptoms compared with the unvaccinated cohort.
At Week 4, bivalent-vaccinated participants had a significantly lower prevalence of general long COVID symptoms compared with unvaccinated participants.
At Week 4, bivalent-vaccinated participants had a significantly lower prevalence of respiratory and heart-related long COVID symptoms compared with unvaccinated participants.

At Week 4, bivalent-vaccinated participants had a significantly lower prevalence of neurologic long COVID symptoms compared with unvaccinated participants; this category was one of the main drivers of the overall reduced risk observed at Month 6.

Fatigue that interferes with daily life and sore throat were significantly less prevalent at Week 4 in bivalent-vaccinated participants compared with unvaccinated participants, and fatigue remained significantly lower through Month 6.

At Month 3, several individual long COVID symptoms — fatigue, sore throat, headache, pins-and-needles feeling, mood changes, depression/anxiety, diarrhea, and stomach pain — were significantly less prevalent in the bivalent cohort than the unvaccinated cohort.
At Month 6, fatigue and chest pain were significantly less prevalent in the bivalent cohort compared with the unvaccinated cohort.

Across ordinal symptom-burden categories (<3, 3-5, >5 symptoms), the bivalent cohort consistently presented with lower overall long COVID symptom burden than the unvaccinated cohort at all three follow-up timepoints.

Across the included survey studies, the proportion of healthcare workers reporting long-term COVID-19 symptoms ranged from 23.1% at 6 months post-infection up to 73% among those with a positive nasopharyngeal swab at a median of 117 days since infection.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported long COVID symptom among healthcare workers, with reported proportions ranging widely from 4% at 8 months to 75% at 1 month after COVID-19 infection.
Headache was reported by healthcare workers with long COVID at proportions ranging from 0.5% beyond 60 days since infection to 42% at 1 month after infection.
Loss of taste and/or smell was reported in healthcare workers with long COVID at proportions ranging from 0.5% at up to and beyond 60 days to 51.1% at more than 3 months after infection.
Other commonly reported long COVID symptoms among healthcare workers included dyspnoea, concentration/attention difficulties, respiratory problems, depression, and anxiety.

Missed working days increased with duration of long COVID symptoms, with a median of 10 missed days for symptoms lasting under 90 days versus a median of 21 missed days for symptoms lasting under 365 days.
Four studies reported that long-term COVID-19 symptoms disrupted healthcare workers' professional working life.
Some healthcare workers reported disruption to their social and home life due to persistent long COVID symptoms, and others reported being unable to participate in leisure activities.
One study reported that around three-quarters of healthcare workers adopted a healthier lifestyle, including increased physical activity or multivitamin use, during the post-COVID-19 recovery period.

Qualitative interviews found that healthcare workers with long COVID experienced unfamiliar, unpredictable, and fluctuating symptoms that did not fit their clinical knowledge, leading to uncertainty about whether and when to return to work.

Healthcare worker participants described problems accessing and navigating care, including delayed, absent, or inappropriate responses and a perceived lack of interest and support from their GPs, sometimes resorting to personal contacts or private consultations.

Combining a professional healthcare-worker identity with the role of patient was described as particularly challenging, with participants struggling to relinquish clinical decision-making and fearing they would be seen as a burden.

Having professional medical knowledge did not protect healthcare workers from uncertainty and fear about the nature and course of their long COVID symptoms, and working in the healthcare sector was not an advantage in obtaining appropriate care.
18.2% of surveyed adults met the case definition for long COVID 90 days after a positive SARS-CoV-2 test during the 2022 Omicron wave.
Women had a higher adjusted risk of developing long COVID compared with men.
Adults aged 50-69 years had a higher adjusted risk of long COVID compared with those aged 18-29 years.
People with pre-existing health conditions had a higher adjusted risk of long COVID.
People who had received two or fewer COVID-19 vaccine doses had a higher adjusted risk of long COVID compared with those who had received four or more doses.
People who had received three COVID-19 vaccine doses had a higher adjusted risk of long COVID compared with those who had received four or more doses.
Fatigue was the most frequently reported symptom among people with long COVID.
Concentration difficulties were the second most commonly reported symptom among people with long COVID, affecting 59.5% of them.
In the month preceding the survey, 38.2% of respondents with long COVID had consulted a general practitioner for related symptoms.
Among respondents with long COVID, 1.6% reported being hospitalised in the month preceding the survey with long COVID-related issues.
Of respondents with long COVID who had been working or studying before infection, 17.8% reported reducing or discontinuing this activity because of long COVID symptoms.
Overall, 38.7% of respondents with long COVID (equivalent to 7.1% of all survey respondents) sought health care for related health concerns two to three months after acute infection.
Patients with long COVID showed hypomagnesemia (serum magnesium ≤1.8 mg/dL) associated with a greater number of clinical manifestations compared to a control group with normal magnesium levels.
Patients with long COVID showed 25-hydroxyvitamin D deficiency (<30 ng/mL) associated with a greater number of clinical manifestations compared to a control group with normal vitamin D levels.
The combined presence of hypomagnesemia and 25-hydroxyvitamin D deficiency was significantly associated with long COVID, with an adjusted odds ratio of 3.1.
Long COVID patients self-reported significant reductions in somatic symptoms after a six-week biofeedback intervention, sustained at three months.
Anxiety symptoms significantly improved in long COVID patients after biofeedback treatment, with effects maintained at 3-month follow-up.
Depressive symptoms significantly improved in long COVID patients after biofeedback treatment, with effects maintained at 3-month follow-up.
Sleep quality improved significantly in long COVID patients after biofeedback treatment, sustained at three months.
Quality of life improved significantly in long COVID patients after biofeedback treatment, sustained at three months.
At the three-month follow-up, participants reported a reduced number of medical doctor visits following the biofeedback intervention.
Prescription drug use over the prior month was reduced at the three-month follow-up after biofeedback treatment.
Emotional wellbeing improved specifically at the three-month follow-up after biofeedback treatment, though not necessarily immediately post-treatment.
No adverse events were reported among the 96% of enrolled long COVID patients who completed the four-week inpatient pulmonary rehabilitation program.
Exercise tolerance measured by the 6-minute walking distance test significantly improved after the four-week pulmonary rehabilitation program.
Overall muscle strength (QMVC) did not show a statistically significant change after pulmonary rehabilitation, although 53% of symptomatic patients individually exceeded the MCID for improvement.
Health-related quality of life (SF-12) improved significantly after pulmonary rehabilitation, with more than 80% of patients with deteriorated QoL before PR reaching normal QoL afterward.
Fatigue significantly improved after pulmonary rehabilitation, with two-thirds of symptomatic patients achieving remission, and a 66% reduction in the proportion of symptomatic patients.
Dyspnea impact and physical-affective dyspnea significantly improved after pulmonary rehabilitation, with 78% of patients achieving remission of dyspnea impact.
Anxiety and depression significantly improved after pulmonary rehabilitation, with two-thirds of anxious patients achieving relief.
Posttraumatic stress disorder symptoms significantly improved after pulmonary rehabilitation, with a 64% reduction in the proportion of symptomatic patients.
Cognitive function significantly improved after pulmonary rehabilitation, with impaired cognition prevalence decreasing by 67%.
Hyperventilation symptoms significantly improved after pulmonary rehabilitation, with a 44% reduction in symptomatic patients.

There was no significant correlation between the delay from acute COVID onset to PR initiation and change in any of the twelve assessed outcomes, arguing against spontaneous recovery explaining the improvements.

Only 1 of 47 long COVID patients in this cohort self-reported post-exertional malaise, markedly lower than the ~73% prevalence at six months post-infection reported in prior literature, likely due to under-recognition/under-reporting of the symptom rather than true absence.

Three isolated cases of partial clinical deterioration (physical QoL in one patient; DYSPNEA-12 scores in two patients) were observed among 47 patients across 12 outcomes, but scores in all three remained below symptomatic thresholds, suggesting these were not clinically meaningful deteriorations.
Female sex, obesity, and presence of comorbidities were common among the study cohort, consistent with previously reported risk factors for developing long COVID.
Among 396 Italian children and adolescents with prior COVID-19, 25.0% developed Long COVID syndrome, with most (68.7%) having symptoms lasting more than 12 weeks.

The most frequently reported Long COVID symptoms in this pediatric cohort were nasal congestion and diarrhea (34.3% each), followed by headache (23.2%), fatigue (21.2%), loss of appetite (13.1%), insomnia (12.1%), abdominal pain (10.1%), cough (8.1%), vision problems (7.1%), and confusion/impaired concentration (5.0%).
Children with concurrent allergic rhinitis had a higher risk of developing Long COVID syndrome than those without.
Children with concurrent atopic dermatitis had a higher risk of developing Long COVID syndrome than those without.
Children with concurrent food allergies had a higher risk of developing Long COVID syndrome than those without.
Children with concurrent respiratory diseases had a higher risk of developing Long COVID syndrome than those without.
Children with concurrent gastrointestinal diseases had a higher risk of developing Long COVID syndrome than those without.
Children with concurrent rheumatologic diseases had a markedly higher risk of developing Long COVID syndrome than those without, though the estimate was highly imprecise.
Children who experienced fatigue during acute COVID-19 had a higher risk of developing Long COVID syndrome.
Children who experienced muscle pain during acute COVID-19 had a higher risk of developing Long COVID syndrome.
Children who experienced abdominal pain during acute COVID-19 had a higher risk of developing Long COVID syndrome.
Female sex was not significantly associated with risk of developing Long COVID syndrome in this pediatric cohort.
Being an adolescent (>12 years) was not significantly associated with risk of developing Long COVID syndrome.
Caucasian ethnicity was not significantly associated with risk of developing Long COVID syndrome.
Vaccine administration prior to infection was not significantly associated with the risk of developing Long COVID syndrome in this pediatric cohort.
Post-COVID patients had significantly lower relative peak torque to body weight in knee extensors compared to healthy controls with a large effect size.
Post-COVID patients had significantly lower relative peak torque to body weight in knee flexors compared to healthy controls with a large effect size.
Post-COVID patients took significantly longer to reach peak torque in knee extensors than healthy controls, suggesting delayed neuromuscular activation.
No significant difference was found in time to reach peak torque for knee flexors between post-COVID patients and healthy controls.
Post-COVID patients showed a smaller joint angle at peak torque for knee extensors than healthy controls, suggesting altered muscle length-tension relationship.
Post-COVID patients showed a larger joint angle at peak torque for knee flexors than healthy controls, suggesting altered muscle length-tension relationship.
Post-COVID patients had significantly lower torque at 30 degrees of knee flexion for extensors compared to healthy controls.
Post-COVID patients had significantly lower torque at 30 degrees of knee flexion for flexors compared to healthy controls.
Post-COVID patients showed significantly higher coefficient of variation of torque in knee extensors, indicating greater measurement variability/inconsistency in muscle performance.
Post-COVID patients performed significantly less relative work per body weight in knee extensors compared to healthy controls.
Post-COVID patients performed significantly less relative work per body weight in knee flexors compared to healthy controls.
Both knee extensors and flexors in the post-COVID cohort showed significantly less work output during the initial third of the exercise compared to healthy controls.
Post-COVID patients showed significantly greater work fatigue (strength loss) in knee extensors compared to healthy controls.
Post-COVID patients showed significantly greater work fatigue (strength loss) in knee flexors compared to healthy controls.
Post-COVID patients exhibited significantly lower knee extensor muscle power compared to healthy controls.
Post-COVID patients exhibited significantly lower knee flexor muscle power compared to healthy controls, with a large effect size.
No significant difference was observed in the agonist/antagonist (hamstring-to-quadriceps) ratio between post-COVID patients and healthy controls.
Among 363 patients referred for cardiovascular evaluation for long COVID symptoms, only 23.4% had an identifiable cardiac cause for their symptoms.
New cardiac disease attributable to COVID-19 was identified in 39 of 363 (10.7%) patients with long COVID cardiovascular symptoms.
Worsening of pre-existing cardiac disease after COVID-19 infection occurred in 13 of 363 (3.6%) long COVID patients.
Six cases of myocarditis were identified among long COVID patients evaluated for cardiovascular symptoms.
Eleven cases of cardiac rhythm disorders were identified among long COVID patients evaluated for cardiovascular symptoms.
Eight cases of pericarditis were identified among long COVID patients evaluated for cardiovascular symptoms.
Five suspected cases of endothelial dysfunction were identified among long COVID patients evaluated for cardiovascular symptoms.
Among the 363 long COVID patients referred for cardiovascular evaluation, 33 cases were attributed to autonomic dysfunction.
Five patients in the long COVID cardiovascular evaluation cohort had suspected endothelial dysfunction.
Most long COVID cases in the cohort (83.7%) were diagnosed during the pre-Delta phase of the pandemic, compared with 13.2% during Delta and 3.1% during Omicron phases.

Long COVID patients had lower ischemic response parameters (IR max and IR index) measured by flow-mediated skin fluorescence compared with healthy controls, indicating reduced residual oxygen bioavailability in skin keratinocytes.
Long COVID patients showed lower reactive hyperemia response (RHR), reflecting reduced nitric oxide-mediated endothelial function, compared with controls.
Long COVID patients showed only minor, non-significant changes in hyperemic response parameters (HR max, HR index) compared with controls.
Serum glycine concentration was decreased in long COVID patients compared with healthy controls.
There were no significant differences in standard red and white blood cell count parameters between long COVID patients and healthy controls.
Platelet distribution width and the percentage of large platelets were higher in long COVID patients than in healthy controls.
Erythrocyte ATP, ADP and AMP concentrations did not differ significantly between long COVID patients and healthy controls.
The erythrocyte ATP/ADP ratio and adenylate energy charge did not differ significantly between long COVID patients and controls.
The erythrocyte ADP/AMP ratio was higher in long COVID patients compared with healthy controls.
In long COVID patients, RBC ATP concentration correlated positively with IR max and IR index (ischemic response) while RBC ADP concentration correlated negatively with these parameters.
RBC ATP/ADP ratio and adenylate energy charge (AEC) showed a strong positive correlation with IR index and IR max parameters in long COVID patients.
The RHR parameter, reflecting endothelial NO production, correlated negatively with RBC ADP concentration and positively with the RBC ATP/ADP ratio and AEC.
The RBC ADP/AMP ratio correlated negatively with log(HS), a parameter reflecting microcirculatory hypoxia sensitivity, in long COVID patients.
A significant positive correlation was found between RBC ATP concentration and the serum arginine/ADMA ratio, a marker of nitric oxide production capacity, in long COVID patients.
RBC ATP correlated positively with serum arginine and citrulline (NO synthesis substrate/co-product) and showed a negative trend with SDMA (arginine transport inhibitor) in long COVID patients.
Erythrocyte ATP and total adenine nucleotide (TAN) concentrations correlated positively with serum glycine concentration in long COVID patients.

No significant correlations were found between erythrocyte adenine nucleotide levels/ratios and standard RBC parameters, although a non-significant trend toward a negative relationship between RBC ATP and RBC count, hematocrit, hemoglobin and RDW was observed.

Erythrocyte ATP and TAN concentrations were significantly related to neutrophil and lymphocyte percentages and showed a strong positive correlation with the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) in long COVID patients.
NLR and LCR significantly correlated with erythrocyte ATP and TAN concentrations in long COVID patients, supporting a link between systemic inflammation status and RBC energetics.
LMR and PLR showed a non-significant tendency to correlate with erythrocyte ATP and TAN concentrations in long COVID patients.
96% of participants identified fatigue as one of their most bothersome long COVID symptoms.
92% of participants identified cognitive problems as one of their most bothersome long COVID symptoms.
40% of participants identified general pain or discomfort as one of their most bothersome long COVID symptoms.
58% of participants reported moderate or severe issues with mobility using the EQ-5D-5L.
Only 15% of participants had moderate or severe difficulty with self-care.
81% of participants experienced moderate to extreme problems performing usual activities, and nearly all reported some difficulty.
61% of participants experienced moderate or severe levels of pain or discomfort related to long COVID.
46% of participants experienced anxiety and/or depression related to their long COVID.
Participants' mean self-reported overall health status on the EQ-5D-5L visual analog scale was 47.3 out of 100, indicating substantially reduced health-related quality of life.
81% of participants reported having sought medical help for their long COVID symptoms, most commonly from family doctors/nurse practitioners (90%), specialists (71%), and physical therapists (52%).

67% of participants had consulted other, non-mainstream healthcare providers (e.g., acupuncturists, chiropractors, massage therapists, social workers, dieticians) or programs to manage long COVID symptoms.
Primary care providers, physical therapists, and acupuncturists were rated as quite helpful by a subset of participants who used them (3/19, 4/11, and 3/4 respectively).
9 of 21 participants who sought medical care reported encountering at least one healthcare provider who was not responsive to their ongoing long COVID symptoms.

Participants most wanted a long-COVID-specialized healthcare provider (88%), a specialized LC clinic (80%), more advertising of local resources (48%), more primary care provider awareness of LC (44%), and a local support group (40%).
Almost one in five (about 19%) of session participants reported not seeking medical help for their long COVID symptoms, consistent with a prior survey finding 18.9% (223/1178) not seeking care.
The patient-oriented long COVID knowledge-sharing session was rated positively by attendees, with high liking, perceived usefulness, and strong interest in future similar events.
Post-COVID participants without cognitive or psychiatric disorders showed lower posterior resting-state EEG alpha source activity compared to matched non-COVID controls.
The reduction in posterior alpha source activity was more pronounced in post-COVID patients reporting two or more fatigue symptoms.
More than 90% of post-COVID participants with brain fog showed no cognitive or psychiatric disorders on clinical/neuropsychological assessment.
Autistic children showed a lower incidence of nonharmonic alpha-theta cross-frequency decoupling at rest compared to nonautistic peers, indicating a higher incidence of spurious neural coupling.
Within autistic children, increased resting-state neural cross-frequency coupling was associated with greater social difficulties.
Increased resting-state neural cross-frequency coupling was associated with lower parasympathetic (high-frequency heart-rate-variability) activity in autistic children.
After 4 weeks of intranasal oxytocin (12 IU twice-daily), autistic children showed an increase in nonharmonic cross-frequency decoupling, indicating reduced spurious neural coupling.
Parallel epigenetic changes in the oxytocin receptor gene accompanied the oxytocin-induced neural effects, suggesting the neural changes were mediated by altered endogenous oxytocinergic signaling.
Individuals with fibromyalgia had significantly higher overall subjective sensory sensitivity (GSQ) scores than non-diagnosed controls, with a large effect size.
Fibromyalgia patients showed markedly increased multisensory hypersensitivity relative to controls, with a large effect size.
Fibromyalgia patients also showed increased (unhypothesized) hyposensitivity scores relative to controls, though with a smaller effect than hypersensitivity.

Group differences in hypersensitivity were significant across all seven sensory modalities assessed (vision, audition, tactile, olfactory, gustatory, vestibular, proprioception), surviving Bonferroni correction.

Among hyposensitivity domains, only touch and proprioception showed group differences surviving Bonferroni correction, potentially reflecting fibromyalgia-specific symptoms like numbness and poor manual dexterity.

A specific tactile hypersensitivity item concerning dislike of haircuts (bits of hair against skin) showed a medium effect size difference between fibromyalgia and controls, resembling a known autism sensory trait.

Fibromyalgia patients scored lower than controls on GSQ items concerning repetitive and self-stimulating behaviours (e.g., spinning around, lining up objects, wearing strong scents), which are typically positively associated with autistic traits, showing a dissociation from the autism sensory profile.
GSQ scores were not significantly associated with age or with male versus female gender within either the fibromyalgia or control groups.
Prior literature cited in this paper reports that individuals with fibromyalgia have lower pain thresholds for auditory stimuli compared to controls.
Prior literature cited in this paper reports increased visual discomfort in fibromyalgia when viewing high spatial frequency patterns, an effect believed to originate in early visual cortex.

Prior literature cited in this paper reports that fibromyalgia is associated with poorer behavioural performance on detection and discrimination of tastes and smells, though it is unknown whether this is accompanied by higher subjective sensitivity to these modalities.
Prior literature cited in this paper indicates that vestibular complaints such as dizziness are common in fibromyalgia.

A related study using an autism-derived sensory sensitivity measure (Tavassoli et al., 2014) in a fibromyalgia group similarly found hypersensitivity for touch, smell, and vision, but not for taste or hearing, partially converging with and partially diverging from the present findings.
MECP2 binds methylated DNA and regulates the transcription of thousands of downstream genes.
MECP2 protein levels below ~80% of normal produce Rett syndrome features, while levels above ~140% produce MECP2 Duplication Syndrome features.

Rett syndrome, occurring predominantly in females, is most often caused by loss-of-function or deletion mutations in MECP2 and presents with developmental regression, motor dysfunction, hand stereotypies, autonomic dysfunction, epilepsy, scoliosis, and autistic-like behavior.
Although MECP2 loss-of-function mutations were originally thought lethal in males, rare hypomorphic or mosaic mutations have been reported in male individuals.

MDS, caused by duplication or triplication of Xq28 including MECP2 and seen primarily in males, presents with developmental delay, early hypotonia, GI problems, refractory epilepsy, neurobehavioral traits, and recurrent respiratory infections.

Individuals with specific MECP2 mutations (R106W, R168X, R255X, R270X, insertion, large deletion) develop hand stereotypies earlier and display the highest frequency and greatest variety of hand movements.
Hand stereotypies show little correlation with overall clinical severity as assessed by the Clinical Severity Scale and Motor Behavior Assessment in Rett syndrome.
Rett syndrome patients show autonomic dysregulation including prolonged QT intervals and reduced heart rate variability, and 20% of Rett deaths occur suddenly while patients are awake.
Rett syndrome patients show increased GI inflammation, reduced microbiotic richness and bacterial metabolic end-products, and altered short-chain fatty acid production.

Approximately 90% of Rett syndrome patients develop seizures during their lifetime, and prior estimates of medication-resistant epilepsy (~36%) were higher than the 16% intractability found in the Rett Syndrome Natural History Study.
About half of Rett syndrome patients develop scoliosis in adolescence, with approximately 20% of those requiring surgical correction, and scoliosis correlates with more severe disease.
Sleep problems are present in about 80% of Rett syndrome individuals, with high rates of night laughing (77%) and night screaming (49%).
Missense MECP2 mutations typically cause milder Rett syndrome phenotypes, late truncating mutations intermediate severity, and early truncating mutations the most severe phenotypes.
MDS incidence has been reported as 1 in 100,000 live male births in Australia.
Epilepsy in MDS is a dynamic feature that becomes nearly universal with age, with atonic seizures most common and most patients developing drug-resistant epilepsy.

Some MDS patients have IgA/IgG2 deficiency and low antibody titers against pneumococci, and duplication of IRAK1 (which acts on the Toll-like receptor pathway) may contribute to impaired humoral immunity and recurrent respiratory infections.
Autism has been found to be universally present in individuals with MECP2 Duplication Syndrome.

Comparing MDS to idiopathic autism (N=10 each), hyposensitivity to pain/temperature was found to be a distinguishing feature of MDS, while core autism behavioral features (social affect, repetitive behavior) were similar between the two groups.

A detailed GI study of MDS found high rates of constipation, feeding difficulty, and GERD, a bimodal age distribution for GERD and gastrostomy feeding, and identified biliary tract disease as a novel finding.
MDS patients whose duplication also includes RAB39B have more severe microcephaly and motor impairments.
MECP2 triplication patients have more severe disease than duplication patients, with more frequent respiratory insufficiency, dysphagia, hearing loss, and cardiac defects.
IRAK1, which acts on the Toll-like receptor pathway, is included in the Xq28 duplication in MDS and may contribute to the recurrent respiratory infections seen in patients.
Some MDS patients have IgA and IgG2 deficiency with low antibody titers against pneumococci, suggesting impaired humoral immunity.

In a small cohort comparison, hyposensitivity to pain/temperature was characteristic of MDS-related autism, whereas core autism features such as social affect and repetitive behavior were similar between MDS and idiopathic autism.

MDS patients commonly display dysmorphic facial and skeletal features including hypotonic face, large ears, flat nasal bridge, posterior skull asymmetry, midface hypoplasia, deep-set eyes, small flat feet, and long thin tapered fingers, features not described in Rett syndrome.

GI dysfunction differs between MDS and Rett syndrome: MDS individuals more commonly and severely experience GERD (bimodal distribution), chewing difficulty and constipation, while air swallowing, excessive gas, and tube feeding dependence are more common in Rett syndrome.
Sleep problems in MDS patients include difficulty with sleep maintenance (48%), sleep initiation (35%), waking in the morning (25%), and snoring (48%).
Scoliosis frequency in MDS varies widely across studies, reported at 53%, 19%, and 37% in different cohorts, and is progressive with age.
Genitourinary anomalies in MDS include cryptorchidism, micropenis, ureteral dilation, and bladder dilation/hypertrophy, with frequencies varying between cohorts.
Visual abnormalities are frequently reported in MDS, including hypermetropia, amblyopia, myopia, strabismus, nystagmus, and astigmatism, along with high rates of eczema and allergy.

Duplication of RAB39B, located near MECP2 at Xq28, is independently associated with intellectual disability and can lead to misdiagnosis as MDS; MDS patients with a RAB39B duplication have more severe microcephaly and motor impairment.
FLNA, a gene near MECP2 at Xq28, has been associated with more severe gastrointestinal symptoms in MDS when included in the duplication.

Mouse models overexpressing only wild-type MECP2 recapitulate many MDS features including spasticity, epilepsy, and stereotypic movements, supporting that MECP2 duplication itself drives the MDS phenotype.

Studies conflict on whether MECP2 duplication size correlates with MDS severity: some found no correlation, while Peters et al. found larger duplications with RAB39B involvement worsened severity, and Pascual-Alonso et al. found translocation outside the X chromosome caused more severe phenotypes.

MECP2 triplication cases present with more severe disease than duplication cases, including respiratory insufficiency, dysphagia, hearing loss, cardiac defects, polyhydramnios, and intestinal pseudo-obstruction.

Unlike Rett syndrome patients who often have poor growth (decreased height/weight) related to GI dysfunction and undernutrition, MDS patients generally have normal growth including height, weight, and occipitofrontal circumference.
Immunoglobulin replacement therapy and prophylactic antibiotic use can reduce the frequency of respiratory infections in MDS patients.
Based on the authors' personal experience, some MDS individuals receiving clobazam experienced worsening seizures and decreased alertness and strength.

AAV9-mediated delivery of MECP2 or activation of endogenous MECP2 expression in mouse models increased survival, improved motor phenotype, and reversed the respiratory phenotype to wild-type function.
In MDS mouse models, antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) therapy that decreases MECP2 mRNA/protein levels improved motor function, hypoactivity, anxiety, and social behavior, and eliminated seizures.
A subsequent study using mice expressing two human MECP2 alleles showed that ASO therapy improved function and corrected behavioral deficits in a dose-dependent manner without toxicity.

The miRARE tool incorporates built-in negative feedback regulation to prevent MECP2 overexpression in gene therapy constructs, and the REVEAL Adult study is assessing safety, tolerability, and efficacy of this therapy in adult females with Rett syndrome.

Neurogene's EXACT (expression attenuation via construct tuning) technology fine-tunes transgene expression to reduce MECP2 toxicity risk, and the company received FDA clearance in January 2023 to begin a clinical trial in children with Rett syndrome.

In a mouse study of AAV9-SMN gene therapy for SMA, permanent overexpression of SMN caused sensorimotor deficits, synapse loss, widespread transcriptome abnormalities in dorsal root ganglion neurons, and ultimately neurodegeneration, raising long-term safety concerns relevant to MECP2 gene therapy.
Activation of mast cells may release inflammatory and neurotoxic molecules that contribute to the pathogenesis of autism spectrum disorder.
Many children with autism spectrum disorder present with allergic symptoms despite negative mast cell activation testing.
Protein-protein interaction network and enrichment analysis identified cytokines, mast cell degranulation marker molecules, associated molecular pathways, and receptors relevant to ASD pathogenesis.
A study of 400 mastocytosis patients found ASD co-occurred in 15 cases (3.75%), a rate about 6.75 times higher than the general population ASD prevalence.
In ten children with autism, cerebrospinal fluid TNF-α levels were significantly higher than corresponding serum levels.
Blood IGF1 levels were significantly elevated in men with ASD who had large head circumference, and head size correlated with IGF1 levels.
Gene expression of the pro-inflammatory microRNA-155 is increased in the amygdala of children with ASD.
Expression of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-38 is decreased in children with ASD.

A transcriptome study of 104 human brain cortical tissue samples found a relationship between the M2 microglia activation gene module and a neuronal module, suggesting dysregulated microglial responses that may alter neuronal activity in ASD.

Multiple studies report elevated proinflammatory cytokines (IL-5, IL-8, IL-13, IL-17, IL-12, IL-21, IL-22, IFN-γ, TNF-α, TNF-receptor II, IL-1β, IL-6) alongside decreased anti-inflammatory IL-10 as immune hallmarks of ASD.
IL-1β is associated with impairments in memory and learning in ASD.
IL-6 is linked with stereotyped behavior and affects synapse formation in ASD.
TNF-α levels are positively related to the severity of ASD symptoms.
Higher levels of IL-8 have been associated with more deviant behavior in ASD patients, including hyperactivity, low language and cognitive ability.
Elevated IL-4 in newborns is associated with higher severity of ASD.
Excessive IL-1β in newborns is linked to a milder form of ASD.
Increased levels of IFN-γ, IL-4, and IL-5 in maternal serum are significantly associated with increased ASD risk in the newborn.
Elevated IL-17 has been reported in the serum and in immune cells of children with ASD.
Significantly increased plasma levels of IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, and IL-12p40 were found in ASD children compared to controls.
A meta-analysis found significantly higher concentrations of IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IFN-γ, eotaxin, and MCP-1 in individuals with ASD compared to controls.
An earlier meta-analysis reported significantly decreased levels of TGF-β1 in ASD patients.
An earlier meta-analysis reported a borderline increase in IL-1RA levels in ASD patients.
A more recent meta-analysis found decreased levels of IL-10 in ASD patients.
In a cohort of 400 patients with mastocytosis, 15 also had ASD, an incidence of 3.75 per 100 that is 6.75 times higher than the reported general-population rate.
CSF levels of TNF-α were significantly higher than corresponding serum levels in ten children with autism, potentially affecting cognitive function.
Neurotensin is found to be elevated in young children with autism and has been proposed as a therapeutic target due to its neurotoxic potential.
VIP and CGRP were reported higher in the serum of children with ASD and in those with intellectual disability without ASD, while substance P and NGF levels were similar to controls.
A later study by the same authors found no differences in VIP, CGRP, substance P or NGF levels between autistic and control groups, contradicting their earlier report.
Extracellular mitochondrial DNA, released by mast cells as a danger signal, is found to be increased in the serum of children with ASD.
In a study of 1638 pregnant women, high stress levels during gestation, especially in the second trimester, were associated with higher risk of ASD in offspring at 6 months of age.
Increased levels of IFNγ, IL-4 and IL-5 in maternal serum were significantly associated with an increased ASD risk in the newborn.
Increased levels of IL-4, IL-10 and TNF-α have been measured in the amniotic fluid of fetuses that later developed ASD.

A study noted that neonatal IL-1β was associated with increased ratios of mild or moderate ASD severity, while high levels of IL-4 were linked with severe ASD, showing that peripheral cytokine profiles at birth differ by symptom severity.

Circulating maternal IgE was shown to lead to vertical transmission of atopic dermatitis to the newborn by stimulating fetal mast cells, indicating fetal mast cells are functionally responsive to maternal IgE and allergens.
In a study of six children with autism, four had high urinary serotonin levels.
Elevated platelet serotonin has been reported in more than 40% of autistic patients.

In a double-blind study of 40 ASD children randomized to haloperidol plus cyproheptadine versus haloperidol plus placebo, the combined H1/serotonin receptor antagonist cyproheptadine was associated with significant clinical improvement.
Mutations leading to decreased PTEN (an mTOR inhibitor) result in proliferation of microglia and mast cells, potentially increasing ASD risk through an epigenetic-like mTOR overactivation signal.
Environmental toxins including mercury, PCBs and aluminum can stimulate mast cells, and mercury and aluminum have been associated with symptom severity in children with ASD.
Herbicides such as glyphosate and atrazine have been reported to stimulate mast cells and promote inflammation and neurotoxic effects.

The natural flavonoid luteolin was shown to be more potent than rapamycin in inhibiting TNF release from human mast cells, and has additional anti-inflammatory, neuroprotective and antioxidant effects relevant to ASD.
Quercetin and other flavonoids inhibit the release of histamine, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α and tryptase from normal human mast cells, suggesting potential as ASD treatment candidates.
Cromolyn is a weak inhibitor of allergic activation of human mast cells and has been reported to potentiate, rather than inhibit, histamine release from mast cells.
Tetramethoxyluteolin was found to be a more potent inhibitor of human mast cells than luteolin.
Adolescents with autism show lower baseline levels of cardiac vagal modulation compared to typical expectations.
Supervised Heart Rate Variability Biofeedback (HRVB) produced a delayed (late-emerging) increase in cardiac vagal modulation in adolescents with autism.
Heart rate increased significantly immediately after supervised HRVB, but this effect did not persist at follow-up.
Cortisol levels decreased significantly immediately after supervised HRVB, but this effect did not persist at follow-up.
Supervised HRVB did not produce a significant change in psychosocial functioning in adolescents with autism.
Adolescents with autism reported lower stress symptoms following home-based HRVB training.
Home-based HRVB training was found to be feasible for adolescents with autism.
Adolescents with autism reported lower stress symptoms following home-based HRVB training.
Compliance with home-based HRVB training significantly decreased over the training period.
During social face-to-face interactions, infants' overall looking and mean look duration declined after 3-4 months of age.
Heart rate-defined sustained attention during social face-to-face interactions remained stable across the decline seen in overall looking behavior.
In the first 6 months of life, all measures of sustained attention were greater for video stimuli than for live interaction conditions.
Within a given task context (screen or interaction), sustained attention to social versus nonsocial stimuli did not differ during the first 6 months.
In the second year of life, sustained attention measured by look duration was greater during social videos than during the other three task conditions.
In the second year of life, heart rate-defined sustained attention was greater for social videos than for nonsocial interactions (toy engagement).
Heart rate change during sustained attention was similar across all four task conditions in the second year of life.
Two-sample Mendelian randomization showed that genetic liability to ADHD significantly increases the risk of temporomandibular disorder (TMD).
ADHD genetic liability was also significantly associated with increased risk of TMD as recorded in the Avohilmo primary care dataset.
ADHD genetic liability significantly increases the risk of TMD-related pain.
ADHD genetic liability significantly increases the risk of TMD muscular pain linked with fibromyalgia.
Genetic liability to Tourette's Disorder was not significantly associated with TMD muscular pain linked with fibromyalgia after Bonferroni correction.
No significant causal relationship was found between genetic liability to Autism Spectrum Disorder and temporomandibular disorder.
No significant causal relationship was found between genetic liability to Tourette's Disorder and temporomandibular disorder overall.
Reverse Mendelian randomization found no evidence that TMD, TMD (including avohilmo), TMD-related pain, or TMD muscular pain linked with fibromyalgia causally increase risk of ADHD, ASD, or TD.
A two-step mediation analysis found that vitamin D does not mediate the causal effect of ADHD on TMD risk.
One of the 20 children (5%) born to mothers with systemic sclerosis was diagnosed with Autism Spectrum Disorder.
Aside from one case of ASD, all children born to SSc mothers showed normal neurological examination, cognitive profile, and adaptive functioning.
There was a notable discrepancy between parents' and children's own perception of quality of life, with children reporting more compromised quality of life than their parents perceived.
Two of the 20 children (10%) were found to be at risk for internalizing behavioral problems.
Three of the 20 children (15%) were found to be at risk for externalizing behavioral problems.
One of the 20 children (5%) was found to be at risk for both internalizing and externalizing behavioral problems combined.
Five of the 20 children (25%) were found to be at risk for problems in social and out-of-school activities.
Among 11 children evaluated for psychological functioning, three (28%) were at risk for anxiety disorders.
Among 11 children evaluated for psychological functioning, one (9%) was at risk for depressive disorders.
Somatic disturbances risk was found in 4 of 11 children (36%) assessed for psychological functioning.
Emotional fragility and poor competence in processing emotional experiences were observed in 9 of 13 assessed children (70%).

Overall, children born to SSc mothers showed normal cognitive and adaptive abilities but increased vulnerability to psychopathological problems and social/emotional fragility, possibly related to the burden of maternal chronic disease.
Neonatal abnormal heart rate characteristics (measured via HeRO scores) in the first 28 days of life were strongly correlated with ASD symptom severity at 12 months corrected age.
In a regression model adjusting for birth gestational age and birth weight, neonatal abnormal HRCs remained a significant, unique predictor of ASD outcomes at 12 months.

Elevated abnormal negative thermal gradients (peripheral temperature exceeding central temperature) in the neonatal period were associated with ASD symptoms at 12 months, though the association was weaker than for HRCs.
Birth gestational age and birth weight were also significantly associated with 12-month ASD symptoms in this VPT cohort.
Developmental delays in this VPT cohort were not apparent early but emerged by 12 months, when over half the sample showed social-communication delays and exceeded the clinical cutoff for ASD risk.

Across the full VPT cohort in the first 28 days of life, average HeRO scores were mildly elevated (just above the abnormality threshold of 1) and infants showed abnormal negative thermal gradients on about 20% of days.
Prior literature reports that very preterm birth (<32 weeks gestation) is associated with a 10-fold increase in the rate of autism spectrum disorder.
Prior literature reports that extremely preterm birth (<28 weeks gestation) is associated with a 20-fold increase in the rate of autism spectrum disorder.
Age at death among COVID-19 autopsy cases was significantly higher during the 2020 Wuhan-variant waves than during the 2021 alpha-variant wave.
Disease duration before death was significantly longer in autopsies from the 2021 alpha-variant wave compared to the 2020 Wuhan-variant waves.
Among COVID-19 autopsies with COVID-19 as underlying cause of death, ARDS was the immediate cause of death in half of cases.

Acute diffuse alveolar damage, (micro)thrombi, and alveolar histiocytes were significantly more frequently reported in pulmonary pathology from 2020 (Wuhan wave) than 2021 (alpha wave), while organizing DAD was significantly more common in 2021.
(Micro)thrombi were found in over half of full-body COVID-19 autopsies, most commonly localized in the lungs.
Myocarditis, pericarditis, and cardiac amyloidosis were observed as cardiac comorbidities in COVID-19 autopsies at varying low rates.
Acute tubular necrosis of the kidney was observed in 10% of COVID-19 autopsies.

Over half of COVID-19 brain autopsies showed a 'COVID-19 encephalitis' pattern of microglial activation with nodule formation and T-lymphocyte infiltration, without significant demyelination, necrosis, or axonal damage.
Intracranial (micro)thrombi were found in a minority of COVID-19 brain autopsies, localized in the pituitary gland, pons, hippocampus, and thalamus.
Post-COVID-19 non-autopsy lung tissue more often showed fibrosis than acute COVID-19 lung tissue, consistent with long COVID pulmonary sequelae.
Chronic histiocytic intervillositis was reported in 4.4% of all COVID-19-related placental pathology reports, a much higher rate than the general population baseline.
Perniosis (chilblain-like skin lesions) was reported in a notable minority of skin biopsies/excisions from COVID-19 patients.

Thrombi were reported not only in the lungs but also in other organs including heart, kidneys, and intestines in both autopsy and clinical-phase histopathology reports, supporting a systemic pro-coagulant effect of COVID-19.
Only a small fraction of Dutch COVID-19 deaths underwent autopsy during the study period, limiting representativeness of autopsy-derived pathology findings.

The Palga registry's automated patient-tracking feature identified a large proportion of post-COVID-19 pathology reports that did not themselves mention prior COVID-19 status, demonstrating utility for long-term post-viral surveillance.

In a subgroup echocardiographic analysis of the same RCT, global longitudinal strain increased in both HBOT and sham groups, but only the HBOT group showed a significant increase in global work efficacy, with 62.5% achieving normal GLS versus 38.4% in the sham group.
