The total COMPASS-31 score significantly increased from pre-infection baseline to 6 months post-COVID in the entire cohort, indicating worsening autonomic function over time.
At 6 months, patients who developed Long-COVID autonomic syndrome (subgroup A) had significantly higher COMPASS-31 total scores than those who did not (subgroup B).

Orthostatic intolerance was the most common autonomic symptom domain reported by subgroup A at 6 months, having started during acute infection, transiently improved at 3 months, then markedly worsened again by 6 months.
The vasomotor autonomic symptom domain was significantly altered only during the acute phase of COVID-19 (T0), without persisting to later time points.

The gastrointestinal, bladder, and pupillomotor autonomic domains were significantly altered at 6 months compared to pre-infection baseline, indicating long-term autonomic dysfunction beyond the acute phase.

VOSS-assessed orthostatic symptoms were reduced at 6 months compared to 1 month, both while supine and during standing, indicating global improvement independent of the gravitational stimulus.
WAI total score was markedly reduced at 1 month compared to pre-infection baseline and remained reduced through 6 months in the entire cohort and in both subgroups.

Patients who developed Long-COVID autonomic syndrome (subgroup A) had substantially longer sick leave (third interquartile 25-99 days) than those without the syndrome (subgroup B, third interquartile <10 days).

There was an inverse relationship between autonomic symptom intensity (COMPASS-31) and work ability (WAI) at 6 months, and this inverse relationship was stronger among patients who developed Long-COVID autonomic syndrome (subgroup A).

The prevalence of specific learning disabilities among NF1 patients is markedly higher than in the general population.
A substantial fraction of individuals with NF1 display behaviors broadly resembling autism spectrum disorder.
Loss of dNf1 in Drosophila significantly impairs associative learning and memory, mirroring human NF1 cognitive deficits.

Nf1+/- mice present elevated GABAergic neurotransmission that is reversible by Ras signaling inhibition, which rescues their cognitive deficits, paralleling the fly findings.
Contrary to earlier reports, elevating cAMP did not reverse the associative learning deficit in dNf1-mutant flies.

Loss of dNf1 causes synaptic overgrowth at the larval neuromuscular junction, engaging the cAMP pathway rather than the Ras-GAP activity.

dNf1 regulates circadian rhythms by modulating cAMP levels in clock neurons, affecting expression of clock genes and downstream targets.

IGF-1 rose significantly during 6 months of GH treatment and returned to near-baseline levels 3 months after treatment was stopped, confirming treatment compliance and pharmacodynamic response.

Peak glucagon-stimulated plasma growth hormone secretion was not significantly different between screening and 12 months, indicating that 9 months of exogenous GH treatment did not alter the underlying endogenous secretory capacity.

Formal cognitive testing (MoCA) showed only a non-significant trend toward improvement after 6 months of GH treatment, though the visuospatial/executive functioning subscale showed near-significant improvement.
Six months of GH treatment did not significantly change resting energy expenditure, respiratory quotient, BMI, or body composition in PASC subjects.

GH treatment significantly increased walking distance at subject-perceived submaximal effort (25% and 50%) and total cumulative distance in a modified 6-minute walk test, while distance at 100% effort was not significantly changed.

GH treatment did not affect maximal leg extension torque, physical endurance, or post-exercise torque recovery, but was associated with increased isometric and isokinetic torque production at submaximal (25%) subjective effort.
Subjective whole-body fatigue ratings on a 0-10 scale were significantly lower after GH treatment, both before and after completion of the leg extension exercise protocol.

The authors interpret the pattern of symptom improvement during treatment and reversion after withdrawal as consistent with GH acting as an adjunct treatment that masks neurologic symptoms without curing the underlying cause, similar to what is seen in TBI-associated brain injury fatigue and altered cognition (BIAFAC).
A separate study of post-infectious ME/CFS reported a similar preference for reduced physical effort, paralleling the submaximal-effort improvements seen with GH treatment in this PASC cohort.
Women are reported to be approximately twice as likely as men to report PASC symptoms, consistent with the disproportionately female composition of this trial's cohort.
Patients reported reduced fatigue at least one month after sequential bilateral stellate ganglion block treatment.
Post-exertional worsening of symptoms following mental and physical activity was reduced after stellate ganglion block treatment.
Memory problems were reduced after stellate ganglion block treatment.
Problems with concentration were reduced after stellate ganglion block treatment.
Sleep problems were reduced after stellate ganglion block treatment.
Anxiety symptoms were reduced after stellate ganglion block treatment.
Depression symptoms were reduced after stellate ganglion block treatment.
Loss of taste did not respond to stellate ganglion block treatment in some individuals, possibly reflecting structural nerve damage from infection.
Loss of taste in some patients did not improve after stellate ganglion block treatment.
Loss of smell in some patients did not improve after stellate ganglion block treatment.

The paper title indicates a study evaluating whether administering RNase has an impact on severe fatigue in patients with post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (long COVID), but no outcome direction or effect size is stated in the available text.
RR interval was significantly lower in long-COVID-19 syndrome patients compared to controls.
RMSSD, a marker of parasympathetic/vagal activity, was significantly lower in long-COVID-19 syndrome patients compared to controls.
SDNN, reflecting overall heart rate variability, was significantly lower in long-COVID-19 syndrome patients compared to controls.
The parasympathetic nervous system (PNS) index was significantly lower in long-COVID-19 syndrome patients compared to controls.
Low-frequency (LF) HRV power was significantly lower in long-COVID-19 syndrome patients compared to controls.
High-frequency (HF) HRV power, associated with vagal tone, was significantly lower in long-COVID-19 syndrome patients compared to controls.
Total HRV power was significantly lower in long-COVID-19 syndrome patients compared to controls.
SD1 (Poincaré plot short-term HRV index) was significantly lower in long-COVID-19 syndrome patients compared to controls.
The heart rate variability parameter SD2 was significantly lower in long-COVID-19 syndrome patients compared to controls.
Resting heart rate was significantly higher in long-COVID-19 syndrome patients compared to controls, remaining significant after adjustment for RR intervals.
The HRV-derived stress index was significantly elevated in long-COVID-19 syndrome patients compared to controls, remaining significant after adjustment for RR intervals.
The sympathetic nervous system (SNS) index was significantly elevated in long-COVID-19 syndrome patients compared to controls, remaining significant after adjustment for RR intervals.
Peak VO2 (cardiorespiratory fitness) partially mediated the reduction in RMSSD observed in long-COVID-19 syndrome patients, accounting for 24.4% of the effect.
Peak VO2 (cardiorespiratory fitness) partially mediated the reduction in SDNN observed in long-COVID-19 syndrome patients, accounting for 25.1% of the effect.
Low cardiorespiratory fitness (peak VO2) and exercise intolerance are common features of long-COVID-19 syndrome and are linked to dysautonomia.
A 15-day course of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir did not significantly improve pooled severity of the six core PASC symptoms at 10 weeks compared with placebo-ritonavir.
Participants in the NMV/r group had higher odds of a more severe rating of their most bothersome symptom at 10 and 15 weeks compared with the placebo group.

Brain fog was the only core symptom for which the change in severity across 15 weeks differed significantly between groups, with the NMV/r group showing decreased odds of experiencing mild or no brain fog symptoms.

There were no significant between-group differences in the proportion of participants experiencing symptom relief at 5, 10, or 15 weeks, alleviation of all core symptoms at 10 weeks, or time to relief of individual and most bothersome symptoms.
PROMIS physical function, fatigue, dyspnea, and cognitive ability change scores, as well as PGIS and PGIC scores, showed no significant between-group difference at 10 weeks.
The 1-minute sit-to-stand test and orthostatic vital signs showed no significant between-group differences from baseline at 10 weeks.
None of the baseline stool specimens from PASC participants had detectable SARS-CoV-2 RNA, providing no evidence of a gut viral reservoir in this cohort.
Dysgeusia was markedly more common in the NMV/r group than the placebo group during the 15-day treatment period.
Serious adverse events were rare and similar between groups, with those in the NMV/r group assessed as unrelated to study drug and the single PBO/r serious event assessed as possibly related.
The trial was stopped early for futility after an interim analysis showed conditional power below the prespecified 10% threshold, resulting in a smaller-than-planned sample size.
Reported COVID-19 reinfection rates during the study period were similar between the NMV/r and placebo groups.
At enrollment, fatigue was reported by all participants and brain fog by 95.5%, confirming these as the most prevalent PASC symptoms in this cohort.

Among participants with laboratory-confirmed (RNA+) prior SARS-CoV-2 infection, antibody (serology) status was not associated with differences in symptoms, number of symptoms, or health domains consistent with long COVID.
Among antibody-positive participants, dyspnea prevalence did not differ significantly between those with RNA-confirmed infection and those RNA-negative or untested.

Compared with true controls without prior COVID-19, participants with confirmed COVID-19 infection and antibody response (Ab+/RNA+) reported worse physical health, cognitive function, and fatigue, and a higher prevalence of palpitations and headaches affecting work function.

In secondary analyses, Ab+/RNA+ participants reported worse physical health and more fatigue, diarrhea, sleep disturbance, dyspnea, chest pain, pain interference, neuropathic pain, nociceptive pain, and overall pain compared with Ab+/RNA-negative participants.
Contrary to expectation, the group without RNA or antibody evidence but reporting prior COVID-19 reported more impairment (e.g., mental health) than the Ab+/RNA+ group.
Participants who were hospitalized during their initial COVID-19 infection reported more severe long COVID symptoms than those who were not hospitalized.
There was no association between COVID-19 vaccination status and physical or mental health in the overall sample.
In sensitivity analyses using continuous T scores, health domain scores for the study groups were close to pre-COVID-19 US general population norms.
Among RNA-positive participants, physical health T-scores were worse (lower) in the antibody-positive group than the antibody-negative group, while other health domains were similar.

Among the subset with antibody testing within 3 months of RNA testing, no difference in fair/poor physical or mental health was found between antibody-positive and antibody-negative RNA-positive groups.
Adjusting for comorbidity burden (modified Charlson index) did not substantively change the association between antibody status and symptoms.
Participants with an EHR-documented long COVID diagnosis at one site reported a significantly higher mean number of symptoms than those without such a diagnosis.

Among people with prior laboratory-confirmed or self-reported COVID-19, about half reported persistent symptoms, nearly a third recurrent symptoms, and roughly a quarter new symptoms on a 31-symptom checklist.
Among people with persistent symptoms consistent with long COVID, fatigue, brain fog, and dyspnea were the most commonly reported.
A higher proportion of the Ab+/RNA+ group reported any persistent symptoms than the antibody-positive/RNA-negative, antibody-negative/RNA-positive, or true control groups.

Patients with multiple sclerosis and fatigue showed greater hypometabolism (via FDG-PET) than long COVID fatigue patients and COVID-recovered controls in the caudate nucleus, putamen, thalamus, and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, but not the globus pallidus.
No significant differences in glucose metabolism were found between long COVID patients with fatigue and COVID-recovered controls across the studied brain regions.

Standardized uptake values (SUVs) were symmetrical between brain hemispheres in all groups studied, suggesting fatigue may relate to global or network-level rather than hemisphere-specific alterations.
About one fifth of surveyed students showed moderate Internet dependence, while most did not report high fatigue levels.
Students with long COVID symptoms showed significantly higher fatigue impact scores than those without long COVID symptoms.
A positive correlation between Internet dependence level and fatigue was found, and this correlation was stronger among students with long COVID symptoms.
Four weeks of Myelophil administration significantly reduced overall fatigue severity as measured by the mKCFQ11 primary outcome.
Both physical and mental fatigue subscales of the mKCFQ11 showed marked reductions after Myelophil treatment.
Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory (MFI-20) scores decreased significantly after Myelophil treatment.
Fatigue VAS scores decreased significantly after 4 weeks of Myelophil treatment.
Brain fog VAS scores decreased significantly after Myelophil treatment.
Quality of life scores (SF-12) improved significantly after 4 weeks of Myelophil treatment.
Plasma cortisol levels increased significantly after 4 weeks of Myelophil treatment, potentially reflecting HPA axis recalibration.
Improvement in mKCFQ11 scores showed a strong positive correlation with improvement in MFI-20 scores.
Improvement in mKCFQ11 scores showed a strong positive correlation with improvement in Fatigue VAS scores.
Improvement in mKCFQ11 scores showed a moderate-to-strong positive correlation with improvement in Brain Fog VAS scores.
Improvement in mKCFQ11 scores showed a strong negative correlation with improvement in SF-12 quality-of-life scores.
The rise in cortisol levels did not significantly correlate with the reduction in mKCFQ11 fatigue scores.
Myelophil was well tolerated with only one mild adverse event (indigestion) reported and no abnormalities in liver or kidney function tests.
The proportion of participants with ME/CFS-level fatigue severity (mKCFQ11 >60) dropped markedly after Myelophil treatment.
Female outpatients had a significantly higher Fatigue Assessment Scale (FAS) score than male outpatients after acute SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Fatigue prevalence after acute SARS-CoV-2 infection was substantially higher in women than men.
Men reported significantly better mental and physical health than women as measured by the VR-12 questionnaire.
Multiple correspondence analysis of 42 acute SARS-CoV-2 symptoms identified seven distinct symptom clusters representing impairment of specific body regions or functions.
In univariate models, the acute symptom cluster of eyes, hair, skin and stings in arms or legs showed the strongest positive association with subsequent Long COVID fatigue severity.
The acute symptom clusters of ear/nose/throat symptoms and loss of taste/smell showed the weakest associations with later fatigue severity.

After mutual adjustment for all seven symptom clusters, only the cognitive and mental symptoms cluster during acute infection remained independently associated with higher Long COVID fatigue severity.
The association between the cognitive/mental symptoms cluster and FAS score was significant in both men and women in sex-stratified models, with a somewhat stronger effect in women.
In the mutually adjusted logistic regression model, each additional cognitive/mental symptom during acute infection was associated with a 42% increase in the odds of later fatigue.
After sex stratification, the association between the cognitive/mental symptoms cluster and fatigue risk remained statistically significant only in women.
In men, the association between the cognitive/mental symptoms cluster and later fatigue risk was not statistically significant after sex stratification.
Interaction terms between symptom clusters and sex were included in all regression models but never reached statistical significance.
Overall, 35.8% of outpatients experienced fatigue at a median of 240 days after acute SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Health care workers with Long COVID showed significantly lower detectability of the spontaneous systolic blood pressure oscillation at 0.1 Hz (Mayer wave - baroreflex arc) during spontaneous breathing compared to never-infected and fully-recovered COVID-19 workers.
Health care workers with Long COVID reported significantly more psychosomatic symptoms than never-infected and fully-recovered controls, assessed via validated questionnaires.

During slow-paced breathing, the detectability of the systolic pressure oscillation at 0.1 Hz increased in Long COVID HCWs to a level close to that of controls, indicating improved baroreflex sensitivity.
Aside from the Mayer wave/baroreflex measure, no other heart rate variability parameters differed significantly among Long COVID, never-infected, and fully-recovered HCWs.
16.4% of Long-COVID patients (11 of 95) had anemia 3-6 months after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Mean hemoglobin concentration increased by 0.3 mmol/L at 3-6 months post-infection compared to levels measured during the acute phase of COVID-19.
A 1 mmol/L greater increase in hemoglobin over follow-up was associated with lower odds of experiencing fatigue in Long-COVID patients.
No correlation was observed between hemoglobin concentration and any of the inflammatory blood biomarkers examined in Long-COVID patients.
Among SARS-CoV-2 infected patients with cancer, 79.6% (39/49) developed long COVID, a substantially higher rate than reported in the general population.
The most commonly reported long COVID symptoms in this cancer cohort were myalgia, fatigue and disrupted sleep.
Linear mixed model analysis found no significant effect of time, COVID-19 status, or their interaction on QoL, functional/symptom, HADS, or CFQ scores over the one-year follow-up.
A BMI above 25.0 was associated with up to a 4.5-fold increased risk of developing long COVID after SARS-CoV-2 infection, though this only reached a trend towards significance.

Cancer patients who developed long COVID had significantly worse scores on all assessed clinical outcome scales, except the HADS Anxiety subscale, compared to infected patients who did not develop long COVID.
Among long COVID patients, males reported significantly higher HADS Depression Scores than females.
Current or former smokers with long COVID reported higher HADS Depression Scores than patients who never smoked, a trend towards significance.
Long COVID patients with comorbidities tended to report more long COVID symptoms than patients without comorbidities.
Long COVID patients with metastatic cancer reported lower quality of life than those with non-metastasized cancer.
In long COVID patients, a higher number of comorbidities correlated with a greater number of long COVID symptoms, at trend-level significance.
In long COVID patients, a higher number of comorbidities correlated with higher EORTC Symptom Scores.
In long COVID patients, a higher number of symptoms was negatively correlated with quality of life.
A moderate positive correlation was found between pre-infection anti-S1 IgG SARS-CoV-2 antibody titers and post-infection cognitive failures (CFQ) scores in long COVID patients.
No significant correlations were observed between anti-S1 IgG SARS-CoV-2 antibody titers and outcome measures other than CFQ scores (e.g., QoL, HADS, symptom counts) in long COVID patients.
Older age was a significant predictor of long COVID symptoms among people with spinal cord injury.
Higher BMI was a significant predictor of long COVID symptoms in people with spinal cord injury.
A higher ASIA motor score was a significant predictor of long COVID symptoms in spinal cord injury patients.
A longer duration since spinal cord injury was a significant predictor of developing long COVID symptoms.
Fatigue was the longest-lasting long COVID symptom in people with spinal cord injury, persisting on average over a year.
Musculoskeletal pain was the second longest-lasting long COVID symptom in this SCI cohort.
Depression symptoms in long COVID SCI patients with pre-existing depression persisted for over a year on average.
Limitations in activities of daily living persisted for a prolonged average duration among SCI patients with long COVID.
Work participation problems persisted for a prolonged average duration among SCI patients with long COVID.
Total ASIA motor score was significantly higher in SCI patients with long COVID compared to those without.
Total ASIA sensory score was significantly higher in SCI patients with long COVID compared to those without.
Remaining years of life lost to premature death (YLL) were lower for long COVID SCI patients than for non-long COVID SCI patients, reflecting their older age and shorter remaining life expectancy.
Overall years lived with disability (YLD) differed significantly between non-long COVID and long COVID SCI patients, being lower in the long COVID group.
SCI patients with long COVID were on average substantially older than those without long COVID symptoms.
Twelve distinct long COVID symptoms were identified in SCI patients using the C19-YRS, spanning physical, cognitive, and mental health domains.
A cited prior study found no increased mortality risk from COVID-19 among people with a history of spinal cord injury, though long COVID symptoms may still worsen disability after infection.
Motor deficit was the most prevalent symptom, reported by 95.29% of evaluated long-COVID patients.
Fatigue was reported by 94.12% of patients and was the symptom most commonly co-occurring with other symptoms.
Weakness, along with respiratory symptoms and cognitive deficits, was reported by 76.47% of patients, less frequently than motor deficit and fatigue.
The number of concurrent symptoms (most patients reported 5-8, usually including fatigue) did not correlate with health-related quality of life as measured by the SF-12.
COVID-19 vaccination status did not significantly affect SF-12 quality-of-life scores or the number of reported symptoms in long-COVID patients.
Overall subjective health status improved during rehabilitation with medium to large effect sizes.
Participation restrictions and physical quality-of-life impairments continued to decrease during the 12-month follow-up after rehabilitation.
Fatigue and mental health impairments (anxiety, depression) worsened during the 12-month follow-up period after rehabilitation ended, though still below admission levels.

The number of reported Long COVID symptoms decreased from baseline to 12-month follow-up in both IR (16 to 15) and FuR (14 symptoms at baseline) groups, with IR patients reporting significantly more symptoms at baseline than FuR patients.
In the follow-up rehabilitation (FuR) group, word-finding difficulty increased markedly from baseline to 12-month follow-up.
Days of incapacity to work in the prior six months decreased significantly from baseline to the 12-month follow-up.
Occupational performance and subjectively perceived ability to work improved significantly from baseline through the 12-month follow-up.
Twelve months after rehabilitation, a substantial minority of patients in both groups still had an increased risk of leaving the labor market prematurely (26.2% FuR, 33.1% IR).
Among IR patients, the proportion considering applying for a disability pension increased significantly to 20.6% over follow-up.
There were no statistically significant differences in the SPE (subjective employment prognosis) scale between the IR and FuR groups or over time.
FuR patients rated satisfaction with rehabilitation as good to excellent more often than IR patients (98.4% vs 88.4%).
FuR patients rated their perceived rehabilitation success as good to excellent more often than IR patients (93.7% vs 77.3%).
IR patients used rehabilitation aftercare more often than FuR patients in the year after rehabilitation (64.1% vs 48.8%), though satisfaction with aftercare was higher among FuR patients.
More IR patients than FuR patients reported that they missed something during rehabilitation aftercare.
Despite most patients failing to reach their goal of increasing subjective work ability, the large majority (88%) returned to work within the year following rehabilitation.
FuR patients took significantly longer than IR patients to return to their first day of work after rehabilitation.

The inpatient rehabilitation (IR) group, enrolled mostly after mild/moderate COVID-19, was predominantly female, while the follow-up rehabilitation (FuR) group, enrolled after severe/critical COVID-19 and hospitalization, was predominantly male.

Initial COVID-19 severity differed markedly between groups: IR patients had mostly mild/moderate disease, while FuR patients had mostly severe/critical disease requiring more hospitalization, ICU admission and ventilation.
In the FuR group, participants who dropped out of the study had a less severe initial COVID-19 course than those who remained.
14 days of hydrogen-rich water consumption produced a significantly greater percent reduction in Fatigue Severity Scale score than placebo water in Long-COVID patients.
HRW did not significantly improve dyspnea (mMRC score) compared to placebo water in Long-COVID patients.
HRW consumption produced a significantly greater percent increase in 6-Minute Walk Test distance than placebo water, indicating improved cardiorespiratory endurance.
HRW consumption produced a significantly greater percent increase in 30-second Chair Stand Test repetitions than placebo water, indicating improved musculoskeletal function.
Within the HRW group, greater fatigue alleviation was significantly associated with greater improvement in musculoskeletal function (30s-CST performance).
No significant association was found between percent change in fatigue (FSS score) and percent change in cardiorespiratory endurance (6MWT distance) within the HRW group.
Among Long-COVID patients with difficulty sleeping, HRW produced a significantly greater percent reduction in PSQI score (improved sleep quality) than placebo water.
Among Long-COVID patients with anxiety/depression, HRW did not significantly improve depression, anxiety, or stress scores (DASS-21) compared to placebo water.

Post-COVID patients with persistent fatigue showed a marked reduction of TMS-evoked beta frequency oscillatory activity in both the left primary motor area and the supplementary motor area compared to healthy controls.
Lower levels of TMS-evoked beta oscillations from the supplementary motor area were significantly correlated with higher fatigue severity scores on the Fatigue Rating Scale in post-COVID patients.
Among 1905 hospitalized COVID-19 patients during the Omicron wave, 657 (34.5%) reported long COVID symptoms 4-8 weeks after discharge.
The most frequently reported long COVID symptoms were fatigue or muscle weakness (16.8%), sleep difficulties (11.1%), and cough (9.5%).
Older age was independently associated with increased risk of developing long COVID in multivariate logistic regression and was retained in the final LASSO-selected prediction model.
A history of diabetes was independently associated with increased risk of long COVID and was included as a predictor in the final nomogram model.
A history of chronic kidney disease was independently associated with increased risk of long COVID and was included as a predictor in the final nomogram model.
Vaccination status conferred a significant protective effect against development of long COVID, with unvaccinated patients comprising the largest share (46.5%) of the cohort.

Higher interleukin-6 levels at admission were independently associated with increased risk of long COVID and were retained in the final prediction model, consistent with IL-6's role in driving cytokine storm and inflammatory/coagulation cascades.
Elevated procalcitonin at admission was independently associated with increased long COVID risk and included in the final prediction model.
Leukocyte count at admission was an independent predictor of long COVID risk, with reduced white blood cell levels suggested to reflect high viral load or compromised immune function.
Lymphocyte count at admission was an independent predictor of long COVID risk in the final model, with reduced lymphocytes hypothesized to reflect T-cell involvement in SARS-CoV-2 pathology.

Elevated D-dimer at admission was independently associated with increased long COVID risk and included in the final prediction model, consistent with prior identification of D-dimer as a marker of COVID-19 severity via coagulation activation.

A nomogram combining age, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, vaccination status, IL-6, procalcitonin, leukocytes, lymphocytes, and D-dimer predicted long COVID risk with AUC 0.762 in the training cohort and 0.713 in the validation cohort, with good calibration and clinical net benefit on decision curve analysis.
Of 21 people who expressed interest in the theatre-based wellness programme, 20 (95%) participated and 19 (90%) completed the full 6-week programme.
Participants attended an average of 4.8 of 6 sessions, with just over half completing all six sessions.
Number of sessions completed did not differ significantly between in-person (mean 5.1) and online (mean 4.5) delivery modes.
Participants who chose in-person delivery were significantly older (mean 53.1 years) than those who chose online delivery (mean 38.3 years); no other baseline characteristics differed between modes.
Nearly all participants (94%) met criteria for post-exertional malaise at baseline, despite none meeting scoring criteria for ME/CFS diagnosis.
At baseline, participants reported relatively severe chronic fatigue symptoms, along with moderate functional limitations and respiratory dysfunction outside the normal range.
Self-rated health index (EQ-5D) improved significantly from baseline to 8-week follow-up after participation in the wellness programme.
Chronic fatigue syndrome scores decreased significantly from baseline to 8-week follow-up after the programme.

Descriptive improvements were observed in generalised anxiety, depressive symptoms, loneliness, dyspnoea, respiratory dysfunction, mental well-being and social support after the programme, but these changes were not statistically significant in exploratory paired analyses, likely due to being underpowered.
Qualitative interviews indicated the programme fostered a sense of community and new peer relationships that reduced feelings of isolation and loneliness among participants with long COVID.
Some participants, particularly in the online group, found drama-based exercises self-conscious-inducing or inappropriate, representing a barrier to engagement with the programme.

Fluctuating long COVID symptoms such as fatigue and brain fog interfered with some participants' ability to engage with programme activities, including concentrating and travelling to in-person sessions.
Online participants reported connectivity and sound-quality problems as a barrier to engagement, along with reduced feelings of connection to the group compared with in-person delivery.

Almost half of participants found out about the wellness programme through a healthcare professional (long COVID clinics, GPs, or other clinicians), suggesting feasibility of embedding such creative health programmes within clinical referral/social prescribing pathways.

Acute-phase serum GDF-15 was numerically higher in patients who later developed long COVID and showed moderate predictive ability for long COVID onset, though the group difference was not statistically significant.
At three months post-onset, serum GDF-15 levels no longer differed between the recovered and long COVID groups, suggesting reduced diagnostic utility in the chronic phase.
Acute-phase serum FGF-21 did not significantly differ between groups and showed poor predictive ability for subsequent long COVID.

At three months post-onset, serum FGF-21 was significantly higher in the long COVID group than the recovered group, with good diagnostic performance, though absolute levels remained within the physiological range.
Serum IL-6 levels did not significantly differ between the recovered and long COVID groups in either the acute phase or at three months.
Serum TNF-α levels did not significantly differ between the recovered and long COVID groups in either the acute phase or at three months.
Serum IL-8 levels did not significantly differ between the recovered and long COVID groups in either the acute phase or at three months.
Serum IL-10 (anti-inflammatory) levels did not significantly differ between the recovered and long COVID groups in either the acute phase or at three months.
Acute-phase serum LDH levels did not significantly differ between the recovered and long COVID groups.
Serum CRP levels did not significantly differ between the recovered and long COVID groups in either the acute phase or at three months.
Acute-phase total lymphocyte count did not significantly differ between the recovered and long COVID groups.

Serum VCAM-1 (endothelial marker) levels did not significantly differ between the recovered and long COVID groups in either the acute phase or at three months, despite being elevated overall in both phases.
Serum syndecan-1 (endothelial glycocalyx marker) levels did not significantly differ between the recovered and long COVID groups in either the acute phase or at three months.
Acute-phase D-dimer levels did not significantly differ between the recovered and long COVID groups.
An estimated 65 million people worldwide have suffered from long COVID, with 10-20% of COVID-19 infections resulting in long COVID.

In a cohort of previously healthy COVID-19 patients, the long COVID subgroup most frequently reported weakness, impaired exercise tolerance, palpitations, concentration/memory disturbances, and chest pain.
Severe COVID-19 course and arthralgia during acute infection were identified as risk factors for developing long COVID in previously healthy patients.
Long COVID cluster symptoms were far more common in patients hospitalized in general wards or ICU than in non-hospitalized patients.
Females showed a higher frequency of long COVID cluster symptoms than males at 3 months post-infection, though the frequency declined by 12 months in both sexes.
IHME data indicate long COVID was diagnosed in females almost twice as often as males, with respiratory problems, fatigue/mood/pain, and cognitive problems as the main symptom clusters.
Fatigue and anxiety/depression were commonly reported at 6 months after hospital discharge, with risk of increased morbidity linked to age, female sex, and multimorbidity.
Myalgia, anxiety, and fatigue as long COVID symptoms were reported more frequently in women, and pre-existing diabetes or hypertension increased severity of long COVID symptoms.
One month after hospital discharge, COVID-19 patients with diabetes and hypertension had a higher incidence of cough and chronic fatigue than those without these comorbidities.
Musculoskeletal complaints among university students and employees significantly increased during the COVID-19 pandemic compared to before it, as measured by VAS.
Among 89 former hospitalized COVID-19 patients, neurocognitive symptoms were diagnosed in 60% at 6 months post-discharge, with fatigue and brain fog being most common.
Brain fog persisted 12 months post hospital discharge in nearly 1 in 5 former COVID-19 patients.
About 44% of former COVID-19 patients had at least one persistent symptom 4 weeks after infection onset, most commonly fatigue and alopecia.
Fatigue prevalence in a South Korean long COVID cohort fluctuated over time, being 22.7% at 6 months, 17.4% at 12 months, and 34.8% at 24 months post-discharge, and did not decline monotonically.

Long COVID substantially impaired everyday functioning, with over half of a large UK clinic sample scoring in the severe-impairment range on the Work and Social Adjustment Scale, driven mainly by fatigue.
Long COVID patients had markedly lower overall quality-of-life scores than healthy controls, measured by SF-36.
Self-reported health scores among long COVID patients declined from 3 to 12 months post-discharge as symptom frequency increased, in a Caribbean primary-care cohort.
Suicide attempt rates increased sharply in 2021 among 13-24 year-olds compared to 2020, more than in older age categories.
Women were reported to be at greater risk of suicide attempts than men during the pandemic, with rates rising 20-30% relative to pre-pandemic levels.

A meta-analysis of 37 studies found significantly increased suicidal ideation prevalence and more prevalent suicide attempts during the pandemic in both clinical and non-clinical populations, though pooled estimates varied by population and design.

Among elderly Polish respondents, borderline depression, depressive symptoms, and loneliness were prevalent during the pandemic, with widowed/single status and female sex associated with greater loneliness.
In a cross-sectional survey of Polish residents, depression and anxiety were prevalent, and younger age was positively correlated with anxiety, depression, and loneliness.
Anxiety and depression symptoms increased markedly after COVID-19 infection compared to pre-infection levels in Italian and Austrian cohorts assessed ~79 days post-infection.
In a study using SF-36 and EQ-5D-5L, reduced quality-of-life scores after COVID-19 (pain/discomfort, anxiety, usual activities, physical health domains) were significantly associated with female sex.

Long COVID may affect up to 43% of people who had COVID-19 overall and more than 60% of those who had severe infection, with approximately 36 million people affected across the WHO European Region during the first 3 years of the pandemic.
45.6% of recovered COVID-19 patients (252/553) developed long COVID syndrome, defined as persistent symptoms beyond four weeks post-diagnosis.
Presence of any pre-existing comorbidity was significantly associated with increased odds of long COVID syndrome in univariate analysis.
A previous history of hypertension was significantly associated with long COVID syndrome in both univariate and multivariate regression analyses.
Unvaccinated individuals had higher odds of NOT developing long COVID syndrome, implying vaccination was associated with a higher likelihood of long COVID in this cohort.
Smoking history was significantly associated with the presence of long COVID syndrome.
Persistent fatigue was the most commonly reported symptom among long COVID patients, affecting 33.3% (84/252) of the group.
Persistent dry cough was the second most common symptom in long COVID patients, reported by 28.5% of participants.
Cognitive symptoms including trouble concentrating or forgetfulness were reported in 14.6% of long COVID participants, along with chest pain (6.7%) and dizziness (5.1%).

Respiratory health, assessed by the St. George's Respiratory Questionnaire, did not differ significantly between participants with and without long COVID, although a higher proportion of poor respiratory outcomes was observed in the long COVID group.

Depression, anxiety, and stress scores (DASS-21) were higher in proportion among long COVID patients (e.g., extremely severe depression 9.3%, extremely severe anxiety 16%), but no statistically significant difference was found compared to those without long COVID.
Sleep quality, assessed via the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, was significantly poorer among participants with long COVID compared to those without.

No statistically significant difference in quality of life was found between participants with and without long COVID syndrome across physical, psychological, social, and environmental health domains of the WHOQOL-BREF.
HbA1c levels showed no significant difference between participants with and without long COVID, with 11.9% overall having raised HbA1c >6.5%.
Peripheral smear examination revealed abnormalities including transformed lymphocytes in 8.2% of recovered COVID-19 participants and activated monocytes in 3%.
Elevated absolute neutrophil count was observed in 19% of recovered COVID-19 participants tested.
Elevated absolute eosinophil count was observed in 8% of recovered COVID-19 participants tested.
In subgroup-A HCWs (n=17), nHF (a vagal heart modulation index) increased significantly at 6-month follow-up compared to the post-acute baseline.
In subgroup-A HCWs, nLF (index of combined sympathetic/vagal and baroreflex modulation) decreased significantly at 6-month follow-up versus baseline.
LF/HF ratio (sympathovagal balance index) decreased significantly at 6-month follow-up in subgroup-A compared to baseline, indicating resolution of sympathetic dominance.
Diastolic blood pressure was significantly lower at 6-month follow-up compared with baseline in subgroup-A HCWs.
In subgroup-B HCWs (n=37), nHF increased significantly at 13-month follow-up compared to baseline.
LF/HF ratio decreased significantly at 13-month follow-up in subgroup-B compared to baseline (nLF also decreased), indicating resolved sympathetic dominance.
RMSSD (time-domain HRV parameter reflecting short-term/vagal modulation) was higher at 13-month follow-up than at baseline in subgroup-B HCWs.
Mean heart rate at 13-month follow-up was significantly lower than at baseline in subgroup-B, though it remained within normal resting range.

In subgroup-C HCWs (n=13, followed at both 6 and 13 months), nHF was higher and nLF lower than baseline at both timepoints, with LF/HF ratio significantly reduced by 13 months (borderline at 6 months).
In subgroup-C, mean heart rate at 13-month follow-up was lower than baseline, remaining within normal range.
At 6-month follow-up, 41.2% of subgroup-A HCWs continued to report at least one persistent symptom, most commonly palpitations, dyspnea on exertion, and attention/memory problems.
At 13-month follow-up, 37.8% of subgroup-B HCWs continued to report at least one persistent symptom, most commonly palpitations and mental fog.
No significant differences in LF/HF (autonomic control of the heart) were found between HCWs with persistent COVID-19 symptoms versus those without, at 6- and 13-month follow-up.
A sex difference in LF/HF was found in subgroup-A HCWs at the post-acute baseline (about 1 month post-infection), with males showing higher LF/HF (greater sympathetic dominance) than females.
In group 2 HCWs (n=29, tested before and about 1 month after SARS-CoV-2 infection), nHF decreased significantly post-infection compared to pre-infection baseline.
Group 2 HCWs showed increased nLF and LF/HF ratio at ~1 month post-infection compared to pre-infection baseline, confirming sympathetic dominance following mild SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Multiple linear regression identified elapsed time since negative SARS-CoV-2 NPS as the principal determinant of delta LF/HF, which trended toward decreasing (normalizing) over time, approaching zero at about two months post-infection.
In group 2 HCWs, a sex difference in LF/HF reached significance only at the 1-month post-infection follow-up, with males showing higher LF/HF than females.

The authors propose that SARS-CoV-2-induced sensitization/upregulation of vagal sensory TRPV1/TRPA1 ion channels by endogenous mediators (e.g., PGE2, bradykinin) may mechanistically underlie the observed cardiac autonomic imbalance (increased sympathetic, decreased vagal modulation).

The paper cites prior literature that des-Arg9-bradykinin was significantly elevated in COVID-19 ICU patients and associated with disease severity, supporting a bradykinin-signaling link to autonomic dysfunction.
Among the pediatric COVID-19 group, 25% (99/396) met criteria for Long COVID-19 based on Italian National Institute of Health criteria.
Children with Long COVID-19 reported a range of persistent neurological symptoms, most commonly tiredness, need for rest, sleepiness, concentration problems, and decreased muscle strength.
Compared with COVID-19 patients, healthy controls perceived greater increases in appetite, sleeping habits, and physical activity after pandemic onset.
Controls reported a greater reduction in in-person time with friends and a greater increase in remote socializing compared with COVID-19 patients.
Healthy controls sought psychological or medical support for emotional/relational issues at a significantly higher rate than COVID-19 patients.
Within the COVID-19 group, children with Long COVID-19 perceived significantly more fatigue and emotional instability than those without Long COVID-19.

EQ-5D-Y-3L quality-of-life scores across mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, and mood dimensions did not differ significantly between pre- and post-COVID/pandemic responses in either the COVID-19 group or controls.
Long COVID-19 patients reported significantly more pain/discomfort and worry/sadness/unhappiness after SARS-CoV-2 infection than COVID-19 patients without Long COVID-19.

Long COVID-19 patients also reported significantly higher rates of pain/discomfort and mood disorders before their SARS-CoV-2 infection compared with those who did not develop Long COVID-19, suggesting a pre-existing vulnerability.
A greater proportion of Long COVID-19 patients experienced worsening of pain/discomfort and mood from pre- to post-infection compared with Non-Long COVID-19 patients.
Non-COVID-19 controls were more likely to report increased physical activity relative to pre-pandemic than COVID-19 patients, with Long COVID-19 patients showing an intermediate increase.
Fatigue perception was increased in COVID-19 and especially Long COVID-19 patients but not in controls, without gender or age effects.
Long COVID-19 patients showed a significantly higher rate of increased emotional and behavioral instability compared with COVID-19 patients without Long COVID-19.
Increased appetite was more frequently reported in the control group than the COVID-19 group, while reduced appetite was more frequent in the COVID-19 group than controls.
Controls reported a significantly higher need for sleep than the COVID-19 group, without age or gender differences.
A meta-analysis estimated worldwide long COVID prevalence at 45%, with fatigue, dyspnea, and impairment of daily activities as the most prevalent sequelae.
Hospitalization severity and female sex were identified as risk factors for developing long COVID, though risk may vary by specific symptom type.
Pulmonary long COVID symptoms among survivors admitted with COVID-19 included fatigue (52%), dyspnea (37%), chest pain (16%), and cough (14%) three months after discharge.
Inhaled salmeterol improved FEV1 and FVC in patients recovering from moderate-to-severe COVID-19, with greatest benefit in those with a prior history of asthma.

An open-label RCT comparing high-dose versus low-dose prednisolone tapers for post-COVID diffuse parenchymal lung abnormalities found similar improvement in clinical, radiologic, physiologic, and quality-of-life outcomes.
A case report from Japan suggested nintedanib as a possible novel therapeutic for SARS-CoV-2-related pulmonary fibrosis.

Cardiovascular symptoms of long COVID including exercise intolerance, dyspnea, chest pain, and palpitations were reported at prevalences of 29-34.5%, 15-22.3%, 6.7-7.0%, and 4.5-6.0% respectively through 2 years post-infection.
Most cardiac symptoms after COVID-19 improve with time, but diastolic dysfunction may persist.

Cardiovascular symptoms without objective cardiac disease, including tachycardia, palpitations, presyncope, exercise intolerance, and dizziness, may be triggered by dysautonomia or post-bed-rest deconditioning, producing orthostatic intolerance syndromes such as POTS.

Pharmacologic management of PASC-associated orthostatic/hyperadrenergic symptoms includes fludrocortisone for hypovolemia, midodrine to increase vasoconstriction and venous return, and clonidine, methyldopa, or propranolol to attenuate hyperadrenergic symptoms.
Individual case studies and one clinical trial evaluated beta-blockers and ivabradine for PASC-associated tachycardia and palpitations, with variable outcomes.
Elevated cytokine levels have been hypothesized as a potential contributor to persistent, treatment-resistant SARS-CoV-2-related headaches.
Among 100 patients with long COVID, 59% reported neurological complaints, with headache being the most common.

Following severe acute COVID-19 infection, 59% of patients were found to have neuropathy, most commonly small fiber neuropathy, and less frequently multifocal demyelinating or critical illness axonal neuropathy.
A cohort study of 1556 participants demonstrated that previously COVID-19-positive patients had a higher likelihood of neuropathy both post-acutely (within 90 days) and during the long COVID period.
Treatment with intravenous immune globulin and/or corticosteroids provided incomplete recovery in up to 52% of small-fiber neuropathy patients in one study.

A large case series and matched control study from Sweden found the risk of stroke was about 6 times higher two weeks after COVID-19 infection compared to controls, remaining twice as high in weeks 3-4.
The CORE-19 multicenter prospective registry reported that thromboprophylaxis with rivaroxaban or LMWH reduced major thromboembolic events and all-cause death by 46% in high-risk COVID-19 patients.

The MICHELLE RCT randomized 320 high-risk post-COVID patients to extended thromboprophylaxis with reduced-dose rivaroxaban versus no prophylaxis, finding improved clinical thromboembolic outcomes without increased major bleeding.

A study of 24 long COVID patients found that triple therapy (dual-antiplatelet therapy and anticoagulation) restored endothelial function and led to reported exhaustion relief and brain fog resolution in all patients, though bleeding risk limits use outside research settings.
Depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress rates were markedly elevated among COVID-19 survivors, with meta-analyses reporting depression in 21-45%, anxiety in 5-55%, and PTSD in 10-36.4%.

Muscle and joint pain were reported in 48% of a 100-patient long COVID cohort, with findings of myositis, elevated creatine kinase, and elevated autoinflammatory markers typically associated with rheumatologic conditions.

Studies of gut microbiome composition in long COVID patients identified changes in various bacterial species, including Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, supporting a gut dysbiosis component of gastrointestinal long COVID.

A UK randomized controlled trial testing a phytochemical-rich food capsule plus pre/probiotic Lactobacillus capsule in post-acute/long COVID patients found bowel symptom improvement in 82% of the 31 patients who had baseline bowel symptoms.
Collapsing glomerulopathy following COVID-19 has been identified specifically in patients with high-risk APOL1 genotypes.

A study of individuals one year post-COVID-19 found 18% had cognitive dysfunction on neuropsychological testing, associated with lower education and pre-infection history of headache/migraine, as well as headache and sleep disturbance during acute infection.

Mesenchymal stem cell therapy has been proposed as a potential novel treatment for long COVID based on its immunomodulatory and regenerative properties, though no clinical evidence currently supports this use.
Nearly two-thirds of previously hospitalized COVID-19 patients reported some form of long COVID syndrome at six-to-nine month telephonic/in-person follow-up.
Breathlessness was the most commonly reported long COVID symptom among follow-up participants.
Fatigue was the second most common long COVID symptom reported at follow-up.
Female sex was significantly associated with a higher likelihood of experiencing long COVID symptoms compared to male sex.
Fatigability was significantly more common among female participants with long COVID.
Throat irritation was significantly more common among female participants with long COVID.
About a quarter of participants at long COVID follow-up displayed a restrictive pattern on spirometry.
Spirometry parameters (FEV1, FEV1% predicted, FVC, FVC% predicted) were significantly lower with increasing mMRC grades of breathlessness.
Six-minute walk test distance progressively decreased as mMRC breathlessness grade worsened.
Baseline resting SpO2 declined progressively with worsening mMRC breathlessness grade.
Spirometry parameters were significantly associated with higher grades of WHO COVID-19 severity recorded at the time of acute hospitalization.
Restrictive PFT pattern prevalence was significantly associated with higher acute COVID-19 severity categories, with almost half of restrictive-pattern patients in severity categories 2-3.
16.8% of children and young persons developed Long COVID with one or more persistent symptoms at 3 or more months post-infection.
Long COVID prevalence decreased to 8.7% when measured at 6 or more months post-infection, indicating roughly half of cases resolved between 3 and 6 months.
CYPs with confirmed prior SARS-CoV-2 infection (cases) had significantly higher odds of developing Long COVID than uninfected controls.
Persistent cough was one of the most common Long COVID symptoms, present in 7.4% of participants.
Nasal congestion was one of the most common Long COVID symptoms, present in 7.6% of participants.
Fatigue was one of the most common Long COVID symptoms, present in 3.0% of participants.
Male sex was significantly associated with higher odds of developing Long COVID in the pediatric cohort.
Vaccinated children and young persons had lower odds of developing Long COVID compared to unvaccinated ones, but this reduction did not reach statistical significance.
Fatigue was the most common persistent symptom at 6 months post-COVID-19, present in 38.88% of the sample.
Persistent anxiety, measured by scores above the HAD cut-off, was present in 45.3% of patients at 6 months.
Persistent depression, measured by scores above the HAD cut-off, was present in 35.18% of patients at 6 months.
There was no association between illness severity group and presence of subjective cognitive complaints (SCC).
Women were significantly more likely than men to have any persistent symptom at 6 months post-COVID-19.
Cognitive complaints were more frequently reported by women (45.5%) than men (28.1%) at 6 months.
Patients with subjective cognitive complaints performed significantly better on the TAVEC-B verbal recognition subtest than those without complaints.
Patients with subjective cognitive complaints had significantly higher anxiety scores than those without complaints.

Patients who had initial dysgeusia showed worse neuropsychological performance at 6 months on verbal memory, visual memory, working memory, and naming tasks compared to those without initial dysgeusia.
Initial headache or anosmia at disease onset were not associated with differences in neuropsychological performance at 6 months.
No significant differences in neuropsychological performance were found at 6 months between the four illness severity groups (non-hospitalized, hospitalized, oxygen therapy, ICU).
Persistent dyspnea at 6 months was associated with significantly greater anxiety and depression scores.
Persistent headache at 6 months was associated with significantly greater anxiety and depression scores.

Persistent fatigue at 6 months was associated with lower neuropsychological performance across visual memory, attention, complex working memory, cognitive flexibility, processing speed, and language domains, along with higher anxiety and depression.
No association was found between initial ferritin or D-Dimer levels and the development of persistent fatigue.

Persistent anxiety was associated with lower neuropsychological performance in most cognitive areas, and persistent depression was associated with lower performance on nearly all subtests except TAVEC-B and Reverse Digits.

Among patients with persistent fatigue, those with cognitive complaints did not differ in objective neuropsychological performance from those without complaints, though they had higher anxiety and depression scores.

Among patients with persistent fatigue, anxiety, or depression, women showed lower neurocognitive performance than men across all neuropsychological subtests, including visual memory, attention, working memory, processing speed, executive function, and language.

A higher percentage of patients with SCC, fatigue, or ICU admission fell 1-2 SD below normal on processing-speed tests (Stroop, SDMT, TMT-A/B), suggesting these tests are most sensitive to subtle cognitive changes in this population.
No individuals showed cognitive impairment at two SD below normal, regardless of disease severity or presence of cognitive complaints.
Pre-existing malaise and fatigue diagnoses were associated with more than double the risk of severe COVID-19 requiring hospitalisation.
Pre-existing malaise and fatigue diagnoses were strongly associated with increased risk of developing Long COVID.
Pre-existing chronic fatigue classified as post-viral fatigue syndrome showed convergent genetic correlation with severe COVID-19 risk, alongside its established survival-analysis association.
Pre-existing anxiety disorders were associated with increased risk of Long COVID, replicating prior reports.
Pre-existing pseudomonal pneumonia was strongly associated with increased risk of COVID-19 hospitalisation.
Acute renal failure was a strong risk factor for COVID-19 hospitalisation and acted as a multimorbidity hub in the disease-disease network.
Type 2 diabetes with renal complications was strongly associated with COVID-19 hospitalisation.
Immune deficiencies such as humoral immunodeficiency conferred markedly increased risk of severe COVID-19.
A history of suicide attempt was associated with markedly increased risk of severe COVID-19, an association not previously well recognised.
Dementias were strongly associated with COVID-19 hospitalisation and death, but showed no significant association with severe respiratory failure, indicating outcome-specific heterogeneity.
Gout showed a stronger association with COVID-19 hospitalisation in women compared to men, one of 16 disease-outcome pairs with significant effect modification.
Vitamin D deficiency was more strongly associated with COVID-19 hospitalisation risk among Europeans than non-Europeans.
Disorders of magnesium metabolism were associated with much higher risk of death with COVID-19 among younger participants than older participants, likely reflecting underlying renal failure.
A disease-disease network community enriched for circulatory and respiratory diseases was strongly enriched for association with severe respiratory failure due to COVID-19.
A network community reflecting renal and diabetic multimorbidity showed that each additional acquired disease within it raised risk of hospitalisation and death with COVID-19.
Abdominal pain showed significant genetic correlation with severe COVID-19 risk.
Adverse reactions such as poisoning by antibiotics showed significant genetic correlation with severe COVID-19 risk.
Mendelian randomization provided nominal evidence that genetic liability to gout causally increases risk of COVID-19 hospitalisation.
Mendelian randomization suggested a possible causal effect of unspecified arthropathy on risk of severe COVID-19.
The loss-of-function TYK2 missense variant rs34536443 increased risk of severe COVID-19, raising concern about TYK2-inhibitor drugs currently in trials for other diseases.

The same TYK2 loss-of-function variant that increases severe COVID-19 risk was protective for rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune diseases such as psoriasis, illustrating opposing pleiotropic effects.

Post-inflammatory pulmonary fibrosis showed high genome-wide genetic correlation with severe COVID-19 and death, yet the strongest single locus for pulmonary fibrosis (MUC5B) was protective for severe COVID-19, indicating discordance between genome-wide and locus-specific effects.

Pre-existing disease codes classified under the ICD-10 'symptoms' chapter were more than 13-fold enriched among diseases associated with increased Long COVID risk, and also enriched for hospitalisation and death.
Across 1128 significant disease-COVID-19 outcome associations, pre-existing diseases were almost exclusively associated with increased risk of severe COVID-19, with a median hazard ratio of 2.39.

Imatinib added to standard of care was not associated with a statistically significant difference in 30-day or 1-year mortality compared to standard of care alone, despite numerically higher death rates in the imatinib group.
Self-reported recovery at 1 year was lower in the imatinib group (79.0%) than in the standard-of-care group (88.5%), but the risk ratio did not indicate a statistically robust difference.
No convincing difference was observed in quality of life or long COVID symptoms between the imatinib and standard-of-care groups at 1 year.
Fatigue was one of the most frequently reported bothersome symptoms among hospitalized COVID-19 trial participants at one year follow-up, affecting about a quarter of patients.
Sleep issues were a commonly reported bothersome symptom among hospitalized COVID-19 trial participants at one year follow-up, affecting one in five patients.
Fatigue was a frequently reported bothersome symptom at one year in 24% of hospitalized COVID-19 patients in the trial.
Sleep issues were reported as a frequently bothersome symptom at one year in 20% of hospitalized COVID-19 patients in the trial.
There was no significant difference in the time from symptom onset to MIS-C diagnosis across different SARS-CoV-2 variant waves.
Hospitalization length of stay did not significantly differ across pandemic waves.
Inflammatory markers remained normal for up to two years of follow-up in all but one MIS-C patient, indicating sustained resolution of the acute inflammatory state.
A small subset of patients (6.9%) remained in active multidisciplinary follow-up, primarily for cardiology and gastroenterology concerns, at long-term assessment.
At 2-year follow-up, the main self-reported residual symptoms among MIS-C patients were abdominal pain and myalgia.
Fatigue, present in approximately a quarter of patients at admission, progressively declined over subsequent follow-up visits, becoming rare by 2 years.
A small subset of MIS-C patients (11/160, 6.9%) remained under specialist follow-up for cardiology, gastroenterology, or nephrology concerns.
At 2 years post-MIS-C, the most commonly self-reported residual symptoms were abdominal pain and myalgia.
Nearly half of tested MIS-C patients showed concurrent Epstein-Barr virus positivity, yet this was not associated with high rates of chronic fatigue or long-COVID symptomatology.
A survey of hospitalized COVID-19 patients found that 19.6% experienced arrhythmias, making it a major complication.
Among COVID-19 patients admitted to intensive care units, the prevalence of arrhythmias rose to 44.4%.
A clinical bulletin from the American College of Cardiology reported that about 16.7% of hospitalized COVID-19 patients had cardiac arrhythmias.
Heart Rhythm Society data indicated atrial fibrillation was the most common tachyarrhythmia in COVID-19 patients, occurring in 21% of cases.
SARS-CoV-2 binding to ACE2 downregulates ACE2 expression, reducing protective angiotensin 1-7/1-9 and allowing angiotensin II accumulation, which contributes to myocardial injury and arrhythmia.
A lysosomal protein, TMEM106B, was identified as an alternative receptor enabling SARS-CoV-2 entry into cells with low or absent ACE2 expression, such as brain, immune, and lung adenocarcinoma cells.

SARS-CoV-2 was detected in hamster sinoatrial node cells and can directly invade cardiac conduction cells, inducing ferroptosis-like cell injury and sinoatrial node dysfunction that promotes arrhythmia.
Elevated bloodstream levels of IL-6 and IL-10 in hospitalized COVID-19 patients were strongly associated with the occurrence of atrial and ventricular arrhythmias.

Patch-clamp studies showed IL-6 inhibits the rapid delayed rectifier potassium current (IKr) in cardiomyocytes, prolonging action potential duration and triggering early after-depolarizations that induce arrhythmia.
IL-1 inhibits the transient outward potassium current (Ito) in cardiomyocytes, contributing to prolonged action potential duration and arrhythmogenesis.
TNF-α inhibits Ito, IKr, and the slow delayed rectifying potassium current (IKs), resulting in prolonged action potential duration or QT interval and promoting arrhythmia.

TNF-α induces abnormal expression and distribution of gap junction proteins connexin 40 and 43 in cardiomyocytes, disrupting cell-to-cell electrical communication and promoting ectopic excitation or re-entry arrhythmias.
The CDC reported that myocarditis occurs in less than 0.2% of COVID-19 cases overall, yet accounts for about 7% of COVID-19-related deaths.
Among patients with COVID-19-related myocarditis, 78.7% had arrhythmia, and fulminant myocarditis can induce various malignant, life-threatening arrhythmias.
32% of COVID-19 patients develop hypoxemia and 76% require oxygen support, which can cause myocardial hypoxia/ischemia and impair cardiac ion channel function, increasing arrhythmia risk.
A case study of 416 COVID-19 patients found 7.2% experienced electrolyte disturbances, including hypokalemia, hyponatremia, and hypocalcemia, which can predispose to arrhythmia.
In a retrospective study, combined hydroxychloroquine and azithromycin treatment led to corrected QT interval prolongation in 33% of COVID-19 patients, compared with 5% for hydroxychloroquine alone.

Long-term azithromycin use increases the late cardiac sodium current and intracellular calcium overload, prolonging the QT interval and raising the risk of arrhythmia and cardiac death, alone or combined with lopinavir/ritonavir and chloroquine.
A global vaccination study found increased risk of myocarditis, pericarditis, and arrhythmias in individuals who contracted SARS-CoV-2 after receiving mRNA COVID-19 vaccination.

Post-infection stress, anxiety, fatigue, pain, quarantine, and sleep disorders combined with medication effects can cause autonomic nervous system dysfunction, activating the sympatho-adrenal medulla and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axes, releasing catecholamines that can cause myocardial damage or malignant arrhythmia.
Marked increases in IL-6 can stimulate the central hypothalamus, leading to overactivation of the cardiac sympathetic nervous system and increased risk of arrhythmia.
Autistic features were present in over half of the individuals in the MSL2 cohort.
Behavioral abnormalities including anxiety, OCD, aggressivity, hyperactivity, and sensory processing disorder were predominant in the cohort.
Most individuals showed motor delay, speech delay, and hypotonia, defining core features of the MSL2-related disorder.
Coordination and feeding difficulties, including dyspraxia and ataxic/heel-toe gait, were present in roughly a third to half of the cohort.
Over a third of individuals had seizures, and nearly half had MRI abnormalities such as delayed myelination or malformations.
EEG abnormalities including hypsarrhythmia and burst suppression were observed in about a quarter of assessed individuals.
Connective tissue disease signs such as joint subluxations, translucent skin, and inguinal hernias were present in about half of the cohort.
The majority of individuals had dysmorphic craniofacial features including deep-set eyes, downslanted palpebral fissures, and low-set ears.
Males in the cohort more frequently exhibited dysmorphisms, connective tissue disease signs, gastrointestinal anomalies, and sleep problems compared to females.
Females with MSL2 variants were more frequently affected by OFC abnormalities, attention deficit, psychiatric concerns, and especially motor/coordination issues than males.

Variants disrupting the N-terminal MSL1-interacting region of MSL2 were associated with a higher frequency of behavioral abnormalities, autistic features, seizures, and sleep issues than variants causing isolated loss of the CXC DNA-binding domain.
The two frameshift variants predicted to undergo nonsense-mediated decay and reduce MSL2 levels were both associated with early-onset seizures, unlike the start-loss variant.
Population genetic constraint metrics indicate that MSL2 is highly intolerant of loss-of-function variation, consistent with haploinsufficiency as a disease mechanism.
A blood-based DNA methylation episignature comprising 239 CpG probes robustly separated MSL2 variant carriers from matched controls in hierarchical clustering and multidimensional scaling.

A support vector machine classifier trained on the 239-probe episignature produced a methylation variant pathogenicity (MVP) score that showed high specificity, with nearly all testing controls and other-disorder samples scoring near zero.
Eight differentially methylated regions were identified between MSL2 cases and controls, but gene ontology enrichment analysis of these regions did not reach statistical significance.
Patient-derived iPSCs carrying truncating MSL2 variants showed reduced overall levels of full-length MSL2 protein compared to control iPSCs, despite detectable expression from the intact allele.
The missense p.Met317Val variant iPSC line showed full-length MSL2 protein levels comparable to control, unlike the truncating variants.

Unlike MSL3- or MOF-related disorders, global H4K16 acetylation levels were unchanged in MSL2 patient-derived iPSCs relative to control, indicating MSL2 variants do not bulk-impair MOF catalytic activity.
MOF protein levels were similar across all MSL2 patient-derived iPSC lines compared to control, indicating MSL2 variants do not destabilize MOF.

Human orthologs of putative MSL2 target genes were significantly downregulated in MSL2 patient-derived iPSCs compared to control, indicating both intact MSL2 alleles are required for their normal expression.
Expression of MSL2 and MSL1 was also downregulated in patient-derived iPSCs, which may have contributed to downregulation of MSL2 target genes.

Dysregulation of MSL2 target genes persisted after differentiation of patient iPSCs into ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm, with truncating variants showing more pronounced downregulation than the missense variant, particularly after differentiation.
Aortic dilatation was noted as a shared, highly specific clinical trait between the MSL2-related disorder and the MSL3-related Basilicata-Akhtar syndrome, both members of the MSL complex.

Joint hypermobility and, in some prior reported cases, formal hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome diagnoses have been observed alongside autism, OCD, and intellectual disability in individuals with MSL2 variants across this and prior studies.
Average dermal echogenicity was significantly higher in patients who required revision surgery after posterior lumbar fusion compared to those who did not.
Upper dermal (UD) echogenicity was significantly higher in patients requiring revision surgery than in non-revision controls.
Lower dermal (LD) echogenicity was significantly higher in patients requiring revision surgery than in non-revision controls.
Pre-MI acute sleep deprivation increased serum epinephrine levels within 24 hours of myocardial infarction.
Acute sleep deprivation before myocardial infarction upregulated oxytocin expression in paraventricular nucleus neurons.
Acute sleep deprivation before myocardial infarction upregulated cFos expression in paraventricular nucleus neurons, indicating neuronal activation.
Pre-MI acute sleep deprivation resulted in decreased serum PAB (oxidative stress biomarker) levels 14 days after myocardial infarction.
Animals subjected to acute sleep deprivation before MI showed reduced infarct size compared to MI-alone animals.
TIMP1 was elevated in the left ventricle of sleep-deprived MI animals compared to MI alone.
MMP2 was elevated in the left ventricle of sleep-deprived MI animals compared to MI alone.
Acute sleep deprivation prior to MI increased left ventricular TIMP1 levels 14 days post-MI compared to MI alone.
Acute sleep deprivation prior to MI increased left ventricular MMP2 levels 14 days post-MI compared to MI alone.
Acute sleep deprivation prior to MI increased left ventricular MMP9 levels 14 days post-MI compared to MI alone.
Echocardiographic parameters differed notably between MI and sham groups, with acute sleep deprivation prior to MI conferring a protective effect on these changes.
The prevalence of ASD among children with CCHS (8.7%) was higher than the reported general population prevalence in Europe (0.38-1.55%).
The severity of the PHOX2B mutation (moderate PARM-25/26 vs severe PARM≥27/NPARM) was not significantly associated with the presence of ASD.
The duration of the initial hospitalization was longer in CCHS children with ASD compared to those without ASD.
Glycemic dysfunction (hypo- or hyperglycemia), reflecting severity of autonomic dysfunction, was associated with ASD development in CCHS children.
Normalized low-frequency heart rate variability power (LFnu), reflecting sympathetic modulation, was significantly higher in CCHS children with ASD than in those without ASD.
Normalized high-frequency heart rate variability power (HFnu), an index of parasympathetic modulation, was significantly lower in CCHS children with ASD than in those without ASD.
The LF/HF ratio, an index of sympathovagal balance, was significantly higher in CCHS children with ASD than those without, indicating a combined sympathetic gain and parasympathetic deficit.
Children with CCHS and ASD had significantly lower Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scale scores in the communication, daily living skills, and socialization domains compared to CCHS children without ASD.
The motor skills domain of the VABS did not differ significantly between CCHS children with and without ASD.

Daytime RMSSD, an index of parasympathetic modulation, positively correlated with the VABS communication, daily living skills, and socialization domains (but not motor skills), with the strongest correlation for the daily living skills sub-domains of personal, domestic, and community functioning.
LF/HF ratio was negatively correlated with VABS communication, daily living skills, and socialization domains, but not with motor skills.
Daytime RMSSD did not significantly correlate with age in the CCHS cohort.

Age was negatively correlated with the VABS communication, daily living skills, and socialization domains, but not with motor skills, suggesting neurobehavioral function deteriorates with age in CCHS.
Among 15 CCHS patients carrying PARM mutations, the number of polyalanine repeat expansions did not significantly correlate with any of the four VABS sub-domains.
SDNN did not significantly correlate with any of the four VABS sub-domains.
Wireless HRV (ECG-based RMSSD) collection was highly feasible and well tolerated in autistic youth with emotion dysregulation across multiple study visits and tasks.
Baseline task HRV showed good test-retest reliability between screening and baseline pre-intervention visits.
Relaxation task HRV showed good test-retest reliability pre-intervention.
Breathing task HRV showed only fair test-retest reliability pre-intervention.
Higher pre-intervention Breathing-task HRV predicted lower (improved) caregiver-reported Dysphoria (EDI-D) scores 10 weeks after completing the emotion regulation intervention.
Higher pre-intervention Breathing-task HRV predicted greater improvement (lower difficulty scores) in caregiver-rated Social Flexibility at 10-week follow-up.
Higher pre-intervention Breathing-task HRV predicted greater improvement in caregiver-rated Transitions/Change flexibility at 10-week follow-up.
Higher pre-intervention Breathing-task HRV predicted greater improvement in overall caregiver-rated flexibility (FS Total Score) at 10-week follow-up.
Pre-intervention Baseline and Relaxation task HRV were not significantly related to any clinical outcome measures over time.

Increases in Baseline HRV across treatment time points were associated with reduced caregiver-rated Reactivity (EDI-R) at 5-week follow-up but increased Reactivity at 10-week follow-up, an inconsistent pattern.
Increases in Relaxation-task HRV over time were marginally associated with reduced Transitions/Change flexibility difficulties at 10-week follow-up.
Older age was associated with higher (worse) scores on the Flexibility Scale Total scale in models examining pre-intervention Breathing and Baseline HRV.

A two-sample Mendelian randomization study found that genetically predicted higher serotonin, an intestinal flora-dependent metabolite, appears to causally increase the risk of autism spectrum disorder.
The same Mendelian randomization study found that genetically predicted higher choline levels appear to causally reduce the risk of autism spectrum disorder.

An exploratory study of 253 children, 203 of whom had ASD, found that convergence insufficiency and refractive errors were the most commonly observed ocular conditions in autism, consistent with known motor and sensory processing alterations in ASD.
A national survey found that the prevalence of urinary symptoms in individuals with autism spectrum disorder was related to higher severity of the ASD condition.

The authors hypothesize that factors beyond obesity, potentially connective tissue involvement, contribute to stretch marks in people with autism spectrum disorder and may impact behavior, posture, and motor skills.
A study on long-term behavioral supports for dental care in children with autism spectrum disorder found a significant improvement in compliance with regular dentistry visits and treatments.

A mini review discusses how exercise, nutrition, and sleep interact with the immune, musculoskeletal, and gut systems and proposes comprehensive support across these three pillars to improve core symptoms of autism spectrum disorder.
All three long COVID phenotypes (cardiological, pulmonary, psychiatric) showed significantly decreased seroprevalence of anti-nucleocapsid IgG antibodies compared to convalescents without long COVID.
Long COVID status was associated with significantly decreased odds of testing seropositive for anti-nucleocapsid antibodies.
Among seropositive individuals, those with long COVID had lower anti-S1 spike subunit antibody levels than those without long COVID.
Among seropositive individuals, those with long COVID had lower anti-S2 spike subunit antibody levels than those without long COVID.
