Patients with pulmonary or psychological long COVID phenotypes had decreased anti-receptor binding domain (RBD) antibody concentrations compared to those without long COVID.
A cited Chinese cohort study found that olfactory dysfunction persisted in 11% of COVID-19-positive patients at 6 months and 4% at 12 months post-infection.

Across four studies (298 participants) reporting symptom disappearance rate of post-viral olfactory dysfunction, two RCTs and one non-RCT (268 participants) showed no significant difference between TCM therapies and comparators.
In one RCT, acupuncture alone or acupoint injection produced a better symptom remission rate than no treatment for post-viral olfactory dysfunction.
One RCT found acupuncture alone gave better symptom remission results than western medicine (mometasone furoate nasal spray) for post-viral olfactory dysfunction.

One RCT found that adding acupoint injection to western medicine (prednisone acetate) plus supplements (mecobalamin + ginkgo biloba extract) improved symptom remission versus western medicine and supplements alone.
Borderline statistical significance for symptom remission rate was found in a non-RCT comparing acupuncture with no treatment and in a cohort study comparing acupuncture with oral vitamin B complex.

Three trials showed no significant difference in symptom remission rate for acupuncture compared with placebo, acupuncture plus acupoint injection, western medicine, supplements, and olfactory training combinations.

In one RCT comparing acupuncture plus conventional nasal steroid (mometasone furoate) with the steroid alone, the Sniffin' Sticks test showed a beneficial result for the addition of acupuncture, but the T&T olfactory test on the same comparison did not reach statistical significance.

One RCT found that combining acupuncture, acupoint injection, olfactory training and western medicine (prednisone acetate) with supplements improved olfactory dysfunction symptom score compared with olfactory training plus the same western medicine and supplements alone.

Overall, all TCM intervention groups (acupuncture, acupoint injection) failed to show a statistically significant effect on olfactory dysfunction symptom scores compared with control groups across the included studies.

Adverse events were reported in only five of nine trials; four reported no adverse events while one trial reported nine participants experienced adverse effects, with no serious adverse events overall, indicating a high level of safety for acupuncture and acupoint injection.
A cited study suggested acupuncture may exert a therapeutic role in olfactory disorders by promoting regeneration of olfactory neurons and improving nasal ventilation.

The review describes two proposed mechanistic types of post-viral olfactory dysfunction: a transitory/short-term type from airway blockage, sensorineural or central dysfunction, and a chronic/permanent type from loss of olfactory epithelium or disruption of central olfactory processing networks.

The review's overall conclusion is that TCM, specifically acupuncture, showed a few positive effects for post-viral olfactory dysfunction in symptom remission, but methodological quality of included trials was generally low.
At 16 months after hospitalization for COVID-19, 68% of assessed patients reported at least one new symptom, most commonly fatigue.
Dyspnea was reported by 37% of patients at the 16-month telephone assessment.
Memory difficulties were reported by 24% of patients at the 16-month telephone assessment.
A quarter of patients who were asymptomatic at four months developed at least one new symptom by 16 months after discharge.
Cognitive impairment prevalence remained largely stable, from 45% at four months to 40% at 16 months in patients evaluated at both time points.
Depression symptom prevalence remained stable between the four-month and 16-month assessments.
Post-traumatic symptom prevalence remained stable between the four-month and 16-month assessments.
The prevalence of anxiety significantly decreased between the four-month and 16-month assessments after COVID-19 hospitalization.
Dysfunctional breathing was detected in 32% of patients assessed at the outpatient facility.
The proportion of patients with lung CT-scan abnormalities decreased from 61% at four months to 38% at 16 months after hospitalization.

More than one-third of individuals with a prior SARS-CoV-2 infection show involvement of both the central and peripheral nervous systems, with an approximately threefold higher incidence of neurological symptoms reported in observational studies.

The review identifies viral persistence and neuro-invasion by SARS-CoV-2, neuroinflammation, autoimmunity, coagulopathy, and endotheliopathy as reported pathogenic mechanisms underlying neurological complications of long COVID.
At 3 months post-COVID, fatigue was the most common symptom in athletes with PASC, reported by 69% of subjects.
Shortness of breath was reported by 63% of PASC subjects at 3 months, the second most common symptom.
Over 30% of PASC subjects endorsed chest pain at 3 months following COVID infection.
Over 40% of PASC subjects endorsed tachycardia at 3 months post-infection.
PASC subjects exercised significantly fewer hours per week than non-PASC subjects at 3 months post-COVID.
Nearly one-third (31%, 10/32) of PASC athletes reported a complete inability to engage in any cardiovascular endurance exercise at 3 months.
PASC subjects reported a median 27% decrease in self-reported cardiopulmonary endurance from baseline compared with a median 0% change in non-PASC controls.
PASC subjects had significantly higher (worse) Modified Oslo scores than non-PASC subjects, indicating greater sport-related health problem burden.
PASC subjects had significantly worse Dyspnea Scale scores than non-PASC subjects, with half reporting breathlessness with hurrying or walking uphill.
PASC subjects reported a lower but not statistically significant EQ Index score compared to non-PASC subjects.
PASC subjects reported significantly lower EQ-VAS scores (self-reported change from baseline health) compared to non-PASC subjects.
The PASC group had a significantly greater proportion of females compared to the non-PASC group among post-COVID endurance athletes.

Women were less represented among PNP than NNP patients.
PNP patients had fewer years of education than NNP patients.
PNP patients had a higher body mass index than NNP patients.
History of a second SARS-CoV-2 infection was less frequent among PNP than NNP patients.
Hypertension was more prevalent among PNP than NNP patients.
Type II diabetes was more prevalent among PNP than NNP patients.
Numbness or tingling was significantly more frequent among post-hospitalization (PNP) than non-hospitalized (NNP) Long COVID patients.
Abnormal body sensations were significantly more frequent among PNP than NNP patients.
Shortness of breath was significantly more frequent among PNP than NNP patients.
Depression symptoms were significantly more frequent among PNP than NNP patients.
Abnormal neurological examination findings overall were more common among PNP than NNP patients.
Sensory, gait, and motor dysfunction on neurological exam were each significantly more frequent in PNP than NNP patients.
Perceived cognitive function was worse in NNP than in PNP patients, although both groups scored below the normative mean.
Objective executive function performance was more impaired in NNP than in PNP patients.
Processing speed was numerically more affected in PNP than NNP patients but the difference was not statistically significant.

LASSO modeling showed that the risk of persistent tinnitus increased with each additional month lived with Long COVID (RR = 1.50).
LASSO modeling showed that the risk of persistent anxiety increased with each additional month lived with Long COVID (RR = 1.4).

LASSO modeling showed that the risk of persistent brain fog increased with each additional month lived with Long COVID (RR = 1.22), though it remained the most frequently reported symptom across all durations.

Fatigue was among the most persistent symptoms, with risk increasing by RR = 1.05 for each 10% decrease in perceived recovery, remaining present in about half of patients even at high recovery levels.
Brain fog risk increased by RR = 1.09 for each 10% decrease in perceived recovery, remaining present in about one third of patients even at high recovery.
Sleep problems' risk increased by RR = 1.10 for each 10% decrease in perceived recovery.
Myalgia risk increased by RR = 1.10 for each 10% decrease in perceived recovery.
Numbness or tingling risk increased by RR = 1.16 for each 10% decrease in perceived recovery.

Persistent sleep problems were associated with significantly higher PROMIS Anxiety and Sleep Disturbance T-scores.

Abnormal findings on the neurological exam were associated with significantly higher PROMIS Anxiety and Depression T-scores.

Patients with a history of critical COVID-19 requiring life-sustaining treatment had significantly lower executive function and processing speed, and higher sleep disturbance scores.

The discussion cites prior evidence that autoantibodies associated with systemic lupus erythematosus have been found in Long COVID patients, including those with mild acute COVID-19, as a possible explanation for severe symptoms in non-hospitalized patients.

The discussion cites a preprint reporting autoantibodies directed against the central nervous system in Long COVID that, when transferred to mice, caused loss of balance and coordination, supporting an autoimmune mechanism for neurological PASC.
Female sex predominated among Long COVID patients in this cohort (63% women), cited as supporting an autoimmune mechanism hypothesis for PASC given similar female predominance reported elsewhere.
The discussion cites evidence of abnormal resting-state EEG rhythms among Long COVID patients with brain fog who have no pre-existing cognitive or affective disorders.
Within individual Neuro-PASC patients, a mean of 69% of test results across all domains remained the same (persistently abnormal) between initial testing and follow-up at least one year later.
Across the four domains of the extended autonomic system (central, autonomic, neuroendocrine, immune/inflammatory), 71% of abnormalities noted at initial evaluation were still present at follow-up.
Individual CSF catecholamine levels measured at initial testing and at follow-up were highly correlated, indicating stable individual biochemical phenotypes over time.
Three of seven Neuro-PASC patients had abnormal oligoclonal band patterns in CSF and serum at initial testing that persisted unchanged at follow-up.
Four of seven patients had brain white matter hyperintensities on MRI present at both the initial and follow-up visits.

One patient had persistently low, and two patients persistently high, CSF DOPA, DOPAC, and DHPG levels at both visits, with the low pattern suggesting decreased central catecholamine biosynthesis similar to that seen in postinfectious ME/CFS.
Two patients showed tilt-evoked sudden hypotension (TESH) at both initial and follow-up testing.
One patient had persistent sympathoadrenal imbalance, a centrally evoked pattern, at both visits, which may underlie a tendency toward fainting or presyncope.
Three patients had persistently low plasma epinephrine levels at both initial and follow-up visits, possibly reflecting increased forearm vasoconstriction and catecholamine extraction.
Three patients had persistently attenuated orthostatic increments in plasma norepinephrine at both initial and follow-up testing.
Three patients had persistently elevated serum chromogranin A, a protein co-released with norepinephrine during sympathetic stimulation.
One patient had persistently decreased immunoreactive tyrosine hydroxylase relative to smooth muscle actin in arrector pili muscles on skin biopsy, indicating sympathetic noradrenergic nerve loss.

Four patients had persistently decreased low high-frequency power of heart rate variability, indicating decreased baroreflex-cardiovagal function, which may be a consequence of COVID-19 rather than a preexisting trait.
Four patients had persistently increased forearm vascular resistance based on finger cuff hemodynamic data at both visits.
None of the seven Neuro-PASC patients was found to be hypovolemic on blood volume testing.
Five patients had persistently elevated copeptin levels, suggesting increased activity of paraventricular nucleus neurons involved in AVP release and central stress regulation.
Three patients had persistently increased blood glucose levels at both initial and follow-up testing.
In the three patients with an abnormal CSF/serum oligoclonal band pattern, antibody-secreting B cells were persistently detected in the CSF at follow-up, matching the initial finding.
Four patients had persistently increased neutrophil/lymphocyte ratios in blood at both initial and follow-up testing.
None of the seven patients had persistently increased IL-6 levels.
Nearly half of surveyed Medicaid managed care members with prior COVID-19 diagnosis reported at least one PASC symptom persisting 6 months or longer.
HIV serostatus was not significantly associated with the prevalence of PASC symptoms lasting 6 months or more.
Among the 49 PASC symptoms examined, only pricking/tingling/creeping skin sensation showed a statistically significant association with HIV-positive status.

The most frequently reported PASC symptoms lasting over 6 months were musculoskeletal (low back pain, joint pain, muscle aches, body aches) and neurocognitive (brain fog, memory problems), along with fatigue, sleep difficulty, mood changes, word-finding problems, and dry eyes.
Older age (50+) was associated with higher prevalence of persistent muscle aches compared to younger age groups.
Older age (50+) was associated with higher prevalence of persistent neck, back, or low back pain compared to younger age groups.
Age over 50 was a strong predictor of heat/cold intolerance as a persistent PASC symptom, while no younger participants reported this symptom.

Individuals with inadequate income reported a wide range of PASC symptoms, including sleep difficulty, rib cage pain, brain fog, dry eyes, muscle aches, neck/back/low back pain, and hair loss, at higher rates than those with adequate income.
Individuals with inadequate income were significantly more likely to experience heat/cold intolerance and body aches than those with adequate income.
In multivariable OLS regression, reporting inadequate income was the only sociodemographic variable significantly associated with a higher number of PASC symptoms lasting six months or more.
A comorbid history of stroke or cardiac condition was significantly associated with a higher number of PASC symptoms lasting 6 months or more.
A comorbid history of cancer was significantly associated with a higher number of PASC symptoms lasting 6 months or more.
A comorbid diagnosis of fibromyalgia was significantly associated with a higher number of PASC symptoms lasting 6 months or more.
Depression/anxiety, bone/joint problems, and tobacco use were not significantly associated with the number of long-duration PASC symptoms after controlling for other factors.
Hypertension was significantly more common among HIV-positive participants than HIV-negative participants, possibly reflecting the older age of the HIV-positive group.
Maximal oxygen consumption (VO2max) measured during exercise testing was significantly lower in COVID-19 survivors than non-COVID-19 controls.
6-minute walk test (6MWT) distance was significantly lower in COVID-19 survivors compared with non-COVID-19 controls.
Resting VO2 was comparable between COVID-19 survivors and non-COVID-19 controls, with impairment only apparent during exercise testing.
Anaerobic threshold (AT) was significantly decreased in COVID-19 survivors compared to non-COVID-19 controls.
Peak workload achieved during exercise testing was significantly lower in COVID-19 survivors compared to non-COVID-19 controls.
Peak blood lactate levels during exercise testing were significantly lower in COVID-19 survivors compared to non-COVID-19 controls.
Physical activity levels were significantly reduced in COVID-19 survivors compared to non-COVID-19 controls, potentially explained by impaired aerobic and anaerobic exercise capacity.
O2 pulse during exercise testing was significantly lower in COVID-19 survivors than non-COVID-19 controls.
Respiratory exchange rate (RER) during exercise testing was significantly lower in COVID-19 survivors than non-COVID-19 controls.
Breathing reserve (BR) during exercise testing was significantly lower in COVID-19 survivors than non-COVID-19 controls.
End-tidal CO2 (ETCO2) during exercise testing was significantly lower in COVID-19 survivors than non-COVID-19 controls.

No significant differences were found between COVID-19 survivors and non-COVID-19 controls in fatigue, dyspnea, peak heart rate, SpO2, peak ventilation, exercise duration, cardiac output, and blood pressure during exercise testing.
At rest, heart rate, SpO2, blood pressure, and end-tidal CO2 were comparable between COVID-19 survivors and non-COVID-19 controls.

VE per unit CO2 production (VE/VCO2) was altered at rest but was not different between COVID-19 survivors and controls after exercise, an unusual pattern distinct from other measures which were normal at rest but abnormal post-exercise.
Nearly half of adult patients with lab-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection developed at least one incident PASC condition within 31-180 days post-infection.
Patients hospitalized during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection had a significantly increased risk of developing any incident PASC condition compared to non-hospitalized patients.
Patients admitted to the ICU during acute infection had an even greater increased risk of developing any incident PASC condition compared to non-hospitalized patients.

Hospitalized patients showed increased risk of several respiratory and metabolic post-acute conditions including COPD, pulmonary fibrosis, dyspnea, pulmonary embolism, chest pain, malnutrition, and sleep disorders compared to non-hospitalized patients.
ICU patients had a markedly elevated risk of incident myopathy in the post-acute period compared to non-hospitalized patients.
ICU patients also showed increased risk of cognitive problems, anxiety disorder, pulmonary fibrosis, malnutrition, and malaise/fatigue in the post-acute period.
Hospitalized and ICU patients had substantially higher risk of receiving the general post-COVID-19 condition diagnosis codes (U099/B948) than non-hospitalized patients.
Patients aged 75 or older had a substantially increased risk of incident dementia diagnosis in the post-acute period compared to those aged 55-64.
Patients aged 75 or older also had increased risk of incident cerebral ischemia and malnutrition in the post-acute period compared to those aged 55-64.
Female patients had a markedly increased risk of incident hair loss diagnosis in the post-acute period compared to male patients.

Patients self-identified as Black had an increased risk of incident diabetes mellitus compared to White patients, but this association was not significant when requiring a significant marginal increase attributable to infection.
Underweight patients had a modestly increased risk of any incident PASC condition compared to normal-weight patients.
Underweight patients were specifically at increased risk of incident malnutrition and diabetes mellitus compared to normal-weight patients.
Patients infected during the Delta-variant-dominant period had increased risk of incident acute pharyngitis compared to those infected during the first pandemic wave.
Patients with five or more baseline comorbidities had increased risk of incident anemia, fluid disorders, and acute kidney failure compared to patients without documented baseline conditions.

Patients with baseline cancer had increased risk of several incident post-acute conditions including pulmonary fibrosis, hypotension, malnutrition, and fibromyalgia compared to patients without baseline cancer.
Patients with baseline pulmonary circulation disorder had substantially increased risk of incident pulmonary embolism compared to those without this baseline condition.
Patients with documented baseline weight loss had increased risk of receiving unspecified PASC diagnosis codes and malaise/fatigue compared to patients without baseline weight loss.

Machine learning models predicted several PASC conditions with high accuracy (C-index ≥0.8), including dementia, myopathies, cerebral ischemia, COPD, heart failure, hypotension, malnutrition, acute kidney failure, and non-specific PASC diagnoses (U099/B948).

Several PASC conditions were predicted with moderate accuracy (C-index 0.7-0.8), including encephalopathy, hair loss, atelectasis, pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary embolism, thromboembolism, anemia, fluid disorders, and diabetes mellitus.

More subjective, symptom-based PASC conditions such as sleep disorders, headache, depressive disorders, anxiety disorder, paresthesia, dermatitis, joint pain, malaise/fatigue, and dizziness were poorly predicted by baseline covariates and acute severity (C-index <0.7).
The association between older age and incident dementia was replicated in the independent OneFlorida+ validation cohort.
The association between female sex and incident hair loss was replicated in the independent OneFlorida+ validation cohort, though with a smaller effect size than the primary cohort.
The association between Black race and incident diabetes mellitus was replicated in the independent OneFlorida+ validation cohort.
The association between Delta-period infection and general PASC diagnosis codes was replicated in the independent OneFlorida+ validation cohort.

Patients infected during the Delta-variant-dominant period (July-November 2021) had a 3.2-fold higher risk of incident acute pharyngitis in the post-acute phase compared to those infected during the first pandemic wave.
Patients with five or more baseline comorbid conditions had a 2.0-fold higher risk of incident anemia in the post-acute phase compared to those without any documented baseline conditions.
Patients with five or more baseline comorbid conditions had a 2.0-fold higher risk of incident fluid disorders in the post-acute phase compared to those without baseline conditions.
Patients with five or more baseline comorbid conditions had a 1.3-fold higher risk of incident acute kidney failure in the post-acute phase compared to those without baseline conditions.
Patients with a baseline cancer diagnosis had a 1.5-fold higher risk of incident pulmonary fibrosis in the post-acute phase compared to patients without cancer.
Patients with a baseline cancer diagnosis had a 1.7-fold higher risk of incident hypotension in the post-acute phase compared to patients without cancer.
Patients with a baseline cancer diagnosis had a 2.2-fold higher risk of incident malnutrition in the post-acute phase compared to patients without cancer.
Patients with a baseline cancer diagnosis had a 1.3-fold higher risk of incident fibromyalgia diagnosis in the post-acute phase compared to patients without cancer.
Cancer patients also showed increased post-acute risk of atelectasis, fever, and anemia, though specific fold-increases were not reported for these outcomes.

Patients with baseline pulmonary circulation disorder had a 3.3-fold higher risk of incident pulmonary embolism post-COVID, though the authors caution this may partly reflect ICD coding/grouping overlap rather than a true COVID-specific effect.
Patients with a baseline weight loss diagnosis had a 2.2-fold higher risk of being diagnosed with unspecified post-COVID condition codes (U099/B948) than patients without baseline weight loss.
Patients with a baseline weight loss diagnosis had a 1.4-fold higher risk of incident malaise and fatigue than patients without baseline weight loss.
In the subgroup not hospitalized during acute infection, older age (≥75 years) and baseline cancer were associated with an increased risk of a range of incident PASC conditions.
In the subgroup hospitalized during acute infection, ICU admission and baseline dementia or pulmonary circulation disorder were associated with increased risk of different incident PASC conditions.

Using a regularized Cox model, dementia, myopathies, cerebral ischemia, COPD, heart failure, hypotension, malnutrition, acute kidney failure, and unspecified post-COVID diagnoses (U099/B948) were the most reliably predictable PASC conditions from baseline covariates (C-index ≥0.8).

A second tier of PASC conditions—encephalopathy, hair loss, atelectasis, pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary embolism, thromboembolism, anemia, fluid disorders, and diabetes mellitus—showed moderate predictability (C-index 0.7-0.8).

Subjective/symptom-based PASC conditions including sleep disorders, headache, depressive disorders, anxiety disorder, paresthesia, dermatitis, joint pain, malaise and fatigue, and dizziness were poorly predicted from baseline covariates (C-index <0.7).

Increasing model complexity (regularized logistic regression, gradient boosting machine, deep neural network) did not substantially change the heterogeneous predictability patterns observed with the regularized Cox model.

Replacing clinician-selected baseline covariates with a high-dimensional feature set of 1593-1698 ICD-10 codes and 2309-4366 medications did not meaningfully change the predictive performance or heterogeneous predictability patterns of PASC conditions.
In the independent OneFlorida+ validation cohort, patients aged 75 or older had a 5.4-fold higher risk of incident dementia post-COVID, consistent with the INSIGHT primary cohort finding.
In the OneFlorida+ validation cohort, female patients had a 2.2-fold higher risk of incident hair loss post-COVID, replicating the direction seen in the INSIGHT cohort.
In the OneFlorida+ validation cohort, patients self-identified as Black had a 1.5-fold higher risk of incident diabetes mellitus post-COVID versus White patients, replicating the INSIGHT finding.

In the OneFlorida+ validation cohort, infection confirmed between July and November 2021 (Delta-dominant) was associated with a 1.7-fold higher risk of being diagnosed with unspecified post-COVID condition codes (U099/B948).

In OneFlorida+, the same predictability hierarchy was replicated: malnutrition, COPD, dementia, and acute kidney failure remained highly predictable (C-index >0.8), while fatigue, anxiety, sleep disorders, and depression remained poorly predictable (C-index around or below 0.6).

Without applying the criterion requiring COVID-specific marginal risk (Criterion 3), pre-existing cancer was also associated with higher risk of encephalopathy, thromboembolism, fluid disorders, edema, acute kidney failure, and malaise/fatigue among non-infected patients, indicating these associations are not specific to SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Baseline pregnancy was associated with incident anemia post-COVID; the authors note this may partly reflect the known high baseline prevalence of anemia in pregnancy but suggest SARS-CoV-2 infection during pregnancy could further exacerbate iron deficiency anemia via hyperinflammation.
Intermittent hypoxia exposure improved six-minute walk distance more than normoxia exposure in PASC patients.
Intermittent hypoxia exposure improved forced vital capacity (FVC and FVC %pred) more than normoxia exposure in PASC patients.
Intermittent hypoxia exposure improved FEV1 and FEV1 %pred more than normoxia exposure in PASC patients.
Intermittent hypoxia exposure improved tidal volume more than normoxia exposure in PASC patients.
Intermittent hypoxia exposure reduced dyspnea scores (Borg and mMRC scales) more than normoxia exposure in PASC patients.
Intermittent hypoxia exposure reduced fatigue scores (FAS and CFQ-11) more than normoxia exposure in PASC patients.
A longer duration of intermittent hypoxia exposure (≥10 days) had a greater impact on functional and symptom measures than shorter duration (<10 days).
Among 1,502 pregnant individuals with SARS-CoV-2 infection, the prevalence of PASC at a median of 10.3 months post-infection was 9.3%.
Postexertional malaise was the most common symptom among individuals with PASC, occurring in 77.7% of PASC-positive participants.
Fatigue was reported in 76.3% of participants with PASC, making it one of the most common symptoms.
Gastrointestinal symptoms were reported in 61.2% of participants with PASC.
History of obesity before first SARS-CoV-2 infection was associated with increased prevalence of PASC.
Pre-existing depression or anxiety disorder before first SARS-CoV-2 infection was associated with increased prevalence of PASC.
Self-reported economic hardship (difficulty covering expenses) was associated with increased prevalence of PASC.
Treatment with oxygen during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection (indicating more severe acute illness) was associated with increased prevalence of PASC.
Hospitalization status did not significantly predict objective cognitive performance in patients with Neuro-PASC referred for abbreviated neuropsychological assessment.
Independent t-tests revealed no significant differences in subjective cognitive impairment ratings between hospitalized and non-hospitalized Neuro-PASC patients.
Greater self-reported fatigue and depression/mood symptoms were associated with greater subjective cognitive impairment, with fatigue independently explaining the majority of the variance.
When controlling for fatigue as a covariate, subjective cognitive impairment still did not significantly differ between hospitalized and non-hospitalized groups.

Patients overall endorsed significantly more fatigue and depression/mood symptoms than the PROMIS normative sample, but there were no significant differences between hospitalized and non-hospitalized groups on these measures.
Both hospitalization groups performed approximately one standard deviation below the normative mean on the objective cognitive composite, with little variability across or within groups.
Performance was most reduced on measures of delayed memory in the non-hospitalized group, whereas performance was most reduced on a measure of lexical fluency in the post-hospitalization group.

Both hospitalization groups performed best (largely within normal limits) on the Oral Trail Making Test Part B, a measure of executive attention and set shifting, contrary to expectations based on prior Written Trail Making Test B findings.
Post-hospitalization patients were on average approximately 10 years older than non-hospitalized patients, with a trend toward fewer females in the post-hospitalization group.

A prior study (Baker et al., 2023) found that somatosensory gating did not differ between individuals without long COVID and those with long COVID fatigue that had a moderate-to-severe impact on daily living.

Individuals with long COVID reported greater subjective fatigue than those without long COVID despite showing a similar degree of objective performance decline on an isokinetic fatigue task, indicating a dissociation between perceived fatigue and fatigability.
A large survey of individuals with long COVID found that 66% were classified as having moderate to severe autonomic dysfunction based on the COMPASS-31 score.
In a pilot test of the modified cognitive task battery in 15 young healthy individuals, self-reported fatigue on a visual analogue scale increased significantly from before to after the task.
The same pilot testing showed a significant increase in fatigue on the Brunel Mood Scale fatigue subscale from before to after the modified cognitive task battery.
Autonomic dysfunction is described as prevalent in long COVID, potentially reflecting an imbalance between sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous system activity.
Depression and anxiety are reported as features of long COVID, and long COVID symptoms are described as having a profound impact on self-identity and illness beliefs.
Sensory changes are described as common among individuals with long COVID, though the sensory attenuation model of fatigue has not been fully explored in this population.
Estimated proportions of CD8+T, CD4+T, NK, B cells, monocytes, and granulocytes did not differ significantly between post-COVID-19 cases and controls.

Genome-wide differential methylation analysis identified 42 CpG sites overlapping 53 genes significantly differentially methylated between post-COVID-19 cases and controls, with 24 hypo-methylated and 18 hyper-methylated sites.
Differentially methylated CpG sites were significantly enriched within CpG islands relative to the genomic background.

Over-representation analysis of differentially methylated genes nominally implicated amino acid metabolism pathways, including alanine/aspartate/glutamate metabolism and D-glutamine/D-glutamate metabolism.
GLUD1 (glutamate dehydrogenase 1) showed significant hyper-methylation at CpG site cg00167275 in post-COVID-19 patients versus controls.
ATP1A3 (Na+/K+ ATPase alpha-3 subunit) showed significant hypo-methylation at CpG site cg13628106 in post-COVID-19 patients versus controls.
RNASEH2C showed significant hypo-methylation at CpG site cg25294185 in post-COVID-19 patients versus controls.

SMAD2 showed significant hyper-methylation at CpG site cg05100634 in post-COVID-19 patients and was also among the 13 genes replicating in the meta-analysis with an independent post-COVID methylation dataset.
TNIP1 (TNFAIP3 interacting protein 1) showed significant hypo-methylation at CpG site cg22178392 in post-COVID-19 patients versus controls.
PRKCI (protein kinase C iota) showed significant hyper-methylation at CpG site cg18139307 in post-COVID-19 patients versus controls.

ARRB2 (beta-arrestin 2) showed significant hyper-methylation at CpG site cg10047026 in post-COVID-19 patients versus controls; beta-arrestin 2 is implicated in IFN-beta production, viral clearance, and TLR signaling.
Gene ontology enrichment of the top 200 nominally significant differentially methylated genes showed significant over-representation of Golgi apparatus-related cellular component terms.
Region-level differential methylation analysis found significant hyper-methylation in a CpG island on chromosome 6 spanning the 3' end of NFYA and the first exon of the pseudogene ADCY10P1.

A meta-analysis integrating this study's nominal p-values with those from an independent post-COVID-19 methylation study (Lee et al.) identified 13 CpG sites/genes with concordant direction of effect across both datasets, including DYRK2, ATP5PF, B4GAT1, PRKXP1, SLC25A21-AS1, NRDC, SMAD2, OSBPL6, IFI44L, PATJ, PRH1-PRR4, UBAC2, and an intergenic probe mapping to ACAN/ISG20.
Post-COVID-19 patients showed a slight but statistically significant epigenetic age acceleration across the Horvath, Hannum, PhenoAge, and SkinBlood clocks, but not the GrimAge predictor.
DNA methylation-estimated, age-adjusted telomere length (DNAmTLadjAge) was significantly lower in post-COVID-19 patients than in controls, indicating accelerated telomere shortening.
The global burden of stochastic epigenetic mutations (Global epimutation load) was significantly increased in post-COVID-19 patients compared to controls, indicating enhanced epigenetic drift.
Gene-level analysis of SEM burden using SKAT identified 790 genes with statistically significant enrichment of stochastic epigenetic mutations distinguishing post-COVID-19 cases from controls.
Genes showing increased epigenetic drift (SEM enrichment) in post-COVID-19 cases were significantly enriched for the KEGG Insulin resistance pathway, surviving multiple-testing correction.
Genes showing increased epigenetic drift in post-COVID-19 cases were significantly enriched for the VEGF signaling pathway, surviving multiple-testing correction.
Genes showing increased epigenetic drift in post-COVID-19 cases were significantly enriched for the apoptosis signaling pathway, surviving multiple-testing correction.

SEM-enriched genes were also nominally associated with additional pathways—hypoxia response via HIF activation, netrin-mediated axon guidance, relaxin signaling, T-cell activation, and endothelin signaling—that did not survive multiple-testing correction.
Most patients with neuro-PASC had elevated autoantibody levels across 79 autoantigens compared with healthy controls at all study visits.
MDA5 autoantibodies, associated with inflammatory myopathy, were particularly enriched in neuro-PASC patients compared with convalescent controls and healthy controls, peaking postboost.
Scl-70 autoantibodies, associated with systemic sclerosis, were enriched in neuro-PASC patients compared with convalescent and healthy controls.
PM/Scl-75 autoantibodies, linked to systemic sclerosis/myositis, were enriched in neuro-PASC patients compared with convalescent and healthy controls.
KU (p70/p80) autoantibodies, associated with systemic lupus erythematosus, were enriched in neuro-PASC patients compared with convalescent and healthy controls.
Anti-ssDNA autoantibodies, associated with systemic lupus erythematosus, were enriched in neuro-PASC patients compared with convalescent and healthy controls.
LPS, myelin basic protein, nucleolin, proliferating cell nuclear antigen, and Ro/SS-A autoantibody titers were correlated with increased age of study participants.
High titers of GAD65 autoantibody, linked to cerebellar ataxia and stiff-person syndrome, were strongly associated with poor attention performance and presence of depression in neuro-PASC patients.

Presence of pre-existing comorbidities was independently associated with increased odds of not feeling fully recovered from COVID-19.
Incomplete or no COVID-19 vaccination was associated with a threefold increased odds of not fully recovering from COVID-19 compared to full vaccination.
Dyspnoea during the acute stage of COVID-19 was the strongest independent predictor of not fully recovering, acting as a surrogate for acute disease severity in this mostly non-hospitalized cohort.
The initial association between vaccination status and self-perceived full recovery was not replicated in the sensitivity analysis using multiple imputation, nor demonstrated in secondary outcomes.

Female sex, comorbidities, and acute-phase dyspnoea were each associated with higher risk of worsening dyspnoea (MRC), poorer quality of life, and poorer functioning (WG-SS) as secondary outcomes; acute dyspnoea also predicted new/persisting symptoms.
Lower educational level was associated with reduced quality of life and functioning, suggesting reduced healthcare access and health literacy contribute to long COVID severity.
Among reported comorbidities, hypertension, diabetes, and obesity were more frequently associated with self-reported non-recovery from COVID-19 in univariable analysis.
When gaze was cued to the eye region (CROSS condition), children's pupils dilated more in response to images with large pupils than small pupils, demonstrating a pupillary contagion effect.
In the gaze-cued (CROSS) condition, heart rate increased significantly more in response to images with large pupils compared to small pupils, paralleling the pupil contagion effect.
Skin conductance response did not differ significantly between large- and small-pupil images in either the cued or uncued gaze condition, showing no contagion effect for this measure.
In the free-viewing (NO-CROSS) condition, none of the three arousal measures (pupil, heart rate, skin conductance) showed a significant contagion response to large versus small pupil images.
When gaze was cued to the eye region, greater autistic traits (higher AQ z-scores) were associated with a stronger pupillary contagion response, controlling for age and amount of gaze.
In the free-viewing (NO-CROSS) condition, autistic traits (AQ scores) did not correlate significantly with pupil contagion response.
Autistic traits (AQ scores) did not significantly correlate with heart rate or skin conductance contagion responses in either gaze condition.
Children looked significantly more toward the eye region when instructed via a fixation cross (CROSS condition) than during free viewing (NO-CROSS).
Older children looked more toward the eye region than younger children in both gaze conditions.
AQ score (autistic traits) did not correlate with the amount of eye gaze toward the face in either gaze condition after accounting for age.

Differences in image luminosity within the eye region did not significantly correlate with the differential pupil response to large versus small pupils, indicating that luminosity artefacts do not explain the pupillary contagion effect.

Myhre syndrome is caused by recurrent gain-of-function variants in SMAD4 and should be considered by clinicians evaluating young children who present with autism, short stature, and an unusual appearance.
One molecularly confirmed fetus with Myhre syndrome presented prenatally with severe intrauterine growth retardation and crossed fused renal ectopia.
A second molecularly confirmed fetus with Myhre syndrome had pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect, a form of tetralogy of Fallot.
Both fetuses with Myhre syndrome exhibited only mild dysmorphic facial features, notably a wide nasofrontal angle, distinct from the more distinctive facial gestalt typically seen postnatally.
Myhre syndrome can present with autism in young children, and clinicians evaluating children with autism plus short stature and unusual facial appearance should consider this diagnosis.
Prenatal next-generation sequencing (genome or exome sequencing) allowed molecular confirmation of Myhre syndrome in both fetuses, underscoring its value for prenatal diagnosis.
Fetal autopsy following termination of pregnancy was highlighted as important for characterizing the early phenotype of Myhre syndrome, including cardiac and external features.
Connective tissue involvement in Myhre syndrome can cause life-threatening cardiac and pulmonary complications as the disease progresses.

MENSA and serum IgG reactivity against six SARS-CoV-2 antigens were significantly higher in acutely infected patients than in unexposed healthy controls, with MENSA anti-RBD showing near-perfect diagnostic accuracy.
During acute primary SARS-CoV-2 infection, both MENSA and serum anti-RBD IgG rose more frequently and to a greater degree in severe/critical patients than mild/moderate patients.
Anti-nucleocapsid IgG in MENSA and serum was also elevated during acute infection, with slightly higher positivity in severe/critical patients than mild/moderate.
During convalescence, MENSA antibody levels dropped rapidly to negative in the majority of patients while serum antibody titers remained persistently elevated for months to years.

In vaccinated subjects with no prior infection, MENSA anti-RBD IgG rose after each vaccine dose and declined to negative before the next dose, while MENSA anti-N remained negative since nucleocapsid is not a vaccine component.

Self-reported symptom questionnaires in 60 PASC patients showed fatigue as the most common symptom (97%), followed by shortness of breath (75%), brain fog (67%), dizziness (52%), post-exertional malaise (47%), headache (42%), chest and muscle pain (38% each), chronic cough (37%), depression/anxiety (37%), palpitations (32%), sleep disturbance (32%), joint pain/arthralgia (32%), and loss of taste/smell (30%).

Among PASC patients referred for cardiac evaluation (58%), new diagnoses included tachycardia and/or POTS in 31%, arrhythmia/atrial fibrillation in 19%, heart failure in 11%, ongoing chest pain in 11%, and venous reflux/vein compression in 11%.
Dysautonomia was newly diagnosed in 8% of PASC patients following cardiac/autonomic referral.

A 12-symptom PASC severity score (average 11.8 at enrollment) with values ≥12 correlated with confirmed PASC status at 6 months, while lower scores were more likely to indicate indeterminate PASC status.
A subset of PASC patients (33%) had persistently positive MENSA for spike RBD beyond 60 days post-symptom onset, compared to none of the COVID-recovered patients.
A smaller subset of PASC patients (10%) had positive MENSA for nucleocapsid protein compared to none of the CR patients.
Serum antibodies to RBD and N were positive in nearly all PASC and CR patients with no meaningful difference between groups, showing that serum titers cannot distinguish PASC from full recovery.
Unbiased phage-display immunoprecipitation sequencing (PhIP-seq) of MENSA samples from PASC patients identified reactivation signatures against EBV, CMV, and HSV2 in addition to SARS-CoV-2.

In an expanded cohort tested with a combined SARS2/EBV/CMV/HSV2 assay, MENSA was positive for SARS-CoV-2 in 40% of PASC patients versus none of the CR patients, indicating ongoing viral antigen persistence.
MENSA reactivity against EBV antigens was more frequent in PASC patients than in COVID-recovered patients, indicating greater EBV reactivation.
MENSA reactivity against CMV antigens was more frequent in PASC patients than in COVID-recovered patients despite similar CMV seropositivity rates in serum.
MENSA reactivity against HSV2 antigen was more frequent in PASC patients than in COVID-recovered patients.

Overall, 60% of PASC patients had a positive MENSA for at least one of SARS-CoV-2, EBV, CMV, or HSV2, compared to only 17% of COVID-recovered patients, demonstrating viral persistence and/or reactivation as an underlying driver of PASC in the majority of patients tested.
PhIP-seq testing of MENSA against the human peptidome for autoantigens showed no differences between PASC and COVID-recovered patients in a limited sample.

In unexposed healthy controls, MENSA was rarely positive for any tested virus (13%, EBV only) while serum antibodies were positive in the large majority (88%), illustrating that MENSA reflects current/recent activity rather than lifetime exposure captured by serum.
VEGF levels between healthy controls and mild-to-moderate acute COVID-19 patients showed a near-significant trend but did not reach conventional statistical significance.

Aggregated analysis of the 14-cytokine panel plus derived indices showed no statistically significant difference between healthy controls and mild-moderate acute COVID-19 patients, supporting combination into a single 'Not Perturbed' class.

The gradient boosting machine (GBM) classifier achieved the best overall weighted performance among three tree-based models on the 20% hold-out evaluation set, distinguishing Not Perturbed, LC/PASC, and CLD.

In an independent, randomly-selected validation cohort of 124 patients (18 CLD, 106 LC/PASC), the GBM model achieved weighted sensitivity 97.58% and specificity 90.36%, with high class-specific performance for both LC/PASC and CLD.
The GBM surrogate decision tree showed that high IL-2 levels were associated with classification as LC/PASC, whereas lower IL-2 levels were associated with CLD and Not Perturbed individuals.
Altered VEGF levels were associated with chronic CLD, consistent with a prior published finding.
LC/PASC patients showed increased levels of IFN-γ together with IL-2, consistent with activation of pro-inflammatory effector T cells.
LC/PASC patients exhibited a chemotactic milieu of lower CCL4 and higher CCL3, promoting myeloid cell attraction and inflammation linked to persistent symptoms.
CLD patients showed increased concentrations of TNF-α, which was incorporated into the CLD Index to help distinguish them from LC/PASC patients.
CLD patients showed elevated IL-4, a type-2 associated cytokine, potentially reflecting a compensatory Th2-polarized response to TNF-α-driven inflammation.

Increased IFN-γ in LC/PASC promotes myeloid cell activation, previously associated with an increased frequency of inflammatory CD14+, CD16+, and CCR5+ monocytes in the PASC group compared to healthy donors.

A two-feature CLD/Lyme Index, combining TNF-α and IL-4 (CLD-associated) in the numerator with IFN-γ, IL-2, and CCL3 (LC/PASC-associated) in the denominator, achieved 100% sensitivity and specificity for discriminating CLD from LC/PASC on both the hold-out evaluation set and an independent 25-patient CLD dataset.
Chronic inflammation and elevated TNF-α have been reported to lower serotonin levels, potentially contributing to depression symptoms observed in CLD and LC/PASC patients.
Long COVID/PASC occurs in approximately 10-20% of individuals infected with SARS-CoV-2.
A systematic review and meta-analysis found that up to 45% of COVID-19 survivors, regardless of hospitalization status, had unresolved symptoms at four months.

In the RECOVER adult cohort, 37 symptoms across multiple systems were more common in SARS-CoV-2-infected participants at six months than in uninfected participants, with fatigue, post-exertional malaise, brain fog, dizziness, palpitations, and GI symptoms being most prevalent.
PASC positivity at six months was higher among participants hospitalized during acute COVID-19 than among non-hospitalized participants.
Women had a higher rate of PASC positivity than men in the RECOVER adult cohort.
Middle-aged adults (46-65 years) had higher PASC positivity than younger adults (18-45 years) in the RECOVER cohort.

RECOVER data analysis identified four distinct PASC symptom cluster phenotypes among adults, characterized by differing combinations of smell/taste changes, post-exertional malaise, fatigue, brain fog, dizziness, GI symptoms, and palpitations.

The RECOVER-Pediatrics Consortium identified 14 symptoms of long COVID/PASC in both school-age children and adolescents with confirmed prior SARS-CoV-2 infection compared with uninfected controls, affecting nearly every organ system.

In children of school age, neurocognitive symptoms, pain, and gastrointestinal symptoms were associated with reduced quality of life, while in adolescents pain, changes in smell or taste, and fatigue-related symptoms were associated with reduced quality of life.

Middle age (40-69 years), female gender, COVID-19 hospitalization, longer hospital stay, mechanical ventilation, depression, chronic lung disease, and obesity were associated with increased risk of a long COVID/PASC diagnosis in the N3C case-control study.

Younger age (18-29 years), male gender, non-Hispanic Black race, and absence of comorbidities such as substance abuse, psychosis, dementia, and cardiomyopathy were associated with lower risk of a long COVID/PASC diagnosis in the N3C study.

Using EHR data from two large PCORnet networks (INSIGHT and OneFlorida+), dementia, pressure ulcers, hair loss, pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary embolism, dyspnea, chest pain, cardiac dysrhythmias, malaise, and fatigue were risk factors for long COVID/PASC replicated in both cohorts, though overall risk factor profiles differed between the two geographic populations.

Individuals with a history of confirmed COVID-19 had increased risk of heart failure, myocardial infarction, and ischemic stroke at 12 months compared with controls, independent of cardiovascular risk factors.

In a US Veterans Affairs cohort of 153,760 individuals with COVID-19, there was significantly increased risk of myocarditis, cerebrovascular disease, dysrhythmias, pericarditis, ischemic and non-ischemic heart disease, thromboembolic disease, and heart failure at 30 days post-infection, including in non-hospitalized individuals.

In the RECOVER-Adult biomarker study, participants with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection had lower platelet counts and higher HbA1c and urinary albumin-creatinine ratio than uninfected participants, though differences were of modest clinical significance.

Among participants with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection, there was no significant difference in mean laboratory values between those with a high PASC symptom index (≥12) and those with a PASC index of zero, indicating that none of 25 routine clinical laboratory tests served as a useful biomarker for long COVID/PASC.

SARS-CoV-2 enters host cells via binding of its spike protein to the ACE2 receptor, which is expressed on endothelial cells, cardiac myocytes, and vascular smooth muscle cells, providing a mechanistic basis for cardiovascular involvement in long COVID.
Ongoing research suggests SARS-CoV-2 can alter mitochondrial function, potentially explaining the fatigue and malaise reported by many long COVID/PASC patients.
Evidence indicates SARS-CoV-2 is not a purely transient infection, with viral fragments detectable in the body more than six months after initial infection.
Research in the US, South Africa, and the UK has shown that SARS-CoV-2 infection can alter clotting proteins and induce autoimmune reactions, mechanisms proposed to contribute to long COVID/PASC.

As of 2020, an estimated 2.5 million people in the US and 24 million people worldwide had myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome, a post-infectious illness associated with herpesvirus and enterovirus infections, cited as a historical analogy for long COVID/PASC.
Microglial activation was significantly higher in PASC patients with neurological symptoms compared with PASC patients without neurological symptoms, based on postmortem brain tissue analysis.
Brain tissue from PASC patients showed impaired hippocampal neurogenesis, myelin loss, and reduced oligodendrocyte numbers, in addition to microglial reactivity.

In a study of CSF from PASC patients with neurological symptoms, a quarter had elevated CSF protein levels and 13% showed blood-brain barrier dysfunction as measured by the CSF/serum albumin quotient.
Severely ill COVID-19 patients showed higher CMV seroprevalence compared with the general population.

COVID-19 patients with CMV infection showed a Th17-dominated immune shift marked by elevated CMV-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cell responses and increased IFNγ, IL-17, and TNFα production in both mild and severe cases.
Post-COVID-19 patient subgroups (mild, severe, without chronic symptoms) showed significantly higher IgG response against EBV and HSV-1 compared with healthy donors.
Elevated HHV-6 antibody titers were observed specifically in the ME/CFS subgroup of a post-COVID-19 comparison study, suggesting a possible link between HHV-6 and symptom persistence.

ACE2, the SARS-CoV-2 receptor, promotes the Z transcriptional activator, enhancing latent EBV reactivation, while EBV reactivation in turn increases ACE2 expression on epithelial cells, potentially promoting SARS-CoV-2 viral entry.

In serologic testing of 280 adults with post-COVID-19 conditions, fatigue and neurocognitive dysfunction were significantly associated with EBV early antigen-diffuse (EA-D) IgG positivity or high EBV nuclear antigen (EBNA) levels.

Among patients assessed 21-90 days and over 90 days post-SARS-CoV-2 infection, 30.3% had elevated anti-EBV antibody titers, suggesting symptom overlap between EBV reactivation and post-COVID-19 conditions.

An Austrian study of 400 previously SARS-CoV-2-infected patients (72 with PASC) found no EBV viremia in PASC patients and no significant differences in EBV serology between those with and without PASC.
A study could not detect EBV via PCR in throat washings, stool, or blood samples from post-COVID-19 patients with neurological symptoms.

Williams et al. found no significant differences in EBV/CMV-specific T cell responses between PASC patients with neurological symptoms and healthy individuals, though PASC patients showed an increased CD8+ T cell response to non-Spike antigens, a finding not consistently replicated.
CMV-specific T cells in the context of PASC often show signs of immunosenescence, including loss of CD28 expression and accumulation of CD57 and KLRG1.
A high prevalence of active HHV-6 infection has been reported in ME/CFS patients, accompanied by increased plasma proinflammatory cytokines and correlation with PASC-like clinical symptoms.
HHV-6 has been linked to ME/CFS, although the evidence for this association remains inconclusive.
The presence of CMV in endothelial cells has been causally linked to impairments in endothelium-dependent regulation of blood flow and endothelial barrier function.
Elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, including IL-6, TNF-alpha, and CCL11, have been identified in the cerebrospinal fluid and blood of PASC patients.
Over one-third of patients aged 65 and older who had COVID-19 develop persistent symptoms lasting more than 6 months, leading to a considerable reduction in quality of life.

In SARS-CoV-2 infected patients, high sympathetic nervous activity manifesting as POTS is present in earlier disease stages, with alterations persisting as further PASC symptoms develop and gradually decreasing over time.
Serum serotonin levels were similar between PASC patients and healthy controls, with no evidence of reduced peripheral serotonin in PASC.
Serotonin levels did not differ between PASC patients with predominantly physical versus mental fatigue.
Serotonin levels did not differ between PASC patients with high versus low depression scores.
The majority of both PASC patients and healthy controls had serotonin levels within the normal range, and no individual had subnormal serotonin levels.

The authors note that prior studies by Sadlier et al. and one of three cohorts studied by Wong et al. found significantly lower serotonin levels in PASC patients compared with controls, along with dysregulated tryptophan metabolism, though these findings were not consistently replicated across cohorts.
About 6.2% of people infected with SARS-CoV-2 experience at least one of three PASC symptom clusters (fatigue with pain/psychological problems, neurocognitive problems, or respiratory issues).
PASC prevalence rates vary across studies and are highest among women and among patients who required hospitalization for the initial SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Roughly one-fifth of PASC patients have mental health comorbidities including anxiety, depression, PTSD symptoms, and sleep disruption.
Depressive symptoms were present in 23% of individuals 12 months after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Anxiety symptoms were present in 22% of individuals 12 months after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Estimates of insomnia/sleep disturbance prevalence after SARS-CoV-2 infection ranged widely, from 12% in one study to as high as 45% in another.
Posttraumatic stress symptoms after SARS-CoV-2 infection range from 6.5% to 42.8%, and are particularly high among those who had severe infection.
Preexisting psychological/psychosomatic conditions such as depression, anxiety, loneliness, and perceived stress are proposed vulnerability factors for developing PASC symptoms.
In an initial study, psychological distress associated with persistent symptoms during the first pandemic year predicted the presence of at least one persistent symptom 6-10 months later.
Outpatient cognitive behavioral interventions improved fatigue symptoms and coping in PASC patients in prior studies.
Multimodal inpatient rehabilitation with psychotherapeutic elements reduced psychological and somatic symptoms and improved activity and social participation in prior PASC studies.
Aerobic exercise was shown to be effective and safe as an early intervention after (severe) SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Aerobic exercise was shown to improve PASC-related fatigue and functional capacity in prior studies.
Activity pacing as a self-management strategy has been shown to positively impact fatigue severity in chronic diseases.
Initial studies suggest computerized neurocognitive training shows promising results for neurocognitive impairment in PASC patients.
The PCS Score, a 12-item weighted yes/no symptom questionnaire (range 0-59) used as the primary outcome measure, has been validated in a German population.
Overall PASC symptom severity measured by the PCS-S decreased significantly between baseline (T0) and 3+ month follow-up (T1).
Depressive symptom severity significantly decreased from T0 to T1 in the long-COVID cohort.
Somatic symptom severity showed the largest significant decrease from T0 to T1 among the mental-health measures.
Anxiety symptom severity decreased modestly but significantly from T0 to T1.
At follow-up, PASC patients' depression, somatization, and anxiety scores remained significantly higher than published normal-population reference values despite improvement over time.
Fatigue severity did not significantly improve between T0 and T1, remaining at a clinically high level, and was the most common PASC symptom in the cohort.
PEM severity and frequency did not significantly decrease between T0 and T1, consistent with a non-self-limiting course similar to ME/CFS.
Older age was associated with higher depressive symptom (PHQ-9) scores at follow-up in mixed-model analysis.
A longer time span between acute infection and baseline presentation was associated with higher PEM severity and frequency scores at follow-up.
Sex, severity/course of the acute COVID-19 infection, and a pathologic echocardiogram were not significantly associated with mental health outcomes in mixed-model analysis.
Patients with a history of mental illness and prior psychotherapy had significantly higher depression, anxiety, somatic, and PASC symptom scores at follow-up compared to those without such a history.
Severe PASC (PCS-S >26.25) was present in 80.8% of patients at the 22.5-month follow-up, a higher prevalence than reported in comparable studies.

At follow-up, clinically relevant depression, somatic symptoms and anxiety were prevalent in 55.8%, 72.5% and 18.9% of patients respectively, exceeding rates reported in most other longitudinal PASC studies.
Unemployment and sick-leave/incapacitation rates increased between baseline and follow-up in the long-COVID cohort.
Elevated IL-6 and CRP after the initial period of SARS-CoV-2 replication were correlated with increased risk of respiratory failure and need for mechanical ventilation.
Tocilizumab, an IL-6 pathway-targeting monoclonal antibody, showed positive early reports for treating patients during the early inflammatory phase of COVID-19.
The RECOVERY trial demonstrated a mortality benefit from low-dose dexamethasone given after the first week during the early inflammatory phase of COVID-19.
Repeated SARS-CoV-2 infections can increase an individual's risk of developing postacute sequelae of COVID-19.
The natural history of long COVID is that most affected individuals improve over time, with only a minority still having a persistent condition at 2 years.
Long COVID is associated with exhausted SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells and miscoordination between T-cell and B-cell responses, producing immune dysregulation.

Long COVID is marked by increased soluble C5bC6 complexes and decreased C7-containing terminal complement complex formations, associated with elevated platelet activation markers and monocyte-platelet aggregates.
Longer time to clear SARS-CoV-2 RNA from the upper respiratory tract during acute infection correlates with long COVID brain fog and muscle pain.

SARS-CoV-2 viral RNA has been detected in liver, kidney, stomach, intestine, brain, blood vessels, lung, breast, skin, and thyroid for months after infection, potentially correlating with long COVID symptom development.

Metagenomic sequencing shows depletion of Bifidobacterium adolescentis and Roseburia hominis, and enrichment of Clostridium bolteae and Flavonifractor plautii, in the fecal microbiota of individuals with long COVID, with specific gut enterotypes associated with individual symptoms.
Persistently high, CD8+ T-cell-mediated interferon-gamma levels are seen in long COVID patients, and normalization of these levels correlates with symptom improvement.
Individuals with long COVID show significantly higher antibody levels against EBV, CMV, and varicella-zoster virus compared to those who recover.
Long COVID patients show low cortisol levels without a compensatory increase in ACTH, suggesting a post-COVID adrenal insufficiency disorder.
EBV viremia detected at the time of initial acute COVID-19 diagnosis is an early risk factor and potentially causative contributor to the development of long COVID.

A subset of long COVID patients have reduced circulating serotonin levels, possibly driven by type I interferons, reduced tryptophan uptake, and thrombocytopenia-related decreased serotonin storage, which may impair cognition via reduced vagal signaling.
Elevated neurofilament light chain levels in COVID-19 patients with ongoing neurocognitive symptoms suggest neuroaxonal damage and may correlate with cognitive loss and long COVID exacerbations.
There is a high incidence of autonomic dysfunction and POTS in patients with PASC, documented in both pediatric and adult patients.
Downregulation of core mitochondrial genes during acute COVID has been suggested as a mechanism triggering postexertional malaise and resulting myopathy and focal necrosis.
Ultrasound imaging in some long COVID patients shows thickened, hyperechogenic vagal nerves along with reduced intestinal peristalsis, consistent with ongoing vagal nerve dysfunction.

Long COVID patients can be clustered into three symptom groups: cluster 1 predominantly pain (joint pain, myalgia, headache), cluster 2 predominantly cardiovascular (chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations), and cluster 3 with significantly fewer symptoms overall.

Formal cognitive testing quantified deficits after mild resolved COVID-19 as equivalent to a 3-point IQ loss, rising to a 6-point loss with unresolved persistent symptoms and a 9-point loss in those admitted to the ICU.
In a Swedish study, vaccine effectiveness against post-COVID conditions was 21% for one dose, 59% for two doses, and 73% for three or more doses.

Early treatment of acute COVID-19 with nirmatrelvir-ritonavir reduces the postacute incidence of congestive heart failure, atrial fibrillation, coronary artery disease, chronic pulmonary disease, interstitial lung disease, and end-stage renal disease.
Early administration of COVID-19 convalescent plasma reduced cytokine levels and was associated with lower odds of developing post-COVID conditions.
Corticosteroids administered appropriately to hospitalized acute COVID-19 patients may exert a protective effect against development of post-COVID-19 syndromes.
Vaccination administered after development of long COVID symptoms has therapeutic benefits, with symptom improvement increasing with each successive dose.
A Swedish study found dose-dependent vaccine effectiveness against post-COVID-19 conditions of 21%, 59%, and 73% for one, two, and three or more doses respectively.
Vaccination prior to infection reduces the risk of developing diabetes after COVID-19.
Vaccination decreases the elevated risk of cardiovascular disease seen after COVID-19 infection.

Early treatment of acute COVID-19 with nirmatrelvir-ritonavir reduces the postacute incidence of congestive heart failure, atrial fibrillation, coronary artery disease, chronic pulmonary disease, interstitial lung disease, and end-stage renal disease.

Treatment of acute COVID-19 with nirmatrelvir-ritonavir reduces the incidence of major adverse cardiac events (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, new-onset heart failure, heart failure hospitalization, or ventricular arrhythmia).

Early administration of COVID-19 convalescent plasma reduces cytokine levels and is associated with lower odds of developing post-COVID conditions, in contrast to monoclonal antibody therapy which has not shown this benefit.
Early monoclonal antibody therapy for acute COVID-19, despite dramatic acute benefits, has not been shown to prevent development of long COVID.
Corticosteroids given appropriately to hospitalized patients with acute COVID may protect against development of post-COVID-19 syndromes.
Early metformin use showed possible promise in reducing risk of long COVID in one trial requiring a challenging regimen, but the finding has not been replicated.
COVID-19 vaccination given after long COVID onset has therapeutic benefits, with symptom benefit increasing dose-dependently from one to three doses.
Vaccination in patients with existing post-COVID conditions is associated with reduced symptoms, increased well-being, and downregulation of systemic inflammatory markers.
Melatonin may benefit individuals with PASC not only for sleep disturbance but also through possible effects on inflammation, symptoms, and recovery time.
Probiotics containing bifidobacteria strains reduced nasopharyngeal viral load, reduced pro-inflammatory immune markers, and restored a healthy gut microbiome during acute infection.

In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, the SUM01 probiotic-prebiotic formulation (containing Bifidobacterium adolescentis, B. bifidum, B. longum plus galacto-oligosaccharides, xylo-oligosaccharides, and resistant dextrin, dosed at 10 billion CFU twice daily) alleviated fatigue, memory loss, concentration problems, gastrointestinal symptoms, and general unwellness compared with placebo.

Graded exercise training may benefit a properly selected subset of long COVID patients without postexertional malaise, but studies supporting GET or pacing are criticized for selecting only patients able to participate rather than proving general benefit.
Inducing postexertional malaise through exertion can be harmful, triggering metabolic disturbances, myopathy, amyloid-containing deposits, and focal necrosis.
Measuring heart rate recovery at the first minute after exercise termination can identify individuals who might benefit from inspiratory muscle training and allow monitoring of treatment response.
Active cycle breathing techniques such as box breathing have been recommended for long COVID patients because these patients show lower parasympathetic tone and autonomic dysfunction.
Slow-paced breathing may modulate autonomic tone in long COVID, decreasing systolic blood pressure oscillation and heart rate variability while improving symptoms.

The ME/CFS literature does not support any significant or sustained benefit of cognitive behavioral therapy for severe post-COVID fatigue, and recommending it is contradictory to NICE ME/CFS guidelines.
Case reports suggest immunoglobulin therapy may provide benefit for some patients suffering from long COVID.

Case studies suggest guanfacine (an alpha-2A-adrenoreceptor agonist, 1 mg at bedtime titrated to 2 mg) combined with N-acetylcysteine 600 mg daily may benefit long COVID patients with working memory and executive function impairment.
Antihistamines or low-histamine diets, including combinations of H1 and H2 antihistamines, may provide benefit for long COVID patients with an immune/allergic phenotype.
Reduced circulating serotonin levels in long COVID have suggested use of higher-dose serotonin reuptake inhibitors or alternative agents such as SNRIs or NDRIs.
Early treatment of acute COVID-19 with nirmatrelvir-ritonavir was associated with reduced postacute incidence of major adverse cardiac events and several chronic organ conditions.
Early administration of COVID-19 convalescent plasma reduced cytokine levels and lowered the odds of developing post-COVID conditions.
Corticosteroids administered appropriately to hospitalized patients with acute COVID may protect against development of post-COVID-19 syndromes.
Early use of metformin has shown possible benefit against developing long COVID but this required a challenging regimen and has not been replicated.
Early monoclonal antibody therapy for acute COVID-19 did not show benefit in preventing long COVID despite dramatic impacts on acute outcomes.

A randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial of the SUM01 probiotic/prebiotic formulation showed alleviation of fatigue, reduced memory loss, improved concentration, reduced GI symptoms, and less general unwellness compared with placebo in long COVID patients.
Graded exercise training may benefit a properly selected subset of long COVID patients without postexertional malaise, but poorly designed studies and potential harms are a concern.

Cognitive behavioral therapy for severe fatigue after COVID-19 remains controversial, and ME/CFS literature does not support significant or sustained benefit, contradicting NICE ME/CFS guidelines to recommend it.
Case studies suggest a potential benefit of the alpha-2A-adrenoreceptor agonist guanfacine combined with N-acetylcysteine for working memory and executive function impacts in long COVID.
Antihistamines or low-histamine diets, including combinations of H1 and H2 antihistamines, may provide benefit for individuals with long COVID, particularly those with immune/allergic phenotype.
Reduced circulating serotonin levels in a subset of long COVID patients led to trials using higher-dose serotonin reuptake inhibitors, alternative reuptake inhibitors, or increased tryptophan intake.
Topical nasal steroids may be beneficial for olfactory dysfunction after COVID-19, while systemic steroids do not appear to provide benefit.
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy has been tried in long COVID with some suggestion of short- and longer-term impacts on quality of life, sleep, and pain, though data remain limited.
Treatment with catalytically active human RNase fused to human IgG, designed to degrade remnant viral RNA, did not produce a statistically significant impact on fatigue in long COVID.

Formal cognitive testing found that about half of long COVID patients have episodic memory deficits and about a quarter have impaired overall cognitive function including attention, working memory, processing speed, and verbal fluency.

Formal testing quantified cognitive deficits in long COVID as equivalent to a 3-point IQ loss in mild resolved cases, 6-point loss with unresolved persistent symptoms, and 9-point loss in those admitted to intensive care.

The cognitive profile of long COVID's neurological phenotype resembles that of multiple sclerosis in attention and processing speed impacts, but MS shows more episodic memory impairment while long COVID shows more severe fatigue.
Some individuals with the gastrointestinal phenotype of long COVID have documented intestinal methanogen overgrowth from methane-producing archaea with carbohydrate malabsorption.
COVID-19 infection during the first pandemic year, prior to vaccine availability, was associated with a significantly increased risk of new-onset erectile dysfunction.
After acute COVID-19, men showed increased incidence of urinary retention, hematuria, and urinary tract infections regardless of COVID-19 severity, attributed to prostatic hyperplasia deterioration.
Semen quality, including sperm count and motility, can be significantly reduced after SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Women experience reproductive health impacts of long COVID including menstrual irregularity, symptom exacerbation around menstruation, dyspareunia, infertility, pelvic congestion syndrome, adverse pregnancy outcomes, and endometriosis.
There is an elevated risk of a wide range of rheumatological and autoimmune disorders developing after acute COVID-19.

COVID-19 vaccination administered after long COVID onset was associated with reduced symptoms, increased well-being, and downregulation of systemic inflammatory markers, with benefit increasing with additional doses.
Melatonin may offer benefit for long COVID beyond sleep disturbance, with possible impacts on inflammation, symptoms, and recovery time.
Probiotics containing bifidobacteria strains reduced nasopharyngeal viral load, reduced pro-inflammatory immune markers, and restored a healthy gut microbiome in COVID-19.

Fecal microbiota temporal changes in COVID-19 patients show increased Bacteroides and decreased Prevotella, with disease severity negatively correlated with butyrate-producing bacteria such as Lachnospiraceae, Roseburia, and Faecalibacterium.
Patients in the cardiovascular long COVID cluster show evidence of endothelial dysfunction with impaired myocardial flow reserve, calculated as the ratio of stress to rest myocardial blood flow.
There is an increased risk of new-onset persistent hypertension after acute COVID-19.
Using the Composite Autonomic Symptom Score-31 or Work Ability Index, unrecognized autonomic dysfunction can be identified in long COVID patients with significant reduction in their ability to work.

Endocrine long COVID phenotype includes impacts on thyroid function and increased incidence of type 2 diabetes, in addition to post-COVID adrenal insufficiency with low cortisol and no compensatory ACTH rise.
PASC is a recognized syndrome with its own ICD-10 code (U09.9), and a subset of PASC patients meeting ME/CFS criteria can carry that diagnosis (G93.32) separately or in addition.

Children and adolescents with documented SARS-CoV-2 infection had a 34% higher relative risk of any of 96 examined health outcomes within 0-3 months after infection compared to matched uninfected controls.
Smell or taste disturbance showed very high excess relative risk following COVID-19, detected almost equally in younger children and adolescents.
Malaise/exhaustion was significantly more frequent following COVID-19, with a slightly higher relative risk in adolescents than in younger children.
Adolescents with prior COVID-19 showed a significant increase in risk of new-onset ME/CFS diagnosis, an effect that was more pronounced and statistically robust than in younger children.
The relative risk of respiratory insufficiency in adolescents increased rather than declined between the early and late follow-up periods after COVID-19.
Hepatomegaly and splenomegaly were among the most frequently diagnosed conditions in adolescents following COVID-19.

Children aged 0-11 years showed a striking and persistent excess risk of inflammatory disorders (including MIS-C/PIMS, SIRS, systemic-onset juvenile rheumatoid arthritis) throughout all four follow-up quarters after COVID-19.
Among diagnostic symptom complexes, pulmonary symptoms had the highest relative risk in adolescents following COVID-19.
Negative control outcomes (prescription glasses and acne), chosen to detect detection bias, showed no statistical association with prior COVID-19.

Within 0-3 months after infection, children with COVID-19 had about twice the risk of the WHO-defined post-COVID condition (based on fatigue, smell/taste disturbance, and anxiety) compared with controls.
Anxiety, one of the three WHO-designated most specific PCC symptoms, showed only a modest and much smaller excess relative risk than smell/taste disturbance and fatigue.

When anxiety was excluded from the WHO PCC definition, the excess relative risk of the remaining specific symptoms (smell/taste disturbance and fatigue) rose considerably, with adolescents more frequently affected than children.

At the individual level, cardiac symptoms, gastrointestinal symptoms, inflammatory disorders, respiratory insufficiency, fatigue (malaise/exhaustion or ME/CFS), and sensation/perception disorders showed both initial excess risk and more prolonged persistence in the COVID-19 group compared to controls.
Myalgia, joint pain, sleep disorders, mood swings, and hyperhidrosis showed faster recovery in the COVID-19 group, with persistent case numbers ultimately converging with the control group.

Stratified analysis by sex found no relevant differences in relative risk (IRR) of health domains or symptom complexes between girls and boys, although absolute incidence of outcomes was generally higher among girls.

Among adolescents, excess incidence of dyspnea decreased over the year following COVID-19 while excess incidence of respiratory insufficiency doubled, suggesting an aggravation shift in respiratory pathology over time.
