At the individual level, most incident post-acute symptoms showed similar persistence trajectories between COVID-19 cases and controls, with persistence rates falling below 10% after one year for the majority of outcomes.
Black adults with long COVID reported significantly more anxiety symptoms than those with SARS-CoV-2 but no long COVID.
Black adults with long COVID reported significantly more depressive symptoms than those with SARS-CoV-2 without long COVID.
Black adults with long COVID reported significantly more hopelessness than those with SARS-CoV-2 without long COVID.
Persons with long COVID were significantly more likely to report experiencing psychosis within the last year compared to those with SARS-CoV-2 without long COVID.
Persons with long COVID were significantly more likely to report suicidal ideation within the last year compared to those with SARS-CoV-2 without long COVID.
Persons with long COVID were significantly more likely to report suicide plans within the last year compared to those with SARS-CoV-2 without long COVID.
Persons with long COVID were significantly more likely to report suicide attempts within the last year compared to those with SARS-CoV-2 without long COVID.

Qualitative accounts from Black adults with long COVID predominantly described physical health problems including prolonged coughing, cardiovascular concerns, troubled breathing, fatigue, headaches, memory loss, and bodily pains.

After 12 weeks of herbal medicine treatment, fatigue treatment success (VAS improvement of more than 15 points) was achieved in 80% of the Bojungikgi-tang group, 53.33% of the Kyungok-go group, and 46.67% of the Cheonwangbosim-dan group, with no significant difference between groups.

Treatment success rates for cognitive dysfunction (VAS improvement >15 points) were comparatively low: 40% in BIT, 46.67% in KOG, and 13.33% in CBD groups, with no significant between-group difference.

The Checklist Individual Strength (CIS) fatigue severity score significantly improved from baseline at 13, 25, and 37 weeks in all three herbal medicine groups, with no significant differences between groups.
VAS fatigue scores significantly improved from baseline at 13, 25 and 37 weeks in all three groups, with no significant between-group differences.

Chalder Fatigue Scale total, physical, and mental health scores significantly improved from baseline in all three groups at 13 weeks, with the mental health subscale showing a significant between-group difference.
No group showed a significant improvement in the cognitive dysfunction VAS score at 13, 25, or 37 weeks.
Only the Kyungok-go (KOG) group showed a significant improvement in K-MoCA cognitive score at 13, 25, and 37 weeks.

Cognitive Failure Questionnaire scores significantly improved in all three groups by 37 weeks, with the largest reduction in the Cheonwangbosim-dan (CBD) group, suggesting a potential effect of CBD on cognitive dysfunction recovery.
Digit span forward and backward test scores showed no significant improvement in any group at 13, 25, or 37 weeks.
The Korean-Boston Naming Test-15 language proficiency score showed no significant improvement in any group at 13, 25, or 37 weeks.
Health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L) did not differ significantly between groups at 13, 25, or 37 weeks, though a slight improvement was seen in the BIT group at 13 weeks.
Sleep quality (PSQI-K) significantly improved only in the Kyungok-go (KOG) group at 13, 25, and 37 weeks, with no significant improvement in the other groups.
Beck's Depression Inventory scores significantly improved in the BIT and KOG groups at 13, 25, and 37 weeks.
Ten of 45 participants (22.22%) reported adverse events with no significant difference in incidence across groups; all AEs were mild and none were judged causally related to the herbal medications.

Fourteen of 45 participants (31%) dropped out over the study period, largely due to unexpected illness including six COVID-19 reinfections, with no withdrawals attributed to drug-related adverse events.
Medication adherence among participants who completed the 12-week course was high across all three herbal medicine groups.
The target enrollment of 45 participants was achieved over 12 months at a recruitment rate of 4 participants per month, supporting overall feasibility of the trial design.
Exercise interventions significantly improved fatigue in long COVID patients across pooled RCTs.
Exercise interventions significantly improved dyspnea in long COVID patients across pooled RCTs.
No significant effect of exercise interventions was found on anxiety in long COVID patients.
No significant overall effect of exercise interventions was found on depression in long COVID patients, though multimodal exercise showed benefit in subgroup analysis.
No significant effect of exercise interventions was found on cognitive impairment in long COVID patients.
Subgroup analysis found multimodal exercise had the broadest benefit, improving fatigue, dyspnea, and depression in long COVID patients.
Supervised exercise delivery showed a positive effect on some long COVID symptoms in subgroup analysis.
An intervention frequency of 4 or fewer times per week showed a positive effect on some long COVID symptoms in subgroup analysis.
94% of long COVID patients undergoing stellate ganglion block reported moderate-to-severe autonomic dysfunction on the COMPASS-31 survey prior to the procedure.
Patients had significantly lower Fatigue Severity Score after stellate ganglion block compared to pre-procedure.
Heart rate was significantly lower after stellate ganglion block compared to baseline.
PCL-5 (PTSD checklist) scores decreased after stellate ganglion block in a clinically meaningful but statistically non-significant manner.
No significant difference was found in GAD-7 anxiety scores before and after stellate ganglion block.
All 17 patients reported some degree of symptomatic improvement following stellate ganglion block, and the procedure was considered safe and low-risk.
Presence of fatigue was associated with a significantly lower daily step count after adjustment for covariates.
Post-exertional malaise was associated with a significantly lower daily step count after adjustment for covariates.
Post-exertional malaise was negatively associated with minutes per week of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity.
Greater co-occurrence of adverse physical symptoms (2, 3, or 4 concurrent symptoms) was associated with progressively lower daily step counts compared to ≤1 symptom.
Co-occurrence of 3 or 4 adverse physical symptoms was associated with lower light physical activity time compared to ≤1 symptom.
Dyspnea was negatively associated with the composite functional score (based on 6MWT, 30-s CST, and TUG) after adjustment for covariates.
Dyspnea was associated with a longer (worse) timed up and go completion time after adjustment for covariates.
Dyspnea and myalgia showed no significant association with sedentary time, light physical activity, MVPA, or step count.
Fatigue, post-exertional malaise, and myalgia showed no significant association with 6MWT, 30-s CST, or TUG performance.
Individuals who had severe acute COVID-19 (ICU admission) exhibited a higher daily step count than those with mild or moderate acute illness.
Fatigue, dyspnea, post-exertional malaise, and myalgia were highly prevalent among the Long COVID cohort, with fatigue and dyspnea most common.
The majority of participants with Long COVID did not meet current physical activity guidelines of at least 150 minutes/week of MVPA.
A large majority of Long COVID participants performed below age/sex/BMI-predicted norms on 6MWT, 30-s CST and TUG.

In an Italian case-control study cited by the authors, people who had contracted SARS-CoV-2 were more likely to be prescribed antidepressants afterward, particularly if unvaccinated, elderly, or having had severe COVID-19.
Comparable increases in prescriptions of opioids and sleeping pills after COVID-19 are noted, suggesting disease-related induction of sleep disorders and pain syndromes.
The elevated risk of depression following COVID-19 appears to normalize over time.
In contrast to depression, the increased risk of psychotic disorders and dementia after COVID-19 appears to persist over time rather than normalize.

Fluvoxamine added to standard therapy for 10-14 days in mild-to-moderate COVID-19 resulted in significantly fewer severe courses and deaths compared with placebo or standard therapy alone, with good tolerability, supported by at least 8 meta-analyses, 7 placebo-controlled RCTs and 5 prospective studies.

At least four large retrospective studies, each including more than 20,000 hospitalized patients, indicate that antidepressants as a drug class may protect against severe COVID-19 outcomes, though this warrants further well-controlled trials.
Initial small clinical trials show that various antidepressants relieve at least fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, and other psychiatric symptoms of Long COVID.

Antidepressants as a class are thought to have a pronounced protective anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effect against oxidative-stress-mediated tissue destruction resulting from prolonged hyperinflammation following SARS-CoV-2 cell entry.
Antiviral properties have been described for many antidepressants, including activity against SARS-CoV-2 infection.

A serotonin deficit was recently reported in the serum of Long COVID patients, potentially resulting from SARS-CoV-2-related gut microbiome dysbiosis, since more than 95% of the body's serotonin is localized in the gastrointestinal tract.

Much of the neuropsychiatric symptomatology of Long COVID, including depression, anxiety, fatigue, and cognitive dysfunction, may be promoted by premature (potentially reversible) 'aging' of midbrain dopaminergic neurons.

Proposed biological mechanisms for Long COVID discussed include persistence of SARS-CoV-2 in immune-privileged sites (eye, brain, testis), reactivation of other latent viruses, autoimmunity or misdirected immune responses, persistent hyperinflammation with subsequent mitochondrial dysfunction, respiratory/gastrointestinal microbiome dysbiosis, and protracted sickness behavior, alongside organic sequelae such as pulmonary fibrosis, heart disease, stroke, and kidney damage.
The author proposes that Long-COVID arises from an immune network mechanism in which the anti-SARS-CoV-2 immune response is redirected toward autoimmune targets, producing autoantibodies.
The paper suggests several therapeutic interventions aimed at suppressing the proposed autoimmune pathway underlying Long-COVID.
Among patients with preexisting neurological disease who had recovered from COVID-19, neurological symptoms were the most commonly reported category of long COVID symptoms.
Fatigue was the most frequently reported persistent long COVID symptom in the cohort.
Within the neurological symptom category, tingling sensation, headache, and dizziness were the most commonly reported individual symptoms.
About one-third of participants with preexisting neurological disease subjectively reported worsening of their neurological condition after contracting COVID-19.
A higher number of long COVID symptoms significantly predicted subjective deterioration of preexisting neurological conditions in logistic regression models.
The number of long COVID symptoms significantly influenced anxiety levels, remaining significant after adjustment for COVID-19-related and demographic variables.
The number of long COVID symptoms significantly influenced depression, remaining significant after adjustment for COVID-19-related and demographic variables.
The number of long COVID symptoms significantly influenced fatigue, remaining significant after adjustment for COVID-19-related and demographic variables.
Subjective deterioration of preexisting neurological condition was associated with depression in unadjusted analysis but lost significance after controlling for COVID-19-related variables.
Subjective deterioration of preexisting neurological disease continued to significantly impact anxiety and fatigue even after adjusting for COVID-19-related and demographic variables.
Female sex was associated with greater fatigue in the fully adjusted logistic regression model.
Participants reported significantly reduced quality of life across most domains after COVID-19 infection compared to before infection.
Hyposmia and hypogeusia were reported at relatively low rates in this cohort compared to prior studies of COVID-19-related olfactory/gustatory dysfunction.
Decreased attention and cognitive decline (brain fog symptoms) were reported by a subset of patients following COVID-19 infection.
Left external oblique muscle activation during the plank exercise significantly increased after the 12-week plank-based core-stabilization program, with a medium effect size.
Right external oblique muscle activation significantly increased post-intervention, with a small effect size.
Right latissimus dorsi muscle activation increased significantly post-intervention, with a small effect size.

Activation of the remaining muscles (rectus abdominis, internal oblique, gluteus maximus, gluteus medius, left latissimus dorsi, and erector spinae) improved numerically after the intervention but did not reach statistical significance.
Total Modified Fatigue Impact Scale (MFIS) score significantly decreased after the 12-week plank-based training program, indicating reduced fatigue, with a medium effect size.
The physical fatigue subscale of the MFIS improved significantly post-intervention, with a large effect size.
The psychosocial fatigue subscale of the MFIS improved significantly post-intervention, with a small effect size.
The cognitive fatigue subscale of the MFIS improved numerically but did not reach statistical significance.
At baseline, nearly all participants (19 of 21, 90.5%) had MFIS scores indicating significant fatigue, reflecting the high prevalence of fatigue among long COVID patients.
The plank-based core-stabilization program was well tolerated, with no adverse effects reported and full participant adherence (all 21 subjects completed the 12-week intervention with no attrition).

Adults in the multi-symptomatic acute symptom cluster (flu-like, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, and neurological symptoms) had over six times the prevalence of long COVID compared with the nasal congestion cluster.
Adults with a predominance of shortness of breath during acute illness had nearly four times the prevalence of long COVID compared with the nasal congestion cluster.
Adults with a flu-like acute symptom cluster (fever, chills, muscle aches) had nearly three times the prevalence of long COVID compared with the nasal congestion cluster.
Adults with a predominance of fatigue during acute illness (without other prominent symptoms) had over twice the prevalence of long COVID compared with the nasal congestion cluster.
Long COVID prevalence was not statistically different between the fever-predominant cluster and the nasal congestion cluster.
Females had greater odds than males of membership in the multi-symptomatic, flu-like, and fatigue-predominant acute symptom clusters relative to the nasal congestion cluster.
Adults aged 65 years and older had lower odds of membership in the multi-symptomatic, shortness of breath, flu-like, and fever symptom clusters compared with adults aged 18-34 years.

Adults with household income below US $35,000 had 1.6-2.5 times greater odds of membership in the multi-symptomatic, shortness of breath, and fatigue-predominant clusters compared with those earning US $75,000 or more.
Obese adults had greater odds of membership in the shortness of breath and flu-like acute symptom clusters.

Having a pre-existing physical condition was associated with greater odds of membership in the multi-symptomatic, shortness of breath, flu-like, and fatigue-predominant acute symptom clusters compared with no pre-existing conditions.
Adults with a pre-existing psychological condition had greater odds of membership in the multi-symptomatic and flu-like acute symptom clusters compared with those without one.
Overall, nearly 1 in 6 adults (15.9%) with PCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection reported long COVID, defined as new or worsening symptoms lasting at least 90 days post-infection.

The multi-symptomatic cluster with the highest long COVID prevalence also had the highest probability of acute gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhea, echoing a small prior study linking acute diarrhea to long COVID.
Responding to the survey via telephone rather than online was associated with higher long COVID prevalence, likely reflecting demographic differences between response modes.

Structuring creative writing workshops as half-hour sessions with small groups (two to six participants) increased accessibility for Long COVID patients living with fatigue and brain fog and limited their exposure to post-exertional malaise.
Participants reported that both the writing itself and sharing it with the group produced a sense of catharsis regarding their Long COVID experience.
The workshops fostered a supportive atmosphere and solidarity among participants who face similar disbelief and scepticism about their illness from others.
Humorous character-writing prompts about Long COVID symptoms enabled a shared sense of solidarity and catharsis among participants.

Participants described breathlessness in divergent, subjective ways when responding to the same writing prompt, with one describing it as 'thin air'/air hunger (a deficiency) and another as 'thick' air associated with nausea (an excess).
The authors note that the exertion required for imaginative writing work could itself negatively impact fatigue and be complicated by brain fog, motivating the short workshop duration.
Preclinical studies showed fluvoxamine and other antidepressants exert antiviral and anti-inflammatory activity against SARS-CoV-2.

Retrospective large-scale studies found that patients already taking SSRIs or SSNRIs for other conditions prior to SARS-CoV-2 infection had significantly fewer infections and a milder course of COVID-19.
Meta-analyses found that fluvoxamine used as add-on to standard therapy for mild-to-moderate COVID-19 significantly reduced mortality, intubation, and hospitalization rates by 40-70%.
Fluvoxamine was more effective when administered early in COVID-19 than when given later in advanced, severe disease stages such as severe pneumonia or final sepsis.

An indirect meta-analytical comparison found that paxlovid and molnupiravir achieved larger risk reductions against progression to severe COVID-19 than fluvoxamine, although fluvoxamine add-on was still more effective than standard therapy alone.
A common Long COVID phenotype with predominant anxiety and depression symptoms has been identified, which responds to antidepressants, relaxation therapy, and/or psychotherapy.
Case reports (casuistics) describe positive effects of antidepressants on fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, and autonomic dysfunction in Long COVID.

A large prospective open-label RCT found that fluvoxamine treatment for mild-to-moderate COVID-19 led to more favorable clinical courses, lower viral load, and lower pro-inflammatory cytokines compared to standard treatment, along with reduced subsequent development of neuropsychiatric and pulmonary Long COVID or fatigue.
The majority of maintenance hemodialysis patients developed long COVID after SARS-CoV-2 infection, affecting 285 of 366 patients followed for 12 months.
Fatigue was the most common long COVID symptom, reported by 84.69% of affected MHD patients.
Muscle weakness was the second most common long COVID symptom, reported by 72.45% of affected MHD patients.
Mobility problems were significantly more prevalent among long COVID patients than among non-long COVID patients.
Anxiety and depression were significantly more prevalent among long COVID patients than among non-long COVID patients.
Breathlessness was significantly more prevalent among MHD patients with long COVID than those without.
Patients with persistent long COVID reported problems across all EQ-5D-5L domains more frequently.
Older age was identified as a risk factor for developing long COVID in MHD patients.
Female sex was identified as a risk factor for developing long COVID in MHD patients.
Inadequate dialysis, defined as Kt/V less than 1.2, was a risk factor for developing long COVID.
Coagulation abnormalities, indicated by D-dimer greater than 1 mg/L, were a risk factor for developing long COVID.
Having more comorbidities was a risk factor for developing long COVID in MHD patients.
Elevated CRP above 10 mg/L was an additional risk factor specifically for the persistence of long COVID symptoms in MHD patients.
More than 80% of long COVID symptoms resolved within one year after SARS-CoV-2 infection among maintenance hemodialysis patients.
The sixth month after COVID-19 infection was identified as a critical turning point in the trajectory of long COVID symptom persistence versus resolution in MHD patients.
Low economic status (income below the provincial per-capita monthly income) was associated with a 48% higher adjusted odds of long COVID compared with high economic status.
Patients with a low-level healthy lifestyle (based on smoking, drinking, weight, physical activity and diet) had 26% higher adjusted odds of long COVID than those with a high-level healthy lifestyle.

The association between low economic status and long COVID was significantly stronger among patients with a low-level healthy lifestyle (aOR 1.86) than among those with a high-level healthy lifestyle (aOR 1.28), indicating effect modification.
The association between low economic status and long COVID was significant among men (aOR 1.98) but not among women (aOR 1.21), indicating sex modifies this relationship.
The association between low economic status and long COVID was particularly strong among ethnic minority patients.
The association between low economic status and long COVID was significant among patients living in urban areas.
57.3% of the 4804 older patients with probable or confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection reported at least one long COVID symptom beginning within 3 months of infection and lasting at least 2 months.
Among long COVID patients, fatigue, cough and muscle pain were the three most prevalent symptoms.
Mediation analysis showed that healthy lifestyle did not significantly mediate the relationship between economic status and long COVID.

The decentralised trial recruited 85 of a target 100 adults with self-reported Long COVID (85% of target), averaging 14 participants per week over a 6-week recruitment period via social media and other routes.
The study population was disproportionately female (82.3%) compared with the estimated female share of the general Long COVID population (58.2%).

During recruitment, 111 fraudulent 'imposter' registrations traced to a single location were detected within one day, of which 28 had already been randomised, completed questionnaires and received vouchers before removal from the dataset.
Completion of patient-reported outcome measures declined markedly over follow-up, from 91.7% at baseline to 51.7% at weeks 4 and 8 and 44.7% at week 12.
At baseline, almost all participants (94.9%) reported having used healthcare services at least once in the preceding three months, most commonly GP visits/calls and Long COVID clinics.

Over half of participants reported using prescribed medication (52.9%) and non-prescription products, mainly nutritional supplements (69.4%), at baseline, with over 60 different prescribed medicines and over 40 different non-prescribed products reported.

Long COVID substantially affected participants' employment, with 36.5% of previously employed participants having stopped working because of illness, and work or education time decreased for 34.1% of all participants.

Among participants reporting lost working hours, the mean change was 11.6 hours per week at baseline, and among those reporting time off work, the mean number of days affected was 129.9 days at baseline.
Among participants who used the pacing book, 90% used it at least once, and the majority (8 of 9 users, 80%) read the whole book over at least two weeks.
All participants who used the pacing video (10/10) watched it at least once, but only 30% watched it over a period of at least two weeks, with an average of 1.8 viewings.
Uptake of the pacing app was lower than the other intervention arms, with only 62.5% of allocated users using it at least once, although 80% of those who used it did so daily for three months.
Only one of the 85 randomised participants formally withdrew specifically because of dissatisfaction with their allocated intervention (the pacing app), having previously tried and disliked that app.

Only 6 of 85 participants (7.1%) recruited via the digital platform were from ethnic minority backgrounds, raising concern that decentralised trial recruitment may exclude underserved populations due to a digital access divide.

Participants generally viewed the digital platform's clinical alert functionality, which triggered a research nurse phone call when red-flag symptoms were reported, positively, describing it as reassuring, though some wanted advance warning of the call.

Data collection for the health economic evaluation (healthcare resource use, prescriptions, private costs) was largely feasible, but the volume of healthcare service use was not fully captured, with 13% of participants at baseline and 11% at follow-up reporting service use without providing further detail.

In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, lithium aspartate 10-15 mg/d showed no significant difference from placebo in change in combined FSS-7 and BFSS scores (fatigue and cognitive dysfunction) or any secondary outcome.

In a small open-label dose-finding sub-study, lithium aspartate 40-45 mg/d was numerically associated with greater reductions in fatigue and cognitive dysfunction scores than 15 mg/d, particularly in patients achieving serum lithium levels of 0.18-0.49 mEq/L.

PET imaging studies cited by the authors show widespread increases in microglial and astrocyte activation in patients with neurologic long COVID compared with healthy controls, most pronounced in the ventral striatum, dorsal putamen, and thalamus.

In a pilot trial in Parkinson disease patients, lithium aspartate 45 mg/d was associated with reductions in the MRI neuroinflammation biomarker free water in several brain sites, including the thalamus.

Prior to the RCT, 9 of 10 patients with neurologic long COVID reported satisfactory benefit to fatigue and/or cognitive dysfunction within 3-5 days of starting lithium aspartate 5-10 mg/d, with 5 reporting additional benefit at 15 mg/d, prompting the RCT.

One patient who self-titrated lithium aspartate up to 40 mg/d after the double-blind study (reaching serum lithium 0.17 mEq/L) reported satisfactory benefit for fatigue and cognitive dysfunction, having had no improvement during blinded placebo or open-label 15 mg/d phases.
AXA1125, an anti-inflammatory investigational therapy, is reported as the only pharmacotherapy shown to benefit neurologic long COVID fatigue in an RCT to date, though it remains in development.
The antidepressant vortioxetine showed benefit for long COVID cognitive dysfunction as a secondary outcome in another RCT, but only among patients with increased serum C-reactive protein levels.
Elevated serum C-reactive protein was associated with a positive response to vortioxetine for long COVID cognitive dysfunction, suggesting CRP may predict treatment response.

In an RCT of amnestic mild cognitive impairment (a precursor to Alzheimer disease), serum lithium levels of 0.25-0.50 mEq/L were associated with slowed cognitive decline and significantly reduced cerebrospinal fluid p-tau levels.

In a Parkinson disease lithium biomarker pilot trial, 4 patients with serum lithium levels of 0.23-0.50 mEq/L showed more robust and consistent reductions in brain free water (a neuroinflammation biomarker) than 2 patients with levels below 0.10 mEq/L.

Recent MRI studies cited by the authors show disrupted blood-brain barrier integrity and microstructural gray matter changes in several brain regions, including the thalamus, in patients with neurologic long COVID compared with controls.
Long COVID causes substantial disability and financial impact, with about 45% of patients requiring reduced working hours and about 22% unable to be employed.
PCC symptoms persist for more than 6 months in approximately 10% of patients, with fatigue, postexertional malaise, and cognitive dysfunction being the most common symptoms.
SPECT imaging in a woman with post-COVID-19 insomnia revealed a significant reduction of regional cerebral blood flow specifically confined to the bilateral thalamus.
The patient developed complete insomnia lasting three weeks after contracting COVID-19, occurring without accompanying daytime drowsiness.
Rehabilitation interventions significantly improved 6-minute walk test distance compared with usual/standard care in older adults with long COVID.
Improvement in 6-minute walk test distance was more pronounced in participants receiving exercise training, those with non-severe acute infection, and those aged 60-65 years.
Rehabilitation interventions were associated with improved 30-second sit-to-stand test performance compared with control.

Overall, rehabilitation interventions did not significantly improve hand grip strength compared with control, though effects were significant in subgroups with severe/critical acute infection and age over 65.
Overall pulmonary function (FEV1/FVC) was not significantly improved by rehabilitation, but respiratory rehabilitation, non-severe infection, and age over 65 subgroups showed significant improvement.
Rehabilitation interventions were associated with alleviation of fatigue, with greater benefit in exercise training, older (>65) and severe/critical infection subgroups.

Rehabilitation interventions significantly improved all eight domains of SF-36 quality of life (physical functioning, bodily pain, general health, role-physical, vitality, social functioning, mental health, role-emotional) compared with control.
Rehabilitation interventions were associated with improved independence in activities of daily living compared with control.
Rehabilitation interventions were associated with alleviation of depression symptoms compared with control, more pronounced with exercise training and non-severe acute infection.
Rehabilitation interventions were associated with alleviation of anxiety symptoms compared with control, more pronounced with exercise training and non-severe acute infection.
Nearly half of children with long COVID showed decreased exercise capacity on cardiopulmonary exercise testing compared to normal reference ranges.
Deconditioning was identified as the cause of exercise limitation in 30% of children with long COVID.
Body habitus was identified as a limiting factor for exercise capacity in 22% of children with long COVID.
Bronchospasm was identified as a cause of exercise limitation in 13% of children with long COVID.
Ventilation to perfusion mismatch was identified as a contributing factor to exertional symptoms in children with long COVID.
Volitional hyperventilation was identified as a contributing factor to exertional symptoms in children with long COVID.
Among children with long COVID, dyspnea on exertion, chest pain, and dizziness were the most frequently reported exertional symptoms.
Ventilation to perfusion mismatch was identified as a contributing factor to exercise limitation in some children with long COVID during cardiopulmonary exercise testing.
Volitional hyperventilation was identified as another contributing factor to exercise limitation in children with long COVID.
Headache at COVID-19 diagnosis was significantly more frequent in female patients than male patients.
Fatigue was the most frequent general symptom reported at the time of COVID-19 diagnosis.
Cough was one of the most common respiratory symptoms at the time of COVID-19 diagnosis.
Palpitations at COVID-19 diagnosis were common and occurred at similar rates between men and women.
Chest pain at diagnosis was reported by a higher proportion of women than men, though this was not statistically significant.
Patients with moderate COVID-19 had significantly higher systolic and diastolic blood pressure at diagnosis compared to those with mild disease.
A significant difference in mean blood pressure between mild and moderate COVID-19 groups emerged at the 6-month follow-up, despite no difference at baseline mean values.
A statistically significant increase in QTc interval was observed at diagnosis in patients with mild, rather than moderate, COVID-19.
Antiviral therapy was administered significantly more often in patients with moderate COVID-19 than those with mild disease.
At the 2-year follow-up, ophthalmologic symptoms were significantly more prevalent among female patients than male patients.
Asthenia and decreased effort tolerance were the most commonly reported symptoms at the 2-year long COVID follow-up.
Memory disorders were among the most frequent neuropsychiatric symptoms reported at the 2-year long COVID follow-up.
The prevalence of headache substantially decreased from the time of COVID-19 diagnosis to the 2-year follow-up.

Cardiovascular symptoms (dyspnea, palpitations, chest pain) showed fairly strong concordance between the time of diagnosis and the 2-year follow-up, unlike most other symptoms, which showed poor concordance and largely did not persist.
Menstrual disorders were reported by a notable proportion of female patients at the 2-year long COVID follow-up.
Women who developed a moderate form of COVID-19 were significantly older than those with a mild form of the disease.
The weighted prevalence of at least mild-to-moderate fatigue (FAS score >21) among German adults in 2023 was 29.7%.
Fatigue prevalence was higher in women (32.6%) than in men (26.6%), and this sex difference persisted after adjustment for other determinants.

Fatigue prevalence varied strongly by age, being highest in 18-29 year-olds (39.6%), lowest in 65-79 year-olds (20.6%), and rising again in adults over 79 (33.2%); after adjustment, younger age groups retained markedly higher risk relative to the 65-79 reference group.

Adults with only basic (low) education had substantially higher fatigue prevalence (36.2%) than those with higher education (21.4%), and this association remained significant after adjustment, more pronounced in men.

Adults without a steady partner had higher fatigue prevalence than those in a partnership (35.8% vs 25.9%), with a larger gap in men than women; however, the association weakened and lost significance after full adjustment.
Adults reporting a chronic disease or long-lasting health problem had markedly higher fatigue prevalence than those without (40.7% vs 18.1%), an association that remained strong after adjustment.

Fatigue was more than three times as prevalent among adults screening positive for depressive symptoms (PHQ-2) compared to those without (70.1% vs 21.1%), an association that remained strong after full adjustment.

Self-reported current Long COVID/post-COVID condition was associated with roughly double the fatigue prevalence compared to adults with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection but no Long COVID or adults without infection.

In multivariable Poisson regression adjusting for sex, age, education, chronic disease and depressive symptoms, self-reported current Long COVID remained significantly associated with higher fatigue risk relative to no SARS-CoV-2 infection, whereas prior infection without Long COVID showed no significant association.

The authors note that the FAS does not capture post-exertional malaise (PEM), the cardinal symptom of ME/CFS, so this study cannot draw conclusions about the presence of ME/CFS despite its symptomatic overlap with Long/Post-COVID.
Among children hospitalized with COVID-19, exercise intolerance was the most frequent post-COVID symptom between 3 and 12 months after acute infection, with a pooled prevalence of 29%.
Nonspecific respiratory symptoms had a pooled prevalence of 12% among hospitalized children between 3 and 12 months after acute COVID-19.
Psychological disorders had a pooled prevalence of 10% among hospitalized children between 3 and 12 months after acute COVID-19.
Nonspecific gastrointestinal symptoms had a pooled prevalence of 10% among hospitalized children between 3 and 12 months after acute COVID-19.
Beyond 12 months after acute COVID-19, exercise intolerance prevalence fell to a pooled 6%, lower than in the 3-12 month window.
Beyond 12 months after acute COVID-19, fatigue had a pooled prevalence of 3% in hospitalized children.
In the first block of variables, BMI was significantly associated with gender.
BMI and active smoking status significantly increased the probability of ICU admission during the acute phase of COVID-19.
Peak oxygen consumption (VO2) at follow-up was associated with length of follow-up, age, BMI and gender, but was no longer related to prior ICU admission after conditioning on these covariates.
Serum D-dimer levels at follow-up showed dependency on age, gender and BMI, and were independent of VO2 after conditioning on these covariates.
FEV1 at follow-up was significantly reduced in patients complaining of fatigue compared to those without fatigue.
After adjustment, FEV1 was independently related to fatigue, and fatigue was in turn significantly associated with depression score.
Neither fatigue nor depression scores were significant responses to intermediate block-2 variables, including ICU admission or length of follow-up.
VO2 was not influenced by smoking status or by D-dimer levels after conditioning on length of follow-up, age, BMI and gender.

Type II diabetes mellitus and hypertension were independently associated with increased D-dimer levels, while statin use was associated with decreased D-dimer levels; no other comorbidities or medications significantly affected block-3 outcome variables.
Persistence of ground-glass opacities and fibrotic signs on follow-up HRCT was independently predicted by VO2, age, gender, ICU admission and follow-up duration.
Follow-up duration did not have a significant impact on FEV1.

Obesity, together with age and female gender, negatively affected FEV1 and peak oxygen consumption at follow-up, outlining a phenotype of obese long-COVID patients prone to ICU admission and later reduced pulmonary/exercise function.

An inverse relationship was found between the presence of residual lung lesions at HRCT and duration of follow-up, suggesting a progressive healing process, and HRCT findings were inversely associated with peak oxygen consumption independent of other outcome variables.
In contrast to other studies, fatigue symptoms in this cohort were not directly correlated with lung features observed at HRCT.
Fatigue was the most frequently reported persistent symptom among long COVID patients in the cohort.
82% of the 364 COVID-19 patients in the cohort reported at least one persistent symptom consistent with long COVID.
High resolution chest CT showed radiological alteration in 76% of long COVID patients examined.
Pulmonary function testing revealed alterations in 44.7% of long COVID patients evaluated.
Patients treated with corticosteroids during acute infection had a higher risk of presenting at least one persistent long COVID symptom.
Hospitalized (in-patient) COVID-19 patients had a higher risk of showing residual chest CT lesions at follow-up compared to home-isolated patients.
Patients who received hydroxychloroquine treatment had a higher risk of presenting residual chest CT lesions after COVID-19 infection.
Older patients had a higher risk of altered pulmonary function after COVID-19 infection.
Among 4,757 infected primary healthcare workers, 12.61% self-reported long COVID symptoms persisting ≥91 days after infection.
Among patients with long COVID, 44.00% reported experiencing two or more concurrent symptoms.
Hypomnesia (memory impairment) was the most frequently reported long COVID symptom, occurring in 4.90% of infected healthcare workers.
Sleep difficulties were reported in 2.73% of infected healthcare workers as a long COVID symptom.
Fatigue was reported in 2.35% of infected healthcare workers as a long COVID symptom.
Disturbances of the reproductive system were reported in 1.93% of infected healthcare workers as a long COVID symptom.
Hair loss was reported in 1.85% of infected healthcare workers as a long COVID symptom.
Myalgia/arthralgia was reported in 1.51% of infected healthcare workers as a long COVID symptom, showing a slight increase compared to the acute/ongoing symptom phase.
Breathing difficulties and cough, common in the acute/ongoing symptom phase, showed a marked decrease in prevalence by the long COVID (≥91 day) follow-up survey.
Individuals aged 30-45 years had nearly twice the odds of developing long COVID compared to those under 30 years old.
Individuals aged 45-60 years had nearly three times the odds of developing long COVID compared to those under 30 years old.
Female healthcare workers had a higher risk of developing long COVID compared to males in multivariate analysis, despite no difference being seen in univariate analysis.
Healthcare workers reporting high work stress had increased odds of long COVID.
Healthcare workers reporting extremely high work stress had increased odds of long COVID.
Having an education level below a bachelor's degree was associated with a reduced risk of developing long COVID.
Receiving four or more doses of the COVID-19 vaccine was associated with a reduced risk of developing long COVID.
Receiving 2-3 doses of the COVID-19 vaccine did not emerge as a significant protective factor against long COVID in multivariate analysis, unlike 4+ doses.
Healthcare workers with a prior medical history had a higher univariate prevalence of long COVID than those without.
Healthcare workers who worked in a fever clinic had a higher univariate prevalence of long COVID compared to those who did not.
Healthcare workers who normally rested on weekends or holidays had a notably lower univariate prevalence of long COVID compared to occasional normal resters.
Healthcare workers in middle management positions had a significantly higher univariate prevalence of long COVID compared to ordinary employees and unit leaders.

No statistically significant differences were found between long COVID and non-long COVID groups for gender, BMI, profession, smoking status, drinking status, dietary structure, weekly exercise frequency, daily working hours, or weekly working days in univariate analysis.
Ten weeks of supervised, CPET-individualized aerobic exercise training significantly increased peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak) in long COVID patients.
Peak work rate on CPET significantly increased after the 10-week exercise training program.
Ventilatory efficiency and dead-space to tidal volume ratio were normal at baseline and did not change with exercise training.
Peak perceived dyspnea and leg fatigue Borg scores at peak exercise did not significantly change with training.
The 6-minute walk distance did not significantly change after exercise training, highlighting its limited sensitivity compared to CPET measures.
Accelerometer-measured daily step count, total energy expenditure, and time spent at sedentary/light/moderate/vigorous activity levels did not change after training.

Most SF-36 subscales improved statistically and with clinically important differences after exercise training, including physical functioning, energy/fatigue, emotional well-being, social functioning, and general health.
Depression scores decreased from moderate to mild severity after exercise training.
Anxiety scores (GAD-7), which were mild at baseline, remained unchanged after exercise training.
Fatigue Severity Score showed an important minimal-clinically-important-difference reduction after training, although the change was not statistically significant.
The modified Medical Research Council dyspnea score improved by a clinically meaningful margin after exercise training.
MMSE scores increased significantly with training, though the increase did not reach the accepted minimal clinically important difference of 1.5-2.0 points.
Post-COVID-19 Functional Status scale scores decreased significantly after exercise training, though no established MCID exists for this instrument.

The proportion of participants meeting PEM criteria on the modified DePaul Symptom Questionnaire did not significantly change after the exercise training program (78.6% at baseline vs 64.3% after training).
Daily-tracked fatigue, brain fog, and overall health ratings significantly improved following exercise training, while other symptom domains improved numerically but not statistically.
Acute exercise (rest to peak CPET) significantly increased WBC counts as expected, but exercise training had no additional effect on WBC counts or their acute-exercise response.

Acute exercise significantly increased circulating CD3+ T cells, CD4+ T cells, CD16++CD14+ non-classical monocytes, CD80+/CD86+ monocytes, and CD56+ NK cells (and subsets), reflecting exercise-induced immune cell mobilization; these acute responses were not altered by 10 weeks of training.
Neither acute exercise nor exercise training affected circulating regulatory T cell, regulatory B cell, or activated monocyte counts.

The acute-exercise-induced rise in CD19+ B cells at peak exercise was significantly greater after exercise training than before, indicating an interaction between training and acute immune mobilization.
Classical monocytes showed a significant acute exercise x training interaction, with the post-hoc peak response after training approaching but not reaching significance.
Plasma IL-8 concentration significantly increased in response to acute exercise during CPET.
Plasma IL-6 showed a non-significant trend toward an increase with acute exercise.
No effect of acute exercise or exercise training was found on plasma TNF-alpha, IL-10, IFN-gamma, or IFN-lambda1 levels.

Pre-exercise CPET screening identified previously unrecognized, potentially serious comorbidities mimicking long COVID symptoms in 5 of 21 enrolled participants (25%), two of which were life-threatening.
At study entry, long COVID participants had reduced cardiorespiratory fitness, with VO2peak averaging only about 86.5% of predicted values, consistent with prior long COVID CPET literature.
32.6% of children and adolescents hospitalized with COVID-19 developed at least one long COVID symptom, whereas essentially no one in the non-COVID-19 control group reported such symptoms.
Among children with long COVID, the most commonly reported symptoms were fatigue, impaired attention/concentration, depression or anxiety, and hair loss.

Among children with long COVID, a substantial proportion reported functional impairment: 17.4% had difficulty with quality of life/studying, 15.2% with school attendance and group activities, 10.9% with self-care, and 6.5% with daily activities and sports.
Greater severity of acute-phase COVID-19 was significantly associated with persistence of muscle and joint pain as a long COVID symptom.
Diarrhea as a long COVID symptom was significantly more prevalent in children under 2 years old compared to other age groups.
Abdominal pain as a long COVID symptom was significantly more common in children aged 2 to 5 years compared to other age groups.
Longer hospital stay during the acute COVID-19 phase was significantly associated with a higher likelihood of persistent cough as a long COVID symptom.
Longer hospital stay was significantly associated with higher likelihood of persistent weight loss as a long COVID symptom.
Longer hospital stay was significantly associated with higher likelihood of depression or anxiety symptoms in long COVID.
History of exposure to tobacco smoke was an independent risk factor for long COVID symptoms, with an adjusted odds ratio of 12.45.

Older age was an independent predictor of long COVID symptoms, with adjusted odds ratios of 3.18 for children aged 6-11 years and 4.57 for those aged 12 years and older, relative to children under 2 years.
No significant association was found between history of NICU/PICU admission and the occurrence of long COVID symptoms, despite a numerically higher rate in the long COVID group (19.6% vs 12.6%).
No significant association was found between gender, ethnicity, or multiple-ward admission and the manifestation of long COVID symptoms.
Non-Bushehri ethnicity was associated with a substantially higher likelihood of hospitalization due to COVID-19 compared to Bushehri individuals.
Having other medical histories was associated with a substantially higher likelihood of COVID-19 hospitalization compared to the non-COVID-19 group.

Anosmia, ageusia, brain fog, hair loss, dyspnea, diarrhea, and chest pain/discomfort were significantly more frequent in patients infected during the Delta-and-before period than during the Omicron period.
Fatigue, dizziness/auditory disorder, and throat pain/discomfort were significantly more frequent in patients infected during the Omicron period than during the Delta-and-before period.
Fatigue was the single most frequent long COVID complaint, reported by more than 40% of patients in both strain groups, and pain symptoms were reported by nearly half of patients in each group.
Patients infected in the Delta-and-before period reported significantly more distinct long COVID symptoms per person (mean 3.7) than those infected in the Omicron period (mean 2.7).
In the Omicron group, patients seen ≥180 days after diagnosis had significantly fewer symptoms per person than those seen <180 days, whereas no such reduction occurred in the Delta-and-before group.
Fatigue rates in the Omicron group and cough rates in the Delta-and-before group were both significantly lower at ≥180 days than at <180 days after diagnosis.
Muscle pain was reported at a higher rate at ≥180 days than <180 days in the Delta-and-before group.

Patients with poor performance status (PS 7–9) had significantly higher rates of fatigue, headache, dizziness/auditory disorder, insomnia, and nausea/vomiting than patients with good performance status (PS 1–2).
Anosmia and ageusia were significantly more frequent in patients with good performance status (PS 1–2) than in those with poor performance status (PS 7–9).
Female sex was significantly associated with a longer time to remission from long COVID in Cox proportional hazard analysis.
Higher body mass index (BMI) was significantly associated with a longer time to remission from long COVID.
Dyspnea was significantly associated with a longer time to remission from long COVID.
Cough and insomnia were associated with a shorter duration until remission from long COVID.
The type of infectious SARS-CoV-2 strain (Delta-and-before vs Omicron) was not significantly associated with the time to remission from long COVID.
Acute COVID-19 severity at onset was significantly greater in the Delta-and-before group than in the Omicron group.
Vaccination coverage prior to long COVID onset was significantly lower in the Delta-and-before group than in the Omicron group.
Significantly more patients in the Omicron group than in the Delta-and-before group had poor performance status (PS 7–9) at their first long COVID visit.

About a quarter of patients (23.5%, 247/1053) sought care for long COVID symptoms before the 60-day symptom duration required by the WHO case definition, and most of these (185/247) still met WHO criteria by the time of assessment.

Hierarchical cluster analysis of 37 self-reported Long COVID symptoms at 9 months identified four clusters: no/minor symptoms (Cluster 1, n=368, 67%), joint pain (Cluster 2, n=47, 8%), multi-symptom (Cluster 3, n=22, 4%), and neurocognitive symptoms (Cluster 4, n=115, 21%).
At 9 months, the largest cluster (Cluster 1, n=368, 67%) comprised individuals with no or minor Long COVID symptoms, with runny nose and fatigue as the most frequent symptoms (10% each).
Cluster 2 at 9 months (n=47, 8%) was characterised by a high frequency of joint pain (85%) and myalgia (47%).
Cluster 3 at 9 months (n=22, 4%) included individuals with multi-organ symptoms, most frequently fatigue (86%), memory loss (77%) and headache (77%).
Cluster 4 at 9 months (n=115, 21%) was characterised by cognitive-related symptoms, with memory loss (89%) and concentration issues (53%) most frequent.
At 12 months, Cluster 1 (n=327, 71%) remained the no/minor symptoms group, with memory loss (6%), cough (5%) and runny nose (4%) most prevalent.

At 12 months, Cluster 2 (n=32, 7%) included individuals with multi-organ symptoms, with fatigue (84%) and myalgia (72%) most prevalent, and the highest proportion of females (84%) among the 12-month clusters.

At 12 months, Cluster 3 (n=37, 8%) was characterised mainly by joint pain (57%) and fatigue (70%), with the highest median age (58 years) and highest tobacco consumption (30%) among 12-month clusters.
At 12 months, Cluster 4 (n=28, 6%) included individuals with cognitive-related symptoms; concentration issues were the most prevalent (93%) and all reported memory loss (100%).
Within the neurocognitive cluster, memory loss and concentration issues increased in frequency from 9 to 12 months, contrary to the general decline seen for most other Long COVID symptoms.
Tobacco use was more frequent among individuals in the joint pain cluster, consistent with prior evidence linking smoking to Long COVID pain-related symptoms.
Asthma was the most frequent pre-existing condition in the joint pain cluster at 9 months, consistent with prior evidence linking asthma to general fatigue in Long COVID.

Hypertension was the most frequent pre-existing health condition among individuals in the multi-symptom cluster, suggesting possible overlap with the cardiorespiratory Long COVID phenotype reported elsewhere.
The multi-symptom cluster had the highest frequency of individuals with a prior SARS-CoV-2 reinfection, consistent with reinfection being associated with increased Long COVID symptom prevalence.
Females were predominant across all Long COVID symptom clusters at 9 months, with the highest proportion (90%) found in the no/minor symptoms cluster.

The authors suggest that self-reported symptoms such as 'balance issues' and 'palpitations' could reflect autonomic dysfunction or postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) potentially triggered by COVID-19 infection or vaccination, an interpretation raised as a limitation rather than tested directly.
Overall, the frequency of most Long COVID symptoms decreased between 9 and 12 months after the positive SARS-CoV-2 test.
Memory loss, fatigue/weakness, and joint pain were the most frequently reported Long COVID symptoms overall at both 9 and 12 months.
COVID-19 patients who received glucocorticoid treatment during infection were diagnosed with long COVID more frequently than those who did not receive glucocorticoids.
Older age was a significant risk factor for developing long COVID.
Female gender was a significant risk factor for developing long COVID.
Patients who received glucocorticoid treatment during acute COVID-19 infection were subsequently diagnosed with long COVID more frequently than those who did not receive glucocorticoids.
Post-COVID-19 condition is commonly characterized by fatigue, dyspnoea, and cognitive dysfunction including brain fog.
Meta-analyses cited in the paper indicate yoga practice is associated with improvements in fatigue, depression, anxiety, and sleep quality compared with control conditions.
Yoga has been shown to improve heart rate variability, a proxy marker of autonomic nervous system regulation and cardiovascular health.
Yoga is discussed to have anti-inflammatory effects, potentially mediated by enhanced melatonin production.
Yoga practice may beneficially affect gut microbiome diversity and composition, which is proposed to reduce fatigue and improve immunity and mental health.
Isometric yoga poses have been associated with reduced fatigue and increased vitality in chronic fatigue syndrome, a condition sharing features with post COVID.
In the authors' prior collaborative trials, yoga was found to be safe and feasible for inexperienced adults and associated with fewer adverse events than moderate-intensity aerobic exercise.

Individuals with a diagnosis of postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) are excluded from this post-COVID yoga trial, reflecting recognized overlap between POTS and post-COVID condition requiring differentiated clinical management.
HIV infection was associated with an increased risk of developing long COVID compared to people without HIV.
Approximately 52% of people with HIV who had SARS-CoV-2 infection developed at least one long COVID symptom.
The most common long COVID symptoms reported among people with HIV were cough, fatigue, and asthenia.
A history of moderate-to-severe COVID-19 illness was a risk factor for long COVID among people with HIV.
Increased levels of interferon-gamma-induced protein 10 (IP-10) were identified as a risk factor for long COVID among people with HIV.
Increased levels of tumour necrosis factor-alpha were identified as a risk factor for long COVID among people with HIV.
Decreased levels of interferon-beta were identified as a risk factor for long COVID among people with HIV.
Female participants reported more symptoms than male participants in fatigue, memory, mental health, and well-being domains during the chronic post-COVID phase.
The comet assay showed no significant differences in DNA damage among the control, acute post-COVID, and chronic post-COVID groups.
Within the acute post-COVID group, male participants showed higher levels of genetic instability (DNA damage) than female participants.
Multiple linear regression identified gender, age, and waist circumference as significant predictors of DNA damage levels.
Among females in the acute post-COVID group, sexual health symptoms and eye-related symptoms significantly influenced increased DNA damage.
The digital therapeutic AKL-T01 did not significantly improve sustained attention (Digit Symbol Matching Task) compared to waitlist control.
Task-switching performance improved in the AKL-T01 intervention group relative to waitlist control.
Processing speed improved significantly in the AKL-T01 intervention group relative to waitlist control.
Disability scores improved (reduced) in the AKL-T01 intervention group relative to waitlist control.
Quality of life improved in the AKL-T01 intervention group relative to waitlist control.
Total fatigue was reduced to a greater degree in the AKL-T01 intervention group compared to control in exploratory analyses.
Exploratory analysis showed a greater reduction in cognitive fatigue in the AKL-T01 intervention group relative to waitlist control.
Exploratory analysis showed a greater reduction in anxiety symptoms in the AKL-T01 intervention group relative to waitlist control.
Children with autism spectrum disorder show enhanced pitch perception, suggested to reflect brain plasticity and reorganization influenced by genetic factors.
Listening to music activates the dopaminergic reward system in individuals with autism spectrum disorder, contributing to emotional regulation and mood.

Engaging in music activities stimulates multiple brain regions associated with memory, emotion, pleasure, and auditory processing in children, and appropriate pitch, tone and tempo enhance melodic memory and brain processing.

Music therapy's effectiveness in autism is proposed to stem from top-down reward-based cortical modulation that supports learning of non-musical behaviors like social interaction, plus bottom-up sensorimotor integration through auditory-motor processing that enhances social communication skills.

In children with autism, the arcuate fasciculus is reported to appear thicker on the right hemisphere than the left, which the authors propose may explain heightened engagement with music in this population since the right hemisphere is primarily responsible for interpreting musical sounds.

Individuals with autism spectrum disorder show intact emotion recognition from music, reflected in typical behavioral ratings and activation of limbic and paralimbic reward regions during processing of emotional music.
The review proposes that music therapy can improve social interactions, attention, and sensory processing in individuals with autism spectrum disorder, promoting overall well-being and development.
Meta-analysis showed that non-autistic individuals exhibit larger pupil dilation in response to social compared to non-social stimuli.
Autistic individuals showed no significant difference in pupil size between social and non-social stimuli, though results were highly heterogeneous across studies.
The authors propose that pupillary responses may serve as an objective physiological marker of social processing differences in autism.
Stool studies show that patients with autism have decreased levels of the short-chain fatty acid butyrate compared to typical composition.
Patients with autism showed higher levels of acetate and propionate in stool compared to typical microbiota composition.
Depressed patients show a significant reduction in the composition of butyrate-producing gut microbiota.
Germ-free mice are more susceptible to anxiety-like behaviour, while fecal microbiota transplantation eases this anxiety.
Citrobacter infection increases anxiety-like behaviour and c-Fos protein expression in the vagal ganglia of mice.

Lactobacillus rhamnosus improves anxiety and depressive behaviour in stressed mice and restores gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) expression to normal levels in the hippocampus, hypothalamus and prefrontal lobes.

Gut microbiota colonization of specific-pathogen-free mice reverses the elevated sympathetic ganglion (celiac-superior mesenteric ganglion) activity seen in germ-free and antibiotic-depleted mice, indicating microbiota depletion raises intestinal sympathetic nerve activity.
Intestinal colonization with Campylobacter jejuni caused anxiety-like behaviour in mice, linked to higher c-Fos expression in vagal afferent brain areas.
Lactobacillus reuteri improved social impairments in mice modeling autism spectrum disorder by raising oxytocin levels in the paraventricular nucleus through vagal nerve stimulation.

Germ-free mice show dramatically reduced jejunal and ileal interosseous plexus network density and neuron number compared to specific-pathogen-free animals, which is restored after microbiota colonization.
Germ-free and antibiotic-treated animals exhibit reduced numbers of enteric glial cells, indicating the microbiota is critical for their development and homeostasis.
Mice receiving fecal transplants from depressed patients exhibited increased anxiety-like behaviour and high levels of kynurenine.
Germ-free mice show abnormalities in neuromuscular junction function and reduced serum choline, the acetylcholine precursor.

Combination probiotic therapy with Chlorella acidophilus KABP021 and Lactobacillus plantarum KABP022/023 alleviates IBS-associated inflammation and gut microbiota dysbiosis by producing acetate and acetylcholine.
Germ-free mice have significantly lower serum 5-HT concentrations and altered enterochromaffin cell morphology, changes that are restored after gut microbiota colonization.

Antibiotic-treated mice showed decreased Tph1 gene expression with no change in enterochromaffin cell number, while colonization of germ-free mice with spore-forming bacteria upregulated colonic Tph1 and downregulated the serotonin transporter SLC6A4, increasing 5-HT levels in colon and blood.

The abundance of Bacteroidetes spp. associated with the GABA production pathway was negatively correlated with depressive brain features, and GABA dysregulation is often present in depressed patients.
Serum GABA levels are considerably lower in germ-free animals, showing that gut microbiota may generate or deplete GABA and impact circulating GABA levels.
Cyanobacteria produce the neurotoxic compound BMAA, which causes neurological degeneration and contributes to neurodegenerative disorders including Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease.

The abundance of pro-inflammatory bacteria Akkermansia, Oscillospira and Bacteroides was dramatically elevated in fecal samples from Parkinson's disease patients, resulting in local intestinal inflammation.
Elevated levels of p-cresol and phenylacetylglutamine metabolites in Parkinson's disease patients are closely linked with the severity of constipation.

Injection of alpha-synuclein into the intestinal lining of rats caused it to accumulate first in enteric nerve then retrograde via the vagus system to the dorsal motor nucleus and brain, inducing Parkinson's disease pathology; vagotomy blocked this progression.

Germ-free mice overexpressing alpha-synuclein (ASO-GF) showed no significant alpha-synuclein aggregation and significantly less impaired locomotion than specific-pathogen-free ASO mice, and transplanting feces from Parkinson's disease patients into ASO-GF mice increased dyskinesia, implicating microbiota in alpha-synuclein-mediated motor impairment.
Approximately 40% of individuals with autism have gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhoea, abdominal pain and constipation, and GI symptom severity correlates with autism severity.
Stool samples from children with autism showed increased levels of Lactobacillus, Clostridium and Desulfovibrio.
Weekly vancomycin treatment in children with autism significantly improved both neurological and gastrointestinal symptoms.
Approximately 40% of individuals with autism experience gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain and constipation, and symptom severity correlates with autism severity.
Stool samples from children with autism showed increased levels of Lactobacillus, Clostridium and Desulfovibrio.
Weekly vancomycin treatment in children with autism significantly improved neurological and gastrointestinal symptoms.

Some evidence suggests a negligible direct association between autism and gut microbiota but a strong association with diet, which shapes dietary preferences that reduce gut microbiota diversity in autistic children.
The abundance and composition of gut microbiota are altered in Alzheimer's disease patients, though the temporal relationship to brain pathology remains unclear.

Cyanobacteria produce the neurotoxic compound β-N-methylamino-L-alanine (BMAA), which causes neurological degeneration and contributes to neurodegenerative disorders including Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease.

Constipation is the most common bowel dysfunction symptom in Parkinson's disease and typically presents 10-20 years before motor symptom onset, suggesting PD may originate in the gastrointestinal tract.

Injection of α-synuclein into the intestinal lining of rats caused accumulation first in enteric neurons, then retrograde transport via the vagus nerve to the dorsal motor ganglion and brain, inducing PD-like pathology; vagotomy blocked this progression.

SPF mice overexpressing α-synuclein (ASO) exhibited increased α-synuclein aggregation and impaired locomotion, whereas germ-free ASO mice (ASO-GF) showed no significant α-synuclein aggregation and significantly less impaired locomotion.
ASO-germ-free mice transplanted with fecal microbiota from PD patients exhibited increased dyskinesia, indicating microorganisms contribute to α-synuclein-mediated dyskinesia.

The abundance of pro-inflammatory bacteria Akkermansia, Oscillopsia and Bacteroides was dramatically elevated in fecal samples from Parkinson's disease patients, resulting in local intestinal inflammation.
Elevated levels of the metabolites p-cresol and phenylacetylglutamine were found in Parkinson's disease patients and both correlate closely with constipation severity.
Gut microbiomes of depressed patients differ significantly from healthy individuals, mainly showing enrichment of pro-inflammatory bacteria and depletion of anti-inflammatory bacteria.
Fecal microbiota transplantation from depressed patients into rodents induced depression-like behavior, suggesting dysbiosis may be causally involved in depression pathogenesis.
Mycobacterium spp was enriched in depressed patients and significantly increased susceptibility to depression.
Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) were found to be reduced in depressed patients.
Exogenous butyrate supplementation may alleviate depression via modulation of the HPA axis.

Overactivation of the HPA axis is one cause of depression, and gut microbiota dysbiosis can produce pro-inflammatory cytokines and microbial antigens that activate the HPA axis across the blood-brain barrier.
A high-fat diet may increase amyloid angiopathy and oxidative stress, predisposing to cognitive dysfunction and Alzheimer's disease.
The Mediterranean diet may attenuate the progression of Alzheimer's disease, with beneficial effects potentially mediated by gut microbiota and its anti-inflammatory properties.
Ketogenic diets, high in fat and low in carbohydrates, may limit glycolysis and increase fatty acid oxidation to produce ketone bodies, ameliorating neurodegenerative diseases.

Long-term supplementation with the probiotic preparation SLAB51 reduced neuronal protein hydrolysis and amyloid-beta aggregation and attenuated cognitive decline and brain damage in transgenic AD mice, potentially via reduced oxidative stress through the SIRT3 pathway.

Saccharomyces boulardii alleviated neuroinflammation and synaptic damage by regulating gut microbiota, inhibiting microglial activation and the TLR pathway, and ameliorating cognitive impairment in AD mice.

Weekly vancomycin treatment significantly improved neurological and gastrointestinal symptoms in children with autism.

Fecal microbiota transplantation from depressed patients induced depression-like behavior in rodents, supporting a causal role for dysbiosis in depression pathogenesis.

A 2018 case study of two patients with autism spectrum disorder showed significant symptom reduction after fecal microbiota transplantation.

Individuals who had experienced severe COVID-19 showed higher antibody responses to latent viruses compared with those with less severe or no COVID-19.
People who ever had PASC showed higher IgG antibody levels against EBV early antigen-diffuse, even among those without prior severe COVID-19.
People who ever had PASC showed higher IgG antibody levels against VZV, even among those without prior severe COVID-19.
People who ever had PASC showed higher IgG antibody levels against WU polyomavirus, even among those without prior severe COVID-19.
Individuals with active persistent PASC had higher IgG to EBV early antigen-diffuse compared with those without persistent PASC.
Individuals with active persistent PASC had higher IgG to VZV compared with those without persistent PASC.
72.2% (13/18) of patients with new-onset chronic musculoskeletal pain after COVID-19 met the ACR 2010 diagnostic criteria for fibromyalgia syndrome.
Patients had a high average Widespread Pain Index score, indicating pain spread across multiple body regions.
The average Symptom Severity score, reflecting fatigue, unrefreshed waking, cognitive symptoms and somatic symptom burden, was high across the cohort.
A very high proportion of patients reported myalgia, most of whom also had arthralgia.
Most patients reported generalised widespread pain, and those who did not still had pain in at least four distinct body areas.
All participants experienced pain and fatigue as new-onset PCS symptoms, and nearly all experienced exertional breathlessness.
Cognitive issues and anxiety were prevalent new-onset symptoms in the majority of patients with PCS-related MSK pain.
The majority of patients reported new-onset sleep problems following COVID-19 infection.

Acute-phase eye conjunctivitis was an independent predictor of long COVID in the post-infection model.
Acute-phase headache/dizziness was an independent predictor of long COVID in the post-infection model.
The post-infection prediction model, incorporating age, inability to concentrate, and several acute-phase symptoms, achieved higher predictive accuracy for long COVID than the pre-infection model.
The pre-infection model, based on age, long-term medication use, and pre-infection psychological problems, showed moderate accuracy for predicting long COVID risk in non-infected individuals.
A 2021 cohort study found that 82% (3069/3743) of COVID-19 patients reported neurological complaints, suggesting SARS-CoV-2 may infect and damage the CNS.

A retrospective study of 214 hospitalized COVID-19 patients in Wuhan found that >36.4% had acute cerebrovascular disease, skeletal muscle damage, disturbance of consciousness, and neurological symptoms.

POTS patients have been found to have lower plasma volumes as well as renin and aldosterone levels, suggesting RAAS deficiency contributes to POTS etiology, likely via partial renal sympathetic denervation.
Hypovolemia, often from fever, anorexia, nausea, night sweats, and extended bed rest in long-COVID, may increase cardiac sympathetic noradrenergic outflow and precipitate hyperadrenergic POTS.
Post-COVID hyperadrenergic POTS may be treated with large amounts of water and salt intake along with other non-pharmacological measures to increase venous return and intravascular volume.
SARS-CoV-2 has been linked to brain stem dysfunction via direct viral invasion, neuroinflammation, and vascular activation.

SARS-CoV-2 spike protein S1 subunit binds host ACE-2 receptor to mediate viral entry into cells, including neurons, intestinal epithelial, kidney, endothelial, monocyte/macrophage, and neuroepithelial cells.

The olfactory nerve is proposed as the most likely peripheral route for SARS-CoV-2 neuroinvasion into the CNS, supported by SARS-CoV-2 RNA and S protein detection in olfactory mucosa neural cells, underlying COVID-19 anosmia.

The vagus nerve, which expresses ACE-2 and neuropilin-1 (NRP-1) receptors, provides a route for SARS-CoV-2 antero- and retrograde transmission between brainstem neurons and duodenal cells, and to the enteric nervous system.
Post-mortem investigations of COVID-19 patients revealed axonal degeneration and cell death in the trigeminal nerve, along with high SARS-CoV-2 RNA levels in the trigeminal ganglia.
Zeng et al. analyzed blood samples from more than 100 COVID-19 patients and found that 41% tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 RNA, supporting a hematogenous route of viral dissemination.
SARS-CoV-2 infection of cerebral endothelial cells via ACE-2 disrupts the blood-brain barrier, increasing permeability and causing cerebral edema and intracranial hypertension.
A meta-analysis found that heart rate variability (HRV) is inversely correlated with inflammation and can serve as a measure of dysautonomia.
Higher plasma GFAP levels in COVID-19 patients are associated with greater astrocyte activation/injury, indicating SARS-CoV-2 may inflict neurological harm.
Higher plasma neurofilament light chain (NfL) levels in COVID-19 patients are associated with axon damage.

NLRP3 inflammasome activation, a key trigger of cytokine storms, causes pyroptosis via Gasdermin D cleavage and is linked to COVID-19-related neuronal injury, similar to processes seen in Alzheimer's disease.

An observational single-center study of 78 reproductive-aged women found that COVID-19 infection was associated with signs of ovarian damage, including decreased ovarian reserve and reproductive endocrine dysfunction.

Wang et al. found SARS-CoV-2 infection was associated with notably reduced blastocyst formation rates despite comparable oocyte counts, fertilization rates, implantation, abortion, and clinical pregnancy rates versus healthy mothers.

Basigin (BSG), a SARS-CoV-2 entry receptor expressed in ovary stroma, cumulus, and granulosa cells, is implicated in corpus luteum formation, follicle development, and embryo implantation, and its disruption may impair implantation.

NLRP3 and proinflammatory cytokines are more prevalent within the endometrium of women who have undergone repeated miscarriages, suggesting SARS-CoV-2-related inflammation could similarly harm fertility.
XX chromosomes and estrogen have been found to lessen COVID-19 severity among females, though this protective effect is lost with age.

Shimabukuro et al., using VAERS and V-safe monitoring, found that pregnant women had more adverse effects than non-pregnant women after mRNA COVID-19 vaccination, with 13.9% experiencing pregnancy loss, 86.1% having a normal pregnancy, and 9.4% delivering early.

A multicenter trial in Israel showed mothers develop IgG antibodies after BNT162b2 vaccination that cross the placental barrier and are detectable in newborns, indicating protective maternal-fetal antibody transfer.
MCC950, an FDA-approved oral NLRP3 inhibitor, has been proposed to reduce the likelihood of COVID-19-associated neurological damage.

Pharmacological treatments for COVID-19-related dysautonomia include vasoconstrictors, volume-expanding agents, beta-blockers, and sympatholytic drugs such as clonidine and methyldopa for hyperadrenergic presentations.

Non-pharmacological measures for COVID-19-related dysautonomia include aerobic progressive exercise training, compression garments, liberal water and salt consumption, head-of-bed elevation, avoidance of aggravating triggers, and psychological therapies.
Patients receiving IHHT on top of standard rehabilitation showed a 2.8-fold greater improvement in 6-minute walk distance than controls receiving standard rehabilitation alone.
Stair climbing power improved significantly more in the IHHT group than in controls, a 3.7-fold greater improvement.
Symptomatic dyspnoea (Borg scale) improved twice as much in the IHHT group compared to controls.
Fatigue improved in the IHHT group while it worsened in the control group over the rehabilitation period.
Patient global assessment of well-being was significantly better in the IHHT group than in controls at discharge.
Health-related quality of life measured by the EQ-5D analogue scale improved far more in the IHHT group than in controls.
The overall MEDIAN Corona Recovery Score, capturing somatic and psychological symptoms and social implications, improved significantly more in the IHHT group than controls.
Maximum handgrip strength and nine-hole peg test performance (dexterity) improved significantly in the IHHT group but not in controls.
Spirometric respiratory function improved after rehabilitation in the IHHT group but not in the control group.
Blood pressure, resting heart rate, resting SpO2 and body weight improved significantly in the IHHT group after rehabilitation, with no changes seen in controls.
Haemoglobin increased while fasting glucose and CRP decreased significantly in the IHHT group after rehabilitation, with no such change in controls.
IHHT using a breathing mask was well tolerated with no adverse events, serious adverse events, or dropouts due to intolerance in either group.

The timed up-and-go test improved similarly in both groups without between-group difference, and functional ambulatory category (FAC) showed no significant change in either group, likely due to a ceiling effect.
