The authors describe HIF-1α activation, which is increased following IHHT, as the mediating mechanism of the physiological benefits of intermittent hypoxic-hyperoxic training via regulation of cellular respiration, erythropoiesis, angiogenesis, antioxidant enzymes, inflammation control, and mitochondrial biogenesis.
The combined plant extract (CPE) supplement did not significantly reduce CRP levels compared to placebo after 7 days.
The CPE group showed a significantly greater reduction in total long COVID symptom score compared to placebo.
CPE reduced the risk of overall moderate to severe long COVID symptoms compared to placebo.
CPE substantially reduced the risk of moderate to severe fatigue compared to placebo.
CPE reduced the risk of moderate to severe post-exertional malaise (PEM) compared to placebo.
Changes in health-related quality of life (HRQOL) scores did not differ significantly between the CPE and placebo groups.
Adverse events with CPE were mostly mild and resolved by the end of the follow-up period, indicating an acceptable safety profile.

GPs' estimates of how often they saw Long-COVID varied widely, from 20-25% of infected patients according to one physician to about 10% by another, while one-fifth of interviewees said it occurred only rarely.
GPs used inconsistent symptom-duration thresholds (4, 6, or 8 weeks) to decide when to diagnose a patient with Long-COVID, reflecting confusion over the NICE/WHO/CDC definitions.
GPs reported that standard laboratory panels in Long-COVID patients were almost entirely normal, with vitamin D being the only value sometimes found abnormal.
Specialist (pulmonology, cardiology) examinations of suspected Long-COVID patients most often produced no significant abnormal findings, complicating diagnostic confirmation.

GPs commonly used physiological treatments for Long-COVID including vitamin C and zinc infusions, vitamin D substitution, rehabilitation, and physiotherapy, despite lack of formal evidence at the time.

Other physiological interventions reported by GPs included inhaled steroids/betamimetics, oral vitamin C, COVID-19 vaccination for unvaccinated patients, cortisone, antihistamines, massage, and electrolytes.

Psychological treatment approaches used by GPs for Long-COVID included dedicated support groups, psychotherapy, social worker involvement, and psychiatric referral including antidepressant medication.
Rehabilitation programs (full-time or part-time/part-work) were considered by GPs among the most effective Long-COVID treatments, but capacity was insufficient, causing long waiting times.
POTS, an autonomic dysfunction subtype of postacute COVID condition, can be mistaken by GPs for panic disorder unless a Schellong orthostatic test is performed.

Post-exertional malaise, POTS, and MCAS-like syndromes, which characterize the postacute COVID condition subgroup after mild infection, were never spontaneously mentioned by the interviewed GPs, suggesting under-recognition of these Long-COVID subtypes.

Recommending graded exercise therapy without recognizing post-exertional malaise can potentially worsen a Long-COVID/ME-CFS patient's condition; pacing should be established first when PEM is present.

GPs working in team-based practices (primary care centres, PVE) were better equipped to manage Long-COVID patients, with better knowledge of therapeutic options, regardless of urban or rural location.

Long-COVID patients frequently had to pay out-of-pocket for treatments such as vitamin C infusions that were not reimbursed by social insurance, and GPs sometimes had to intervene with insurers over automatically terminated sick-leave for Long-COVID.

The authors note that, contrary to information GPs commonly gave patients that symptoms would resolve within weeks to months, an increasing number of studies show approximately 20-30% of affected patients still have Long-COVID symptoms after two years.
Cited literature indicates that in approximately 5% of infected persons, Long-COVID symptoms had even worsened after two years rather than improving.
A minority of GPs (3/30, 10%) reported skepticism that some patients only believed or pretended to have Long-COVID, though even skeptical GPs acknowledged having genuine Long-COVID cases.
GPs found it difficult to differentiate Long-COVID from depression/burnout syndrome due to lack of knowledge and diagnostic tools for the specific Long-COVID symptom clusters.

The ÖGAM Long-COVID guideline was viewed positively by GPs for diagnosis and training, but its length was seen as limiting practicability in daily general practice, and its short-form and webtool were underused despite being available on the same site.
The few public Long-COVID outpatient clinics in Austria had waiting times of 6-12 months in the first half of 2022 and closed entirely by 2023, leaving GPs without a secondary-care referral pathway.
Light therapy administered to five long-COVID patients improved sleep and its architecture across the case series.

In case 1, a shift-worker with long-COVID, evening light therapy caused sleep deterioration for three days, but switching administration to the morning (7:30 AM) produced slight-to-moderate improvement in sleep and psychiatric parameters within 1.5 weeks and moderate-to-marked improvement by week 3.
In case 2, evening light therapy improved all long-COVID and Parkinsonian symptoms except Raynaud's disease and anosmia, which were suspected to predate COVID infection.
In case 4, severe fatigue, depression, brain fog, mood disturbance, and anxiety showed marked improvement by 8 weeks after starting light therapy, sustained for at least 16 weeks.

Case 5 developed cardiac symptoms including palpitations, POTS, irregular heartbeat, and weakness starting 15 weeks after COVID infection, in addition to persistent fatigue, body pain, insomnia, and brain fog.
In case 5, all symptoms improved substantially within 1 week of starting morning light therapy and were markedly improved by weeks 2-5, allowing return to normal daily activity.

Light therapy was well tolerated across the case series; the only adverse event was transient sleep deterioration in case 1 due to incorrect (evening) timing of administration, which resolved upon switching to morning light.

The post-encephalitic brain reportedly exhibits fivefold hypersensitivity to psychotropic and neuropsychiatric drugs, suggesting that repurposing melatonin or SSRIs for long-COVID could be problematic.
Melatonin is suggested to have pro-Parkinsonian properties, consistent with already elevated plasma melatonin levels observed in Parkinson's disease and its animal models.
Light therapy is proposed to elevate serotonin and its precursor tryptophan, which may underlie its therapeutic effect on long-COVID symptoms.
Darker, winter climates are reported to have higher COVID incidence while warmer climates report lower infection rates, supporting a role for ambient light in COVID survival and proliferation.
Shift workers who contract COVID-19 have been identified in prior literature as predisposed to developing long-COVID.
Long-COVID and prodromal Parkinson's disease share overlapping symptoms including sleep disturbance, fatigue, depression, anxiety, and cognitive change, suggestive of shared circadian dysfunction.

Case 2 developed suspected Parkinsonian features—bradykinesia, muscular rigidity, hand tremor, shortened gait, reduced arm swing, anosmia, and impaired balance—shortly after contracting COVID, consistent with possible viral Parkinsonism.
Of 11,860 hospitalised COVID-19 patients followed up, 37.0% reported not feeling fully recovered at 2 to <6 months and 46.5% at 6 to <12 months postdischarge.

At 2 to <6 months, participants in high-income countries (HICs) were significantly more likely to report moderate-to-severe fatigue, incomplete recovery, fever, and at least one persistent or new symptom than those in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).

Similar HIC vs LMIC differences persisted at 6 to <12 months, with higher fatigue, incomplete recovery, fever, symptom prevalence, anxiety/depression, pain/discomfort and impaired usual activities in HICs.

Unlike other symptoms, the proportion of participants with moderate-to-severe breathlessness did not differ significantly between HICs and LMICs or across follow-up time points, affecting approximately 1 in 10 participants.
Neurocognitive symptoms were the most commonly reported symptom cluster and were significantly more frequent in HICs than LMICs at both follow-up time points.

Patients with severe acute COVID-19 during hospitalisation had a higher risk of developing Long Covid, moderate-to-severe fatigue, and decreased functioning and quality of life at 2 to <6 months follow-up than patients with moderate acute COVID-19.
Male sex was associated with a lower risk of developing Long Covid, moderate-to-severe fatigue, and reduced functioning and quality of life compared with females.
Participants from LMICs had a lower risk of developing Long Covid, moderate-to-severe fatigue, and decreased functioning and QoL compared with participants in HICs.
Being 45-65 years old was associated with a significantly increased risk of experiencing reduced functioning and quality of life compared with younger adults.
Pre-existing asthma, chronic pulmonary disease and rheumatological disease were identified as significant risk factors for developing Long Covid and fatigue.
Hypertension and chronic cardiac disease were additional risk factors for experiencing reduced functioning and quality of life following COVID-19 hospitalisation.

There was a significant increase in the proportion of people experiencing breathlessness at follow-up compared with prior to their COVID-19 illness, with worsening more common than improvement, though frequency declined somewhat by 6-12 months.

The authors propose that persistent SARS-CoV-2 infection and reactivation of Epstein-Barr virus have been suggested as possible underlying causative agents of Long Covid, potentially explaining the high proportion of persistent fever observed.
Microclots and hypercoagulation biomarkers indicating endothelial activation and abnormal clotting have been implicated as causative agents for some Long Covid symptoms, based on cited literature.

The authors suggest that differing symptom presentation between settings and clusters may relate to different underlying aetiologies, including organ damage, infection-triggered autoimmunity, and dysautonomia.
The predominant autonomic dysfunction shifted from sympathetic withdrawal pre-COVID-19 (45.7%) to parasympathetic excess post-COVID-19 (46.7%), with sympathetic withdrawal falling to 36.2%.
Autonomic therapy prior to COVID-19 reduced the average number of P&S dysfunctions from 2.34 to 0.95 (of 7 possible), a statistically significant improvement.
After COVID-19 infection, patients demonstrated a significant increase in average P&S dysfunctions to 3.67 of 7, up from the post-therapy pre-COVID baseline of 0.95.
Continued and adjusted autonomic therapy after COVID-19 reduced the average number of P&S dysfunctions from 3.67 to 1.63 of 7.
Autonomic therapy prior to COVID-19 reduced the average number of reported symptoms (of 28) from 9.74 to 6.25.
After COVID-19 infection, patients reported a significant increase in symptoms to an average of 14.6 of 28.
Continued autonomic therapy after COVID-19 reduced average symptom count from 14.6 to 7.44 of 28.
COVID-19 infection increased the number of autonomic dysfunctions demonstrated by these patients by 56.8%.
COVID-19 infection increased the number of associated symptoms reported by these patients by 49.9%.

Patients with low resting sympathovagal balance (vagal excess) reported more significant depression/anxiety and fatigue symptoms, while those with high sympathovagal balance (sympathetic excess) reported more significant pain and hypertension symptoms.
At initial presentation prior to COVID-19, 8.6% of the cohort had orthostatic dysfunction attributable to POTS.
A quarter (25.7%) of the cohort of autonomic dysfunction/long-COVID patients were diagnosed with Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome-Hypermobility.
Over a third (36.9%) of the cohort reported fatigue at initial presentation.
Sympathetic withdrawal and associated orthostatic dysfunction were treated with 2.5 mg tid of Midodrine, an alpha-adrenergic agonist.
Alpha-Lipoic Acid, an antioxidant selective for nerves, was used up to 600 mg tid as adjunct therapy for sympathetic withdrawal.
Parasympathetic excess was treated with low-dose (10 mg qd) Nortriptyline as an anti-cholinergic agent.
Up to 40 minutes of low-and-slow exercise was used as a non-pharmacologic adjunct therapy for parasympathetic excess.
Central autonomic dysfunction may be related to microglial hyperactivation within brainstem autonomic centers, which has been associated with parasympathetic excess.

While acute COVID-19 infection is traditionally associated with increased resting sympathetic activity and decreased parasympathetic activity, this cohort's post-COVID-19 (>12 weeks) data showed a significant shift toward parasympathetic dominance instead.
High antibody responses to the EBV protein VCAp18 during acute COVID-19 disease were significantly associated with reporting fatigue during acute disease.
High antibody responses to the EBV protein BXLF1 during acute COVID-19 disease were significantly associated with reporting fatigue during acute disease.
High antibody responses to the EBV protein BaRF1 during acute COVID-19 disease were significantly associated with reporting fatigue during acute disease.
High antibody responses to the CMV protein pp28 during acute COVID-19 disease were associated with a decrease in taste during acute disease.
High antibody responses to the EBV protein Zebra (BZLF1) measured during acute COVID-19 disease were significantly associated with fatigue occurring at ≥1 follow-up time-point (5, 12, or 20 months).
High antibody responses to the EBV protein BGLF2 during acute COVID-19 disease were significantly associated with fatigue occurring during PASC follow-up.
High antibody responses to the EBV protein BGLF2 during acute COVID-19 disease were significantly associated with dyspnea occurring during PASC follow-up.
High antibody responses to the CMV protein pp150 during acute COVID-19 disease were associated with concentration problems occurring during PASC follow-up.
High antibody responses to the CMV protein pp52 during acute COVID-19 disease were associated with concentration problems occurring during PASC follow-up.
High antibody responses to the CMV protein pp28 during acute COVID-19 disease were associated with concentration problems occurring during PASC follow-up.
High antibody responses to the CMV protein pp52 during acute COVID-19 disease were associated with a decrease in taste occurring during PASC follow-up.
High antibody responses to the CMV protein pp28 during acute COVID-19 disease were associated with a decrease in taste occurring during PASC follow-up.
High antibody responses to the CMV protein pp65 during acute COVID-19 disease were associated with a decrease in taste occurring during PASC follow-up.

Antibodies to the classical EBV reactivation marker EA-D and the infection marker EBNA-1 were not associated with symptom occurrence in this study, potentially because responses were near assay saturation, hindering dichotomization.

Herpesvirus antibody levels did not change substantially between the acute COVID-19 time-point and up to 20 months of follow-up, questioning the use of static antibody levels as a marker of transient viral reactivation.
Long-COVID healthcare workers reported a significantly higher number and intensity of psychosomatic (physical, cognitive and emotional) symptoms compared to matched controls at baseline.
The prevalence of dysfunctional breathing symptoms decreased significantly after one month of slow-paced breathing intervention.
After the one-month at-home breathing intervention, participants showed a significant reduction in cognitive deterioration, headache, asthenia and chest tightness symptoms.
Cardiovagal modulation, measured by RMSSD during slow breathing, showed no significant change after the one-month rVNS intervention.
LF power (a marker of sympathovagal balance) during slow breathing showed no significant change after the one-month intervention.
Manual dexterity (two-handed assembly task on the Purdue Pegboard test) showed only a slight, non-significant increase after the breathing intervention, approaching statistical significance.

At baseline, long-COVID healthcare workers showed impairment in fine manipulative skills (Purdue Pegboard performance) compared to controls, which only marginally improved after the breathing intervention.

Three-quarters of long-COVID cases had a total psychosomatic symptom count of 6 or more on the M.U.S. questionnaire, a threshold previously associated with low heart rate variability (RMSSD), an indirect marker of parasympathetic dysfunction.
Long-COVID cases showed a markedly higher SARS-CoV-2 antibody titre compared to never-infected but vaccinated controls.
The intensity of psychosomatic symptoms (M.U.S./Distress) did not change significantly between baseline and follow-up after the breathing intervention.
Histological analysis by Shi et al. found that epimysium and perimysium fibrosis was more than twice as common in the diaphragms of COVID-19 ICU patients compared with non-COVID ICU controls.

Studies in dystrophic mice show that excessive IL-6 expression disrupts redox balance in the diaphragm, intensifying oxidative stress and contributing to progressive muscle atrophy, a mechanism proposed as relevant to COVID-19-related cytokine effects on the diaphragm.
Human tissues infected with SARS-CoV-2 show increased ACE2 expression, which may facilitate viral invasion of neuronal and muscular tissue, including the diaphragm.
Diaphragm thinning has been observed in COVID-19 patients across the severity spectrum, occurring in both severe and milder cases.
Reduced diaphragm thickness has been identified as an independent risk factor for progression to severe COVID-19, potentially limiting inspiratory pump force and accelerating respiratory failure.
Regmi et al. used invasive testing to show that diaphragmatic weakness persisted for up to 15 months following SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Steier et al. showed that in-depth respiratory muscle assessment techniques can improve diagnostic accuracy for diaphragmatic weakness by up to 40%.
COVID-19 patients show reduced transdiaphragmatic systolic pressure, similar to patterns seen in neuromuscular disease patients with severe dyspnea.
Long COVID patients commonly experience musculoskeletal dysfunction, with muscle pain and general weakness reported in approximately 25% to 50% of cases.

Appelman et al. found that long COVID is associated with reduced skeletal muscle oxidative phosphorylation capacity, a shift toward more fatigue-prone fiber types, and reduced mitochondrial respiration, contributing to diminished exercise capacity.

Radiological studies show that people with obstructive sleep apnea have greater diaphragm thickness on ultrasound compared with healthy individuals without OSA, potentially reflecting compensatory hypertrophy from increased respiratory effort.

In COVID-19, cytokine storm leads to elevated CRP, IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha, which trigger muscle proteolysis, promote fibrogenesis, activate fibroblasts, and inhibit muscle progenitor cells needed for regeneration.
A small number of case reports describe diaphragmatic palsy following COVID-19, occurring unilaterally more often than bilaterally, independent of mechanical ventilation.
Voice problems in COVID-19 and post-COVID syndrome are attributed in part to impaired diaphragm activity, abnormal respiratory patterns, and disrupted respiratory-phonatory-articulatory coordination.
Recurrent coughing, a prominent COVID-19 symptom, is hypothesized to cause pelvic floor muscle fatigue and weakness in affected individuals.
ACE2, the SARS-CoV-2 host receptor, is highly expressed in the small intestine and moderately expressed in the bladder, potentially explaining gastrointestinal and urinary effects of infection.
Musculoskeletal dysfunction, manifesting as muscle pain and general weakness, affects approximately 25% to 50% of COVID-19 patients, often accompanied by dizziness, swaying, or loss of balance.
Reduced diaphragm thickness has been identified as an independent risk factor for progression to severe COVID-19, limiting inspiratory pump force and accelerating respiratory failure.
Quantitative CT COVID scores at admission serve as an independent prognostic factor for predicting rapid escalation to severe COVID-19 pneumonia.
A reduction in transdiaphragmatic systolic pressure has been observed in COVID-19 patients, similar to that seen in patients with neuromuscular diseases and severe shortness of breath.
Steier et al. demonstrated that in-depth respiratory muscle assessment techniques can increase the accuracy of diagnosing diaphragmatic weakness by up to 40%.

Voice problems observed during and after COVID-19 infection result from impaired diaphragm activity, abnormal respiratory patterns, and impaired respiratory, phonatory, and articulatory coordination, sometimes requiring speech therapy.

Weakness of the pelvic floor muscles following COVID-19 is hypothesized to result from recurring coughing episodes causing fatigue in these muscles, given their synergistic function with the diaphragm.
Radiological studies show that people with obstructive sleep apnea exhibit greater diaphragm thickness on ultrasound compared to healthy individuals without the condition.
Invasive tests in patients with severe obstructive sleep apnea showed lower functional efficiency and greater fatigue of the diaphragm.
SARS-CoV-2 patients frequently exhibit sleep disturbances including insomnia and respiratory disorders during sleep (RDDS), most commonly obstructive sleep apnea.

Farr et al. describe critical illness myopathy as multifactorial, involving muscle membrane dysfunction, microcirculatory changes during inflammation, high-dose corticosteroid exposure, and impaired translocation of glucose transporter type 4 to muscle membranes.
Mechanically ventilated COVID-19 patients face a significant risk of developing pneumomediastinum.

Extensive changes in tracheal and major airway cartilage, characterized by fibrous-hyaline degeneration and unusual regenerative tissue remodeling processes, are distinctive markers directly linked to COVID-19.
Diaphragmatic palsy following COVID-19, unrelated to mechanical ventilation, can be bilateral or (more commonly) unilateral, with only a small number of such cases reported in the literature.

Prolonged bed rest during hospitalization, particularly in older sarcopenic patients, accelerates decreased muscle mass, reduced contractile strength, increased fatigue, diminished muscle power, and deteriorated neuromuscular conduction.
SARS-CoV-2-positive participants reported memory problems at markedly higher odds than negative participants at 3-6 months and beyond 18 months post-infection.
SARS-CoV-2-positive participants reported concentration problems at higher odds than negative participants at 3-6 months and beyond 18 months post-infection.
Fatigue was reported more frequently by SARS-CoV-2-positive participants than negative participants persisting after infection.
Dyspnea was reported more frequently by SARS-CoV-2-positive participants than negative participants persisting after infection.
Anosmia was reported more frequently by SARS-CoV-2-positive participants than negative participants persisting after infection.
Dysgeusia was reported more frequently by SARS-CoV-2-positive participants than negative participants persisting after infection.

SARS-CoV-2-positive participants reported worsening of overall self-rated health compared with negative participants, persisting up to 22 months after infection even after adjusting for pre-COVID symptoms.
Long COVID patients showed higher fatigue levels than healthy controls on the FAS scale, with 59.6% classified as having fatigue and 23.9% as having extreme fatigue.
A higher proportion of long COVID patients reported low levels of physical activity compared to controls.
No significant difference in sleep quality was found between the long COVID and control groups, both groups showing poor sleep quality.
A much smaller proportion of long COVID patients reported an ideal overall health status compared to controls on the EQ-5D-5L scale.
Self-reported overall health score (EQ VAS) was significantly lower in the long COVID group than in controls.
Despite a subset of long COVID patients showing impaired scores on individual cognitive tests, no significant overall differences in cognitive test performance were found compared to controls.
Normalised TMT-A scores were lower (worse) in the long COVID group compared to controls, at borderline significance.
Right cerebellar grey matter volume was significantly reduced in the long COVID group compared to controls, and this remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons.
Left cerebellar grey matter volume was significantly reduced in the long COVID group in the ANCOVA analysis, but this did not survive correction for multiple comparisons.
Reduced grey matter volumes were observed in the left lingual gyrus and left inferior parietal lobule in long COVID patients, but this did not survive correction for multiple comparisons.

Long COVID patients showed reduced cortical thickness in multiple regions including bilateral postcentral gyrus and precuneus, right superior temporal gyrus, left banks of the superior temporal sulcus, left lingual gyrus, and left supramarginal gyrus, with significance surviving multiple-comparison correction in five of these regions.
No significant correlations were found between brain regions showing atrophy and cognitive test scores or standardised questionnaire measures.
No significant differences in global grey matter, white matter, or total brain volume were found between long COVID patients and controls after controlling for age.
The long COVID group reported a high prevalence of persistent symptoms, most commonly memory problems, fatigue, brain fog, and attention problems, nearly two years after infection.
The proportion of participants reporting Long COVID symptoms declined across the three interview sessions, from 88% at session 1 to 82% at session 2 and 68% at session 3.
Brain fog, fatigue, and headache were consistently the most frequently reported Long COVID symptoms across all three interview sessions and across variant cohorts.
Older participant age was negatively correlated with the number of Long COVID symptoms reported, contrary to prior literature associating older age with higher Long COVID risk.
Females reported significantly more Long COVID symptoms on average than males.
Participants with one, or three or more, comorbidities reported significantly more Long COVID symptoms than those with no comorbidities.
Vaccination status at the time of the first interview session was not significantly associated with the average number of Long COVID symptoms reported.
Homologous versus heterologous vaccine combination was not significantly associated with the number of Long COVID symptoms reported.
Vaccine type(s) taken were not significantly associated with the number of Long COVID symptoms reported.
The average number of reported Long COVID symptoms did not differ significantly among Alpha, Beta, Delta, Omicron, and Theta variant cohorts.
The average number of Long COVID symptoms varied significantly with acute disease severity, though pairwise comparisons did not identify specific significant group differences.
The total number of tested SARS-CoV-2 infections was not significantly associated with the average number of Long COVID symptoms reported.
Timing of vaccination relative to infection (either before or after infection) was not significantly correlated with the number of Long COVID symptoms reported.
Between the second and third interview sessions (3 months apart), the number of asymptomatic cases significantly increased while symptomatic cases significantly decreased.
General symptoms and neuropsychiatric symptoms were consistently the top two most frequently reported Long COVID symptom categories across all sessions and variant cohorts.

The majority of brain fog reports came from the Alpha and Beta variant cohorts, suggesting possible differences in neurotropism across variants that could increase risk of brain fog and neurocognitive impairment.

The majority of headache reports came from the Alpha or Beta cohorts, and headache was a consistently top-reported symptom in the Omicron cohort across all sessions, suggesting a variant-specific association with Long COVID headache.
The majority of fatigue reports came from the Alpha or Beta cohorts, with fewer from Omicron or Theta cohorts, mirroring the pattern seen for brain fog.

Central sensitization, characterized by CNS hypersensitivity to sensory stimuli, has been proposed as a mechanism explaining the co-occurrence and amplification of brain fog, headache, and fatigue in Long COVID.

The Theta variant, despite carrying Beta-like spike mutations associated with immune evasion, was associated with fewer reported Long COVID symptoms than the Delta variant that circulated in the same period, suggesting a possibly milder clinical phenotype.
Self-reported fatigue prevalence (22.7%) was higher than fatigue prevalence measured objectively using the Fatigue Severity Scale (14.4%) among post-COVID-19 patients.
A positive PHQ-2 depression screening result was the strongest independent predictor of post-COVID-19 fatigue in multivariate logistic regression, with an odds ratio of 14.3.
Higher acute COVID-19 clinical severity was an independent predictor of post-COVID-19 fatigue, with an odds ratio of 1.87.
In univariate analysis, female gender was significantly associated with fatigue among COVID-19 survivors, though this association did not remain significant in multivariate analysis.
Presence of comorbidities was significantly associated with fatigue in univariate analysis but not in the multivariate model.
Being on regular chronic medications was significantly associated with fatigue in univariate analysis but not after multivariate adjustment.
Smoking status was significantly associated with fatigue in univariate analysis but not in the multivariate model.
Age was not significantly associated with post-COVID-19 fatigue.
Body mass index (BMI) was not significantly associated with post-COVID-19 fatigue.
COVID-19 vaccination status was not significantly associated with post-COVID-19 fatigue.

In the multivariate logistic regression model, smoking, female gender, comorbidities, and fatigue-related medications were no longer significantly associated with fatigue after adjustment for other variables.
COVID-19-positive respondents were substantially more likely to report at least one persistent new symptom than close-contact controls at a mean of 12.6 months after infection.
14.2% of all respondents met the study's criteria for clinical long COVID, defined as at least one persistent new symptom combined with less than 80% recovery at three months post-infection.
A small minority of those with clinical long COVID reported at least moderate problems with usual daily activities at 12 months after infection.
Respondents with more recent SARS-CoV-2 infections had a lower proportion of clinical long COVID than those infected earlier in the pandemic.
Female sex was identified as a risk factor for developing clinical long COVID.
Female sex was identified as a risk factor for developing clinical long COVID.
Being aged 40-49 years was identified as a risk factor for developing clinical long COVID.
Greater acute infection severity was associated with increased risk of clinical long COVID.
Pre-existing chronic illness was associated with increased risk of clinical long COVID.
A past history of anxiety or depression was associated with increased risk of clinical long COVID.
More recently acquired SARS-CoV-2 infections were associated with a lower proportion of respondents meeting criteria for clinical long COVID.
POTS was the most frequently diagnosed complicating disease among the long COVID cohort, found in 115 of 798 patients.
PSWT, a new diagnostic concept of orthostatic intolerance without meeting POTS hemodynamic criteria, was the second most common complication (65 patients).
Mood disorder was the third most common complicating disease detected, occurring in 60 patients.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported symptom at initial consultation, affecting 523 of 798 patients.
Anxiety was the second most commonly reported symptom, affecting 349 of 798 patients.
Lack of motivation was the third most commonly reported symptom, affecting 344 of 798 patients.
Among patients complaining of fatigue, POTS was the most common accompanying complication (99 patients), followed by PSWT (58), mood disorders (53), and social anxiety disorder (23).
Among patients with palpitations, POTS was the most common complication (49 patients), followed by PSWT (22) and panic disorder (8).
Among patients with dyspnea, POTS was the most common complication (50 patients), followed by asthma/COPD (7) and organizing pneumonia (3).
Of 129 patients complaining of chronic cough, 12 were diagnosed with postinfectious cough or cough-variant asthma, 10 with gastroesophageal reflux disease, and 4 with bronchial asthma.
Of 323 patients with headache complaints, 31 were newly diagnosed with migraine and 18 with tension-type headache.
Of 168 patients reporting dizziness, 38 had POTS and 9 had persistent postural perceptual dizziness (PPPD).
Among patients with joint pain, 2 were diagnosed with reactive arthritis and 13 with other musculoskeletal problems.
Among patients complaining of diarrhea, IBS was diagnosed as a complication in six patients.

Among patients complaining of numbness, small fiber neuropathy was diagnosed in five patients based on clinical presentation, with diagnosis made in the absence of nerve conduction, MRI, and blood test abnormalities since skin biopsy could not be performed.

Among patients with psychiatric symptoms (lack of motivation, low mood, anxiety, insomnia), 60 were diagnosed with unipolar depression or bipolar disorder, 54 with adjustment disorder, 23 with anxiety disorder, and 16 with panic disorder.
Overall, 452 of the 798 long COVID patients evaluated had at least one complicating disease identified by chart review.
Among patients who complained of fatigue, six were found to have hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism.
During the acute phase of infection, 145 (18.2%) of the 798 patients had complications of pneumonia.
At the initial interview, 141 patients reported arthralgia and 150 reported myalgia.
Fatigue was the most frequently reported symptom across EMA assessments, present 83% of the time, followed by cognitive dysfunction and pain/discomfort.
Older participants (60+ years) reported significantly worse breathlessness than those under 40.
Women reported more severe fatigue than men.
Women reported less severe dizziness than men.
Women reported less severe anxiety than men.
Women reported less severe depression than men.
No evidence was found that minority ethnic groups as a whole experienced different symptom severity than White ethnicity participants.
Participants able to remain in full-time employment reported significantly lower fatigue, pain/discomfort, depression, and cognitive dysfunction than those unable to work full-time.
Participants recruited from the community reported more fatigue than those recruited from long COVID clinics.
No evidence of difference in long COVID symptom severity was found between those whose initial infection was asymptomatic, required hospital admission, or ICU admission.
Longer duration of long COVID symptoms was associated with greater pain or discomfort severity.
Small month-on-month improvements over the 12-week study were seen in severity of fatigue and dizziness.
Weekdays were associated with worse symptom severity across most symptoms, particularly cognitive dysfunction, compared to weekends.
Symptom severity, especially fatigue and cognitive dysfunction, increased progressively through the day.
Need for rest or sleep immediately prior to an EMA was associated with greater concurrent fatigue and pain/discomfort, with sleep showing a stronger association than rest.
Rest 3 hours previously was associated with slightly less cognitive dysfunction, while sleep 3 hours previously was associated with slightly worse depression scores.
High effort (8/10) physical and cognitive activity within the preceding 30 minutes were both associated with substantially increased fatigue severity, with physical exertion showing a larger effect.

All measured symptoms increased immediately (within 30 minutes) after effort on all recorded activities; breathlessness was most strongly linked to physical activity specifically, while fatigue increases were as severe after cognitive, social and self-care activities as after physical activity.
Small delayed increases in fatigue and pain/discomfort were observed 3 hours after high physical activity effort (8/10).
Small delayed increases in fatigue, pain/discomfort, anxiety, and cognitive dysfunction were observed 3 hours after high cognitive activity effort (8/10).
High-effort social activity was associated with a small delayed increase in fatigue emerging 3 hours later.
High-effort self-care activity (e.g. showering, cooking) was associated with delayed increases in fatigue, pain/discomfort, anxiety and depression emerging 3 hours later.

Effortful physical activity the day before was associated with increased pain/discomfort and cognitive dysfunction, and decreased palpitations, emerging the next day, with wide credible intervals at higher effort levels.
Greater cognitive activity effort was associated with more severe fatigue and increased cognitive dysfunction emerging the following day.
Social activity effort the day before was associated with worse fatigue emerging the next day.

Effortful self-care activity the day before was associated with increased fatigue and markedly increased severity of palpitations the following day, although mean daily efforts were low and credible intervals were wide.
Subgroup analyses (clinic vs community, men vs women, younger vs older) using the best-fitting model showed broadly consistent conclusions about activity-symptom associations across all subgroups.
Among hospitalized COVID-19 survivors followed at 12-18 months, the incidence of Long COVID-19 was 17.0%.
Long COVID-19 was significantly more prevalent among women than men.
Long COVID-19 was significantly more prevalent in older individuals.
Patients who developed Long COVID-19 had a significantly longer mean duration of oxygen requirement during acute hospitalization compared to those without Long COVID-19.
Use of nonrebreather oxygen masks during acute hospitalization was significantly more common in patients who later developed Long COVID-19 compared to those who did not.
Requirement for noninvasive ventilation during acute illness was significantly more frequent among patients who developed Long COVID-19.
Duration of ICU stay was significantly longer in patients who subsequently developed Long COVID-19 compared to those who did not.
Quality of life measured by EQ-5D was poor overall in survivors, with a median score of 5.0 and only 0.6% scoring above 5.

Using the Birmingham Symptom Burden Questionnaire, fatigue was the most common new-onset symptom reported among Long COVID-19 patients at 12-18 months, followed by feverishness, low energy, exertional dyspnea, and rest dyspnea.
76% of long COVID outpatient clinic attendees had clinically significant fatigue as measured by the FACIT-F scale.
69% of patients had moderate-to-severe breathlessness symptoms measured by the Dyspnoea-12 scale.
55% of patients had moderate-to-severe depression symptoms as measured by PHQ-9.
34% of patients had moderate-to-severe anxiety as measured by GAD-7.
41% of patients reported very poor self-rated overall health as measured by a Visual Analogue Scale.
57% of patients had moderate-to-severe dysfunction in work and social life as measured by the WSAS.
Older long COVID patients (≥50 years) were more likely to experience moderate-to-severe dyspnoea than younger patients.
There were no significant differences between males and females across any of the six baseline symptom questionnaires.
Women reported a significantly higher mean number of Long-COVID symptoms than men.
Patients under age 65 reported a significantly higher symptom burden than those 65 or older.
Patients admitted to intensive care showed a borderline, non-significant trend toward higher symptom burden than those not admitted.
Memory loss was significantly more prevalent among women than men with Long-COVID.
Difficulty concentrating was significantly more common in women than men.
Cough was significantly more common in women than men.
Palpitations or tachycardia were significantly more common in women than men.
Skin disorders or alopecia were significantly more common in women than men.
Brain fog was significantly more common in women than men.
Headache was significantly more common in women than men.
Visual disturbances were significantly more common in women than men.
Weight loss was the only symptom significantly more frequent in men than in women.
Pre-existing autoimmune disease, anxiety and depression were significantly more common comorbidities in women than men in this Long-COVID cohort.
Cardiovascular and respiratory comorbidities (ischaemic heart disease, respiratory failure/COPD, hypertension) were significantly more common in men than women in this Long-COVID cohort.

Hierarchical clustering identified a six-symptom cluster (brain fog, equilibrium or gait disturbances, headache, paresthesia, thoracic pain, and palpitations/tachycardia) suggested to reflect combined sensorial, neurological and autonomic disturbance.
Difficult concentration and memory loss clustered together as a cognitive symptom pair in symptom clustering analysis.
Anxiety and depressed mood clustered together as a mood symptom pair.
Joint pain/swelling and muscle pain clustered together as a musculoskeletal pain pair.
Headache was independently associated with reduced or interrupted working activity in the multivariable model.
Dyspnea was independently associated with reduced or interrupted working activity in the multivariable model.
Difficulty concentrating was independently associated with reduced or interrupted working activity in the multivariable model.
Disturbances of equilibrium or gait were independently associated with reduced or interrupted working activity.
Visual disturbances were independently associated with reduced or interrupted working activity.
Muscular pain was independently associated with reduced or interrupted working activity.
Nearly a quarter of working-age Long-COVID patients reported reduced or interrupted working activity, with no gender difference.
Fatigue was the single most commonly reported Long-COVID symptom, affecting 55.9% of the entire cohort, with similar prevalence in men and women.
Dyspnea was the second most common persisting symptom, affecting 47.2% of the cohort, with no major difference between men and women.
Sleep disturbances were reported by 21.4% of patients, with a non-significant trend toward higher prevalence in women.
Joint pain or swelling was reported in 16.3% of patients, without a statistically significant gender difference.
Muscle pain was reported in 16.1% of patients, without significant gender difference, and was independently associated with reduced/interrupted working activity in multivariable analysis.
Reduced taste and reduced smell each affected roughly 12% of patients, with no significant gender difference, and clustered together in symptom cluster analysis as a sensorial-loss group.
Muscle pain and joint pain/swelling clustered together in the symptom clustering analysis, forming a multidistrict pain phenotype.
Memory loss and difficult concentration clustered together, forming a cognitive dysfunction symptom phenotype in Long-COVID.
Anxiety and depressed mood clustered together as a mood-change symptom phenotype in the Long-COVID cohort.

A six-symptom cluster comprising brain fog, equilibrium or gait disturbances, headache, paresthesia, thoracic pain, and palpitations/tachycardia co-occurred, suggesting a combined sensorial, neurological and autonomic disturbance phenotype.

Five symptoms (skin disorders/alopecia, cough, sleep disturbances, dyspnea, fatigue) did not aggregate with any other symptom, forming single-unit clusters distinct from the rest of the symptom profile.
Women reported a significantly higher mean number of Long-COVID symptoms than men despite having had milder acute infection.
Patients under age 65 reported a significantly higher mean number of Long-COVID symptoms than those 65 or older, contrary to the expectation that advanced age would increase symptom burden.
There was only a borderline non-significant trend toward a higher number of symptoms in patients who had been admitted to intensive care during acute infection.
Nearly a quarter of Long-COVID patients under age 60 reported reduced or interrupted working activity following COVID-19, with no significant difference between women and men.

In the case-clustering analysis, dyspnea and paresthesia were significantly more common in the subpopulation (cluster 2) with older age, more comorbidities, and more severe acute SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Headache, difficult concentration and palpitations/tachycardia were significantly more common in the case-cluster (cluster 1) characterised by younger age, female predominance, and milder acute COVID-19.

A significantly higher proportion of patients in the milder-acute-disease cluster (cluster 1) reported worsened subjective functional status compared to pre-infection, relative to the more severe-disease cluster.

The authors note that severe, persistent fatigue in Long-COVID resembles Chronic Fatigue Syndrome/Myalgic Encephalomyelitis (CFS/ME) and is increasingly viewed as a possible post-viral manifestation triggered by SARS-CoV-2, similar to other viral infections.

A significant three-way interaction among diagnosis, social context, and time point was found for salivary cortisol, indicating that ASD and TD youth show different cortisol response patterns depending on the social stressor and timing.
A significant three-way interaction among diagnosis, social context, and time point was found for heart rate, indicating diagnostic groups respond differently across context and time.
There was no significant three-way interaction (diagnosis by context by time) for respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA).
Youth with ASD showed significantly lower overall RSA compared to TD youth, regardless of context or time point.
State and trait anxiety did not mediate the relationship between diagnosis (ASD vs TD) and physiological responses (cortisol, HR, RSA).
Autism spectrum disorder was diagnosed in 38% of individuals in the present cohort, with a similar prevalence in the combined dataset.
ASD prevalence was numerically higher in patients with PTVb variants (12/14) than PTVa variants (4/10), but this genotype-phenotype trend was not statistically significant.

Signs of autonomic dysfunction, including cutis marmorata, intermittently cold extremities or Raynaud's phenomenon, and altered pain sensitivity, were identified in 17% of individuals, representing a newly recognized manifestation of BCL11A-IDD.
Joint hypermobility/laxity was reported in 36% of individuals with BCL11A-IDD.
Constipation was reported in 35% of individuals with BCL11A-IDD.
All 23 individuals in whom HbF was quantified had levels above the maximum reference for age, confirming persistence of fetal hemoglobin as a constant hallmark of BCL11A-IDD.
HbF levels showed an inverse trend with age, decreasing over time in individuals with sequential measurements while remaining above the reference range for age.
Brain MRI abnormalities were found in 55% of scanned patients, most commonly cerebellar abnormalities (32%) and brainstem abnormalities (32%), with hypoplastic cerebellar vermis in all such cases.

Cortical malformations were significantly less frequent in individuals with variants or deletions affecting BCL11A alone compared with those carrying large contiguous gene CNVs encompassing BCL11A and neighboring genes.

Congenital malformation frequency in the BCL11A-IDD cohort (15%) was significantly lower than in individuals with large CNVs encompassing additional coding genes (60%), a difference that remained significant in the combined dataset.
Postnatal microcephaly emerged as a common, previously underappreciated feature, present in 46% of individuals, with head circumference significantly smaller postnatally than at birth.
Individuals with PTVb class variants had significantly smaller head circumference than those with missense variants.
Hypotonia was significantly more frequent in individuals with PTVa variants than in those with missense variants.
Developmental delay and/or intellectual disability was present in nearly all individuals in the present cohort, ranging from mild to severe/profound with moderate ID most common.
Seizures occurred in 22% of patients, with polymorphic seizure types (generalized tonic-clonic, myoclonic, focal-onset) and no dominant seizure type.
Additional behavioral problems, including aggressiveness, repetitive behavior, sleep disturbances, ADHD, and anxiety, were reported in 69% of patients, some co-occurring in the same individual.

Two novel missense variants, p.His188Arg and p.Asn756Lys, were classified pathogenic by AlphaMissense, with p.Asn756Lys predicted to alter the C-terminal zinc-finger structure required for globin repression.
Germline mosaicism was identified in two sib-pair families where parents tested negative for the variant, indicating a recurrence risk of approximately 4% for parents of a single affected child.
Immunohistochemistry confirmed high BCL11A protein expression in the cerebellar Purkinje cell layer during human fetal development from 12 to 18 weeks post-conception.

GestaltMatcher facial analysis showed only 34.5% of BCL11A-IDD individuals fell below the similarity threshold, indicating the absence of a distinct, objectively recognizable facial gestalt for the condition.
Despite somatic BCL11A variants being reported in sporadic malignant tumors, no individuals in this cohort were diagnosed with solid or hematologic malignancy.
A trend towards a more severe overall phenotype was observed for protein-truncating variants compared to missense and splice variants across the cohort.
Parents of autistic children reported higher trait social anxiety in their children compared to parents of non-diagnosed peers.
Parents of children with Specific Learning Disorders reported higher trait social anxiety in their children compared to parents of non-diagnosed peers.
No group differences emerged in participants' own self-reported trait social anxiety across autistic, SLD, and non-diagnosed groups.
Autistic and SLD participants were rated as having lower quality of public speech during the TSST than non-diagnosed peers.
Autistic children and adolescents reported lower subjective arousal during the TSST than non-diagnosed peers.
Autistic children and adolescents reported higher perceived competence during the social stress task than non-diagnosed peers.
Participants with Specific Learning Disorders reported a lower perception of competence during the social stress task than non-diagnosed peers.
Autistic children and adolescents showed decreased cardiac reactivity across the Trier Social Stress Test compared to both SLD and non-diagnosed peers.
Bulk RNA-Seq of long-COVID PBMCs (8th month post-SARS-CoV-2 infection) showed 866 upregulated and 330 downregulated genes out of ~22,500 expressed genes compared to non-LC samples.
EBV-infected PBMCs (4th day post-infection) showed 3,075 upregulated and 2,806 downregulated genes out of ~19,700 expressed genes.
Intersection of significant DEGs from EBV (7,609 genes) and LC (839 genes) datasets yielded 357 common differentially expressed genes (cDEGs) shared between the two conditions.

Among the top 30 differentially expressed genes, five genes (FST, OR7D2, SERPINE1, TMEM176A, TMEM176B) were specifically dysregulated within the long-COVID sample cluster, with FST (follistatin, an FSH inhibitor) previously reported as upregulated in LC by clinical genomic studies.
Among the top 20 differentially expressed genes in EBV-infected PBMCs, ZBED2 and RGS16 were upregulated while the remaining 18 were downregulated on day 4 post-infection.
Functional enrichment of the 357 common DEGs showed 5 genes enriched in glutathione transferase activity.
24 of the common DEGs were functionally enriched in calcium ion binding.

Protein-protein interaction analysis via STRING identified 125 of the 357 common DEGs forming interactions (score>0.4), from which 43 were classified as hub genes with high connectivity (degree>5) using CytoHubba.
MCODE clustering of hub genes grouped CCL2, MMP2, IL6, CXCL8, CCL20, NRCN1, and CDH2 into cluster 1, the genes with the highest number of network edges.
MCODE cluster 2 grouped NEK2, TOP2A, CDCA2, CEP55, DEPDC1, DIAPH3, PBK, and DLGAP5 as the genes with the highest number of edges, mostly cell-cycle related genes.
CDCA2, CEP55, CKAP2L, DEPDC1, DIAPH3, DLGAP5, E2F8, FGF1, NEK2, PBK, and TOP2A were found upregulated in both long-COVID and EBV-infection samples.
CCL2, CHI3L1, and EGR2 showed opposite expression patterns between the two conditions, with higher expression in EBV samples and lower expression in long-COVID samples.
MMP2 and RETN expression was upregulated in long-COVID samples but downregulated in EBV-infected samples.
CCL20, CCL3, CXCL8, DEPDC1, DIAPH3, DLGAP5, E2F8, IL6, LCN2, and OLR1 were found depleted in both EBV-infected and long-COVID samples.

The transcription factor ARNTL2 was found to control multiple hub genes (EGR2, CCL2, DLGAP5, CEP55, E2F8, PBK, TOP2A, DEPDC1, CDCA2, NEK2, CKAP2L, DIAPH3, CXCL8, IL8), suggesting a shared transcriptional machinery.

Zinc-finger protein family TFs (ZNF-215, ZNF-2670, ZNF-219) and MYB family TFs (MYBL1, MYBL2) were identified as key regulators of ten hub genes (DLGAP5, CEP55, E2F8, PBK, TOP2A, DEPDC1, CDCA2, NEK2, CKAP2L, DIAPH3), consistent with prior reports of these TF families in COVID-19 and EBV infection.

Molecular docking of the OLR1 protein with the bioflavonoid amentoflavone produced the strongest binding among five candidates, with a binding energy of -8.3 kcal/mol involving pi bonds with Phe158/Phe261 and hydrogen bonds with Ser159/Tyr179.
OLR1 docked with apigenin showed a binding energy of -7.6 kcal/mol, with hydrogen bonds formed mainly by Ser207 and Arg209.

OLR1 docked with myricetin showed a binding energy of -6.5 kcal/mol, forming hydrogen bonds with Val230, Leu223, and Pro211, and produced the highest average number of hydrogen bonds (five) during MD simulation among the tested compounds along with orientin.

MMPBSA binding free energy calculations ranked the five bioflavonoid-OLR1 complexes from most to least stable as amentoflavone (-18.48 kcal/mol), myricetin (-14.13 kcal/mol), orientin (-13.75 kcal/mol), ilexgenin A (-11.07 kcal/mol), and apigenin (-9.55 kcal/mol), identifying amentoflavone as the best predicted inhibitor.
In severe COVID-19, OLR1 (oxidized LDL receptor 1) is reported to be positively expressed, contributing to cytokine storms, thrombosis, and activation of inflammatory immune responses.

A cited study reported that individuals co-infected with SARS-CoV-2 and EBV had approximately threefold increased risk of severe symptoms compared to those infected with SARS-CoV-2 alone, suggesting EBV reactivation may worsen COVID-19 severity.

The 22 hub genes identified as shared between EBV infection and long COVID were found to be primarily involved in immune-signaling pathways including JAK-STAT signaling, interleukin signaling, protein kinase signaling, and toll-like receptor pathways.
The COVID-19 Mental Disorders Collaborators estimated a large global rise in major depressive disorder and anxiety disorder cases coinciding with the COVID-19 pandemic.

In a study of neurological and neuropsychiatric effects of post-acute SARS-CoV-2 infection (neuro-PASC), anxiety disorders and depression were the most prevalent symptoms, at rates similar to a comparison influenza cohort.

SARS-CoV-2 infection and type I interferon-driven inflammation reduce serotonin via impaired tryptophan absorption, platelet hyperactivation/thrombocytopenia disrupting serotonin storage, and enhanced MAO-mediated serotonin metabolism.
Parvovirus B19 infection shows a notable odds-ratio association with increased risk of ME/CFS compared to healthy controls.
Coxsackie B virus infection shows a notable odds-ratio association with increased risk of ME/CFS compared to healthy controls.
Among ME/CFS patients stratified by etiology, those who were Herpesviridae carriers had elevated autoantibodies against voltage-gated calcium channels compared to other ME/CFS subgroups.
The stress/distress-associated (non-viral) subgroup of ME/CFS patients had higher levels of dopamine-, glutamate-, and GABA-receptor autoantibodies than the herpesvirus-associated subgroup.
Individuals recovering from HCV infection have a markedly higher likelihood of depression and other psychiatric conditions than the general population.
Clearing HCV infection with antiviral treatment has been linked to improvements in depression and overall quality of life.
HHV-6 seropositivity was significantly higher in children with depression, particularly those exhibiting suicidal ideation, than non-suicidal counterparts.
Latent HHV-6B can invade olfactory astrocytes and express the SITH-1 protein, inducing olfactory bulb apoptosis and activating the HPA axis, contributing to depression risk.

Using UK Biobank genotypic and phenotypic data, HSV-1 infection combined with genetic factors at the SULF2 locus significantly increases depression risk, implicating altered heparan sulfate proteoglycan-mediated glutamatergic signaling.
A longitudinal study from 2000-2010 found an almost twofold increase in depression prevalence among people infected with varicella-zoster virus (herpes zoster).

VZV-specific cell-mediated immunity, which declines with age, inversely correlates with severity of depressive symptoms in elderly adults, and antidepressant treatment is linked to higher VZV-CMI levels.
Infectious mononucleosis, often caused by EBV, has been linked to a 40% higher hazard ratio for a future depression diagnosis.
A Japanese study found EBV serological reactivation was independently associated with psychological distress in older women living in the community, but not in men.
In a postmortem/blood study, CMV seropositivity was associated with mood disorders including bipolar disorder and major depression, suicide, neuroinflammation markers, and microglial activation.

In a longitudinal study of persistent pathogen burden and incident depression in older adults, only CMV antibody positivity (among CMV, HSV, VZV, H. pylori, and T. gondii) was significantly associated with increased odds of incident depression, more prominent in women, independent of CRP or IL-6 levels.
A systematic meta-analysis found the pooled prevalence of depression among adolescents with HIV/AIDS was 26.07%, with higher prevalence in females and older adolescents.

In a large UK-based case-control study using the Clinical Practice Research Datalink, patients with a history of influenza infection had a moderately higher risk of developing depression, especially with recent/repeated infections.

A study of 3,808 mothers in southern China found women with HBV infection were more likely to test positive for postpartum depression, but the difference was not statistically significant after adjusting for other variables.
SSRIs/SNRIs may be effective in reducing mortality in COVID-19 patients, with fluvoxamine showing potential superiority to fluoxetine.

SSRIs (escitalopram, sertraline, fluoxetine) only partially reduced depressive/anxiety symptoms in patients with MDD/GAD post-COVID-19, indicating incomplete restoration of affective state after 6 months of therapy.
Direct-acting antiviral treatment for HCV achieving sustained virological response significantly reduced depressive symptoms from 21.11% before treatment to 1.11% after SVR.

The incidence of clinically significant depression was lower among HIV-infected patients on antiretroviral therapy, including efavirenz-containing regimens, despite efavirenz's known neuropsychiatric toxicity.
A double-blind placebo-controlled RCT found that amantadine significantly improved depressive symptoms in patients also infected with Borna Disease Virus 1, with a safe oral treatment regimen.
A meta-analysis of four studies (152 patients) found no statistically significant effect of infliximab as an adjuvant treatment for treatment-resistant depression.

A systematic meta-analysis found that anti-inflammatory add-on medications (NSAIDs, cytokine inhibitors, statins, minocycline, pioglitazone, glucocorticoids) added to antidepressants showed better therapeutic outcomes than antidepressants alone.

The SULF2 gene locus, which encodes an extracellular sulfatase modulating heparan sulfate proteoglycans, is genetically implicated in the association between HSV-1 infection and increased depression risk in UK Biobank data.

Autoantibodies against NMDA receptors have been detected in patients with herpes simplex encephalitis and varicella-zoster infection, with movement disorder symptoms improving after immunotherapy alongside declining autoantibody titers.

SARS-CoV-2 infection-induced type I interferon-driven inflammation reduces serotonin via diminished tryptophan absorption, disrupted serotonin storage from platelet hyperactivation/thrombocytopenia, and enhanced MAO-mediated serotonin metabolism.

In HCV infection, IFN-γ-induced activation of indoleamine-2,3-dioxygenase shifts tryptophan metabolism toward the kynurenine pathway, reducing tryptophan availability for serotonin synthesis and generating neurotoxic quinolinic acid.

In transgenic mice expressing HIV-1 Tat protein, dopamine uptake through dopamine and norepinephrine transporters was markedly reduced in the prefrontal cortex, with Tat blocking dopamine's entry pathway at the transporter.

HIV-1 Nef protein expression in microglia of mice induced CCL2 expression together with reduced dopamine levels, MAO activity, and dopamine transporter expression in the striatum, producing hyperactive behaviors resembling mania.

Among ME/CFS patient subgroups stratified by etiology, the Herpesviridae-carrier group showed elevated autoantibodies against voltage-gated calcium channels, while the stress/distress group had higher dopamine-, glutamate-, and GABA-receptor autoantibodies.
Direct injection of influenza virulence protein PB1-F2 into the hippocampal dentate gyrus of mice caused depressive-like behavior and disrupted oligodendrocyte development and neural plasticity.
Influenza A virus infection led to subtle, persistent imbalances in glutamatergic synapse transmission affecting synaptic pruning and neuronal alterations in the cortex and hippocampus of mice.

The SSRI escitalopram restored behavioral impairments and synaptodendritic damage induced by HIV-1 in preclinical models, suggesting a role for SSRI therapy in repairing virus-mediated neuronal damage.
Expression of rabies virus glycoprotein enhances both short-term and long-term synaptic plasticity, suggesting viral components can directly influence synaptic function.

Continuous activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in microglia during and after viral infections maintains chronic neuroinflammation thought to underlie mood disturbances and depressive behaviors in post-viral syndromes.

Patients with depression show impaired mitochondrial gene expression, damage to mitochondrial structure and dynamics, and disrupted electron transport chain activity, contributing to oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and apoptosis.
Decreased mitochondrial respiration has been observed in early EBV infection, acting as a barrier to cell proliferation.
SSRIs/SNRIs may reduce mortality in COVID-19 patients, with fluvoxamine showing potential superiority over fluoxetine.

SSRIs such as escitalopram, sertraline, and fluoxetine only partially reduced depressive/anxiety symptoms in patients with MDD/GAD post-COVID-19, indicating incomplete restoration of affective state after 6 months of therapy.

Individuals with major depressive disorder had significantly reduced antibody reactivity to EBV Nuclear Antigen-1, and elevated anti-virion antibodies were linked to increased odds of being in the MDD group.
Untreated chronic hepatitis C patients showed significantly higher rates of clinically significant emotional distress and depression (35%) compared to patients receiving antiviral treatment.
Achieving sustained virological response with direct-acting antiviral agents led to a significant and sustained reduction in depressive symptoms among HIV-HCV co-infected individuals.
Direct-acting antiviral therapy for HCV reduced depressive symptom prevalence from 21.11% before treatment to 1.11% after achieving sustained virological response.

Incidence of clinically significant depression was lower among HIV-infected patients on antiretroviral therapy and anti-protease therapy, including efavirenz-containing regimens, despite efavirenz's known neuropsychiatric toxicity.

Acyclovir inhibits tryptophan-2,3-dioxygenase activity, raising blood and tissue serotonin and 5-hydroxyindole acetic acid levels, and may reduce depressive symptoms in herpes simplex encephalitis by modulating serotonin availability.

In a double-blind placebo-controlled RCT, amantadine treatment in depressed patients infected with Borna Disease Virus 1 showed significant improvement in depressive symptoms with a safe oral treatment regimen.
A meta-analysis of four primary studies with 152 patients found no statistically significant effect of infliximab as an adjuvant treatment for treatment-resistant depression.

Intravenous cytoflavin, an antihypoxic/antioxidant combination of succinic acid, riboflavin, nicotinamide, and inosine, significantly improved overall functional state and reduced depression and fatigue levels in a small trial on post-COVID syndrome rehabilitation.

Epigenetic downregulation of RAC1 in the nucleus accumbens is linked to depression and stress-related behaviors, and this repressive chromatin state can be reversed by histone deacetylase inhibitors, restoring RAC1 expression and reversing depressive behaviors.
Thrombocytopenia, a common sequela of HIV infection, has been associated with reduced levels of BDNF and serotonin, contributing to poor immune responses and depression-like symptoms.

CSF dopamine levels and tyrosine hydroxylase expression are decreased in the brains of chronically HIV-infected patients, and dopamine concentration in brain is consistently decreased in clinical and experimental HIV samples, potentially contributing to apathy/depression and neurocognitive problems.
In the cohort of 201 chronic musculoskeletal pain patients, 78% met ACR2010/FiRST fibromyalgia criteria, 58% had depression, and 22% had a concurrent chronic inflammatory rheumatic disease.
A substantial proportion of patients in the cohort reported worsening of their fibromyalgia-like symptoms following SARS-CoV-2 infection or vaccination.

Unsupervised clustering of the cohort identified five phenotype clusters characterized by prevalent features including alexithymia, sleep impairment, childhood pain, PTSD, migraine, obesity, and loneliness.
One identified digital persona (Persona E) comprises women aged 20-40 with joint hypermobility, childhood-onset chronic pain including migraine, and sometimes PTSD.
Another persona (Persona B) comprises often-perimenopausal obese women aged 45-55 with severe sleep disturbance, low-grade inflammation, and mild-to-moderate depression.

A polypharmacy phenotype (Persona D), involving multiple pain/psychotropic medications and prior spinal surgeries, was associated with very poor response to multimodal treatment and was therefore not prioritized in the digital program.
Personas A-C were predicted to be most likely to respond positively to multimodal treatment and possibly to the digital self-management program.
AI-based text-network analysis of the self-management program content identified 'sleep', 'body', and 'pain' as the most central and interconnected topics, reflecting the program's core focus.

Selective concept relation analysis quantified the network connection between 'pain' and 'covid' concepts as having a significance of 0.48, accounting for 19% of total influence and linked to 23 of 150 nodes (15% of the graph).

Sentiment analysis of 129 unique patient feedback entries showed themes primarily focused on stress, fatigue, resilience, and chronic pain, largely aligning with program content, though social support from family/friends was not addressed.
The authors postulate that perimenopausal loss of anti-inflammatory estrogen contributes to musculoskeletal pain, weight gain, sleep impairment, and emotional imbalance resembling fibromyalgia.
The authors found sleep impairment in a substantial portion of their chronic pain patients, prompting increased program content on this issue.
A considerable rate of peri-/post-menopause, alexithymia, and pain since childhood was found in the cohort, prompting dedicated program modules.

Factorial analysis of mixed data followed by hierarchical clustering on principal components identified three distinct clusters of long COVID patients based on combined clinical and biological variables.
Cluster 1 ("Pain") was characterized by myalgia and was predominantly composed of male patients with the persistent clinical phenotype of long COVID.

Cluster 2 ("Central Nervous System") primarily featured pure neurocognitive disorders (concentration, memory, and phasic disorders), was more prevalent among females, and aligned with the "long" clinical form of long COVID.

Cluster 3 exhibited a diverse multisystem symptom profile including anxio-depressive syndrome with sleep and mood disorders, dysautonomia (POTS, dyspnoea, exercise intolerance, palpitations), neurocognitive disorders, sensory disturbances, myalgia/joint/chest pain, and digestive disorders (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain).
Median C-reactive protein was elevated above normal reference range in this long COVID cohort.
LDL cholesterol and total cholesterol were elevated above normal reference ranges in this long COVID cohort.
The most prevalent symptoms of long COVID at study inclusion were concentration disorders, memory disorders, fatigue, phasic disorders, and sleep disorders.
Female sex, a history of psychiatric conditions, and allergies were identified as primary antecedent risk factors for long COVID.
Anxiety and depression antecedents were present in 31% and 21% of patients respectively in this long COVID cohort.
The average duration from SARS-CoV-2 infection onset to the development of long COVID was 65 ± 42.9 days (approximately 9 weeks).

Cluster 3, with its anxio-depressive syndrome, fatigue, pain, dysautonomia, and neurocognitive disorders, was noted by the authors to share similar symptoms with ME/CFS (myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome).
A cited study suggests that long COVID patients expressing ME/CFS-like symptoms are more prone to anxiety and depression due to reduced sarcosine and serine levels.

Cluster 1, characterized by myalgia-type pain, was likened by the authors to fibromyalgia syndrome, although dysautonomia (a proposed fibromyalgia mechanism) was not sufficiently present in this cluster to fully characterize it as such.
Standard biological laboratory tests could not differentiate between the three identified long COVID clusters, so clinical examination remains necessary to distinguish clinical forms.
The authors hypothesize that Cluster 2's pure neurocognitive disorders may result from cerebral hypoxia together with an inflammatory component involving the interferon-complement system.
The patient tested positive for AChR binding, blocking, and modulating antibodies, confirming the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis.
Bedside spirometry demonstrated a restrictive pattern with a markedly reduced forced vital capacity of 15.8 cc/kg, prompting elective intubation.
The patient developed new-onset very-late-onset myasthenia gravis symptoms four months after resolution of a COVID-19 infection, meeting CDC/WHO criteria for Long COVID.

Among 17 reviewed cases of new-onset very-late MG following COVID-19, the latency between infection and MG symptom onset ranged from five days to eight weeks, shorter than the four-month delay seen in the present case.
Ocular involvement (ptosis and diplopia) was the most common presenting symptom among reviewed post-COVID myasthenia gravis cases, occurring in six of 17 cases.
Bulbar symptoms (dysarthria, dysphagia, dysphonia) following COVID-19 infection have been reported in only one other case besides the present one.

A proposed mechanism for new-onset MG after COVID-19 is molecular mimicry, whereby structural similarity between the SARS-CoV-2 receptor and the acetylcholine receptor triggers an immune response producing anti-AChR antibodies.
Certain genes including HLA-DRB1*1501, HLA-DQ5, and CTLA4 have been linked to myasthenia gravis and its subgroups, though these were not confirmed in this patient.
Hypotheses implicating Epstein-Barr virus in thymic pathology of myasthenia gravis were not corroborated by subsequent controlled studies.

Patients with pre-existing myasthenia gravis are more vulnerable to contracting COVID-19 and to experiencing adverse outcomes compared to individuals without MG, due to immunosuppressive therapy and respiratory muscle weakness.

COVID-19 infection is likely to provoke acute exacerbations in MG patients through immune activation and secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines, potentially causing cytokine storm, ARDS, and multi-organ failure.

Acute treatment with high-dose pyridostigmine, pulse-dose methylprednisolone, and IVIG in the ICU led to resolution of the patient's myasthenic symptoms and improvement in ventilatory function, allowing extubation.
Titration of mycophenolic acid to 1,000 mg every 12 hours resulted in marked improvement in the patient's ventilatory mechanics, and he remained asymptomatic without recurrence at 12-month follow-up.
10-40% of convalescent COVID-19 patients develop long COVID/PASC, and up to 40% of long-term COVID patients develop neurological or psychiatric symptoms.

In a 3-year follow-up of 135,161 infected patients, mortality risk declined after 1 year in non-hospitalized patients but persisted beyond 3 years in hospitalized patients, who also showed increased PASC risk.
Among 226 COVID-19 pneumonia survivors evaluated 1-3 months after discharge, 78% had disability in at least one cognitive domain and 50-57% had impaired psychomotor coordination.
In a cross-sectional study of 57 hospitalized COVID-19 patients, over 80% exhibited significant cognitive impairment, particularly in attention and executive function.
A study of 13,001 individuals found significantly higher rates of memory problems 8 months after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
A cohort study found anosmia, ageusia, memory loss, and headache persisted beyond 60 days post-infection, with memory deficits continuing to the third month.

The SARS-CoV-2 spike protein persists in the skull-meninges-brain axis long after viral clearance, and neurodegeneration biomarkers are elevated in CSF of Long COVID patients; in an animal model, the S1 subunit altered the proteome in this axis, induced anxiety-like behavior, dysregulated IL-18, MAPK and PI3K-AKT signaling, altered NET-formation proteins, and increased caspase-3 activity.

Using a pseudovirus containing the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, researchers demonstrated that the spike protein damages the choroid plexus epithelium, causing barrier leakage that normally prevents pathogens, immune cells, and cytokines from entering the CSF and brain.

The spike protein was observed at extremely high levels in the terminal feet of hypothalamic tanycytes in a patient who died of severe COVID-19, suggesting internalization at fenestrated capillaries and possible transfer to other cell types.

SARS-CoV-2 spike (S), S1, and nucleocapsid (N) antigens are detectable in approximately 65% of PASC patients months after infection, with S protein detected most frequently (60%), S1 less often (~20%), and N rarely, most often in patients reporting gastrointestinal and neuropsychiatric PASC symptoms.
A large percentage of patients with acute COVID-19 had plasma cortisol and ACTH levels consistent with central adrenal insufficiency, indicating impaired adrenocortical response.

In SARS convalescent patients, hypercortisolism persisted for up to 1 year along with central hypothyroidism and low DHEAS in some patients, supporting chronic corticotropin (CRH) deficiency, possibly from reversible hypophysitis or direct hypothalamic damage.
Patients with CFS exhibited blunted HPA axis activity, including reduced 24-hour free cortisol excretion, increased sensitivity to ACTH, and an attenuated response to CRH.

In long COVID patients, fatigue and depression scores correlated positively with serum cortisol and FT4 levels respectively; patients with general fatigue had lower growth hormone and higher FT4, while those with anosmia/dysgeusia had lower cortisol; higher TSH and lower FT4/TSH ratios suggested occult hypothyroidism, and ACTH/cortisol ratios were decreased in patients with high antibody titers.

COVID-19 patient plasma induced glycocalyx shedding causing hyperinflammation and oxidative stress, consistent with high levels of syndecan-1 (SDC-1) reported in convalescent patients, indicating persistent endothelial damage possibly linked to circulating spike protein.

Spike-exposed pericytes displayed elongated/contracted morphology and increased expression of ACE2 and contractile/myofibrogenic proteins, with S protein exposure promoting Ca2+ influx, lipid peroxidation, oxidative/nitrosative stress, and NF-kB pathway activation, potentially impairing pericyte function and contributing to vessel-mediated brain damage.

ACE2 treatment induced mild pericyte-mediated capillary constriction via AT1R activation, which was enhanced by the receptor-binding domain and spike-pseudotyped viral particles in human and hamster brain tissue.

Spike/RBD-triggered mast cell activation induced inflammatory factors in human brain microvascular endothelial cells and microglia, destroyed tight junction proteins, and full-length S protein (but not RBD) stimulated IL-1β and the proteolytic enzymes chymase and tryptase, mediated by TLR4 (IL-1β) and the ACE2 pathway (chymase/tryptase).

Spike protein can activate the NLRP3 inflammasome in LPS-stimulated microglia in an ACE2-dependent manner, and can prime the inflammasome via NF-κB signaling, supporting microglial innate immune activation as a mechanism linking S protein to Parkinson's-like neurological symptoms.

The S1 subunit alone was sufficient to provoke neuroinflammation, including microglial activation and pro-inflammatory cytokine gene expression, and altered animal behavior resembling neurological and cognitive symptoms of COVID-19; S1 can travel along nerve terminals/axons to the brain and activate microglia via TLR4, increasing IL-1β and MHC-II expression.

TLR4 signaling was identified as the primary pathway responsible for long-term cognitive dysfunction after COVID-19 in humans, with the GG genotype of TLR4-2604G>A (rs10759931) serving as a marker for poor cognitive outcome; spike protein infusion in mice impaired cognition via complement-dependent synapse destruction, and blocking TLR4 signaling protected against synapse loss and memory dysfunction.

Both the expression levels and percentage of astrocytes expressing NRP1 mRNA were higher in astrocytes from COVID-19 patients compared to controls, and NRP1-mediated astrocyte infection increased IFN and inflammatory mediator expression while decreasing ion and neurotransmitter transporter expression, contributing to neuronal dysfunction and death.

Administration of the BNT162b2 spike mRNA vaccine during pregnancy in rats significantly altered WNT gene expression and BDNF levels in offspring, and male offspring exhibited autism-like behaviors (reduced social interaction, repetitive behavior), decreased neuronal counts, and impaired motor coordination.
After mRNA vaccination (BNT162b2 or Moderna mRNA-1273), the S1 subunit spike protein has been detected in blood for up to 14 days, in CSF for up to 2.5 months, and in breast milk for up to 45 days.

Prospective studies showed that vaccination with up to two doses, given before or after SARS-CoV-2 infection, reduced the risk of developing PASC-prolonged symptoms, and also reduced the risk of a broader symptom range and mortality.

The apparent protective effect of vaccination against long COVID has been questioned, since high antibody titers induced by successive vaccinations showed opposite effects, raising concerns amid continued infection waves and vaccination programs.

A recent study indicates that active viral infection is not required for cognitive impairment in long COVID, supporting the role of indirect immune-mediated mechanisms over direct viral proliferation in the brain.

ACE2 was upregulated in epithelial cells in some COVID-19 patients with neurological involvement, particularly in white matter and in patients with severe neurological symptoms, despite normally restricted brain ACE2 expression to choroid plexus and ependymal cells.
